0.title: The Prayers of the Kingdom
0.overview:
Open the Psalter and you are standing at the entrance of the Bible's own heart. Here, across 150 poems spanning a thousand years of Israel's life with God, you will find every human emotion — terror and triumph, guilt and gratitude, desolation and ecstasy — brought without editing into the presence of the living LORD. Other books of Scripture speak to us; the Psalter speaks for us. As Athanasius wrote in the fourth century: 'Most of Scripture speaks to us, but the Psalter speaks for us — it puts the very words of the soul in our mouths.' What Israel discovered, and what the church has found in every generation since, is that there is no experience of human life too raw, too shameful, too desolate, too glorious to bring to God. The Psalms give the people of God a language large enough for everything.

But the Psalter is more than a collection of honest prayers. It is the prayer book of Jesus Christ. Dietrich Bonhoeffer, writing from the shadow of the Third Reich, saw this with blazing clarity: Jesus himself prayed these psalms in the days of his flesh. He cried 'My God, my God, why have you forsaken me?' (Ps. 22:1) from the cross — not composing a new prayer in his agony, but reaching for the ancient words his Father had given him. He sang the Hallel psalms at the Last Supper with his disciples (Matt. 26:30), knowing that within hours he would be the fulfillment of everything they sang. He is the Righteous Man of Psalm 1, the anointed King of Psalm 2, the forsaken and vindicated sufferer of Psalm 22, the risen Lord at the right hand of Psalm 110. Every Christian who opens the Psalter and prays these words prays them in him — in the One who has already prayed them perfectly, who has already walked through every valley they describe, and who has emerged on the other side in resurrection glory. This is what gives the Psalms their inexhaustible power: they are not merely ancient poetry. They are the voice of Christ, and the voice of Christ's people united to him.

The Five Books and the great arc of the Psalter: The collection is divided into five books, each closing with a doxology, mirroring the five books of Moses. Book I (Psalms 1–41) is the most personal — the individual soul before God, David in his most intimate moments of trust and terror. Book II (Psalms 42–72) widens the lens to the community and the nation. Book III (Psalms 73–89) is the darkest territory in the Psalter — the shadow of the Exile falls across it, the Davidic covenant seems to have failed, and the great lament of Psalm 88 ends without a single note of resolution. Yet Book IV (Psalms 90–106) answers the darkness with a thunderclap: the LORD reigns. He reigned before David. He reigns when David's throne lies in ruins. He is the everlasting King from generation to generation (Ps. 90:1–2). Book V (Psalms 107–150) moves with gathering momentum toward the great doxological finale — psalm after psalm rising in praise until the last five Hallelujah psalms (146–150) break into pure, unrestrained, universe-wide adoration. The Psalter begins with a quiet beatitude and ends with everything that has breath praising the LORD. That is the arc of redemption. That is the shape of the Christian life. That is where history is going.

Psalm types and their pastoral function: Lament psalms — the largest single category — follow a recognizable structure: address to God, honest complaint, confession of trust, petition, and vow of praise. They teach the church something she desperately needs to learn: that crying out to God in darkness is not a failure of faith but its highest expression. The psalmist who prays 'How long, O LORD? Will you forget me forever?' (Ps. 13:1) is not doubting God — he is taking his doubt to God, which is exactly what faith looks like under pressure. Praise psalms form the great counter-melody — declarations of who God is and what he has done that are meant to be sung, shouted, and danced. Royal psalms (2, 18, 20–21, 45, 72, 89, 101, 110, 132, 144) celebrate the Davidic king and find their ultimate and only sufficient fulfillment in Jesus Christ. Wisdom psalms (1, 37, 49, 73, 112, 119) reflect on Torah, retribution, and the shape of the flourishing life. Zion psalms (46, 48, 76, 84, 87, 122) celebrate the city where God has chosen to dwell — and point forward to the new Jerusalem, the city whose builder and maker is God (Heb. 11:10).

The superscriptions: About two-thirds of the psalms carry headings in the Hebrew text — author attributions (David, Asaph, the Sons of Korah, Moses, Solomon, Ethan, Heman), musical instructions (lamnatseach = to the choirmaster; miktam, maskil, shir), and historical settings. The Reformed tradition has generally taken these as part of the inspired text. The Davidic attribution of 73 psalms is historically trustworthy and pastorally irreplaceable: these are not anonymous liturgical compositions but the prayers of a man who knew the heights and the depths — who danced before the ark and committed adultery, who slew Goliath and fled Absalom, who was chosen by grace and failed by sin and was restored by mercy. David's life is the gospel in miniature, and his psalms carry the full weight of that biography.

Christ in the Psalms: The New Testament cites the Psalms more than any other Old Testament book — over seventy direct citations and hundreds of allusions. The apostles did not impose Christology onto the Psalter from outside; they found it already there, coiled in the very structure of Israel's prayer. Psalm 2: the Father's decree — 'You are my Son; today I have begotten you' — cited at Jesus's baptism, transfiguration, and resurrection (Acts 13:33). Psalm 16: 'You will not abandon my soul to Sheol' — Peter's text for the resurrection on the Day of Pentecost (Acts 2:27). Psalm 22: the desolate cry, the mocking crowds, the casting of lots for garments — the crucifixion narrated in advance with photographic precision. Psalm 40: 'A body you have prepared for me' — the incarnation as the ultimate act of obedience (Heb. 10:5). Psalm 45: 'Your throne, O God, is forever and ever' — applied directly to the Son in Hebrews 1:8. Psalm 69: the zeal that consumed him, the reproaches that fell on him, the betrayal — all in Christ. Psalm 110: 'The LORD says to my Lord: Sit at my right hand' — cited more often in the New Testament than any other verse in the Old Testament, the cornerstone of the apostolic proclamation of Jesus as both Lord and Messiah. To read the Psalms is to find Christ everywhere — not by forcing alien meanings onto ancient texts, but by following the trajectory that Israel's own prayers were always pointing toward.

The Psalms of Ascent (120–134): Fifteen pilgrim songs, sung by Israel on the road up to Jerusalem for the three great festivals — Passover, Pentecost, Tabernacles. Their movement from distress in a foreign land (Ps. 120) to blessing at the sanctuary (Ps. 134) is the shape of the whole Christian life compressed into fifteen short poems. Alec Motyer calls them 'the pilgrim's companion.' Every Christian life is an ascent — from the far country to the Father's house, from exile to the city of God.

The imprecatory psalms: The psalms of cursing (35, 58, 69, 83, 109, 137, 139) disturb every sensitive reader, as they disturbed C. S. Lewis, who called them 'the most frightful' passages in the Bible. But the discomfort is itself instructive. These psalms arise from a world where wickedness was not merely annoying but was actively destroying God's people and dishonoring God's name. They are not personal revenge — they are cries handed to God, appeals to divine justice from people who had no other court of appeal. They are Christological: Jesus applies Psalm 109's curse to Judas (Acts 1:20). And they express a passion for God's justice — a hatred of evil as evil, a refusal to be neutral about sin — that the comfortable, therapeutic church has largely lost. The Christian prays them in Christ, against the true enemies: sin, death, and the devil, whose defeat was accomplished in the darkness of Good Friday and the light of Easter morning.

Psalm 119: The great Torah psalm — 176 verses, 22 acrostic stanzas, every verse a meditation on the Word of God. It is not the record of a legalist who finds security in rules; it is the outpouring of a soul who has discovered that God's Word is 'sweeter also than honey and drippings of the honeycomb' (Ps. 19:10). Spurgeon devoted an entire separate volume of his Treasury of David to Psalm 119 alone. Every preacher should spend a month with it.

The great Hallel (113–118, 136, 146–150): The Egyptian Hallel (Psalms 113–118) was the hymn of Passover — Psalms 113–114 before the meal, 115–118 after. When Matthew 26:30 tells us that Jesus and his disciples 'sang a hymn and went out to the Mount of Olives,' they had just sung Psalms 115–118 — the songs of the Passover table — on the night he was betrayed. He sang 'The stone that the builders rejected has become the cornerstone' (Ps. 118:22) knowing he was that stone. He sang 'This is the day that the LORD has made; let us rejoice and be glad in it' (Ps. 118:24) on the night before his death. The Psalter ends with five unbroken Hallelujahs (146–150) — every instrument, every creature, everything that has breath called to join the chorus. This is where all prayer ends up. This is the destination. Praise the LORD.

1.title: Blessed Is the Man
1.text: <sup>1</sup>Blessed is the man who walks not in the counsel of the wicked, nor stands in the way of sinners, nor sits in the seat of scoffers;<sup>2</sup>but his delight is in the law of the LORD, and on his law he meditates day and night.<sup>3</sup>He is like a tree planted by streams of water that yields its fruit in its season, and its leaf does not wither. In all that he does, he prospers.<sup>4</sup>The wicked are not so, but are like chaff that the wind drives away.<sup>5</sup>Therefore the wicked will not stand in the judgment, nor sinners in the congregation of the righteous;<sup>6</sup>for the LORD knows the way of the righteous, but the way of the wicked will perish.
1.overview: The Psalter opens with a portrait and a fork in the road. Blessed is the man who does not walk, stand or sit in the company of the wicked, but delights in the law of the LORD and murmurs over it day and night (vv. 1-2). He is a tree transplanted beside irrigation channels: fruit in its season, a leaf that does not wither, a life that arrives somewhere (v. 3). The wicked are the opposite of a rooted tree — chaff, weightless, blown off the threshing floor, with no footing in the judgment and no place among the righteous (vv. 4-5). Underneath both ways stands the reason for their ends: the LORD knows one of them, and the other comes to nothing (v. 6).
1.theology:
The psalm is a beatitude before it is an ethic. The blessed man is defined by what he loves and where he is rooted, and the tree is planted — set there by another hand (v. 3). Delight comes first and meditation follows it (v. 2), so this is grace at work, not willpower.

Two ways, and no third. The psalm refuses the middle category our age wants, and its verdict is forensic: the wicked will not stand in the judgment (v. 5).

The ground of it all is God's covenant knowing (v. 6; 2 Tim 2:19; John 10:14). And the portrait is finally a portrait of Christ, the only man who fits verse 1, who took the end of the chaff on a tree (Gal 3:13) so that the rootless could be transplanted. Psalms 1 and 2 are one doorway, bracketed by Blessed is the man (1:1) and Blessed are all who take refuge in him (2:12).
1.examples:
Walks, stands, sits: a descent nobody plans.

Hagah: a lion growling over its prey (Isa 31:4).

Day and night, said first to Joshua before a war (Josh 1:8).

Transplanted, not self-rooted; fruit in its season.

Chaff: not fire first, but weightlessness.

The Lord knows those who are his (2 Tim 2:19).

The blessed man on a tree, cursed for us (Gal 3:13).

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–3 — Planted by Streams of Water
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Blessed is the man who walks not in the counsel of the wicked, nor stands in the way of sinners, nor sits in the seat of scoffers (v. 1); his delight and his murmuring, day and night, are in the law of the LORD (v. 2). He is like a tree planted by streams of water, fruitful in season, unwithered, prospering in all he does (v. 3).
verseByVerse.theology: The blessed life is not described by what it achieves but by where it is rooted and what it loves.

verseByVerse.quote: Blessed is the man who walks not in the counsel of the wicked, nor stands in the way of sinners, nor sits in the seat of scoffers;
verseByVerse.commentary:
Blessed is the man who walks not in the counsel of the wicked, nor stands in the way of sinners, nor sits in the seat of scoffers.

The Psalter opens with a word of congratulation, not a command. Blessed is ashre, a plural form that works like an exclamation: O the happinesses of that man. Before Israel sings anything, she is shown a person and asked whether she wants that life.

He is described first by what he does not do, and the three lines walk downhill. Walks, then stands, then sits: passing through, then stopping to listen, then pulling up a chair. The company worsens at the same rate, from the wicked, to sinners, to scoffers, who have got past arguing about God to laughing at him. Nobody plans the third step. It is reached by taking the first one often enough.

Measure that against a real week rather than in the abstract. Whose counsel actually shapes what you decide? Not who do you agree with on paper: whose voice is in your ear at the moment of choosing? That is the counsel you walk in.

verseByVerse.quote: but his delight is in the law of the LORD, and on his law he meditates day and night.
verseByVerse.commentary:
But his delight is in the law of the LORD, and on his law he meditates day and night.

The engine is not willpower. It is delight. The man is not gritting his teeth over a rule book; he likes it. And meditates is hagah, a word for a low, muttering sound. Isaiah uses it of a lion over its kill, growling as it feeds (Isa 31:4). This is not skimming a page at breakfast. It is a man chewing over a sentence of God all day, under his breath, until it gets into his bones.

The phrase day and night is quoted from the charge given to Joshua on the edge of the conquest: This Book of the Law shall not depart from your mouth, but you shall meditate on it day and night (Josh 1:8). What was said to a general before a war is now said of any blessed man. The battle has not changed much.

And note the order, because it is the whole difference between religion and life. The psalm does not say he meditates until he learns to delight. It says he delights, and therefore he meditates. You cannot manufacture that affection by effort any more than you can order yourself to find something beautiful. You can ask God for it, and put yourself where it is given.

verseByVerse.quote: He is like a tree planted by streams of water that yields its fruit in its season, and its leaf does not wither. In all that he does, he prospers.
verseByVerse.commentary:
He is like a tree planted by streams of water that yields its fruit in its season, and its leaf does not wither. In all that he does, he prospers.

Planted is stronger than it sounds in English: the word means transplanted, lifted and set in place. The tree did not wander to the water. Someone carried it there and dug it in beside the irrigation channels, where it cannot fail for drought. The tree does not make the water. It stands where the water is.

Then three results, and the middle one is the mercy. Fruit, in its season — not every month, not on demand; there are winters in a fruitful life, and the psalm allows for them. A leaf that does not wither, because the roots are into something that does not dry up. And in all that he does, he prospers, which is not a promise of money; the same psalm has this man surrounded by scoffers and will shortly put him in a courtroom. It is the promise that his life arrives somewhere.

Jeremiah took this verse up almost whole and added the drought: He is like a tree planted by water ... for its leaves remain green, and is not anxious in the year of drought (Jer 17:8). Another psalm plants the same tree indoors: They are planted in the house of the LORD; they flourish in the courts of our God. They still bear fruit in old age (Ps 92:13-14). And at the end of the Bible the tree is still standing by the water, yielding its fruit each month, its leaves for the healing of the nations (Rev 22:2). Psalm 1 is the seedling of that tree.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 4–6 — The LORD Knows the Way of the Righteous
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: The wicked are not so, but are like chaff that the wind drives away; they will not stand in the judgment nor in the congregation of the righteous (vv. 4-5). For the LORD knows the way of the righteous, but the way of the wicked will perish (v. 6).
verseByVerse.theology: Two ways, two ends, and underneath them the reason for both: the LORD knows one of them.

verseByVerse.quote: The wicked are not so, but are like chaff that the wind drives away. Therefore the wicked will not stand in the judgment, nor sinners in the congregation of the righteous;
verseByVerse.commentary:
The wicked are not so, but are like chaff that the wind drives away. Therefore the wicked will not stand in the judgment, nor sinners in the congregation of the righteous.

The Hebrew of the first line is three curt words, and the abruptness is deliberate: not so. Against the tree, chaff. Not fire, not violence — weightlessness. Chaff is the dry husk beaten off the wheat at threshing, and the farmer does not need to remove it. He throws the whole heap in the air on a windy evening and the chaff simply goes. A life with no root also has no weight; when the wind gets under it there is nothing there to hold.

John the Baptist put the winnowing fork in the Messiah's hand: he will clear his threshing floor and gather his wheat into the barn, but the chaff he will burn with unquenchable fire (Matt 3:12). The psalm's picture has a day attached to it.

Will not stand is a courtroom word: they will have no footing when the verdict is read, and no place in the assembly of God's people. Be honest about how unwelcome this is. We want a third category — decent, undecided, not really either. The psalm offers two. Everything else in the book, every lament and every hallelujah, is prayed by people on one of these two roads.

verseByVerse.quote: for the LORD knows the way of the righteous, but the way of the wicked will perish.
verseByVerse.commentary:
For the LORD knows the way of the righteous, but the way of the wicked will perish.

Here is the reason under both halves of the psalm, and it is not the man's performance. Knows is yada, the Bible's word for knowing a person rather than a fact — the word used of a husband and wife, of God knowing Israel, of God knowing Jeremiah before he was formed. The righteous way is not merely observed by God. It is known, walked with, kept company. Paul seals the church with this very line: The Lord knows those who are his (2 Tim 2:19). The Shepherd says it warmest: I know my own and my own know me (John 10:14).

The other way is not said to be struck down; it is said to perish, to come to nothing on its own, the way chaff does. It has no destination because it has no root.

Read the psalm honestly and it will not leave you comfortable, because the man in verse 1 is not you. There has been one man who never walked, stood or sat in that company, whose delight was genuinely in the law of God, whose way the Father knew perfectly — and the tree he came to was a gallows: Christ redeemed us from the curse of the law by becoming a curse for us — for it is written, Cursed is everyone who is hanged on a tree (Gal 3:13). The blessed man took the chaff's end so that the chaff could be planted. That is how anyone gets into verse 3, and it is why the doorway has a second half: Blessed are all who take refuge in him (2:12).

2.title: You Are My Son
2.text: <sup>1</sup>Why do the nations rage and the peoples plot in vain?<sup>2</sup>The kings of the earth set themselves, and the rulers take counsel together, against the LORD and against his Anointed, saying,<sup>3</sup>"Let us burst their bonds apart and cast away their cords from us."<sup>4</sup>He who sits in the heavens laughs; the Lord holds them in derision.<sup>5</sup>Then he will speak to them in his wrath, and terrify them in his fury, saying,<sup>6</sup>"As for me, I have set my King on Zion, my holy hill."<sup>7</sup>I will tell of the decree: The LORD said to me, "You are my Son; today I have begotten you.<sup>8</sup>Ask of me, and I will make the nations your heritage, and the ends of the earth your possession.<sup>9</sup>You shall break them with a rod of iron and dash them in pieces like a potter's vessel."<sup>10</sup>Now therefore, O kings, be wise; be warned, O rulers of the earth.<sup>11</sup>Serve the LORD with fear, and rejoice with trembling.<sup>12</sup>Kiss the Son, lest he be angry, and you perish in the way, for his wrath is quickly kindled. Blessed are all who take refuge in him.
2.overview: The nations are in uproar and the kings of the earth conspire against the LORD and his Anointed, calling his rule a rope to be thrown off (vv. 1-3). Heaven's answer is laughter, then wrath, then an announcement: As for me, I have set my King on Zion, my holy hill (vv. 4-6). The King reads out the decree that made him: You are my Son; today I have begotten you; he has only to ask and the nations are his inheritance, to be shattered like pottery if they resist (vv. 7-9). So the psalm turns to the rebels with an offer: be wise, serve with fear, rejoice with trembling, kiss the Son, for blessed are all who take refuge in him (vv. 10-12).
2.theology:
God rules the world through an appointed King, and the world's quarrel with God always lands on that King (v. 2). The church prayed these verses over Herod and Pilate (Acts 4:25-28), naming the crucifixion as the rage of the nations and as God's own plan.

You are my Son; today I have begotten you (v. 7) is applied to the resurrection (Acts 13:33), to the Son's supremacy over angels (Heb 1:5) and to his appointment as priest (Heb 5:5); the Father says it in his own words at the baptism (Matt 3:17). The nations given for an inheritance are claimed by preaching (Matt 28:18) before the rod falls (v. 9; Rev 2:26-27; 19:15).

Fear and joy belong together (v. 11), and judgment and refuge meet in the same person: the Son whose wrath is to be feared is the one in whom all who take refuge are blessed (v. 12). With 1:1 this closes the Psalter's two-psalm doorway.
2.examples:
Bonds and cords: what authority feels like from inside a rebellion.

Heaven laughs — the cure for thinking the rulers rule.

As for me, I have set my King: an announcement, not a threat.

You are my Son, read at the baptism, the tomb and the throne.

Ask, and the nations: mission before the rod.

Rejoice with trembling; kiss the Son while the door is open.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–6 — He Who Sits in the Heavens Laughs
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: The nations rage and the kings of the earth take counsel against the LORD and against his Anointed, wanting their bonds burst (vv. 1-3). He who sits in the heavens laughs; the Lord holds them in derision, then speaks in wrath: As for me, I have set my King on Zion, my holy hill (vv. 4-6).
verseByVerse.theology: The rebellion is real and the outcome is not in doubt. God's answer to a world in revolt is a King he has already installed.

verseByVerse.quote: Why do the nations rage and the peoples plot in vain? The kings of the earth set themselves, and the rulers take counsel together, against the LORD and against his Anointed, saying, "Let us burst their bonds apart and cast away their cords from us."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Why do the nations rage and the peoples plot in vain? The kings of the earth set themselves, and the rulers take counsel together, against the LORD and against his Anointed, saying, Let us burst their bonds apart and cast away their cords from us.

The first psalm showed one man and his book. The second pulls the camera back until the whole earth is in shot, and what it is doing is conspiring. Rage is a word for a crowd in uproar — the ESV notes it can be rendered "noisily assemble" — and the kings are in session with one item on the agenda: God. Notice what they call his rule: bonds and cords, the tackle of a yoke. That is how authority feels from the inside of a rebellion — as rope.

And notice that the plot is against two: against the LORD and against his Anointed. You cannot separate them. The world's quarrel with God always lands on the man God has appointed, which is why this psalm was the first thing the church prayed when the arrests started. Peter and John came back from prison and the believers said these very verses aloud, then named the conspirators: truly in this city there were gathered together against your holy servant Jesus, whom you anointed, both Herod and Pontius Pilate, along with the Gentiles and the peoples of Israel (Acts 4:27). The kings of the earth in verse 2 turned out to be a provincial governor and a puppet king on one Friday morning.

verseByVerse.quote: He who sits in the heavens laughs; the Lord holds them in derision. Then he will speak to them in his wrath, and terrify them in his fury, saying, "As for me, I have set my King on Zion, my holy hill."
verseByVerse.commentary:
He who sits in the heavens laughs; the Lord holds them in derision. Then he will speak to them in his wrath, and terrify them in his fury, saying, As for me, I have set my King on Zion, my holy hill.

God's first response to the rebellion is laughter. Not cruelty — perspective. The one who sits enthroned does not get up, does not consult, does not check whether the plan will work. There is a kind of fear that only this verse cures: the fear that the people running the world might actually be running the world.

Then the laughter stops. Then he will speak to them in his wrath, and terrify them in his fury. The wrath is not a mood God loses control of; it is the settled opposition of a good God to everything that is wrecking his world, and it is aimed here at a conspiracy, not at a weakness. Note too that he speaks before he acts. Words first is mercy: there is still time to be warned, which is exactly what the end of the psalm does.

And the sentence itself is not a threat but an announcement. As for me, I have set my King. It is done; the coronation has already happened. The rebels are debating how to throw off a yoke that has been fastened by decree in heaven. On Zion, my holy hill: a modest ridge in a small country, and God calls it his. That hill is where the temple stood, where the lambs died, and just outside it, where the King was lifted up on a Friday and the nations got their answer. And the church has watched this settled at a graveside outside Jerusalem: the same council that thought it had disposed of him discovered God had enthroned him.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: The King tells the decree: You are my Son; today I have begotten you; ask, and the nations are his heritage, to be broken like a potter's vessel (vv. 7-9). So the kings are warned: be wise, serve the LORD with fear, and rejoice with trembling. Kiss the Son — and the psalm ends, Blessed are all who take refuge in him (vv. 10-12).
verseByVerse.theology: The Son who will break the nations is the refuge of anyone who comes to him, and the New Testament reads every line of this of Jesus.

verseByVerse.quote: I will tell of the decree: The LORD said to me, "You are my Son; today I have begotten you. Ask of me, and I will make the nations your heritage, and the ends of the earth your possession. You shall break them with a rod of iron and dash them in pieces like a potter's vessel."
verseByVerse.commentary:
I will tell of the decree: The LORD said to me, You are my Son; today I have begotten you. Ask of me, and I will make the nations your heritage, and the ends of the earth your possession. You shall break them with a rod of iron and dash them in pieces like a potter's vessel.

Now the King himself speaks and reads out the terms of his appointment. Every king of David's line was called God's son at his coronation, and every one of them died and left the promise unfilled. The New Testament takes these words and puts them where they belong. Paul preaches that God has fulfilled to us their children by raising Jesus, as also it is written in the second Psalm, You are my Son, today I have begotten you (Acts 13:33). Hebrews uses the line twice: to show the Son is greater than any angel (Heb 1:5), and to show he did not grab the priesthood but was appointed to it (Heb 5:5). And the Father said it in his own voice over the water and on the mountain: This is my beloved Son, with whom I am well pleased (Matt 3:17).

Ask of me, and I will make the nations your heritage. The inheritance is not seized; it is requested from a Father and given. The risen Christ says it as an accomplished fact: All authority in heaven and on earth has been given to me (Matt 28:18), and the sentence that follows it is the missionary command. The ends of the earth are claimed by preaching before they are claimed by the rod.

But the rod is there, and it should not be sanded down. Dash them in pieces like a potter's vessel is what happens to power that will not bow. The ESV notes that with different vowels the line reads "you shall rule them", which is how the Greek Old Testament took it — and that is the form John heard in heaven. Break or rule: a pot that will not hold water is smashed, and a people that will bow is governed. The same iron rod does both, depending on what it meets. John hears it three times in Revelation, and once with a startling twist: the authority to rule the nations with a rod of iron is promised to the one who conquers and holds on (Rev 2:26-27). The martyrs get a share in the verdict.

verseByVerse.quote: Now therefore, O kings, be wise; be warned, O rulers of the earth. Serve the LORD with fear, and rejoice with trembling. Kiss the Son, lest he be angry, and you perish in the way, for his wrath is quickly kindled. Blessed are all who take refuge in him.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Now therefore, O kings, be wise; be warned, O rulers of the earth. Serve the LORD with fear, and rejoice with trembling. Kiss the Son, lest he be angry, and you perish in the way, for his wrath is quickly kindled.

The psalm ends by addressing the conspirators directly, and the tone is not triumph over them but an offer to them. Be wise: the word links this psalm back to the first one, where wisdom was delight in God's law. Here wisdom is surrender while surrender is still possible.

Serve the LORD with fear, and rejoice with trembling holds together two things we keep pulling apart. Joy that has no trembling in it has forgotten who God is; trembling with no joy in it has forgotten what he has done. The Christian life is both at once, and a church where only one is audible has lost half the psalm.

Kiss the Son is the gesture of a subject to a sovereign, the act by which a man publicly took his side. Samuel poured the oil on Saul's head and kissed him (1 Sam 10:1); a kiss was how homage was paid and allegiance seen. The psalm is not asking the kings for private agreement. It is asking them to come over publicly, while the door is open.

Blessed are all who take refuge in him.

And there is the last word of the doorway. The Psalter opened with Blessed is the man (1:1) and it closes this pair with blessed are all — not the blameless, not the successful: all who run to him. The King with the iron rod is himself the refuge, and the only safe place from the Son is inside his arms. Everything that follows in this book — every lament, every confession, every hallelujah — is prayed by people who have come in through that door.

And for anyone who reads the news and feels the ground moving: this psalm is not asking you to pretend the rage is harmless. It is asking you to notice who is seated while it happens, and whose Son already holds the title deed to the ends of the earth. Take refuge, and then get on with the work of the eleventh verse — serving with fear, rejoicing with trembling — in whatever small square of the raging earth you have been given.

3.title: A Shield About Me
3.text: A Psalm of David, when he fled from Absalom his son. 1O LORD, how many are my foes! Many are rising against me;2many are saying of my soul, "There is no salvation for him in God." Selah3But you, O LORD, are a shield about me, my glory, and the lifter of my head.4I cried aloud to the LORD, and he answered me from his holy hill. Selah5I lay down and slept; I woke again, for the LORD sustained me.6I will not be afraid of many thousands of people who have set themselves against me all around.7Arise, O LORD! Save me, O my God! For you strike all my enemies on the cheek; you break the teeth of the wicked.8Salvation belongs to the LORD; your blessing be on your people! Selah
3.overview: David prays as he flees from his son Absalom. His enemies are many, and their taunt is theological: There is no salvation for him in God (vv. 1-2). He answers with God himself — a shield around him, his glory, the lifter of his head — and is answered from the holy hill he has just been driven away from (vv. 3-4). He sleeps, wakes, and finds he is not afraid of ten thousand (vv. 5-6). He asks God, not his own sword, to deal with his enemies, and ends by blessing the people who have turned against him: Salvation belongs to the LORD (vv. 7-8).
3.theology:
The superscription is part of the text, and it anchors the psalm in 2 Samuel 15-17: the covered head of the fleeing king (2 Sam 15:30) is lifted by God (v. 3), and the night attack Ahithophel planned (2 Sam 17:1) is slept through (v. 5).

Faith answers a taunt about God with God, and it is God who is asked to act on the enemy (v. 7); the sufferer keeps his own hands clean. Sleep is an act of trust in the one who does not sleep (Ps 121:4; Mark 4:38).

Salvation belongs to the LORD (v. 8) is the Psalter's confession in four words and heaven's song at the end (Rev 7:10), and the prayer that follows it asks blessing on the very people in revolt.
3.examples:
A psalm with a week attached to it: 2 Samuel 15-17.

Three times many, and the cruellest is the theology.

The head covered in grief, lifted by God.

Answered from the hill he had been driven from.

The night raid, and the sleeping king.

Salvation belongs to the LORD, sung in the dark and at the end.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–4 — Many Are Rising Against Me
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: O LORD, how many are my foes! Many say of him, There is no salvation for him in God (vv. 1-2). But you, O LORD, are a shield about me, my glory, and the lifter of my head; he cried aloud and was answered from God's holy hill (vv. 3-4).
verseByVerse.theology: The taunt is about God, not about David, and the answer comes from God's hill, not from David's resources.

verseByVerse.quote: O LORD, how many are my foes! Many are rising against me; many are saying of my soul, "There is no salvation for him in God." Selah
verseByVerse.commentary:
A Psalm of David, when he fled from Absalom his son.

The Psalter's first lament comes with a date on it. These headings above the psalms are part of the Hebrew text, not a later editor's note in the margin, and this one puts us in the worst week of David's life: his own son has taken the kingdom, and the king is walking out of Jerusalem barefoot. David went up the ascent of the Mount of Olives, weeping as he went, barefoot and with his head covered (2 Sam 15:30). Hold that covered head; the psalm comes back to it.

O LORD, how many are my foes! Many are rising against me; many are saying of my soul, There is no salvation for him in God.

Three times many, and the third is the one that hurts. The crowd is not merely against him; they have worked out a theology about him. Shimei shouted it along the road: The LORD has avenged on you all the blood of the house of Saul ... See, your evil is on you (2 Sam 16:8). God has finished with you. When trouble comes with a commentary attached — this is what you deserve, God has dropped you — the commentary wounds deeper than the trouble.

Selah. The ESV's note says its meaning is uncertain and that it may be a musical or liturgical direction — a rest, or a lift in the accompaniment — and it falls here, after the worst sentence in the psalm. Whatever the musicians did with it, the reader is made to stop where he would rather hurry on.

verseByVerse.quote: But you, O LORD, are a shield about me, my glory, and the lifter of my head. I cried aloud to the LORD, and he answered me from his holy hill. Selah
verseByVerse.commentary:
But you, O LORD, are a shield about me, my glory, and the lifter of my head. I cried aloud to the LORD, and he answered me from his holy hill.

But you. Two words, and the psalm turns on them. He does not answer the taunt with evidence; he answers it with God, and with three things at once.

A shield about me: not held in front, but around — the side a man cannot cover himself. My glory: his honour is gone, stripped by his own son, and he says the glory he has left is God. And the lifter of my head — said by the man who walked up the hill with his head covered in grief. He cannot lift it himself. Someone else puts a hand under his chin.

Then: he answered me from his holy hill. David is on the Mount of Olives; the ark is back in the city he has just lost. He is cut off from the place where God is worshipped, and God answers him from there anyway. Distance from the building is not distance from God.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 5–8 — I Lay Down and Slept
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: I lay down and slept; I woke again, for the LORD sustained me; he will not fear ten thousand drawn up around him (vv. 5-6). Arise, O LORD! Save me, O my God! — and the psalm ends, Salvation belongs to the LORD; your blessing be on your people (vv. 7-8).
verseByVerse.theology: A hunted man sleeps, and prays for rescue rather than revenge, and ends by blessing the very nation that has turned on him.

verseByVerse.quote: I lay down and slept; I woke again, for the LORD sustained me. I will not be afraid of many thousands of people who have set themselves against me all around.
verseByVerse.commentary:
I lay down and slept; I woke again, for the LORD sustained me. I will not be afraid of many thousands of people who have set themselves against me all around.

It is one of the quietest miracles in the Bible. That same night Ahithophel was urging Absalom, Let me choose twelve thousand men, and I will arise and pursue David tonight (2 Sam 17:1). A night raid was being planned, and the hunted king slept, and woke up, and was surprised enough by it to write it down.

Sleep is one of the plainest acts of faith there is. To sleep is to stop holding the world together and let someone else hold it, and the psalm gives the reason without embarrassment: the LORD sustained me. The Psalter says elsewhere that the one keeping you will neither slumber nor sleep (Ps 121:4), which is exactly why you can. And when the disciples were bailing water in a gale, they found their Lord in the stern, asleep on the cushion (Mark 4:38). He slept in the storm because he trusted his Father; we sleep in the storm because we trust him.

If you are lying awake tonight doing the arithmetic of everything that could go wrong, this verse is not a rebuke. It is an invitation to hand the watch over to the one who is awake anyway.

verseByVerse.quote: Arise, O LORD! Save me, O my God! For you strike all my enemies on the cheek; you break the teeth of the wicked. Salvation belongs to the LORD; your blessing be on your people! Selah
verseByVerse.commentary:
Arise, O LORD! Save me, O my God! For you strike all my enemies on the cheek; you break the teeth of the wicked.

The language is violent, and it matters who is holding the weapon. David does not strike anyone; he asks God to act and leaves it there. A struck cheek is an insult answered, broken teeth are a predator disarmed — the imagery is of an attacker made harmless, not of a private revenge carried out. David had Shimei within reach and refused to touch him. A man who hands his grievance to God can afford to keep his hands clean.

Salvation belongs to the LORD; your blessing be on your people!

The last line is astonishing from a man in his position. Your people is the nation that just crowned his rival, and he asks for their blessing. And the first half of the line is the sentence heaven itself will sing: Salvation belongs to our God who sits on the throne, and to the Lamb (Rev 7:10). A fugitive king says it on a hillside in the dark, and an uncountable multitude says it in the light at the end. It was true both times.

4.title: In Peace I Will Both Lie Down and Sleep
4.text: To the choirmaster: with stringed instruments. A Psalm of David. 1Answer me when I call, O God of my righteousness! You have given me relief when I was in distress. Be gracious to me and hear my prayer!2O men, how long shall my honor be turned into shame? How long will you love vain words and seek after lies? Selah3But know that the LORD has set apart the godly for himself; the LORD hears when I call to him.4Be angry, and do not sin; ponder in your own hearts on your beds, and be silent. Selah5Offer right sacrifices, and put your trust in the LORD.6There are many who say, "Who will show us some good? Lift up the light of your face upon us, O LORD!"7You have put more joy in my heart than they have when their grain and wine abound.8In peace I will both lie down and sleep; for you alone, O LORD, make me dwell in safety.
4.overview: An evening prayer handed to the choirmaster. David asks to be answered, remembering that God has made room for him before in a tight place (v. 1), and challenges the men of rank who love lies (v. 2). He steadies himself on what God has done: the LORD has set the godly apart for himself and hears them (v. 3). Then counsel to the angry — be angry without sinning, think it over on your bed, be silent, offer right sacrifices and trust (vv. 4-5). Against the crowd's Who will show us some good? he asks for the light of God's face (v. 6), says he has more joy than a good harvest gives (v. 7), and lies down to sleep because the LORD alone keeps him safe (v. 8).
4.theology:
Prayer rests on God's prior action and on belonging to him: he has set apart the godly for himself, and therefore hears (vv. 1, 3).

Anger is not sin, and is not licence either (v. 4; quoted at Eph 4:26). The prescribed cure is reflection, silence, worship and trust rather than speech.

The answer to Who will show us some good? is the Aaronic blessing (v. 6; Num 6:25-26): the face of God, not better circumstances. Joy in God outweighs harvest joy without pretending harvest joy is nothing (v. 7), and peace that does not depend on us makes sleep possible (v. 8; cf. 3:5).
4.examples:
To the choirmaster: your worst night becomes the congregation's hymn.

In a tight place you made room for me.

Set apart for himself, and therefore heard.

Be angry, and do not sin: take it to bed, not to the street.

The face, not the goods (Num 6:25-26).

More joy than grain and wine — a claim you can test.

You alone: the difference between resting and stopping.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–5 — Know That the LORD Has Set Apart the Godly
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Answer me when I call, O God of my righteousness! — he has made room before, and is asked to be gracious again (v. 1). How long will men love vain words and seek lies (v. 2)? But know that the LORD has set apart the godly for himself; the LORD hears when I call to him (v. 3). Be angry, and do not sin: ponder on your bed, be silent, offer right sacrifices, and trust the LORD (vv. 4-5).
verseByVerse.theology: Prayer rests on what God has already done and on whose he is. Anger is not forbidden; acting on it is.

verseByVerse.quote: Answer me when I call, O God of my righteousness! You have given me relief when I was in distress. Be gracious to me and hear my prayer! O men, how long shall my honor be turned into shame? How long will you love vain words and seek after lies? Selah
verseByVerse.commentary:
To the choirmaster: with stringed instruments. A Psalm of David.

Here is the first of fifty-five psalms handed over to the choirmaster, with the band noted: strings. Keep that in mind through the whole book. These prayers are intensely personal and they were written to be sung in public by people who did not write them. Your worst night becomes someone else's hymn.

Answer me when I call, O God of my righteousness! You have given me relief when I was in distress. Be gracious to me and hear my prayer!

The middle line is the ground of the other two, and in Hebrew it is a picture: in a tight place, you made room for me. He is boxed in again, and he prays by remembering the last time the walls moved. That is not sentiment; it is evidence. Keep a record of the times God made room, because you will need it in the next narrow place.

O men, how long shall my honor be turned into shame? How long will you love vain words and seek after lies? The ESV notes these may be "men of rank" — people with the standing to make a lie stick. He does not argue with the slander. He takes it to God and then turns to give the slanderers a warning.

verseByVerse.quote: But know that the LORD has set apart the godly for himself; the LORD hears when I call to him. Be angry, and do not sin; ponder in your own hearts on your beds, and be silent. Selah Offer right sacrifices, and put your trust in the LORD.
verseByVerse.commentary:
But know that the LORD has set apart the godly for himself; the LORD hears when I call to him.

The word for godly is the adjective from God's own covenant love: the loyal one, the man bound to a God who binds himself. He is not claiming to be impressive. He is claiming to be owned. And the two halves belong together — set apart for himself, and therefore heard. Prayer is answered because of a relationship, not because of volume.

Be angry, and do not sin; ponder in your own hearts on your beds, and be silent.

Paul quotes this line straight into a letter about church life (Eph 4:26), which tells you how practical it is. The ESV notes the first verb can be rendered "be agitated": the tremble of a man who has been wronged. Scripture does not tell him to feel nothing. It tells him what to do with what he feels — take it to bed rather than to the street, turn it over in God's presence, and stop talking. Most of the damage anger does is done by the mouth in the hour before it cools.

Offer right sacrifices, and put your trust in the LORD. The two go together: the act of worship and the leaning of the heart. Either one without the other is half a religion.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 6–8 — More Joy Than When Their Grain and Wine Abound
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Many ask, Who will show us some good?, and the psalmist asks instead for the light of God's face (v. 6). You have put more joy in my heart than they have when their grain and wine abound (v. 7). In peace I will both lie down and sleep; for you alone, O LORD, make me dwell in safety (v. 8).
verseByVerse.theology: The harvest is real joy and God's face is a greater one, and the man who has the greater one can sleep.

verseByVerse.quote: There are many who say, "Who will show us some good? Lift up the light of your face upon us, O LORD!" You have put more joy in my heart than they have when their grain and wine abound. In peace I will both lie down and sleep; for you alone, O LORD, make me dwell in safety.
verseByVerse.commentary:
There are many who say, Who will show us some good? Lift up the light of your face upon us, O LORD!

That first question is the sound of a discouraged crowd, and it is perfectly modern: is there any good news at all? The answer he prays is not a better year. It is the priestly blessing, word for word out of Numbers: the LORD make his face to shine upon you and be gracious to you; the LORD lift up his countenance upon you and give you peace (Num 6:25-26). He asks for the face rather than the goods.

You have put more joy in my heart than they have when their grain and wine abound.

And this is the verse to sit with. He is not pretending harvest joy is nothing. Grain and wine in are real gladness — the mortgage covered, the barns full, a good year. He says he has more than that, and he has it while being slandered by men of rank. Any believer can test the claim in a plain way: which piece of news would actually change your evening more, a raise or an hour of the felt nearness of God? The honest answer is usually humbling, and it tells you where your joy is currently plugged in.

In peace I will both lie down and sleep; for you alone, O LORD, make me dwell in safety.

The Psalter's third and fourth psalms both end in bed. There a hunted king slept because God sustained him (3:5); here a slandered man sleeps because God alone keeps him safe. You alone is the whole difference between resting and merely stopping. If safety depends partly on you, some part of you has to stay on watch all night. If it depends on God, you can put your head down.

5.title: In the Morning You Hear My Voice
5.text: To the choirmaster: for the flutes. A Psalm of David. 1Give ear to my words, O LORD; consider my groaning.2Give attention to the sound of my cry, my King and my God, for to you do I pray.3O LORD, in the morning you hear my voice; in the morning I prepare a sacrifice for you and watch.4For you are not a God who delights in wickedness; evil may not dwell with you.5The boastful shall not stand before your eyes; you hate all evildoers.6You destroy those who speak lies; the LORD abhors the bloodthirsty and deceitful man.7But I, through the abundance of your steadfast love, will enter your house. I will bow down toward your holy temple in the fear of you.8Lead me, O LORD, in your righteousness because of my enemies; make your way straight before me.9For there is no truth in their mouth; their inmost self is destruction; their throat is an open grave; they flatter with their tongue.10Make them bear their guilt, O God; let them fall by their own counsels; because of the abundance of their transgressions cast them out, for they have rebelled against you.11But let all who take refuge in you rejoice; let them ever sing for joy, and spread your protection over them, that those who love your name may exult in you.12For you bless the righteous, O LORD; you cover him with favor as with a shield.
5.overview: A morning prayer. The psalmist brings words, groaning and a cry to his King, laying his prayer out like a sacrifice at first light and then watching for the answer (vv. 1-3). He prays because of who God is: one who takes no delight in wickedness, who cannot house evil, who hates all evildoers and destroys liars (vv. 4-6). He himself enters God's house only by the abundance of steadfast love, and asks for a straight path under hostile eyes (vv. 7-8). His enemies' throats are open graves; he asks God — not his own hand — to let them fall by their own counsels (vv. 9-10). The psalm ends in singing for everyone who takes refuge, covered by God's favour as by a shield (vv. 11-12).
5.theology:
God's hatred of evil (vv. 4-6) is not an embarrassment to be softened; it is the sufferer's hope, since a God indifferent to lies would be no help to the lied-about. It stands alongside Rom 5:8: the hatred of evil fell on Christ rather than on us.

Entry to God's house is through the abundance of your steadfast love (v. 7), never merit. And Paul quotes v. 9 of the whole human race (Rom 3:13, 19), so the reader who starts on the psalmist's side of the line ends needing v. 7 as much as the enemies do.

The first imprecation in the Psalter asks God to judge and asks that the wicked fall by their own counsels, on the ground that they have rebelled against God (v. 10) — prayer handed over, not vengeance taken.
5.examples:
Words, groaning, a cry: God considers all three.

Prayer laid out like wood on an altar — and then watched.

You hate all evildoers: the guarantee the cry is taken seriously.

In by steadfast love, not by being unlike them.

A straight path because of my enemies.

An open grave under a smooth tongue (Rom 3:13).

Favour as a body-shield over a man who began by groaning.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–6 — You Are Not a God Who Delights in Wickedness
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Give ear to my words, O LORD; consider my groaning — morning by morning he lays his prayer out like a sacrifice and watches for the answer (vv. 1-3). The reason he can pray at all is who God is: you are not a God who delights in wickedness; the boastful cannot stand before him, and he destroys those who speak lies (vv. 4-6).
verseByVerse.theology: A God who was indifferent to evil would be no use to a man being lied about. God's hatred of evil is the sufferer's hope.

verseByVerse.quote: Give ear to my words, O LORD; consider my groaning. Give attention to the sound of my cry, my King and my God, for to you do I pray. O LORD, in the morning you hear my voice; in the morning I prepare a sacrifice for you and watch.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Give ear to my words, O LORD; consider my groaning. Give attention to the sound of my cry, my King and my God, for to you do I pray.

Three words for what comes out of him: words, groaning, a cry. The middle one is a murmur, the sound a man makes when the sentence will not form. God is asked to consider that too. If you can only groan this morning, you are still praying, and this psalm knows it.

O LORD, in the morning you hear my voice; in the morning I prepare a sacrifice for you and watch.

Twice in the morning, and the verb behind prepare is the priest's word for laying the wood and the pieces in order on the altar. He arranges his prayer the way a priest arranges a sacrifice, and then he does the thing most of us skip: he watches. A lookout on the wall, waiting to see what God will do about what he has just said. The ESV notes the line can be read "I direct my prayer to you". Either way it is deliberate work, at a set hour, with expectation attached.

verseByVerse.quote: For you are not a God who delights in wickedness; evil may not dwell with you. The boastful shall not stand before your eyes; you hate all evildoers. You destroy those who speak lies; the LORD abhors the bloodthirsty and deceitful man.
verseByVerse.commentary:
For you are not a God who delights in wickedness; evil may not dwell with you. The boastful shall not stand before your eyes; you hate all evildoers. You destroy those who speak lies; the LORD abhors the bloodthirsty and deceitful man.

This is the reason he prays at all, and it is stated with no cushioning. God does not merely disapprove of wickedness; he cannot have it in the house. You hate all evildoers is not a slip of the pen or an immature stage of revelation. God's opposition to evil is personal, because evil is not a substance floating about — it is done, by someone, to someone.

And a God who felt nothing about it would be useless to the man in this psalm. If you have been lied about by people with power, a God who shrugs is not a comfort, he is an insult. The hatred of evil in verse 5 is the guarantee that the cry in verse 2 is taken seriously.

Then hold it beside the other sentence: God shows his love for us in that while we were still sinners, Christ died for us (Rom 5:8). Both are true, and neither cancels the other. God's hatred of evil went all the way to the cross, where it fell on his Son instead of on us. Anyone who has cheapened either half has lost the gospel: a God who hates nothing forgives nothing.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 7–12 — Lead Me, O LORD, in Your Righteousness
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: But I, through the abundance of your steadfast love, will enter your house, and he asks to be led in God's righteousness on a straight path (vv. 7-8). His enemies' throats are open graves; let them fall by their own counsels (vv. 9-10). But let all who take refuge in you rejoice: God blesses the righteous and covers him with favour as with a shield (vv. 11-12).
verseByVerse.theology: He enters God's house on steadfast love and not on merit, and leaves judgment with God while he sings.

verseByVerse.quote: But I, through the abundance of your steadfast love, will enter your house. I will bow down toward your holy temple in the fear of you. Lead me, O LORD, in your righteousness because of my enemies; make your way straight before me.
verseByVerse.commentary:
But I, through the abundance of your steadfast love, will enter your house. I will bow down toward your holy temple in the fear of you.

But I — and it would be easy to hear the next clause as: because I am not like them. It says the opposite. He enters through the abundance of your steadfast love, the covenant loyalty that was never earned. The only thing that gets him through the door is the same thing that gets anyone through it. And he goes in in the fear of you: welcomed, and not casual.

Lead me, O LORD, in your righteousness because of my enemies; make your way straight before me.

Notice what the pressure of enemies makes him ask for. Not their ruin first, and not an easier road — a straight path and a righteous walk, because of my enemies. He knows that hostile eyes are on him and that the surest way to lose is to be caught crooked. When people are looking for a reason to discredit you, the prayer to pray is this one.

verseByVerse.quote: For there is no truth in their mouth; their inmost self is destruction; their throat is an open grave; they flatter with their tongue. Make them bear their guilt, O God; let them fall by their own counsels; because of the abundance of their transgressions cast them out, for they have rebelled against you.
verseByVerse.commentary:
For there is no truth in their mouth; their inmost self is destruction; their throat is an open grave; they flatter with their tongue.

A tour of a lying mouth, from the inside out: nothing true in it, ruin at the bottom of it, a throat like a dug grave with the smell of death coming up, and a smooth tongue on top. The flattery is the worst of it, because flattery is what makes the grave look like a garden.

And here is the turn nobody expects. Paul takes this verse, puts it in his long list of Scriptures about human sin, and applies it to every person alive: Their throat is an open grave; they use their tongues to deceive (Rom 3:13). The point of the list is that every mouth may be stopped, and the whole world may be held accountable to God (Rom 3:19). Read the psalm as a believer and you will start on David's side of the line, and end up needing the abundance of steadfast love in verse 7 exactly as much as the men he is praying about.

Make them bear their guilt, O God; let them fall by their own counsels; because of the abundance of their transgressions cast them out, for they have rebelled against you.

The Psalter's first prayer against enemies, and its shape matters. He does not plan anything; he asks God to act, which is the opposite of revenge — revenge is what a man does when he will not wait for God. He asks that they fall by their own counsels, that the trap they built work as designed. And the last clause gives his real reason: they have rebelled against you. This is not wounded pride looking for a weapon; it is a servant asking his King to deal with treason. The Christian prays it with the cross in view, where God dealt with our treason by bearing it, and where the final judgment of every unrepented lie is guaranteed.

verseByVerse.quote: But let all who take refuge in you rejoice; let them ever sing for joy, and spread your protection over them, that those who love your name may exult in you. For you bless the righteous, O LORD; you cover him with favor as with a shield.
verseByVerse.commentary:
But let all who take refuge in you rejoice; let them ever sing for joy, and spread your protection over them, that those who love your name may exult in you. For you bless the righteous, O LORD; you cover him with favor as with a shield.

The psalm that began with a groan ends with singing, and it is not the psalmist's own rescue he sings about but all who take refuge — everyone in the same position as himself. Grief that has been taken to God often comes back out as intercession for other people.

Spread your protection over them is the picture of a covering stretched out, like a tent over people in the open. And the last line makes God's favour a body-shield: not a small round buckler held in one hand, but the tall shield an infantryman crouched behind, covering him from head to foot. The morning began with a man laying out his prayer and watching the horizon. It ends with him hidden behind God's own approval.

6.title: How Long, O LORD?
6.text: To the choirmaster: with stringed instruments; according to The Sheminith. A Psalm of David. 1O LORD, rebuke me not in your anger, nor discipline me in your wrath.2Be gracious to me, O LORD, for I am languishing; heal me, O LORD, for my bones are troubled.3My soul also is greatly troubled. But you, O LORD— how long?4Turn, O LORD, deliver my life; save me for the sake of your steadfast love.5For in death there is no remembrance of you; in Sheol who will give you praise?6I am weary with my moaning; every night I flood my bed with tears; I drench my couch with my weeping.7My eye wastes away because of grief; it grows weak because of all my foes.8Depart from me, all you workers of evil, for the LORD has heard the sound of my weeping.9The LORD has heard my plea; the LORD accepts my prayer.10All my enemies shall be ashamed and greatly troubled; they shall turn back and be put to shame in a moment.
6.overview: A sick and sorrowing believer asks not to be spared discipline but to be spared wrath: be gracious, heal me, my bones are troubled — and the prayer breaks off mid-sentence, But you, O LORD — how long? (vv. 1-3). He pleads God's steadfast love and argues that the dead do not praise him (vv. 4-5). He is exhausted by weeping, his bed flooded, his eyes failing (vv. 6-7). Then, with nothing in his circumstances changed, he knows he has been heard, three times over, and tells the workers of evil to leave (vv. 8-10).
6.theology:
The prayer asks for correction without anger (v. 1) and grounds itself in God's steadfast love rather than the sufferer's record (v. 4). Grief is bodily as well as spiritual (vv. 2-3, 6-7), and the Psalter puts an unfinished question and undignified weeping into the congregation's songbook.

In death there is no remembrance of you (v. 5) is an Old Testament voice before the resurrection had been brought to light (cf. Isa 38:18-19); it is answered by Christ's rising.

The turn comes by assurance, not by circumstance (vv. 8-9), and Depart from me, all you workers of evil is the sentence the Judge himself will pronounce (Luke 13:27; Matt 7:23).
6.examples:
Not "do not correct me" but "not in anger".

Trouble in the bones and in the soul, named with one word.

How long? — a sentence that never finishes.

The argument that wins: for the sake of your steadfast love.

A flooded bed, sung to stringed instruments.

Three times heard, with nothing else changed.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–7 — I Am Weary with My Moaning
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: O LORD, rebuke me not in your anger: he is languishing, his bones and his soul are troubled, and the prayer breaks off — But you, O LORD — how long? (vv. 1-3). Save me for the sake of your steadfast love, for the dead do not praise you (vv. 4-5). Every night he floods his bed with tears and his eye wastes away with grief (vv. 6-7).
verseByVerse.theology: A believer in the dark, asking for mercy rather than a verdict, and hiding nothing about how bad it is.

verseByVerse.quote: O LORD, rebuke me not in your anger, nor discipline me in your wrath. Be gracious to me, O LORD, for I am languishing; heal me, O LORD, for my bones are troubled. My soul also is greatly troubled. But you, O LORD— how long?
verseByVerse.commentary:
O LORD, rebuke me not in your anger, nor discipline me in your wrath. Be gracious to me, O LORD, for I am languishing; heal me, O LORD, for my bones are troubled. My soul also is greatly troubled. But you, O LORD — how long?

The church has long called this the first of the penitential psalms, and the first line shows why. He does not ask to be let off. He asks that the correction not come in anger — discipline from a father's hand rather than a judge's. That is a distinction a guilty man learns to make when he still trusts the one correcting him.

Then the body gives way with the soul. My bones are troubled, and the same word comes again for his soul: the trouble has gone all the way through. Scripture does not divide a suffering person into a spiritual department and a physical one. Grief gets into the bones, and God is asked to heal there too.

And then the sentence stops: But you, O LORD — how long? There is no object; the question runs out before it finishes. It is the Psalter's first how long, and it is broken off in the middle, which is exactly how the question sounds at three in the morning. Scripture gives the unfinished sentence a place in the hymnbook.

verseByVerse.quote: Turn, O LORD, deliver my life; save me for the sake of your steadfast love. For in death there is no remembrance of you; in Sheol who will give you praise?
verseByVerse.commentary:
Turn, O LORD, deliver my life; save me for the sake of your steadfast love. For in death there is no remembrance of you; in Sheol who will give you praise?

He gives God a reason, and it is not his own record. For the sake of your steadfast love: the covenant love God has bound himself to, which is the only argument any of us has. A prayer that pleads God's character instead of the pray-er's is a prayer that cannot be embarrassed.

Then a line that startles Christian readers: the dead do not praise God. Hezekiah prayed the same way — Sheol does not thank you; death does not praise you ... The living, the living, he thanks you (Isa 38:18-19). This is an Old Testament believer speaking from where he stood, before the resurrection had been brought into the light. He is not denying life after death; he is saying that in the grave the congregation loses a voice. It is an argument for rescue, made to a God who wants to be praised.

And it is a prayer this side of the tomb we can answer. The one who said I am the resurrection and the life has been in Sheol and come out, and the dead in Christ are now precisely those who praise him without pause. Psalm 6 asks its question honestly; Easter answers it.

verseByVerse.quote: I am weary with my moaning; every night I flood my bed with tears; I drench my couch with my weeping. My eye wastes away because of grief; it grows weak because of all my foes.
verseByVerse.commentary:
I am weary with my moaning; every night I flood my bed with tears; I drench my couch with my weeping. My eye wastes away because of grief; it grows weak because of all my foes.

Two verses of undignified detail. He is exhausted by his own crying; the bed is soaked; his eyes have gone dim from it. The language is deliberately larger than life, as anyone knows who has cried like that — the flood is how it feels, not how much water there was.

Take the pastoral point plainly. This is in the Bible, in the hymnbook, set to stringed instruments, and it was given to a congregation to sing. Whoever decided that faith means keeping a level voice did not get it from Scripture. There is no hint here that the weeping is unbelief. The man is doing it in God's presence and out loud, which is the difference between grief and despair.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Depart from me, all you workers of evil, for the LORD has heard the sound of my weeping. The LORD has heard my plea; the LORD accepts my prayer (vv. 8-9). His enemies will be ashamed and turn back (v. 10).
verseByVerse.theology: Nothing in his situation has changed. What has changed is that he knows he was heard.

verseByVerse.quote: Depart from me, all you workers of evil, for the LORD has heard the sound of my weeping. The LORD has heard my plea; the LORD accepts my prayer. All my enemies shall be ashamed and greatly troubled; they shall turn back and be put to shame in a moment.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Depart from me, all you workers of evil, for the LORD has heard the sound of my weeping. The LORD has heard my plea; the LORD accepts my prayer. All my enemies shall be ashamed and greatly troubled; they shall turn back and be put to shame in a moment.

The psalm turns on a hinge, and nothing outside the man has moved. He is still ill; the enemies are still there. What he has is a certainty that he was heard — said three times over, as if he can hardly believe it: heard the sound of my weeping, heard my plea, accepts my prayer. Somewhere between verse 7 and verse 8, in a dark room, God gave him that. That is a common experience in prayer, and anyone waiting on it should know it: often the first thing that changes is not the trouble but the knowledge that God has it.

His words to the workers of evil sound severe from a man in bed. They are the words the Judge himself will speak: Depart from me, all you workers of evil! (Luke 13:27). The psalmist is not sentencing anyone; he is handing them the verdict of the court he has just been heard in, and Christ will say it in his own voice on the last day. Those are the two options in front of every reader — to be heard while weeping, or to be told to depart.

7.title: God Is a Righteous Judge
7.text: A Shiggaion of David, which he sang to the LORD concerning the words of Cush, a Benjaminite. 1O LORD my God, in you do I take refuge; save me from all my pursuers and deliver me,2lest like a lion they tear my soul apart, rending it in pieces, with none to deliver.3O LORD my God, if I have done this, if there is wrong in my hands,4if I have repaid my friend with evil or plundered my enemy without cause,5let the enemy pursue my soul and overtake it, and let him trample my life to the ground and lay my glory in the dust. Selah6Arise, O LORD, in your anger; lift yourself up against the fury of my enemies; awake for me; you have appointed a judgment.7Let the assembly of the peoples be gathered about you; over it return on high.8The LORD judges the peoples; judge me, O LORD, according to my righteousness and according to the integrity that is in me.9Oh, let the evil of the wicked come to an end, and may you establish the righteous— you who test the minds and hearts, O righteous God!10My shield is with God, who saves the upright in heart.11God is a righteous judge, and a God who feels indignation every day.12If a man does not repent, God will whet his sword; he has bent and readied his bow;13he has prepared for him his deadly weapons, making his arrows fiery shafts.14Behold, the wicked man conceives evil and is pregnant with mischief and gives birth to lies.15He makes a pit, digging it out, and falls into the hole that he has made.16His mischief returns upon his own head, and on his own skull his violence descends.17I will give to the LORD the thanks due to his righteousness, and I will sing praise to the name of the LORD, the Most High.
7.overview: David sings about words — the slander of a man from Saul's tribe. He takes refuge in God from pursuers who would tear him like a lion (vv. 1-2), and swears an oath with a penalty attached: if the charge is true, let them catch him and lay his glory in the dust (vv. 3-5). He asks God to convene the court of the nations and judge him in this matter (vv. 6-8). God tests the innermost self and saves the upright; he is a righteous judge whose indignation at evil is daily, whose weapons are readied against the man who will not repent (vv. 9-13). The wicked conceives mischief, gives birth to lies, digs a pit and falls into it (vv. 14-16). The psalm ends in thanks and song before anything is settled (v. 17).
7.theology:
A believer may ask to be judged in a particular matter (v. 8) without claiming to be righteous in general — the same man prays enter not into judgment with your servant (143:2). God alone tests the hearts (v. 9), which is where a slandered person finally rests.

A God who feels indignation every day (v. 11) is not a God of moods but of settled moral opposition to evil; and his armoury is conditional — if a man does not repent (v. 12). Judgment is announced before it falls, and a way out is left open.

Evil is conceived, carried and born (v. 14; Jas 1:15), and is built to recoil on its author (vv. 15-16). The righteous may therefore wait, and sing before the verdict (v. 17).
7.examples:
The psalm is about words, and the accuser is from Saul's tribe.

Slander does not argue; it tears like a lion.

An oath with a penalty: if I did it, let them catch me.

Hearts and kidneys: the part no one else can inspect.

Indignation every day — the alternative is a God who does not care.

The pit digger, and the gallows built for Mordecai.

Singing before the verdict comes in.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–8 — If There Is Wrong in My Hands
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: O LORD my God, in you do I take refuge, lest they tear his soul like a lion (vv. 1-2). Then an oath: if I have done this, if there is wrong in my hands — let the enemy overtake him and lay his glory in the dust (vv. 3-5). Arise, O LORD, in your anger; let the peoples be gathered and the Judge take his seat (vv. 6-8).
verseByVerse.theology: He does not merely deny the charge; he swears to it, and then asks God to convene the court.

verseByVerse.quote: O LORD my God, in you do I take refuge; save me from all my pursuers and deliver me, lest like a lion they tear my soul apart, rending it in pieces, with none to deliver. O LORD my God, if I have done this, if there is wrong in my hands, if I have repaid my friend with evil or plundered my enemy without cause, let the enemy pursue my soul and overtake it, and let him trample my life to the ground and lay my glory in the dust. Selah
verseByVerse.commentary:
A Shiggaion of David, which he sang to the LORD concerning the words of Cush, a Benjaminite.

We know nothing else about Cush; he appears here and nowhere else in the Bible. Two details survive. He was a Benjaminite, Saul's tribe, which places this among the years when David was hunted by a king's men. And the psalm is about his words. Someone has said something, and it has been believed.

O LORD my God, in you do I take refuge; save me from all my pursuers and deliver me, lest like a lion they tear my soul apart, rending it in pieces, with none to deliver.

The lion is the right picture for slander. It does not argue with you; it takes you apart. And the last phrase is the fear underneath it — with none to deliver. That is what a whispering campaign does to a man: it makes him feel that there is no one left who will step in.

O LORD my God, if I have done this, if there is wrong in my hands, if I have repaid my friend with evil or plundered my enemy without cause, let the enemy pursue my soul and overtake it, and let him trample my life to the ground and lay my glory in the dust.

This is not a general claim to be a good man. It is an oath with a penalty attached: if I did it, let them catch me. The ESV notes that my friend is literally the one at peace with me — the specific charge seems to be treachery against a man who trusted him, which is what Saul's court said about David. And note the third line: he swears he has not even plundered an enemy without cause. Twice he had Saul within reach of a blade and walked away. He can afford this oath.

Most of us cannot swear it about every charge laid against us, and the psalm is not a script for pretending we can. Where the charge is false, take it to God like this. Where some of it lands, there is Psalm 6 two pages back.

verseByVerse.quote: Arise, O LORD, in your anger; lift yourself up against the fury of my enemies; awake for me; you have appointed a judgment. Let the assembly of the peoples be gathered about you; over it return on high. The LORD judges the peoples; judge me, O LORD, according to my righteousness and according to the integrity that is in me.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Arise, O LORD, in your anger; lift yourself up against the fury of my enemies; awake for me; you have appointed a judgment. Let the assembly of the peoples be gathered about you; over it return on high. The LORD judges the peoples; judge me, O LORD, according to my righteousness and according to the integrity that is in me.

He asks God to hold court, and he does it on the grand scale: not a private hearing but the nations assembled and God taking his seat above them. A man being lied about in one small place asks for the verdict of the last day, because that is the only court whose judgment is final.

Awake for me is bold to the point of rudeness, and the Psalter will say it again: Awake! Why are you sleeping, O Lord? (44:23). God is not asleep, and the psalmist knows it. He is describing how the delay feels and asking God to do something about it, which is prayer rather than complaint.

Judge me, O LORD, according to my righteousness sounds dangerous to Christian ears, and it would be, if he were asking about his standing before God in general. He is not. He is asking about this charge, the one Cush has made. A believer may say, with no arrogance at all: Lord, in that specific matter I am innocent, and you know it. The same man says elsewhere, enter not into judgment with your servant (143:2), and both are true at once.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 9–17 — He Makes a Pit and Falls Into It
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: God tests the heart and saves the upright (vv. 9-10); he is a righteous judge, and a God who feels indignation every day, with sword whetted and bow bent if a man will not repent (vv. 11-13). The wicked man conceives mischief and gives birth to lies; he makes a pit, digging it out, and falls into the hole that he has made (vv. 14-16). So the psalm ends in thanks and song (v. 17).
verseByVerse.theology: God's daily indignation is good news for the slandered, and evil is built so that it recoils on the head that plans it.

verseByVerse.quote: Oh, let the evil of the wicked come to an end, and may you establish the righteous— you who test the minds and hearts, O righteous God! My shield is with God, who saves the upright in heart. God is a righteous judge, and a God who feels indignation every day. If a man does not repent, God will whet his sword; he has bent and readied his bow; he has prepared for him his deadly weapons, making his arrows fiery shafts.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Oh, let the evil of the wicked come to an end, and may you establish the righteous — you who test the minds and hearts, O righteous God!

The ESV notes that minds and hearts is, in Hebrew, hearts and kidneys: the deepest interior, the part of a man nobody else can inspect. This is the only place a slandered person can finally rest. Reputation is public and can be stolen; the inside of you is known by God alone, and he is the one who will speak last.

My shield is with God, who saves the upright in heart. The third shield in five psalms — around him (3:3), over him like favour (5:12), and here simply held by God and not by David. A man under attack keeps wanting to pick his own shield up. The psalm says it is in better hands.

God is a righteous judge, and a God who feels indignation every day.
