This is not a rule against banking; it is a rule against making money out of a neighbour's disaster. Loans in that world were rarely for business — they were for a family that had run out of grain. And the bribe is the same sin in a courtroom: turning someone else's vulnerability into your gain.

So the list is almost entirely about how a man treats people, and there is not one ritual item in it. No sacrifices, no festivals, no rules about food. The gate into God's presence turns out to be guarded by the neighbours.

He who does these things shall never be moved.

And now read the list again and ask honestly whether you are through the gate. Speaks truth in his heart; never carries a reproach; keeps a promise that has turned costly; never profits from another's trouble. One man has the whole list without a gap, and he kept his word at a cost he alone could calculate. The letter to the Hebrews tells Christians where they now stand: you have come to Mount Zion and to the city of the living God ... and to Jesus, the mediator of a new covenant (Heb 12:22-24). We do not come in on our record. We come in with him — and then this list stops being a barrier and becomes the description of what living there makes of you.

16.title: My Chosen Portion and My Cup
16.text: A Miktam of David. 1Preserve me, O God, for in you I take refuge.2I say to the LORD, "You are my Lord; I have no good apart from you."3As for the saints in the land, they are the excellent ones, in whom is all my delight.4The sorrows of those who run after another god shall multiply; their drink offerings of blood I will not pour out or take their names on my lips.5The LORD is my chosen portion and my cup; you hold my lot.6The lines have fallen for me in pleasant places; indeed, I have a beautiful inheritance.7I bless the LORD who gives me counsel; in the night also my heart instructs me.8I have set the LORD always before me; because he is at my right hand, I shall not be shaken.9Therefore my heart is glad, and my whole being rejoices; my flesh also dwells secure.10For you will not abandon my soul to Sheol, or let your holy one see corruption.11You make known to me the path of life; in your presence there is fullness of joy; at your right hand are pleasures forevermore.
16.overview: David asks God to keep him and states his ground: I have no good apart from you (vv. 1-2). His delight is in God's people; the sorrows of idolaters multiply, and he will not touch their rituals or say their gods' names (vv. 3-4). Using the language of the land settlement, he calls the LORD his portion, his cup and his lot, and says the surveyor's lines fell for him in pleasant places (vv. 5-6). God counsels him by day and his own heart instructs him at night; with the LORD before him he is not shaken (vv. 7-8). So heart, whole being and flesh rest secure, because God will not abandon his soul to Sheol or let his holy one see corruption (vv. 9-10), and the psalm ends on the path of life, fullness of joy, and pleasures at God's right hand forever (v. 11).
16.theology:
Contentment begins where verse 2 begins: God is not the best of a man's goods but the whole category. The inheritance language (vv. 5-6) is the Levites' arrangement — no land, because I am your portion and your inheritance (Num 18:20) — chosen deliberately, and set against the wicked man's cup (11:6) and the men whose portion is in this life (17:14).

Idolatry is described by its yield: multiplied sorrows (v. 4). Stability comes from deliberate practice — setting the LORD before oneself (v. 8).

Peter preached vv. 8-11 at Pentecost and pointed out that David's tomb was still occupied, so the psalm speaks of Christ's resurrection (Acts 2:25-31; 13:35). The hope reaches the body (v. 9), and the psalm's end is presence rather than rescue: fullness of joy and pleasures forevermore (v. 11).
16.examples:
I have no good apart from you: not the best good, the only one.

Delight in God and delight in his people arrive together.

Every substitute god charges more and delivers less.

The surveyor's cord, and the tribe that was given God instead of land.

Two cups: fire and sulphur (11:6), or the LORD.

The night shift working for him instead of against him.

Peter: David's tomb is down the road, so whose psalm is this?

Fullness of joy — a cup that cannot hold more.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–6 — The Lines Have Fallen for Me in Pleasant Places
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Preserve me, O God, for in you I take refuge; I have no good apart from you (vv. 1-2). The saints in the land are his delight; those who run after another god multiply their sorrows, and he will not pour their offerings or speak their names (vv. 3-4). The LORD is my chosen portion and my cup; you hold my lot. The lines have fallen for me in pleasant places; indeed, I have a beautiful inheritance (vv. 5-6).
verseByVerse.theology: A man surveys his life as if it were land he has been allotted, and finds that his share is God himself.

verseByVerse.quote: Preserve me, O God, for in you I take refuge. I say to the LORD, "You are my Lord; I have no good apart from you." As for the saints in the land, they are the excellent ones, in whom is all my delight. The sorrows of those who run after another god shall multiply; their drink offerings of blood I will not pour out or take their names on my lips.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Preserve me, O God, for in you I take refuge. I say to the LORD, You are my Lord; I have no good apart from you.

The psalm opens by asking to be kept alive — preserve me — and it will end with a promise about a grave. Hold the two ends together: the prayer of a man who wants to survive the week is answered with something far larger than the week.

Six words hold the whole psalm: I have no good apart from you. Not "you are the best of my good things" — there is no other category. Everything he goes on to enjoy in this psalm, he enjoys as something that comes out of that one relationship.

As for the saints in the land, they are the excellent ones, in whom is all my delight.

The second thing he says he loves is God's people, and the word is strong: the excellent ones, the noble ones. Not the impressive people in the land — the holy ones. Anyone who genuinely delights in God finds, usually to their surprise, that they have started to enjoy his people, including the awkward ones. The two loves arrive together.

The sorrows of those who run after another god shall multiply; their drink offerings of blood I will not pour out or take their names on my lips.

And here is the alternative, described without heat. Idolatry is not portrayed as wicked fun; it is portrayed as multiplying sorrows. Every substitute god charges more and delivers less as time goes on, which is a thing people discover slowly and always the same way. David will not go near the rituals — he will not even say the names out loud. There is a kind of distance from an old idol that has to be physical and verbal, not just intentional. Ask anyone who has kept one contact in their phone.

verseByVerse.quote: The LORD is my chosen portion and my cup; you hold my lot. The lines have fallen for me in pleasant places; indeed, I have a beautiful inheritance.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The LORD is my chosen portion and my cup; you hold my lot. The lines have fallen for me in pleasant places; indeed, I have a beautiful inheritance.

Every word here comes out of the land settlement. When Israel took Canaan, each tribe got its portion, measured out with lines — the surveyor's cord — and assigned by lot. One tribe got nothing. The Levites were given no territory at all, and the reason was this: I am your portion and your inheritance among the people of Israel (Num 18:20). No fields, no border, no deeds — God himself, instead.

David takes that arrangement, which looked on paper like the worst deal in Israel, and says he chooses it. He surveys his own life the way a man walks his boundary, and reports that the cord fell in good ground: the lines have fallen for me in pleasant places. Read the verse remembering that he wrote a lot of psalms in caves.

And the cup: five psalms earlier, the wicked man's cup was fire and sulphur and a scorching wind (11:6). Every person is handed a cup, and the difference is what is in it. Here the cup is God. Later a man in Lamentations says the same thing with Jerusalem in ruins around him — The LORD is my portion, says my soul, therefore I will hope in him (Lam 3:24). That sentence is not a way of pretending you have what you wanted. It is the discovery that what you have is enough because of who it is.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 7–11 — You Will Not Abandon My Soul
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: He blesses the God who counsels him by day and instructs him at night, and keeps the LORD before him so that he is not shaken (vv. 7-8). Therefore heart, whole being and flesh rest secure, for you will not abandon my soul to Sheol, or let your holy one see corruption (vv. 9-10). You make known to me the path of life; in your presence there is fullness of joy; at your right hand are pleasures forevermore (v. 11).
verseByVerse.theology: Peter preached these verses at Pentecost and pointed out that David's tomb was down the road: the psalm is about a grave that stayed empty.

verseByVerse.quote: I bless the LORD who gives me counsel; in the night also my heart instructs me. I have set the LORD always before me; because he is at my right hand, I shall not be shaken.
verseByVerse.commentary:
I bless the LORD who gives me counsel; in the night also my heart instructs me. I have set the LORD always before me; because he is at my right hand, I shall not be shaken.

Two times of day. By daylight God counsels him; at night his own inner self keeps teaching him — the ESV notes the Hebrew is that his kidneys instruct him, the deep interior that speaks when the house is quiet. Wakefulness at 2 a.m. is usually a courtroom where we prosecute ourselves. In a man who has been taking God's counsel by day, the night shift works for him instead: what he has heard goes on being turned over when he is too tired to defend himself against it.

I have set the LORD always before me is deliberate practice, not a mood — putting God in the field of vision on purpose, repeatedly, as the day requires. And the result is stability: at my right hand, in the supporter's position, the place where an advocate stood. Not shaken does not mean not troubled. It means not dislodged.

verseByVerse.quote: Therefore my heart is glad, and my whole being rejoices; my flesh also dwells secure. For you will not abandon my soul to Sheol, or let your holy one see corruption. You make known to me the path of life; in your presence there is fullness of joy; at your right hand are pleasures forevermore.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Therefore my heart is glad, and my whole being rejoices; my flesh also dwells secure. For you will not abandon my soul to Sheol, or let your holy one see corruption.

Gladness runs all the way down: heart, whole being (the Hebrew is my glory, says the ESV's note), and then my flesh. The body is included in the confidence, and the reason is a promise about the grave: God will not leave him in Sheol or let his loyal one rot. The ESV notes the last phrase may be rendered see the pit.

Fifty days after the crucifixion, Peter stood in Jerusalem and read these verses to a crowd, then said the obvious thing: Brothers, I may say to you with confidence about the patriarch David that he both died and was buried, and his tomb is with us to this day (Acts 2:29). David's body did see corruption; everyone knew where he was lying. So either the psalm failed, or David was speaking as a prophet about someone else — and Peter's conclusion was that he foresaw and spoke about the resurrection of the Christ (2:31). Paul preached the same verse the same way in Antioch (Acts 13:35).

That is how the earliest Christian preaching worked: not a new idea imposed on an old poem, but an old poem that had been waiting for a body it fitted. One man's flesh dwelt secure in a borrowed tomb and came out.

You make known to me the path of life; in your presence there is fullness of joy; at your right hand are pleasures forevermore.

The psalm does not end with a rescue from the enemies it never named, or with better circumstances. It ends with a path, a presence and a pleasure that does not run out. Fullness of joy — not a topped-up cup but one that cannot hold more. If you have ever wondered whether the Christian hope is finally rather thin — harps and clouds — this verse is the correction. What is coming is not less enjoyment than this life holds, but the unmixed version of it, at the right hand of the God who said, I have no good apart from you, and was right.

17.title: The Apple of Your Eye
17.text: A Prayer of David. 1Hear a just cause, O LORD; attend to my cry! Give ear to my prayer from lips free of deceit!2From your presence let my vindication come! Let your eyes behold the right!3You have tried my heart, you have visited me by night, you have tested me, and you will find nothing; I have purposed that my mouth will not transgress.4With regard to the works of man, by the word of your lips I have avoided the ways of the violent.5My steps have held fast to your paths; my feet have not slipped.6I call upon you, for you will answer me, O God; incline your ear to me; hear my words.7Wondrously show your steadfast love, O Savior of those who seek refuge from their adversaries at your right hand.8Keep me as the apple of your eye; hide me in the shadow of your wings,9from the wicked who do me violence, my deadly enemies who surround me.10They close their hearts to pity; with their mouths they speak arrogantly.11They have now surrounded our steps; they set their eyes to cast us to the ground.12He is like a lion eager to tear, as a young lion lurking in ambush.13Arise, O LORD! Confront him, subdue him! Deliver my soul from the wicked by your sword,14from men by your hand, O LORD, from men of the world whose portion is in this life. You fill their womb with treasure; they are satisfied with children, and they leave their abundance to their infants.15As for me, I shall behold your face in righteousness; when I awake, I shall be satisfied with your likeness.
17.overview: A prayer, without music or instrument. David asks God to hear a just cause from honest lips and to let vindication come from his own presence (vv. 1-2); God has examined him by night and will find nothing in this matter, for he has kept to God's paths by God's word (vv. 3-5). He calls on the Saviour of all who seek refuge: Keep me as the apple of your eye; hide me in the shadow of your wings (vv. 6-8). His enemies have closed their hearts, opened their mouths, and surrounded him like a lion (vv. 9-12). Let God confront them — men of the world whose portion is in this life, full of treasure and children and inheritance (vv. 13-14). As for me, I shall behold your face in righteousness; when I awake, I shall be satisfied with your likeness (v. 15).
17.theology:
Vindication is asked for from God's presence rather than from public opinion (v. 2), and the claim of innocence is about one charge, not about a life (v. 3; cf. 143:2). What kept him off the violent road was the word of your lips (v. 4).

God's care is described by reflex and instinct: the pupil of the eye (v. 8; Deut 32:10; Zech 2:8) and a bird covering her young (Ruth 2:12; Matt 23:37).

Cruelty begins by closing the heart (v. 10). The psalm's spine is the contrast of portions: everything one life can hold, given generously by God and stopping at the grave (v. 14), against the face of God on waking (v. 15; cf. 16:5; 1 John 3:2). Both parties are satisfied; only one satisfaction survives the night.
17.examples:
No instrument, no choir: just a prayer.

God's night visit, when a man is least guarded.

Kept off the road by what God said, not by temperament.

The pupil of the eye: protection you cannot decide to give.

The hen and her brood, wept over Jerusalem.

Full bellies, heirs, estates — and all of it inside one life.

Two satisfactions, and the one that survives waking.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–9 — You Have Visited Me by Night
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Hear a just cause, O LORD ... Give ear to my prayer from lips free of deceit! (v. 1). Let vindication come from God's presence (v. 2). You have tried my heart, you have visited me by night, you have tested me, and you will find nothing (v. 3); he has kept to God's paths and his feet have not slipped (vv. 4-5). He calls, certain of an answer, on the Savior of those who seek refuge, and asks to be kept as the apple of your eye, hidden in the shadow of your wings from deadly enemies (vv. 6-9).
verseByVerse.theology: A man asks God to examine him on one specific charge, and appeals to the God whose habit is to save people who run to him.

verseByVerse.quote: Hear a just cause, O LORD; attend to my cry! Give ear to my prayer from lips free of deceit! From your presence let my vindication come! Let your eyes behold the right! You have tried my heart, you have visited me by night, you have tested me, and you will find nothing; I have purposed that my mouth will not transgress. With regard to the works of man, by the word of your lips I have avoided the ways of the violent. My steps have held fast to your paths; my feet have not slipped.
verseByVerse.commentary:
A Prayer of David. Hear a just cause, O LORD; attend to my cry! Give ear to my prayer from lips free of deceit!

Only five psalms are headed simply a prayer, and this one earns the title: there is no music note, no instrument, no choirmaster. A man is in trouble and talking.

From your presence let my vindication come! Let your eyes behold the right! He is not asking the court of public opinion for a hearing. Vindication has to come out from where God is, or it does not hold; a reputation restored by clever handling is a different thing altogether.

You have tried my heart, you have visited me by night, you have tested me, and you will find nothing; I have purposed that my mouth will not transgress.

God's inspection is described as a night visit — the hours when a person is least guarded and most himself. And the claim, again, is narrow: about this business, in this dispute, you will find nothing. The same man prays elsewhere enter not into judgment with your servant (143:2). A clean conscience on a particular charge and a clean record before God in general are two different claims, and only the first is being made here.

With regard to the works of man, by the word of your lips I have avoided the ways of the violent. My steps have held fast to your paths; my feet have not slipped.

And note how he kept out of trouble: by the word of your lips. Not by temperament, not by keeping good company — by what God had said. The word is what actually steered him away from the violent men's road, which is a claim any Christian can test by asking what has kept him out of the last thing he nearly did.

verseByVerse.quote: I call upon you, for you will answer me, O God; incline your ear to me; hear my words. Wondrously show your steadfast love, O Savior of those who seek refuge from their adversaries at your right hand. Keep me as the apple of your eye; hide me in the shadow of your wings, from the wicked who do me violence, my deadly enemies who surround me.
verseByVerse.commentary:
I call upon you, for you will answer me, O God; incline your ear to me; hear my words. Wondrously show your steadfast love, O Savior of those who seek refuge from their adversaries at your right hand.

For you will answer me is said before the answer comes. He is not hoping aloud; he is stating the character of the one he is calling. And that character is given a title: Savior of those who seek refuge. This is what God does; it is his line of work.

Keep me as the apple of your eye; hide me in the shadow of your wings.

Two of the tenderest images in Scripture, side by side. The apple of your eye is the pupil, the part of the body we protect without thinking — you cannot decide whether to blink. God used the phrase of Israel in the desert: he kept him as the apple of his eye (Deut 32:10), and Zechariah made it a warning to anyone who touches God's people: he who touches you touches the apple of his eye (Zech 2:8).

The second picture is a bird covering her young. Boaz blessed Ruth as one who had come under whose wings ... to take refuge (Ruth 2:12), and Jesus wept over Jerusalem in the same words: How often would I have gathered your children together as a hen gathers her brood under her wings, and you were not willing! (Matt 23:37). Reflex and instinct: God protects his own the way you protect your eye and the way a bird covers her chicks.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 10–15 — I Shall Behold Your Face
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: They close their hearts to pity and open their mouths; they have surrounded him like a lion eager to tear (vv. 10-12). Arise, O LORD! Confront him, subdue him! — deliver me from men of the world whose portion is in this life, full-bellied and well provided for (vv. 13-14). As for me, I shall behold your face in righteousness; when I awake, I shall be satisfied with your likeness (v. 15).
verseByVerse.theology: Two portions are set side by side: everything this life can hold, or the face of God on waking.

verseByVerse.quote: They close their hearts to pity; with their mouths they speak arrogantly. They have now surrounded our steps; they set their eyes to cast us to the ground. He is like a lion eager to tear, as a young lion lurking in ambush. Arise, O LORD! Confront him, subdue him! Deliver my soul from the wicked by your sword, from men by your hand, O LORD, from men of the world whose portion is in this life. You fill their womb with treasure; they are satisfied with children, and they leave their abundance to their infants.
verseByVerse.commentary:
They close their hearts to pity; with their mouths they speak arrogantly. They have now surrounded our steps; they set their eyes to cast us to the ground. He is like a lion eager to tear, as a young lion lurking in ambush.

Before that, notice verse 9's plain description of what he is asking rescue FROM: the wicked who do me violence, my deadly enemies who surround me. This is not hurt feelings. The psalm is prayed by someone in physical danger, and its tenderness in verse 8 is not sentimentality — it is what a man reaches for when he is genuinely being hunted.

Three moves in three verses: the heart shuts, the mouth opens, the body closes in. That is the order in which cruelty happens. Pity has to be switched off first — and the psalm says they do it themselves, they close their hearts. Nobody is born unable to feel for the person in front of him.

Arise, O LORD! Confront him, subdue him! Deliver my soul from the wicked by your sword, from men by your hand, O LORD, from men of the world whose portion is in this life. You fill their womb with treasure; they are satisfied with children, and they leave their abundance to their infants.

The prayer is that God would do it — his sword, his hand — and then comes one of the most piercing descriptions in the Psalter. These are men of the world whose portion is in this life. And look at what their portion contains: full bellies, treasure, children they are satisfied with, an estate to leave the grandchildren. It is not a picture of misery. That is the point. God gives them a great deal, and all of it is inside the span of one life, and then it stops.

The previous psalm said, The LORD is my chosen portion and my cup (16:5). Here is the alternative portion, set out honestly and enviably. The choice is not between a full life and an empty one; it is between a full life that ends and a portion that does not.

verseByVerse.quote: As for me, I shall behold your face in righteousness; when I awake, I shall be satisfied with your likeness.
verseByVerse.commentary:
As for me, I shall behold your face in righteousness; when I awake, I shall be satisfied with your likeness.

Everything the psalm has been holding back arrives in one sentence. As for me — over against the men with the treasure and the heirs. What he wants is not a larger share of what they have. It is a face.

In righteousness is how he expects to see it — not by talking his way in, but put right. And the seeing is the reward itself; nothing else is named.

When I awake: from sleep, and from something deeper than sleep. He has spent the psalm among people who may kill him, and he speaks of waking up satisfied. The word satisfied was used in the previous verse of the men with their children and their wealth — they are satisfied too, for now. Two kinds of satisfaction, and only one of them survives the night.

John says what this will look like: we know that when he appears we shall be like him, because we shall see him as he is (1 John 3:2). Seeing his face is what makes us like him; the likeness the psalm wants is caught from the sight of it. Whoever is reading this psalm with their own list of things they do not have — the treasure, the security, the family, the vindication that never came — the psalm's last word is not a consolation prize. It is the thing everything else was a picture of.

18.title: The LORD Is My Rock
18.text: To the choirmaster. A Psalm of David, the servant of the LORD, who addressed the words of this song to the LORD on the day when the LORD delivered him from the hand of all his enemies, and from the hand of Saul. He said: 1I love you, O LORD, my strength.2The LORD is my rock and my fortress and my deliverer, my God, my rock, in whom I take refuge, my shield, and the horn of my salvation, my stronghold.3I call upon the LORD, who is worthy to be praised, and I am saved from my enemies.4The cords of death encompassed me; the torrents of destruction assailed me;5the cords of Sheol entangled me; the snares of death confronted me.6In my distress I called upon the LORD; to my God I cried for help. From his temple he heard my voice, and my cry to him reached his ears.7Then the earth reeled and rocked; the foundations also of the mountains trembled and quaked, because he was angry.8Smoke went up from his nostrils, and devouring fire from his mouth; glowing coals flamed forth from him.9He bowed the heavens and came down; thick darkness was under his feet.10He rode on a cherub and flew; he came swiftly on the wings of the wind.11He made darkness his covering, his canopy around him, thick clouds dark with water.12Out of the brightness before him hailstones and coals of fire broke through his clouds.13The LORD also thundered in the heavens, and the Most High uttered his voice, hailstones and coals of fire.14And he sent out his arrows and scattered them; he flashed forth lightnings and routed them.15Then the channels of the sea were seen, and the foundations of the world were laid bare at your rebuke, O LORD, at the blast of the breath of your nostrils.16He sent from on high, he took me; he drew me out of many waters.17He rescued me from my strong enemy and from those who hated me, for they were too mighty for me.18They confronted me in the day of my calamity, but the LORD was my support.19He brought me out into a broad place; he rescued me, because he delighted in me.20The LORD dealt with me according to my righteousness; according to the cleanness of my hands he rewarded me.21For I have kept the ways of the LORD, and have not wickedly departed from my God.22For all his rules were before me, and his statutes I did not put away from me.23I was blameless before him, and I kept myself from my guilt.24So the LORD has rewarded me according to my righteousness, according to the cleanness of my hands in his sight.25With the merciful you show yourself merciful; with the blameless man you show yourself blameless;26with the purified you show yourself pure; and with the crooked you make yourself seem tortuous.27For you save a humble people, but the haughty eyes you bring down.28For it is you who light my lamp; the LORD my God lightens my darkness.29For by you I can run against a troop, and by my God I can leap over a wall.30This God—his way is perfect; the word of the LORD proves true; he is a shield for all those who take refuge in him.31For who is God, but the LORD? And who is a rock, except our God?—32the God who equipped me with strength and made my way blameless.33He made my feet like the feet of a deer and set me secure on the heights.34He trains my hands for war, so that my arms can bend a bow of bronze.35You have given me the shield of your salvation, and your right hand supported me, and your gentleness made me great.36You gave a wide place for my steps under me, and my feet did not slip.37I pursued my enemies and overtook them, and did not turn back till they were consumed.38I thrust them through, so that they were not able to rise; they fell under my feet.39For you equipped me with strength for the battle; you made those who rise against me sink under me.40You made my enemies turn their backs to me, and those who hated me I destroyed.41They cried for help, but there was none to save; they cried to the LORD, but he did not answer them.42I beat them fine as dust before the wind; I cast them out like the mire of the streets.43You delivered me from strife with the people; you made me the head of the nations; people whom I had not known served me.44As soon as they heard of me they obeyed me; foreigners came cringing to me.45Foreigners lost heart and came trembling out of their fortresses.46The LORD lives, and blessed be my rock, and exalted be the God of my salvation—47the God who gave me vengeance and subdued peoples under me,48who rescued me from my enemies; yes, you exalted me above those who rose against me; you delivered me from the man of violence.49For this I will praise you, O LORD, among the nations, and sing to your name.50Great salvation he brings to his king, and shows steadfast love to his anointed, to David and his offspring forever.
18.overview: David's great song of deliverance, from the day God freed him from Saul and all his enemies; the same song stands as 2 Samuel 22. He begins with love and a pile of names for God — rock, fortress, deliverer, shield, horn, stronghold (vv. 1-3). Caught in the cords of death, he cried out and was heard (vv. 4-6), and God came down in an earthquake of smoke, darkness, cherub, hail and lightning (vv. 7-15) to pull one man out of deep water into a broad place, because he delighted in me (vv. 16-19). He was dealt with according to clean hands kept through the Saul years (vv. 20-24); God meets people as they have dealt with him, saving the humble and bringing down haughty eyes (vv. 25-27); he lights the lamp of a man in the dark (vv. 28-30). God equips him for war and your gentleness made me great (vv. 31-36); enemies are scattered and nations submit (vv. 37-45). The LORD lives: praise among the nations, and steadfast love to David's offspring forever (vv. 46-50).
18.theology:
The whole storm follows one cry (v. 6): God spends an earthquake on a single hunted man, and the reason given for the rescue is delight (v. 19), not merit.

The claim of clean hands (vv. 20-24) concerns the Saul years, and the same author wrote Psalm 51. Even the blamelessness is credited to God (v. 32), who is the blameless one first (v. 30).

God is met as a person has dealt with him (vv. 25-27) — the moral grain of things, not divine moodiness — and he opposes haughty eyes while saving the humble.

He lights a lamp rather than removing the darkness (v. 28), equips people for the work in front of them (vv. 33-34), and makes men great by gentleness (v. 35). The battle report is a king's duty, not a church's method; the psalm's own trajectory runs to the nations praising God with Israel (v. 49; Rom 15:9) and to David's offspring forever (v. 50).
18.examples:
The Old Testament prints this song twice (2 Sam 22).

Eight names for God, all out of the terrain that kept him alive.

Heaven bowed like a man ducking through a low door.

An earthquake spent on one fugitive.

Drawn out of many waters — the verb behind Moses' name.

Because he delighted in me.

A lamp in the dark, not daylight.

Your gentleness made me great, in the middle of a war song.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–19 — He Bowed the Heavens and Came Down
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: I love you, O LORD, my strength, piled with names — rock, fortress, deliverer, shield, horn, stronghold (vv. 1-3). The cords of death and the snares of Sheol closed on him, and he cried out (vv. 4-6). Then the earth shook: smoke, fire, thick darkness, a cherub, hail and thunder and arrows, as God came down (vv. 7-15). He sent from on high, he took me; he drew me out of many waters and brought me out into a broad place ... because he delighted in me (vv. 16-19).
verseByVerse.theology: Heaven is emptied and the mountains shake, and the whole operation is for one hunted man.

verseByVerse.quote: I love you, O LORD, my strength. The LORD is my rock and my fortress and my deliverer, my God, my rock, in whom I take refuge, my shield, and the horn of my salvation, my stronghold. I call upon the LORD, who is worthy to be praised, and I am saved from my enemies.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The heading dates this song: on the day when the LORD delivered him from the hand of all his enemies, and from the hand of Saul. It is the whole fugitive decade looked back on from safety. And the Old Testament thought it important enough to print twice — the same song stands as 2 Samuel 22, with small differences, one of very few passages given to us in duplicate.

I love you, O LORD, my strength.

The verb is a warm, intimate word, the kind used of a mother or a lover, and no one else in the Psalter uses it of God. After years of caves and close escapes, the first thing out of him is not analysis but affection.

The LORD is my rock and my fortress and my deliverer, my God, my rock, in whom I take refuge, my shield, and the horn of my salvation, my stronghold.

I call upon the LORD, who is worthy to be praised, and I am saved from my enemies. That is the psalm in one line, and the tense is the habit of a lifetime rather than a single event: I call, and I am saved. Fifty verses follow to fill it in.

Eight images in one verse, tumbling over each other, and all of them from the years he is describing: the rock faces of Engedi, a hill fort, a shield in a skirmish, the horn of a strong animal. This is not a theology seminar's list of divine attributes. It is a soldier naming God after the terrain that kept him alive, and it invites the same thing from any reader: what has God actually been to you this year? Name it out of your own landscape.

verseByVerse.quote: The cords of death encompassed me; the torrents of destruction assailed me; the cords of Sheol entangled me; the snares of death confronted me. In my distress I called upon the LORD; to my God I cried for help. From his temple he heard my voice, and my cry to him reached his ears.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The cords of death encompassed me; the torrents of destruction assailed me; the cords of Sheol entangled me; the snares of death confronted me.

Death is described as a hunter: ropes, nets, snares, and a flash flood in a dry wadi. He was not merely frightened — the ESV notes the first line can be read terrified me — he was caught. Anyone who has been in a crisis that kept tightening knows the imagery is exact.

In my distress I called upon the LORD; to my God I cried for help. From his temple he heard my voice, and my cry to him reached his ears.

One verse, and it is the hinge of fifty. He called; God heard. Everything else in this psalm — the earthquake, the cherub, the armies — follows from a man in a tight place shouting for help. And notice the last clause: his cry reached his ears. Not overheard in general; it arrived.

verseByVerse.quote: Then the earth reeled and rocked; the foundations also of the mountains trembled and quaked, because he was angry. Smoke went up from his nostrils, and devouring fire from his mouth; glowing coals flamed forth from him. He bowed the heavens and came down; thick darkness was under his feet. He rode on a cherub and flew; he came swiftly on the wings of the wind. He made darkness his covering, his canopy around him, thick clouds dark with water. Out of the brightness before him hailstones and coals of fire broke through his clouds. The LORD also thundered in the heavens, and the Most High uttered his voice, hailstones and coals of fire. And he sent out his arrows and scattered them; he flashed forth lightnings and routed them. Then the channels of the sea were seen, and the foundations of the world were laid bare at your rebuke, O LORD, at the blast of the breath of your nostrils.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Then the earth reeled and rocked; the foundations also of the mountains trembled and quaked, because he was angry. Smoke went up from his nostrils, and devouring fire from his mouth ... He bowed the heavens and came down; thick darkness was under his feet. He rode on a cherub and flew; he came swiftly on the wings of the wind.

What follows the cry is nine verses of storm. This is the language of Sinai, where the mountain shook and smoke went up (Exod 19:16-18), and of the old war songs where God marched out and the earth trembled. God does not send an angel with a message; he bows the heavens like a man ducking through a low door, and comes down himself, with darkness as his tent and a cherub for a chariot.

Sit for a moment with verse 11: He made darkness his covering, his canopy around him, thick clouds dark with water. Two psalms ago a man was asking why God hides himself (10:1), and another was asking how long the face would stay hidden (13:1). Here the darkness is not absence at all — it is the tent God travels in. He was never not coming; he was coming wrapped in the very thing that looked like his absence.

Out of the brightness before him hailstones and coals of fire broke through his clouds. The LORD also thundered in the heavens ... And he sent out his arrows and scattered them; he flashed forth lightnings and routed them. Then the channels of the sea were seen, and the foundations of the world were laid bare at your rebuke.

The sea beds are exposed and the world's foundations laid bare — creation itself pulled back like a sheet. Now hold the scale of it against the fact underneath: none of this was a national emergency. David was one man, on the run, with a few hundred followers and a price on his head. Scripture is perfectly happy to spend an earthquake on an individual. Whatever else you take from this psalm, take that: when a believer in trouble calls, what answers is not a sympathetic presence but the God who bows the heavens.

verseByVerse.quote: He sent from on high, he took me; he drew me out of many waters. He rescued me from my strong enemy and from those who hated me, for they were too mighty for me. They confronted me in the day of my calamity, but the LORD was my support. He brought me out into a broad place; he rescued me, because he delighted in me.
verseByVerse.commentary:
He sent from on high, he took me; he drew me out of many waters. He rescued me from my strong enemy and from those who hated me, for they were too mighty for me. They confronted me in the day of my calamity, but the LORD was my support. He brought me out into a broad place; he rescued me, because he delighted in me.

After all that noise, the rescue itself is described very simply: a hand comes down and lifts him out. The verb for drew me out is the one behind the name Moses, who was named for what Pharaoh's daughter said, I drew him out of the water (Exod 2:10). David is a man pulled out of the river a second time.

And do not skip verse 18: They confronted me in the day of my calamity, but the LORD was my support. Two things arrived on the same day. The trouble came on schedule, and so did the support — a word for something you lean your whole weight on. God did not cancel the day; he held the man up inside it.

They were too mighty for me — he says it without embarrassment. And the destination is not another cave but a broad place, room to stand after years of hiding in crevices.

Then the reason, and it is the last thing a self-made man would write: he rescued me, because he delighted in me. Not because David was necessary to the plan, not because he had earned it. God liked him. That is the engine of the whole psalm, and it is what the New Testament says over every believer who has been drawn out of deep water: God takes pleasure in his people.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 20–30 — This God: His Way Is Perfect
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: God dealt with him according to my righteousness — he had kept the LORD's ways through the Saul years (vv. 20-24). With the merciful you show yourself merciful ... with the crooked you make yourself seem tortuous; God saves the humble and brings down haughty eyes (vv. 25-27). It is you who light my lamp; by God he can run at a troop and leap a wall; This God — his way is perfect (vv. 28-30).
verseByVerse.theology: People meet God as they have dealt with him, and the man in the dark is given a lit lamp rather than an explanation.

verseByVerse.quote: The LORD dealt with me according to my righteousness; according to the cleanness of my hands he rewarded me. For I have kept the ways of the LORD, and have not wickedly departed from my God. For all his rules were before me, and his statutes I did not put away from me. I was blameless before him, and I kept myself from my guilt. So the LORD has rewarded me according to my righteousness, according to the cleanness of my hands in his sight.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The LORD dealt with me according to my righteousness; according to the cleanness of my hands he rewarded me. For I have kept the ways of the LORD, and have not wickedly departed from my God ... I was blameless before him, and I kept myself from my guilt.

Five verses of a man saying he deserved to be rescued, and Christian readers stiffen. Two things keep it in focus. First, the subject: this is about the Saul years. Twice he had the king asleep in front of him and did not kill him. He refused to take the throne by blood. In that matter his hands were clean and he says so.

And look at what the loyalty actually consisted of: all his rules were before me, and his statutes I did not put away from me (v. 22; the ESV notes the word may be rendered just decrees). He kept God's instructions where he could see them during a decade when nobody would have blamed him for improvising. Most moral collapse happens after the rules quietly go out of the field of vision.

Second, the same man wrote Psalm 51 after Bathsheba, where there is not a word about clean hands and the only plea is mercy. Both psalms are true, and Scripture prints them both. A believer can say of a particular fight, before God, I did not cheat — while knowing that his standing with God rests on nothing of the kind.

And the word he uses of himself, blameless, is the word this psalm will give to God in verse 30 and credit God with in verse 32: the God who equipped me with strength and made my way blameless. Even the clean hands were issued to him.

verseByVerse.quote: With the merciful you show yourself merciful; with the blameless man you show yourself blameless; with the purified you show yourself pure; and with the crooked you make yourself seem tortuous. For you save a humble people, but the haughty eyes you bring down.
verseByVerse.commentary:
With the merciful you show yourself merciful; with the blameless man you show yourself blameless; with the purified you show yourself pure; and with the crooked you make yourself seem tortuous. For you save a humble people, but the haughty eyes you bring down.

God meets people in the manner they have brought. That is not divine moodiness; it is the moral grain of the universe. A merciful man finds God merciful, because mercy is what he has trained himself to recognise. The crooked man finds God devious and hard to pin down, because a bent rule makes a straight line look crooked.

Which explains a great deal about how differently people describe the same God. Some find him warm and some find him impossible to deal with, and the difference is not always in their theology. The last line puts it plainly: what God actively opposes is haughty eyes, and what he saves is a humble people. Come as a beggar and you will find him generous.

verseByVerse.quote: For it is you who light my lamp; the LORD my God lightens my darkness. For by you I can run against a troop, and by my God I can leap over a wall. This God—his way is perfect; the word of the LORD proves true; he is a shield for all those who take refuge in him.
verseByVerse.commentary:
For it is you who light my lamp; the LORD my God lightens my darkness. For by you I can run against a troop, and by my God I can leap over a wall. This God — his way is perfect; the word of the LORD proves true; he is a shield for all those who take refuge in him.

Three small mercies, and the first is the one people in the dark should hold on to: God does not always remove the darkness, he lights a lamp in it. A lamp is not daylight. It is enough to take the next step, which is all anyone actually needs.

Then energy for exactly what is in front of him. A troop and a wall were not metaphors in David's life. Notice too that God does not lift him over the obstacles: he still has to run, and still has to jump. And the credit is given away twice in one verse: by you, by my God. And then the summary: his way is perfect, which the ESV notes can be read blameless, the same word David used of himself. The perfection is God's first; anything of it in a man is borrowed.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 31–50 — Your Gentleness Made Me Great
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: God equips him: feet like a deer, hands trained for war, the shield of your salvation, and your gentleness made me great (vv. 31-36). The enemies are pursued, overtaken and scattered like dust; nations he never knew submit (vv. 37-45). The LORD lives, and blessed be my rock: he gave vengeance, rescued him from the man of violence, and shows steadfast love to his anointed, to David and his offspring forever (vv. 46-50).
verseByVerse.theology: The victory song credits God with the strength AND the gentleness, and ends on a promise that outlives David.

verseByVerse.quote: For who is God, but the LORD? And who is a rock, except our God?— the God who equipped me with strength and made my way blameless. He made my feet like the feet of a deer and set me secure on the heights. He trains my hands for war, so that my arms can bend a bow of bronze. You have given me the shield of your salvation, and your right hand supported me, and your gentleness made me great. You gave a wide place for my steps under me, and my feet did not slip.
verseByVerse.commentary:
For who is God, but the LORD? And who is a rock, except our God? — the God who equipped me with strength and made my way blameless. He made my feet like the feet of a deer and set me secure on the heights. He trains my hands for war, so that my arms can bend a bow of bronze.

The gifts are specific and practical: sure feet on broken ground, the strength to draw a heavy bow, high places to stand on. God's help here is not a mood of comfort; it is competence for a hard job. He equips people for the work he has given them, which is a thing to ask for by name.

You have given me the shield of your salvation, and your right hand supported me, and your gentleness made me great. You gave a wide place for my steps under me, and my feet did not slip.

And there, in the middle of a war song, is the loveliest line in the psalm: your gentleness made me great. Not your power, not your discipline — your gentleness. The man who has just described an earthquake says that what actually made him is the way God stooped and handled him carefully. Anyone who has been dealt with gently by God at a point where he deserved otherwise knows how much weight that word carries, and how much of whatever he has become came from it.

verseByVerse.quote: I pursued my enemies and overtook them, and did not turn back till they were consumed. I thrust them through, so that they were not able to rise; they fell under my feet. For you equipped me with strength for the battle; you made those who rise against me sink under me. You made my enemies turn their backs to me, and those who hated me I destroyed. They cried for help, but there was none to save; they cried to the LORD, but he did not answer them. I beat them fine as dust before the wind; I cast them out like the mire of the streets. You delivered me from strife with the people; you made me the head of the nations; people whom I had not known served me. As soon as they heard of me they obeyed me; foreigners came cringing to me. Foreigners lost heart and came trembling out of their fortresses.
verseByVerse.commentary:
I pursued my enemies and overtook them, and did not turn back till they were consumed ... They cried for help, but there was none to save; they cried to the LORD, but he did not answer them. I beat them fine as dust before the wind.

This is a battle report, and it is bloody. The psalm does not apologise for it and neither should we pretend otherwise: David was Israel's king, charged with defending a people from raiders who came to take their harvest and their children, and a king who lost those wars got his nation enslaved. The most sobering line is verse 41: his enemies at the end call on the LORD, and he does not answer. Fear at the end is not repentance.

You delivered me from strife with the people; you made me the head of the nations; people whom I had not known served me. As soon as they heard of me they obeyed me; foreigners came cringing to me.

Hold this against the church's charter. The nations here are subdued by the sword and come cringing; in the kingdom this psalm was pointing towards, the nations come in freely, and the Son who rules them was killed by them first. The trajectory runs from David's conquered foreigners to the day when people from every tribe and language and people and nation stand and sing. Christians do not get David's methods; they get his promise.

verseByVerse.quote: The LORD lives, and blessed be my rock, and exalted be the God of my salvation— the God who gave me vengeance and subdued peoples under me, who rescued me from my enemies; yes, you exalted me above those who rose against me; you delivered me from the man of violence. For this I will praise you, O LORD, among the nations, and sing to your name. Great salvation he brings to his king, and shows steadfast love to his anointed, to David and his offspring forever.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The LORD lives, and blessed be my rock, and exalted be the God of my salvation — the God who gave me vengeance and subdued peoples under me, who rescued me from my enemies ... you delivered me from the man of violence.

The LORD lives is the shout that ends the song. Not an idea about God: a fact about him, said by a man who has been kept alive by it. And notice that vengeance is something God gave — it was never David's to take, which is why he could leave Saul asleep in a cave.

For this I will praise you, O LORD, among the nations, and sing to your name.

Paul quotes exactly this verse to prove that God always meant the Gentiles to be in on the praise: Therefore I will praise you among the Gentiles, and sing to your name (Rom 15:9). David sang it as a king making his name known among neighbouring peoples. Paul reads it as a promise that those peoples would one day be singing with him, which is what happened.

Great salvation he brings to his king, and shows steadfast love to his anointed, to David and his offspring forever.

The last word of this very personal song is not about David at all. It is about his offspring forever — the line that runs from a cave in Judah to a manger and an empty tomb. The rescue of one hunted man turns out to be an instalment in the covenant God made with David's house, and the psalm ends by looking down the generations to the King who would need no rescue from the man of violence because he walked into his hands on purpose.

19.title: The Heavens Declare the Glory of God
19.text: To the choirmaster. A Psalm of David. 1The heavens declare the glory of God, and the sky above proclaims his handiwork.2Day to day pours out speech, and night to night reveals knowledge.3There is no speech, nor are there words, whose voice is not heard.4Their voice goes out through all the earth, and their words to the end of the world. In them he has set a tent for the sun,5which comes out like a bridegroom leaving his chamber, and, like a strong man, runs its course with joy.6Its rising is from the end of the heavens, and its circuit to the end of them, and there is nothing hidden from its heat.7The law of the LORD is perfect, reviving the soul; the testimony of the LORD is sure, making wise the simple;8the precepts of the LORD are right, rejoicing the heart; the commandment of the LORD is pure, enlightening the eyes;9the fear of the LORD is clean, enduring forever; the rules of the LORD are true, and righteous altogether.10More to be desired are they than gold, even much fine gold; sweeter also than honey and drippings of the honeycomb.11Moreover, by them is your servant warned; in keeping them there is great reward.12Who can discern his errors? Declare me innocent from hidden faults.13Keep back your servant also from presumptuous sins; let them not have dominion over me! Then I shall be blameless, and innocent of great transgression.14Let the words of my mouth and the meditation of my heart be acceptable in your sight, O LORD, my rock and my redeemer.
19.overview: The sky talks without stopping: day hands the message to day and night to night, and though there is no speech or language, the voice reaches the end of the world (vv. 1-4). The sun comes out like a bridegroom and runs its circuit like an athlete, and nothing is hidden from its heat (vv. 4-6). Then six lines on God's word — law, testimony, precepts, commandment, fear, rules; perfect, sure, right, pure, clean, true — reviving the soul, making the simple wise, gladdening the heart and enlightening the eyes (vv. 7-9), more desirable than gold and sweeter than honey (vv. 10-11). Having read both books, the psalmist asks to be cleared of faults he cannot see and kept from deliberate sins that want to master him, and offers his speech and his thinking to my rock and my redeemer (vv. 12-14).
19.theology:
Creation is a continuous, wordless, universal testimony to God's glory (vv. 1-4), and Paul applies the same verse to the spread of the gospel (Rom 10:18). What the sky cannot do is forgive: it leaves everyone without excuse and no one with a Saviour, which is why the psalm turns to the word.

Six names, six qualities, six effects (vv. 7-9) describe what Scripture does to a person: revival, wisdom for the teachable, joy, light. Its worth is measured against gold and honey — a claim about desire, not merely about usefulness (v. 10).

Read properly, the word exposes three layers of sin: undiscernible errors, hidden faults, and presumptuous sins that seek dominion (vv. 12-13). The remedy asked for is a verdict and a restraint, and the psalm's last word is redeemer — the kinsman who pays (v. 14; Lev 25:25; Ruth 4; Job 19:25).
19.examples:
Day briefing day, night briefing night, since the beginning.

No language, and therefore all of them.

The sun as bridegroom and as runner, both glad.

Nothing hidden from its heat — and then, the law.

Six answers to "what will the Bible do to me?"

More desirable than gold: a claim about appetite.

Errors, hidden faults, and sins that apply to be master.

The last word: a relative who pays.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–6 — Day to Day Pours Out Speech
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: The heavens declare the glory of God, and the sky above proclaims his handiwork; day and night hand the message on without a word being said, and their voice reaches the end of the world (vv. 1-4). The sun comes out of its tent like a bridegroom leaving his chamber and runs its course, and there is nothing hidden from its heat (vv. 4-6).
verseByVerse.theology: Creation talks constantly and says one thing: glory. Nobody is out of earshot.

verseByVerse.quote: The heavens declare the glory of God, and the sky above proclaims his handiwork. Day to day pours out speech, and night to night reveals knowledge. There is no speech, nor are there words, whose voice is not heard. Their voice goes out through all the earth, and their words to the end of the world. In them he has set a tent for the sun,
verseByVerse.commentary:
The heavens declare the glory of God, and the sky above proclaims his handiwork. Day to day pours out speech, and night to night reveals knowledge.

The verbs are in the present tense and they do not stop. The sky is not a piece of evidence lying about for clever people to interpret; it is a mouth, and it is talking now. And the message is handed on in shifts — day tells the next day, night briefs the next night — so that the testimony has not missed an hour since the world began. The ESV notes the Hebrew word behind heavens is the expanse of Genesis 1: the psalm is walking through the creation account with its head tipped back.

There is no speech, nor are there words, whose voice is not heard. Their voice goes out through all the earth, and their words to the end of the world.

A deliberate paradox: no speech, no words, and yet a voice that carries everywhere. Creation does not preach in any language, which is exactly why it preaches in all of them. There is no country where the stars are untranslated.

Paul takes this verse and uses it of the gospel: Their voice has gone out to all the earth, and their words to the ends of the world (Rom 10:18). He is arguing that Israel has had every chance to hear — the message has gone out as universally as daylight. The witness of the sky and the preaching of Christ get the same verse, which tells you something about how far God intends his word to travel.

Notice where Paul puts it. He has just asked, How are they to hear without someone preaching? and said that faith comes from hearing, and hearing through the word of Christ (Rom 10:14, 17). Then he quotes this psalm. The sky's testimony is universal; the gospel's must be carried by people, and God intends it to travel just as far.

What creation cannot do is tell you how to be forgiven. It announces glory, which is why the second half of the psalm is necessary; the stars leave everyone without excuse and no one with a Saviour.

verseByVerse.quote: which comes out like a bridegroom leaving his chamber, and, like a strong man, runs its course with joy. Its rising is from the end of the heavens, and its circuit to the end of them, and there is nothing hidden from its heat.
verseByVerse.commentary:
In them he has set a tent for the sun, which comes out like a bridegroom leaving his chamber, and, like a strong man, runs its course with joy. Its rising is from the end of the heavens, and its circuit to the end of them, and there is nothing hidden from its heat.

Two pictures of the same morning. A bridegroom stepping out of his chamber — scrubbed, dressed, radiant, and not remotely embarrassed to be looked at. And an athlete at the start of a race, all energy and gladness, who will run the whole circuit without tiring. That is the sun coming up, and the psalm says it does it with joy. Nothing in creation is dragging itself round out of duty.

Then the line that turns the psalm: there is nothing hidden from its heat. You can shelter from the light but not from the warmth; it gets into everything. Hold that thought, because the next verse starts talking about the law of the LORD, and the connection is precisely this. The sun reaches everywhere in the sky's world; the word reaches everywhere in a man's.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 7–14 — The Law of the LORD Is Perfect
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Six lines on God's word: law, testimony, precepts, commandment, fear and rules — perfect, sure, right, pure, clean and true — reviving the soul, making the simple wise, rejoicing the heart, enlightening the eyes (vv. 7-9). It is better than fine gold and sweeter than honey, and it warns God's servant (vv. 10-11). Who can discern his errors? Clear me from hidden faults and keep me from presumptuous sins (vv. 12-13), and let the words of my mouth and the meditation of my heart be acceptable in your sight, O LORD, my rock and my redeemer (v. 14).
verseByVerse.theology: The sky shows God's glory; the word shows his will — and the man who has read both ends up asking to be cleared of sins he cannot even see.

verseByVerse.quote: The law of the LORD is perfect, reviving the soul; the testimony of the LORD is sure, making wise the simple; the precepts of the LORD are right, rejoicing the heart; the commandment of the LORD is pure, enlightening the eyes; the fear of the LORD is clean, enduring forever; the rules of the LORD are true, and righteous altogether.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The law of the LORD is perfect, reviving the soul; the testimony of the LORD is sure, making wise the simple; the precepts of the LORD are right, rejoicing the heart; the commandment of the LORD is pure, enlightening the eyes; the fear of the LORD is clean, enduring forever; the rules of the LORD are true, and righteous altogether.

Six lines built the same way: a name for God's word, a quality, and what it does to a person. Read them as six answers to "what will the Bible do to me?"

It revives the soul — literally brings a life back, the word used of reviving someone who has collapsed. It makes the simple wise: not the clever, the open — the person who knows he needs telling. It rejoices the heart, which cuts against the assumption that God's commands are a weight. It enlightens the eyes, the same phrase David used when he was at the end of his strength (13:3). It is clean and stays clean, when everything else is being revised. And it is true, and righteous altogether — no bad clauses hidden in the small print.

Put the six together and they describe a way of reading, not just a book. If you have been coming to Scripture mainly for information, notice that not one of the six effects is information. A man reads and something in him comes back to life; a slow learner gets wise; a heavy heart lifts; eyes that had stopped seeing start again. That is what to expect and what to ask for before you open it.

Notice too that the fifth line names the fear of the LORD as if it were one of God's writings. The reverence the word produces belongs on the same list as the word itself.

verseByVerse.quote: More to be desired are they than gold, even much fine gold; sweeter also than honey and drippings of the honeycomb. Moreover, by them is your servant warned; in keeping them there is great reward.
verseByVerse.commentary:
More to be desired are they than gold, even much fine gold; sweeter also than honey and drippings of the honeycomb. Moreover, by them is your servant warned; in keeping them there is great reward.

Gold and honey: the thing people work hardest to get and the sweetest thing they knew. Not more useful than gold, not more improving than honey — more to be desired, and sweeter. The claim is about appetite. That is a claim every reader can test on himself this week, and most of us discover we believe it in principle and live as though the gold were ahead by some distance.

Then two plain benefits, one negative and one positive. Warned: the word tells a man what is about to go wrong, which is the kindest thing a friend ever does. And in keeping them there is great reward — not a payment afterwards so much as a reward inside the obedience. Some of what God commands is its own wages.

verseByVerse.quote: Who can discern his errors? Declare me innocent from hidden faults. Keep back your servant also from presumptuous sins; let them not have dominion over me! Then I shall be blameless, and innocent of great transgression. Let the words of my mouth and the meditation of my heart be acceptable in your sight, O LORD, my rock and my redeemer.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Who can discern his errors? Declare me innocent from hidden faults. Keep back your servant also from presumptuous sins; let them not have dominion over me! Then I shall be blameless, and innocent of great transgression.

This is what the word does when it has been genuinely read: it drives a man to his knees about sins he is not even aware of. Three layers are named here, and they go from faint to fatal. Errors nobody can discern, including himself. Hidden faults — hidden from him, not from God, the habits everyone else can see and he cannot. And presumptuous sins, the ones done with the eyes open, which do not stay occasional: he asks that they not gain dominion, because deliberate sin always applies for the job of master.

The prayer for the first two is declare me innocent — a courtroom word; he cannot clean what he cannot find, so he asks for a verdict. The prayer for the third is keep back your servant; he does not trust himself with an open door. Anyone serious about holiness ends up praying both halves.

Let the words of my mouth and the meditation of my heart be acceptable in your sight, O LORD, my rock and my redeemer.

He has looked at the sky and read the law, and what he asks at the end is that his own speech and his private thinking would be accepted — the two things this psalm has been about, said outwardly and turned over inwardly, brought in as an offering. Acceptable is sacrificial language.

And the last word is the one the whole psalm has been earning: my redeemer. The word is the family rescuer, the relative with the right and the duty to buy his kinsman out of debt or slavery (Lev 25:25; Ruth 4), the one Job wanted when everything had gone (Job 19:25). A man who has just discovered that he has faults he cannot even see does not need a standard; he needs a relative who will pay. The heavens told him the glory. The law told him the trouble. The last two words tell him where to go.

20.title: Some Trust in Chariots
20.text: To the choirmaster. A Psalm of David. 1May the LORD answer you in the day of trouble! May the name of the God of Jacob protect you!2May he send you help from the sanctuary and give you support from Zion!3May he remember all your offerings and regard with favor your burnt sacrifices! Selah4May he grant you your heart's desire and fulfill all your plans!5May we shout for joy over your salvation, and in the name of our God set up our banners! May the LORD fulfill all your petitions!6Now I know that the LORD saves his anointed; he will answer him from his holy heaven with the saving might of his right hand.7Some trust in chariots and some in horses, but we trust in the name of the LORD our God.8They collapse and fall, but we rise and stand upright.9O LORD, save the king! May he answer us when we call.
20.overview: The congregation prays for the king on the day he goes out to fight: may the LORD answer him, may the name of the God of Jacob protect him, may help come from the sanctuary and support from Zion, may his offerings be remembered, his heart's desire granted and his plans fulfilled — and may they raise banners in God's name when the news comes (vv. 1-5). A single voice answers with certainty: the LORD saves his anointed (v. 6). Some trust in chariots and some in horses, but we trust in the name of the LORD our God. They collapse and fall, but we rise and stand upright (vv. 7-8). The people close: O LORD, save the king! May he answer us when we call (v. 9).
20.theology:
God is invoked as the God of Jacob (v. 1) — the God of a man who received what he could not claim — and the help is sought from the sanctuary on the basis of sacrifice already offered (vv. 2-3), not from the armoury.

Verse 7 is not a case against preparation; Israel still saddled the horse (Prov 21:31), but her kings were forbidden to accumulate them (Deut 17:16), because what an army owns becomes what it leans on. The test is what would remain if the chariots were gone. The promised outcome is not invulnerability but recovery: they fall, we rise (v. 8).

The prayer for the king becomes a prayer for everyone (v. 9), and the King it finally points to came on a donkey, with the war horse cut off (Zech 9:9-10), and was not saved from the day of trouble but carried through it.
20.examples:
A congregation praying hard for the one who carries the weight.

The God of Jacob: the name you choose when you cannot claim anything.

Help from the altar, not the armoury.

Banners chosen before the battle, and in whose name.

Fill in the blank: some trust in ...

Not "we are never knocked down" but "we rise".

Hosanna: save us, we pray — shouted at a King who would not save himself.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–5 — May the LORD Answer You
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: The congregation prays for the king going out to battle: May the LORD answer you in the day of trouble! May the name of the God of Jacob protect you! — help from the sanctuary, support from Zion, his offerings remembered, his heart's desire granted, and banners raised in God's name when the news comes back (vv. 1-5).
verseByVerse.theology: A whole people praying for one man, and asking for nothing but that God would act.

verseByVerse.quote: May the LORD answer you in the day of trouble! May the name of the God of Jacob protect you! May he send you help from the sanctuary and give you support from Zion! May he remember all your offerings and regard with favor your burnt sacrifices! Selah May he grant you your heart's desire and fulfill all your plans! May we shout for joy over your salvation, and in the name of our God set up our banners! May the LORD fulfill all your petitions!
verseByVerse.commentary:
May the LORD answer you in the day of trouble! May the name of the God of Jacob protect you! May he send you help from the sanctuary and give you support from Zion!

The king is going out to war and the congregation is praying for him — every line addressed to him, every request made to God about him. Before you look for yourself in this psalm, notice the shape of it: a people who have learned to pray hard for the one who carries the weight. Most churches have someone in that position this week.

They call God by an old name: the God of Jacob. Not Abraham the friend of God, not Isaac the promised son — Jacob, the schemer who got what he had no right to, and was carried anyway. It is a deliberate choice of name when you are asking for help you cannot claim to deserve.

And the help is asked for from the sanctuary ... from Zion: not from the armoury, from the altar. The next line makes the connection plain — May he remember all your offerings and regard with favor your burnt sacrifices! The king's standing with God on the battlefield rests on what has already been offered at the temple.

May he grant you your heart's desire and fulfill all your plans! May we shout for joy over your salvation, and in the name of our God set up our banners!

They are praying for a man they trust: they can ask God to fulfil his heart's desire and his plans, which is not a thing to pray for just anyone. And they are already planning the celebration — banners up, and in God's name rather than the king's. The victory has not happened and they have chosen whose flag will fly.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 6–9 — We Trust in the Name of the LORD
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Now I know that the LORD saves his anointed, answering from heaven with his right hand (v. 6). Some trust in chariots and some in horses, but we trust in the name of the LORD our God. They collapse and fall, but we rise and stand upright (vv. 7-8). O LORD, save the king! May he answer us when we call (v. 9).
verseByVerse.theology: The contrast is not between weapons and prayer but between what a nation finally leans on.

verseByVerse.quote: Now I know that the LORD saves his anointed; he will answer him from his holy heaven with the saving might of his right hand. Some trust in chariots and some in horses, but we trust in the name of the LORD our God. They collapse and fall, but we rise and stand upright.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Now I know that the LORD saves his anointed; he will answer him from his holy heaven with the saving might of his right hand.

One voice answers the congregation, and the tone changes from asking to certainty: now I know. Something settled it between verse 5 and verse 6 — a word from a priest, or the assurance God gives a praying people. It is a common enough experience: you begin praying for someone in fear and finish praying for them in confidence, with nothing new to report except that God has been asked.

Some trust in chariots and some in horses, but we trust in the name of the LORD our God. They collapse and fall, but we rise and stand upright.

Chariots were the tanks of the ancient world, and Israel's kings were told not to accumulate them: he must not acquire many horses for himself (Deut 17:16). The command was not against competence but against the thing armies do to the people who own them — they become what you lean on. Proverbs puts the balance exactly: The horse is made ready for the day of battle, but the victory belongs to the LORD (Prov 21:31). Israel still saddled the horse.

So the psalm is not praising unpreparedness. It is asking what a nation is finally resting on, and the test is what you would still have if the chariots were gone. Replace the word with whatever your generation counts: the portfolio, the insurance, the reputation, the second passport. Some trust in ... but we trust in the name of the LORD our God. Fill the gap honestly and the psalm has done its work.

And the outcome is put in two words each: They collapse and fall, but we rise and stand upright. Not "we never get knocked down" — we get up.

verseByVerse.quote: O LORD, save the king! May he answer us when we call.
verseByVerse.commentary:
O LORD, save the king! May he answer us when we call.

The congregation has the last word, and it is three syllables in Hebrew and a nation's whole request: save the king. Whole countries have prayed that sentence in one form or another ever since.

Then the door swings open: may he answer us when we call. The psalm began with prayer for one man and ends with prayer for everybody — the king's cause and the people's are the same cause, and the God who answers him answers them.

Which is where the psalm quietly reaches past David. Israel's anointed king rode out with horses he was told not to trust; the King this psalm was pointing to came into his capital humble, and mounted on a donkey, and the promise attached to him is that God will cut off the chariot from Ephraim and the war horse from Jerusalem (Zech 9:9-10). And the crowd that shouted for him to be saved — save us, we pray is what Hosanna means — watched him refuse to save himself. He was not rescued from the day of trouble. He went through it, which is how he saves the people who pray this psalm.

21.title: A Crown of Fine Gold
21.text: To the choirmaster. A Psalm of David. 1O LORD, in your strength the king rejoices, and in your salvation how greatly he exults!2You have given him his heart's desire and have not withheld the request of his lips. Selah3For you meet him with rich blessings; you set a crown of fine gold upon his head.4He asked life of you; you gave it to him, length of days forever and ever.5His glory is great through your salvation; splendor and majesty you bestow on him.6For you make him most blessed forever; you make him glad with the joy of your presence.7For the king trusts in the LORD, and through the steadfast love of the Most High he shall not be moved.8Your hand will find out all your enemies; your right hand will find out those who hate you.9You will make them as a blazing oven when you appear. The LORD will swallow them up in his wrath, and fire will consume them.10You will destroy their descendants from the earth, and their offspring from among the children of man.11Though they plan evil against you, though they devise mischief, they will not succeed.12For you will put them to flight; you will aim at their faces with your bows.13Be exalted, O LORD, in your strength! We will sing and praise your power.
21.overview: The answering half of Psalm 20. The king rejoices in God's strength: he has been given his heart's desire, met with rich blessings, crowned with fine gold, and granted the life he asked for — length of days forever and ever (vv. 1-4). Glory, splendour and majesty are God's gift, and the king is made glad with the joy of God's presence, because he trusts in the LORD and will not be moved (vv. 5-7). God's hand will find out every enemy; their plots will not succeed (vv. 8-12). The congregation ends by looking away from the king: Be exalted, O LORD, in your strength! (v. 13).
21.theology:
Psalms 20 and 21 are one movement: the request of 20:4 is answered in 21:2. Joy is aimed at God's strength and salvation rather than at the victory (v. 1), and the crown is placed by God's own hands (v. 3).

The best gift in the list is not the crown but the face: you make him glad with the joy of your presence (v. 6), and the reason for the whole psalm is trust, not competence (v. 7).

The judgment section belongs to God, whose search does not fail (vv. 8-12); Christians read it through the cross and the command to love enemies, which does not soften the fire but insists it is God's.

Length of days forever and ever (v. 4) outruns any king Israel had; the crown's journey runs through thorns (John 19:2) to glory and honour (Heb 2:9) and many diadems (Rev 19:12).
21.examples:
Psalm 20 asked for it; Psalm 21 says he got it.

Joy aimed at the strength that won, not the win.

God comes out to meet him, and crowns him himself.

Splendour and majesty: God's own wardrobe, lent.

How far down your list is his company?

Find out: a search that no hiding place survives.

The last verse looks away from the king.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–7 — You Have Given Him His Heart's Desire
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: O LORD, in your strength the king rejoices: God has given him his heart's desire, met him with rich blessings and set a crown of fine gold upon his head (vv. 1-3). He asked life of you; you gave it to him, length of days forever and ever; glory, splendour and majesty are God's gift, and the king is made glad with the joy of your presence (vv. 4-6), for the king trusts in the LORD (v. 7).
verseByVerse.theology: Everything the king has, he was given — and the best of it is not the crown but God's own company.

verseByVerse.quote: O LORD, in your strength the king rejoices, and in your salvation how greatly he exults! You have given him his heart's desire and have not withheld the request of his lips. Selah For you meet him with rich blessings; you set a crown of fine gold upon his head. He asked life of you; you gave it to him, length of days forever and ever.
verseByVerse.commentary:
O LORD, in your strength the king rejoices, and in your salvation how greatly he exults! You have given him his heart's desire and have not withheld the request of his lips.

Read this straight after Psalm 20 and you can hear the answer arriving. There the congregation prayed, may he grant you your heart's desire (20:4); here, You have given him his heart's desire. The two psalms are the prayer before the battle and the singing afterwards, and they are printed next to each other so that no reader misses which one produced the other.
