Notice where the joy is aimed. Not in his victory — in your strength, in your salvation. A man can win and still know exactly whose the win was. That is a harder discipline after a success than before one, and it is the difference between a thanksgiving and a boast.

For you meet him with rich blessings; you set a crown of fine gold upon his head. He asked life of you; you gave it to him, length of days forever and ever.

God meets him — comes out to him, the way a host comes out to greet someone arriving — and puts the crown on with his own hands. And then a line the psalm cannot quite spend on David: he asked to live, and was given length of days forever and ever. David asked God to spare his life in a war and was given a sentence that outruns any man's funeral. Israel sang words about her king that only one king would ever be able to hold.

verseByVerse.quote: His glory is great through your salvation; splendor and majesty you bestow on him. For you make him most blessed forever; you make him glad with the joy of your presence. For the king trusts in the LORD, and through the steadfast love of the Most High he shall not be moved.
verseByVerse.commentary:
His glory is great through your salvation; splendor and majesty you bestow on him. For you make him most blessed forever; you make him glad with the joy of your presence. For the king trusts in the LORD, and through the steadfast love of the Most High he shall not be moved.

Splendor and majesty are words the Psalter normally reserves for God himself; here he lends them to a man. That is what God does with people he honours — not diminishing himself, but dressing his servant in his own wardrobe. The ESV notes verse 6 can be read "you make him a source of blessing forever", which is the Abraham promise: blessed, in order to be a blessing.

And then the best line of the psalm, tucked in among the gifts: you make him glad with the joy of your presence. Crown, glory, splendour, long life — and the gladness comes from God's face. Strip the rest away and that one remains; give the rest without it and the man is furnished and miserable. Every reader can run the test on himself: of everything you are hoping God will give you, how far down the list is his company?

Verse 7 gives the reason for all of it, and it is not the king's competence: for the king trusts in the LORD. Psalm 20 said it as a creed before the battle; Psalm 21 records it as the explanation afterwards. He will not be moved, and what holds him is the steadfast love of the Most High, not his own grip.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: God's hand will find out all his enemies; they will be a blazing oven, swallowed in wrath, their line cut off, their plots unable to succeed, put to flight by the bow (vv. 8-12). Be exalted, O LORD, in your strength! We will sing and praise your power (v. 13).
verseByVerse.theology: The psalm of the king's success ends by taking the congregation's eyes off the king.

verseByVerse.quote: Your hand will find out all your enemies; your right hand will find out those who hate you. You will make them as a blazing oven when you appear. The LORD will swallow them up in his wrath, and fire will consume them. You will destroy their descendants from the earth, and their offspring from among the children of man. Though they plan evil against you, though they devise mischief, they will not succeed. For you will put them to flight; you will aim at their faces with your bows.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Your hand will find out all your enemies; your right hand will find out those who hate you. You will make them as a blazing oven when you appear ... You will destroy their descendants from the earth ... Though they plan evil against you, though they devise mischief, they will not succeed.

Five hard verses, and they are addressed to a you — either to the king, whose hand acts for God's, or to God himself; the psalm is content to let the two blur, because the king's war was God's war. Find out is the picture of a search that does not fail: no hiding place holds. The blazing oven and the fire belong to the final judgment, not to a border skirmish.

The hardest line is verse 10, the cutting off of descendants — a sentence on a dynasty rather than a man. It is the language of ending a house that lives by evil, and it is spoken about people who plan evil and devise mischief as a policy. The psalm does not gloat; it states that such plotting will not succeed, which is something to hold on to when you are on the receiving end of it and it is succeeding beautifully this month.

Christians pray these verses through the cross, where the plot did succeed for a Friday and was reversed, and with Jesus' own instruction to love enemies and leave judgment to God. That is not a softening of the psalm. It is an insistence that the fire in it belongs to God and not to us.

verseByVerse.quote: Be exalted, O LORD, in your strength! We will sing and praise your power.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Be exalted, O LORD, in your strength! We will sing and praise your power.

The psalm has spent twelve verses on the king and gives its last one to God. Be exalted, not "long live the king" — the congregation turns its eyes off the man it has been celebrating. Any song about a leader that cannot end like this has become something else.

And the crown in verse 3 has not finished its journey. The New Testament says of Jesus that he was crowned with glory and honor because of the suffering of death (Heb 2:9), and that the rider on the white horse has many diadems (Rev 19:12). Between those two, soldiers twisted together a crown of thorns and put it on his head (John 19:2). The king of Psalm 21 asked life and was given length of days forever; the King this psalm was waiting for was given death first, and rose to hold the promise for everyone who trusts him.

22.title: Why Have You Forsaken Me?
22.text: To the choirmaster: according to The Doe of the Dawn. A Psalm of David. 1My God, my God, why have you forsaken me? Why are you so far from saving me, from the words of my groaning?2O my God, I cry by day, but you do not answer, and by night, but I find no rest.3Yet you are holy, enthroned on the praises of Israel.4In you our fathers trusted; they trusted, and you delivered them.5To you they cried and were rescued; in you they trusted and were not put to shame.6But I am a worm and not a man, scorned by mankind and despised by the people.7All who see me mock me; they make mouths at me; they wag their heads;8"He trusts in the LORD; let him deliver him; let him rescue him, for he delights in him!"9Yet you are he who took me from the womb; you made me trust you at my mother's breasts.10On you was I cast from my birth, and from my mother's womb you have been my God.11Be not far from me, for trouble is near, and there is none to help.12Many bulls encompass me; strong bulls of Bashan surround me;13they open wide their mouths at me, like a ravening and roaring lion.14I am poured out like water, and all my bones are out of joint; my heart is like wax; it is melted within my breast;15my strength is dried up like a potsherd, and my tongue sticks to my jaws; you lay me in the dust of death.16For dogs encompass me; a company of evildoers encircles me; they have pierced my hands and feet —17I can count all my bones— they stare and gloat over me;18they divide my garments among them, and for my clothing they cast lots.19But you, O LORD, do not be far off! O you my help, come quickly to my aid!20Deliver my soul from the sword, my precious life from the power of the dog!21Save me from the mouth of the lion! You have rescued me from the horns of the wild oxen!22I will tell of your name to my brothers; in the midst of the congregation I will praise you:23You who fear the LORD, praise him! All you offspring of Jacob, glorify him, and stand in awe of him, all you offspring of Israel!24For he has not despised or abhorred the affliction of the afflicted, and he has not hidden his face from him, but has heard, when he cried to him.25From you comes my praise in the great congregation; my vows I will perform before those who fear him.26The afflicted shall eat and be satisfied; those who seek him shall praise the LORD! May your hearts live forever!27All the ends of the earth shall remember and turn to the LORD, and all the families of the nations shall worship before you.28For kingship belongs to the LORD, and he rules over the nations.29All the prosperous of the earth eat and worship; before him shall bow all who go down to the dust, even the one who could not keep himself alive.30Posterity shall serve him; it shall be told of the Lord to the coming generation;31they shall come and proclaim his righteousness to a people yet unborn, that he has done it.
22.overview: A sufferer cries the words Jesus would use from the cross: My God, my God, why have you forsaken me? — unanswered by day and by night (vv. 1-2). Yet God is holy and the fathers who trusted were rescued (vv. 3-5). He is a worm, mocked by everyone, his own faith thrown back at him (vv. 6-8); yet God has held him since the womb (vv. 9-11). Bulls, lions and dogs surround him; he is poured out, his bones out of joint, his tongue stuck to his jaws, laid in the dust of death; his hands and feet are pierced and his clothes gambled for (vv. 12-18). He begs for rescue — and mid-sentence the answer comes (vv. 19-21). The rest is praise: he tells God's name to his brothers in the congregation, the afflicted eat and are satisfied, the ends of the earth turn to the LORD, the dying bow, and a people yet unborn are told that he has done it (vv. 22-31).
22.theology:
The loudest complaint in Scripture is made inside faith: my God, twice (v. 1). Three times the psalm answers itself with yet — God's holiness (v. 3), the fathers' rescue (vv. 4-5), and God's hold on him since birth (vv. 9-10).

The New Testament treats this psalm as written about Christ, and the details are not vague: the cry (Matt 27:46), the head-wagging and the taunt (Matt 27:39-43), the thirst (John 19:28), the gambling for his clothes (John 19:24). At v. 16 the ESV's note records the textual division honestly; the case does not rest on it.

The answer arrives inside a sentence with nothing narrated (v. 21), and the psalm's verdict on its own opening is that God has not hidden his face (v. 24) — which interprets the abandonment rather than cancelling it.

The risen sufferer leads the church's praise (v. 22; Heb 2:11-12), and the fruit of his suffering is the conversion of the nations, the worship of the dying, and a finished work proclaimed to the unborn (vv. 27-31; cf. John 19:30).
22.examples:
Jesus reached for this psalm, which means he had all of it in mind.

Day without answer, night without rest — and darkness from noon to three.

Mockers quoting verse 8 without knowing their lines.

God as midwife: trust taught before speech.

Bulls of Bashan: well-fed men enjoying themselves at your expense.

Soldiers throwing dice for a shirt, a thousand years early.

The rescue that arrives mid-sentence.

The last three words, and the last three words from the cross.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: My God, my God, why have you forsaken me? He cries day and night and is not answered (vv. 1-2). Yet you are holy: the fathers trusted and were rescued (vv. 3-5). But I am a worm and not a man, mocked by everyone: He trusts in the LORD; let him deliver him (vv. 6-8). Yet you are he who took me from the womb — so do not be far off, for trouble is near and no one helps (vv. 9-11).
verseByVerse.theology: Faith argues with God out of the dark: the fathers were heard, I was made yours from birth, and yet here I am.

verseByVerse.quote: My God, my God, why have you forsaken me? Why are you so far from saving me, from the words of my groaning? O my God, I cry by day, but you do not answer, and by night, but I find no rest. Yet you are holy, enthroned on the praises of Israel. In you our fathers trusted; they trusted, and you delivered them. To you they cried and were rescued; in you they trusted and were not put to shame.
verseByVerse.commentary:
My God, my God, why have you forsaken me? Why are you so far from saving me, from the words of my groaning? O my God, I cry by day, but you do not answer, and by night, but I find no rest.

These are the words Jesus said from the cross, in his own language, about three in the afternoon (Matt 27:46; Mark 15:34). He did not compose them; he reached for this psalm, which means the whole of it was in his mind while he hung there. Read every verse that follows knowing whose lips they reached.

Notice what the cry is not. It is not God, why have you forsaken me — it is my God, twice. The relationship is being appealed to at the very moment it seems to have failed. This is the loudest complaint in the Bible and it is made inside faith, not outside it.

And notice the two halves of verse 2: by day, no answer; by night, no rest. On the day it was fulfilled, darkness came over the land from noon until three, so that the day itself turned to night while he hung there.

Yet you are holy, enthroned on the praises of Israel. In you our fathers trusted; they trusted, and you delivered them. To you they cried and were rescued; in you they trusted and were not put to shame.

The first yet. He does not resolve the contradiction; he holds both ends. You are holy — the ESV notes the line may read that God is "dwelling in the praises" of his people, at home among their worship. And then the history: three times in two verses, they trusted, and every time it worked. Which makes his position worse, not better. The fathers cried and were rescued; I cry and am not. Faith that knows the track record feels the silence more sharply, not less.

verseByVerse.quote: But I am a worm and not a man, scorned by mankind and despised by the people. All who see me mock me; they make mouths at me; they wag their heads; "He trusts in the LORD; let him deliver him; let him rescue him, for he delights in him!" Yet you are he who took me from the womb; you made me trust you at my mother's breasts. On you was I cast from my birth, and from my mother's womb you have been my God. Be not far from me, for trouble is near, and there is none to help.
verseByVerse.commentary:
But I am a worm and not a man, scorned by mankind and despised by the people. All who see me mock me; they make mouths at me; they wag their heads: He trusts in the LORD; let him deliver him; let him rescue him, for he delights in him!

A worm and not a man: something you step on without noticing. That is how he describes himself, and the crowd confirms it — pulling faces, shaking their heads, and then the cruellest stroke of all, throwing his own faith at him as a joke.

Stand at Golgotha and listen: those who passed by derided him, wagging their heads ... He trusts in God; let God deliver him now, if he desires him (Matt 27:39, 43). The mockery at the cross did not merely resemble this psalm; it quoted it, from people who did not know they were reading their lines. There is no stronger evidence that this psalm was written about someone in particular.

Yet you are he who took me from the womb; you made me trust you at my mother's breasts. On you was I cast from my birth, and from my mother's womb you have been my God.

The second yet, and it reaches back further than the fathers — to his own first minutes. The God who seems absent now is the one who acted as midwife, who taught a baby to trust before the baby could speak. When a believer cannot see God today, this is the direction to look: not at the present evidence but at the record of who has been holding him since before he can remember.

Be not far from me, for trouble is near, and there is none to help. The whole prayer in one line. Near and far are the psalm's words: trouble near, God far, nobody in between.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 12–21 — They Have Pierced My Hands and Feet
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Bulls, a roaring lion and dogs close in (vv. 12-13, 16). He is poured out like water, his bones out of joint, his heart melted, his strength dried up, his tongue stuck to his jaws, laid in the dust of death (vv. 14-15). They have pierced my hands and feet ... they divide my garments among them, and for my clothing they cast lots (vv. 16-18). But you, O LORD, do not be far off! — and the last line of v. 21 turns: You have rescued me (vv. 19-21).
verseByVerse.theology: The suffering is described from inside, and the answer arrives in the middle of a sentence.

verseByVerse.quote: Many bulls encompass me; strong bulls of Bashan surround me; they open wide their mouths at me, like a ravening and roaring lion. I am poured out like water, and all my bones are out of joint; my heart is like wax; it is melted within my breast; my strength is dried up like a potsherd, and my tongue sticks to my jaws; you lay me in the dust of death. For dogs encompass me; a company of evildoers encircles me; they have pierced my hands and feet — I can count all my bones— they stare and gloat over me; they divide my garments among them, and for my clothing they cast lots.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Many bulls encompass me; strong bulls of Bashan surround me; they open wide their mouths at me, like a ravening and roaring lion.

The enemies come as animals, and the choice of animal is precise. Bashan, east of the Jordan, was famous cattle country: these are the prize beasts, heavy and well fed, which is a good description of powerful men enjoying themselves at someone's expense.

I am poured out like water, and all my bones are out of joint; my heart is like wax; it is melted within my breast; my strength is dried up like a potsherd, and my tongue sticks to my jaws; you lay me in the dust of death.

Now the body, described from inside. Poured out and unable to hold shape; joints pulled apart; the heart gone to wax; strength baked dry like a piece of broken pottery; the tongue stuck to the roof of the mouth. Anyone who has read a description of death by crucifixion will recognise the list, written centuries before the Romans invented the method. And at the cross, John says, Jesus, knowing that all was now finished, said (to fulfill the Scripture), I thirst (John 19:28).

For dogs encompass me; a company of evildoers encircles me; they have pierced my hands and feet — I can count all my bones — they stare and gloat over me; they divide my garments among them, and for my clothing they cast lots.

I can count all my bones — they stare and gloat over me. Two horrors in one line. He is so wasted that the ribs stand out and could be counted, and there is an audience doing the counting. Public execution was entertainment in the ancient world, as it has been in most centuries; people brought their lunch. The psalm records not only pain but the humiliation of being looked at while in pain, which anyone who has been ill in public understands in a smaller way.

Verse 16 has a textual question and it should be stated plainly rather than smoothed over. The ESV notes that they have pierced my hands and feet follows some Hebrew manuscripts together with the ancient Greek, Latin and Syriac versions, while most Hebrew manuscripts read something like "like a lion, my hands and feet". The reading the ESV prints is old and well attested — the Greek translation was made long before the crucifixion — but a Christian does not need to win the argument to preach the psalm. Even on the other reading, the hands and feet are the point, and the next lines stand on their own.

Because verse 18 needs no textual defence at all: they divide my garments among them, and for my clothing they cast lots. John watched soldiers do exactly that, split the clothes four ways and gamble for the seamless tunic, and wrote: This was to fulfill the Scripture (John 19:24). A thousand years early, a dying man described soldiers throwing dice for his shirt.

verseByVerse.quote: But you, O LORD, do not be far off! O you my help, come quickly to my aid! Deliver my soul from the sword, my precious life from the power of the dog! Save me from the mouth of the lion! You have rescued me from the horns of the wild oxen!
verseByVerse.commentary:
But you, O LORD, do not be far off! O you my help, come quickly to my aid! Deliver my soul from the sword, my precious life from the power of the dog! Save me from the mouth of the lion! You have rescued me from the horns of the wild oxen!

The third but you, and then the most extraordinary line break in the Psalter. He is still asking — sword, dog, lion — and in the middle of the last sentence the tense changes. Save me from the mouth of the lion! and then, without a pause: You have rescued me. The ESV notes the Hebrew is literally you have answered me.

And there is a mercy here for anyone praying in the dark tonight. Because Jesus prayed this psalm first, no believer prays verse 1 alone or unheard. He went into real forsakenness — the thing itself, not the feeling of it — so that the promise to everyone who is his can be I will never leave you nor forsake you (Heb 13:5). What you may feel is abandonment; what is true is that the abandonment was spent on him.

The answer arrives inside the sentence. Nothing is narrated — no rescue is described, no enemy is driven off. One moment he is begging and the next he is thanking, and everything after verse 21 is praise. Whatever happened in that gap is what the whole second half of the psalm is about, and any believer who has prayed through a long night knows that the change can come exactly like that: mid-sentence, with nothing to point to.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 22–31 — They Shall Proclaim His Righteousness
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: I will tell of your name to my brothers; in the midst of the congregation I will praise you (v. 22). God has not despised or abhorred the affliction of the afflicted (vv. 23-24). The afflicted will eat and be satisfied (vv. 25-26); all the ends of the earth shall remember and turn to the LORD, the dying will bow, and a people yet unborn will be told that he has done it (vv. 27-31).
verseByVerse.theology: The psalm turns from one man's agony to the whole world's worship, and ends on a finished work.

verseByVerse.quote: I will tell of your name to my brothers; in the midst of the congregation I will praise you: You who fear the LORD, praise him! All you offspring of Jacob, glorify him, and stand in awe of him, all you offspring of Israel! For he has not despised or abhorred the affliction of the afflicted, and he has not hidden his face from him, but has heard, when he cried to him. From you comes my praise in the great congregation; my vows I will perform before those who fear him. The afflicted shall eat and be satisfied; those who seek him shall praise the LORD! May your hearts live forever!
verseByVerse.commentary:
I will tell of your name to my brothers; in the midst of the congregation I will praise you.

The first thing the rescued man does is gather a congregation. And Hebrews puts this verse in the mouth of Jesus, as proof that he is not ashamed of us: he is not ashamed to call them brothers, saying, I will tell of your name to my brothers; in the midst of the congregation I will sing your praise (Heb 2:11-12). The one who went through verses 1-18 stands in the middle of the church and leads the singing. That is what the risen Christ is doing in every gathering of his people.

For he has not despised or abhorred the affliction of the afflicted, and he has not hidden his face from him, but has heard, when he cried to him.

Here is the psalm's verdict on its own first line. It began, why have you forsaken me?; it now says God has not hidden his face. Both are in the same poem, and the second does not cancel the first. It interprets it. What felt like abandonment was not contempt, and the cry that seemed to go nowhere had been heard the whole time.

Take verse 24 slowly if you have ever suspected that God finds your trouble distasteful. Three negatives: he has not despised it, has not abhorred it, has not hidden his face from it. God is not embarrassed by the afflicted, does not find weakness disgusting, and does not look away. And the positive at the end is the whole of it: but has heard, when he cried to him.

The afflicted shall eat and be satisfied — the ESV notes the word may be the meek — and his vows are paid in public, which in Israel meant a meal shared with the poor. The man who was starving in verse 15 is hosting dinner.

verseByVerse.quote: All the ends of the earth shall remember and turn to the LORD, and all the families of the nations shall worship before you. For kingship belongs to the LORD, and he rules over the nations. All the prosperous of the earth eat and worship; before him shall bow all who go down to the dust, even the one who could not keep himself alive. Posterity shall serve him; it shall be told of the Lord to the coming generation; they shall come and proclaim his righteousness to a people yet unborn, that he has done it.
verseByVerse.commentary:
All the ends of the earth shall remember and turn to the LORD, and all the families of the nations shall worship before you. For kingship belongs to the LORD, and he rules over the nations.

The psalm now goes as wide as the world. One man's private agony becomes the reason the nations come home, which is a leap no ordinary sufferer's psalm could make and exactly what the cross did. The ends of the earth remember: they had known once and forgotten.

All the prosperous of the earth eat and worship; before him shall bow all who go down to the dust, even the one who could not keep himself alive. Posterity shall serve him; it shall be told of the Lord to the coming generation.

Three groups, and between them there is nobody left out: the prosperous, the dying, and the not yet born. The one who could not keep himself alive is every human being in the end, and even he bows — which in this psalm is not defeat but worship, because the singer himself has been through the dust of death in verse 15 and is standing here.

They shall come and proclaim his righteousness to a people yet unborn, that he has done it.

Three words end the psalm: he has done it. Not "he will", not "he is working on it". The verb is finished. A man who began by asking why God had abandoned him signs off with the announcement that the work is complete, and the news is to be carried to people who do not exist yet — which includes everyone reading this.

On the cross, at the end, Jesus said, It is finished, and he bowed his head and gave up his spirit (John 19:30). He had begun with the psalm's first line. He ended where the psalm ends.

23.title: The LORD Is My Shepherd
23.text: A Psalm of David. 1The LORD is my shepherd; I shall not want.2He makes me lie down in green pastures. He leads me beside still waters.3He restores my soul. He leads me in paths of righteousness for his name's sake.4Even though I walk through the valley of the shadow of death, I will fear no evil, for you are with me; your rod and your staff, they comfort me.5You prepare a table before me in the presence of my enemies; you anoint my head with oil; my cup overflows.6Surely goodness and mercy shall follow me all the days of my life, and I shall dwell in the house of the LORD forever.
23.overview: A shepherd's psalm by a man who had been one. The LORD is his shepherd, so he lacks nothing he needs: he is made to lie down in green pasture, led beside quiet water, restored, and kept on right paths for the sake of the shepherd's own name (vv. 1-3). In the valley of deep darkness the psalm changes from speaking about God to speaking to him: you are with me; your rod and your staff, they comfort me (v. 4). Then the field becomes a house: a table set in front of the enemies, oil on the head, a cup filled past the brim (v. 5), goodness and steadfast love in pursuit all his days, and a home in the house of the LORD (v. 6).
23.theology:
I shall not want promises sufficiency, not everything wanted (v. 1), and the rest is administered — he makes me lie down (v. 2). The guarantee of arrival is God's reputation, for his name's sake (v. 3), not the sheep's worth.

The pronoun turns from he to you in the valley (v. 4): darkness is where speech about God becomes speech to him. The sufferer walks through; rod and staff answer both the predator outside and the sheep's own folly.

Enemies are present and not removed while God hosts a meal (v. 5); the cup overflows because the host is lavish. Goodness and steadfast love pursue the believer through the bad days too (v. 6).

Printed after Psalm 22, the pasture lies beyond the dust of death. The shepherd here is the one who lays down his life for the sheep (John 10:11; cf. Ezek 34:11-12; Isa 40:11), and at the last the Lamb is the shepherd (Rev 7:17).
23.examples:
Written by a man who had done the job, about animals that drown standing in rivers.

A lying-down flock is a report on the shepherd.

Waters of rest: sheep will not drink from a fast stream.

The pronoun that changes in the valley.

Rod for the wolves, staff for the sheep's own stupidity.

The enemies are not removed; they are made to watch a meal.

Goodness and mercy as pursuers.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–4 — Even Though I Walk Through the Valley
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: The LORD is my shepherd; I shall not want. He makes his sheep lie down in green pastures, leads them beside still waters, restores the soul and leads in paths of righteousness for his name's sake (vv. 1-3). Even though I walk through the valley of the shadow of death, I will fear no evil, for you are with me; your rod and your staff, they comfort me (v. 4).
verseByVerse.theology: Three verses about him, and then, in the valley, the psalm starts speaking to him.

verseByVerse.quote: The LORD is my shepherd; I shall not want. He makes me lie down in green pastures. He leads me beside still waters. He restores my soul. He leads me in paths of righteousness for his name's sake.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The LORD is my shepherd; I shall not want.

It is the best known sentence in the Old Testament, and it was written by a man who had done the job. David knew what a shepherd's day was: the walking, the counting, the carrying, the nights out with the flock. He also knew what sheep are — not gentle and wise, but nervous, short-sighted animals that will walk off a ledge or stand in a river and drown.

I shall not want does not mean he gets everything he wants. It means he will not lack what he needs, which is a different promise and a better one. The psalm was written by a man with enemies at his table in verse 5.

He makes me lie down in green pastures. He leads me beside still waters. He restores my soul.

He makes me: sheep do not lie down while they are frightened or hungry, so a lying-down flock is a report on the shepherd. The ESV notes the second line is literally "beside waters of rest"; running water frightens sheep and they will not drink from it. Everything here is arranged for an animal that cannot arrange anything for itself.

And that is the quiet mercy in the verb: some of us are only made to rest. The shepherd knows when the flock has been driven long enough, and stops it, and that stopping is care rather than waste.

He leads me in paths of righteousness for his name's sake. The ESV notes it can be read in right paths — the tracks that actually get somewhere, rather than the ones the sheep would choose. And the reason given is not the sheep's value: for his name's sake. A shepherd who lost half his flock would be shamed in the village. God's reputation is bound up with getting his people home, which is the strongest guarantee anyone could be given.

verseByVerse.quote: Even though I walk through the valley of the shadow of death, I will fear no evil, for you are with me; your rod and your staff, they comfort me.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Even though I walk through the valley of the shadow of death, I will fear no evil, for you are with me; your rod and your staff, they comfort me.

Something happens in this verse that changes the whole psalm, and it is easy to miss: the pronoun. For three verses God has been he — he makes, he leads, he restores. In the valley he becomes you. The psalm stops talking about God and starts talking to him at precisely the point where the light goes.

Say that to anyone in the valley now: the darkness is not where faith goes quiet. It is very often where third-person religion turns into first-hand prayer.

Notice too that he walks through. Not camps in, not settles — through. The ESV notes the phrase may be rendered "the valley of deep darkness", which covers more than dying: depression, disgrace, a diagnosis, the months after a bereavement. And the comfort is not that the valley is short but that it has an exit, and that he is not walking it alone.

The rod is the club a shepherd carried against wolves and lions; the staff is the crook for hooking a sheep out of a hole. One is for enemies, the other for the sheep's own stupidity, and both are comforting to an animal that is threatened from outside and prone to fall in holes. The Christian needs exactly these two.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: You prepare a table before me in the presence of my enemies; you anoint my head with oil; my cup overflows (v. 5). Surely goodness and mercy shall follow me all the days of my life, and I shall dwell in the house of the LORD forever (v. 6).
verseByVerse.theology: The pasture becomes a house, the sheep becomes a guest, and the pursuit that follows him is kindness.

verseByVerse.quote: You prepare a table before me in the presence of my enemies; you anoint my head with oil; my cup overflows. Surely goodness and mercy shall follow me all the days of my life, and I shall dwell in the house of the LORD forever.
verseByVerse.commentary:
You prepare a table before me in the presence of my enemies; you anoint my head with oil; my cup overflows.

The picture changes from field to house. He is no longer a sheep but a guest, and the host is setting a table while the enemies stand there and watch. The enemies are not destroyed in this verse, and they are not asked to leave. They are made to watch a meal.

Oil on the head was the ordinary courtesy of a good host, the thing Jesus noted was missing when Simon the Pharisee received him. And my cup overflows is not measured hospitality: the host keeps pouring after the cup is full, which is what people do when they are enjoying themselves. God is not a careful provider; he is a lavish one.

Surely goodness and mercy shall follow me all the days of my life, and I shall dwell in the house of the LORD forever.

Follow is a strong verb — pursue, chase, hunt down. All his life he has been followed by enemies; now he says two other things are on his trail, and they are God's goodness and God's steadfast love (the ESV notes that second word). They are not trailing behind him at a polite distance. They are after him, and they will catch him.

All the days of my life includes the bad ones. The psalm has already been through the valley and past the enemies; nothing here is sheltered. And the ESV notes the last line can be read "shall return to dwell", and that forever is literally for length of days. The sheep ends up living in the house.

Read the psalm in the place the Bible prints it, immediately after Psalm 22, and one more thing becomes clear. The green pastures come after the dust of death; the table is spread on the far side of he has done it. The shepherd of this psalm said, I am the good shepherd. The good shepherd lays down his life for the sheep (John 10:11) — which is what no shepherd would ever do, since the whole point of a shepherd is that he is worth more than the sheep. And at the end of the Bible the arrangement is stated in the only way it could finally be put: the Lamb in the midst of the throne will be their shepherd (Rev 7:17).

24.text: A Psalm of David. 1The earth is the LORD's and the fullness thereof, the world and those who dwell therein,2for he has founded it upon the seas and established it upon the rivers.3Who shall ascend the hill of the LORD? And who shall stand in his holy place?4He who has clean hands and a pure heart, who does not lift up his soul to what is false and does not swear deceitfully.5He will receive blessing from the LORD and righteousness from the God of his salvation.6Such is the generation of those who seek him, who seek the face of the God of Jacob. Selah7Lift up your heads, O gates! And be lifted up, O ancient doors, that the King of glory may come in.8Who is this King of glory? The LORD, strong and mighty, the LORD, mighty in battle!9Lift up your heads, O gates! And lift them up, O ancient doors, that the King of glory may come in.10Who is this King of glory? The LORD of hosts, he is the King of glory! Selah

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–6 — Who Shall Ascend the Hill of the LORD?
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: The earth is the LORD's and the fullness thereof, founded on the seas (vv. 1-2). Who shall ascend the hill of the LORD? And who shall stand in his holy place? He who has clean hands and a pure heart, who does not lift up his soul to what is false and does not swear deceitfully (vv. 3-4). Such a man receives blessing and righteousness from God; such is the generation of those who seek him (vv. 5-6).
verseByVerse.theology: The whole earth is his, and the question is who may come up the hill — answered by four marks, two of them invisible.

verseByVerse.quote: The earth is the LORD's and the fullness thereof, the world and those who dwell therein, for he has founded it upon the seas and established it upon the rivers.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The earth is the LORD's and the fullness thereof, the world and those who dwell therein, for he has founded it upon the seas and established it upon the rivers.

The psalm begins as wide as it can: the planet, everything in it, and everyone on it. Ownership by right of making. The ESV notes the first line may be read "and all that fills it" — the contents as well as the container.

Paul settled a live church argument with this verse. Christians in Corinth were worried about meat that might have been offered to idols, and he told them to eat what was set in front of them without raising questions, For the earth is the Lord's, and the fullness thereof (1 Cor 10:26). If it is all God's, no piece of it is the devil's to spoil. That is an argument for a free conscience in a world full of things with murky histories.

Founded it upon the seas is picture language, not plumbing: the dry land set above the chaos of water, as in Genesis 1. The world is stable because he holds it there, not because the seas have agreed to behave.

verseByVerse.quote: Who shall ascend the hill of the LORD? And who shall stand in his holy place? He who has clean hands and a pure heart, who does not lift up his soul to what is false and does not swear deceitfully. He will receive blessing from the LORD and righteousness from the God of his salvation. Such is the generation of those who seek him, who seek the face of the God of Jacob. Selah
verseByVerse.commentary:
Who shall ascend the hill of the LORD? And who shall stand in his holy place? He who has clean hands and a pure heart, who does not lift up his soul to what is false and does not swear deceitfully.

The question at the gate again, as in Psalm 15, and this time the answer is four marks instead of eleven. Two of them are visible and two are not. Clean hands: what he has done. A pure heart: what he has wanted — and no gatekeeper on earth can check that one, which is the point of putting it in an entrance liturgy.

Does not lift up his soul to what is false covers the whole of idolatry in one phrase: lifting your inner life up towards something that is not there. And does not swear deceitfully is the same failure in speech — words used to create an impression rather than to tell the truth.

He will receive blessing from the LORD and righteousness from the God of his salvation. Such is the generation of those who seek him, who seek the face of the God of Jacob.

Then the give-away: the righteousness is received, not produced. The man who comes up the hill with clean hands is given the very thing the list required. That is not a contradiction; it is the gospel's shape showing through the Old Testament — what God demands, God supplies.

And the whole class of such people is called the generation of those who seek him. The ESV notes a textual difference in the last phrase: most Hebrew manuscripts read "who seek your face, Jacob", while the ESV follows the Greek and Syriac and two Hebrew manuscripts. Either way they are marked out as seekers, not arrivers. Jesus made the same promise to the same people: Blessed are the pure in heart, for they shall see God (Matt 5:8).

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 7–10 — Lift Up Your Heads, O Gates
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Lift up your heads, O gates! And be lifted up, O ancient doors, that the King of glory may come in. The challenge comes back twice — Who is this King of glory? — and is answered twice: The LORD, strong and mighty, the LORD, mighty in battle, and The LORD of hosts, he is the King of glory! (vv. 7-10).
verseByVerse.theology: The second half reverses the first: not who may go up to God, but who is coming in.

verseByVerse.quote: Lift up your heads, O gates! And be lifted up, O ancient doors, that the King of glory may come in. Who is this King of glory? The LORD, strong and mighty, the LORD, mighty in battle! Lift up your heads, O gates! And lift them up, O ancient doors, that the King of glory may come in. Who is this King of glory? The LORD of hosts, he is the King of glory! Selah
verseByVerse.commentary:
Lift up your heads, O gates! And be lifted up, O ancient doors, that the King of glory may come in. Who is this King of glory? The LORD, strong and mighty, the LORD, mighty in battle!

Now the direction reverses. The first half asked who may come up to God; the second announces that God is coming in, and the city gates are told to make themselves taller to let him through. It is the language of a procession, most likely the ark coming up to Jerusalem while David danced in front of it (2 Sam 6), sung antiphonally: one group outside calling, another inside challenging, Who is this King of glory?

The question is asked twice and answered twice, and the answers are military. Strong and mighty ... mighty in battle, and then the title that closes the psalm: the LORD of hosts, the LORD of armies. This is not a decorative king arriving for a ceremony. He has been fighting, and he has won.

Lift up your heads, O gates! ... Who is this King of glory? The LORD of hosts, he is the King of glory!

The church has always sung this psalm at Advent and at Ascension, and for good reason. The King who came into Jerusalem the second time came on a donkey, through gates that did not need raising, to be executed outside them. He went out of the city carrying a cross and came back through death, and the announcement of what he is at the end of the Bible uses this psalm's vocabulary: the rider called Faithful and True, who judges and makes war (Rev 19:11).

And there is a door in front of every reader of this psalm. It was asked twice, so ask it twice. Who is this King of glory? The gates of a city can be told to lift their heads; a human life has to open its own.

24.title: Who Is This King of Glory?
24.overview: The earth and everything in it belongs to the LORD, who founded it above the seas (vv. 1-2). Then the question at the gate: who may go up the hill and stand in the holy place? The one with clean hands and a pure heart, who does not lift his soul to what is false or swear deceitfully — and what he receives is blessing and righteousness from God (vv. 3-6). Then the direction reverses: Lift up your heads, O gates! ... that the King of glory may come in. Twice the challenge comes back, Who is this King of glory?, and twice the answer: the LORD strong and mighty, mighty in battle; the LORD of hosts (vv. 7-10).
24.theology:
God owns the world by right of making it (v. 1), which Paul uses to free a Christian conscience about food with a murky history (1 Cor 10:26).

The entrance liturgy (vv. 3-4; cf. Ps 15) requires two visible marks and two invisible ones — a pure heart cannot be checked at any gate — and then gives away the secret: the righteousness required is received from God (v. 5). What God demands, God supplies.

The second half reverses the movement: the gates are told to make room for the King who is coming in (vv. 7-10), and the answer to the challenge is military — he has been fighting and has won. Sung at the ark's ascent (2 Sam 6), it points to the King who entered Jerusalem to be executed and came back through death (cf. Rev 19:11).
24.examples:
Ownership by right of making — and a free conscience at dinner.

Dry land set above the chaos, and held there.

Two marks a gatekeeper can check, two he cannot.

Idolatry defined: lifting your soul to what is not there.

The righteousness is received, not produced.

Gates told to stand taller.

The question asked twice, and a door in front of the reader.

25.text: Of David. 1To you, O LORD, I lift up my soul.2O my God, in you I trust; let me not be put to shame; let not my enemies exult over me.3Indeed, none who wait for you shall be put to shame; they shall be ashamed who are wantonly treacherous.4Make me to know your ways, O LORD; teach me your paths.5Lead me in your truth and teach me, for you are the God of my salvation; for you I wait all the day long.6Remember your mercy, O LORD, and your steadfast love, for they have been from of old.7Remember not the sins of my youth or my transgressions; according to your steadfast love remember me, for the sake of your goodness, O LORD!8Good and upright is the LORD; therefore he instructs sinners in the way.9He leads the humble in what is right, and teaches the humble his way.10All the paths of the LORD are steadfast love and faithfulness, for those who keep his covenant and his testimonies.11For your name's sake, O LORD, pardon my guilt, for it is great.12Who is the man who fears the LORD? Him will he instruct in the way that he should choose.13His soul shall abide in well-being, and his offspring shall inherit the land.14The friendship of the LORD is for those who fear him, and he makes known to them his covenant.15My eyes are ever toward the LORD, for he will pluck my feet out of the net.16Turn to me and be gracious to me, for I am lonely and afflicted.17The troubles of my heart are enlarged; bring me out of my distresses.18Consider my affliction and my trouble, and forgive all my sins.19Consider how many are my foes, and with what violent hatred they hate me.20Oh, guard my soul, and deliver me! Let me not be put to shame, for I take refuge in you.21May integrity and uprightness preserve me, for I wait for you.22Redeem Israel, O God, out of all his troubles.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–7 — Make Me to Know Your Ways
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: To you, O LORD, I lift up my soul, trusting and asking not to be shamed (vv. 1-3). Make me to know your ways, O LORD; teach me your paths. Lead me in your truth and teach me, for you I wait all day (vv. 4-5). Remember your mercy ... Remember not the sins of my youth ... according to your steadfast love remember me (vv. 6-7).
verseByVerse.theology: Before he asks to be rescued he asks to be taught, and his plea for pardon rests on God's memory rather than his own record.

verseByVerse.quote: To you, O LORD, I lift up my soul. O my God, in you I trust; let me not be put to shame; let not my enemies exult over me. Indeed, none who wait for you shall be put to shame; they shall be ashamed who are wantonly treacherous. Make me to know your ways, O LORD; teach me your paths. Lead me in your truth and teach me, for you are the God of my salvation; for you I wait all the day long. Remember your mercy, O LORD, and your steadfast love, for they have been from of old. Remember not the sins of my youth or my transgressions; according to your steadfast love remember me, for the sake of your goodness, O LORD!
verseByVerse.commentary:
The heading is as short as they come: Of David. No tune, no occasion, no instrument — and the psalm turns out to need none, because its subject is the thing every day has in it.

The ESV notes that this psalm is an acrostic: each verse begins with the next letter of the Hebrew alphabet. That is a form for memorising, and it shapes the content — this is an A-to-Z of what a believer needs, laid out so it can be carried in the head.

To you, O LORD, I lift up my soul. O my God, in you I trust; let me not be put to shame.

The previous psalm barred from God's hill anyone who does not lift up his soul to what is false — that is, it let in only the man who refuses to (24:4). Here is the same motion pointed the right way, and it is the whole of religion in five words: the inner life raised deliberately towards God rather than towards something that is not there.

Indeed, none who wait for you shall be put to shame. Waiting runs through this psalm like a thread (vv. 3, 5, 21). It is the hardest thing faith does, and the psalm's promise is not that the wait is short but that it will not end in humiliation.

Make me to know your ways, O LORD; teach me your paths. Lead me in your truth and teach me, for you are the God of my salvation; for you I wait all the day long.

Four verses in, and he has not yet asked to be rescued. He asks to be taught — know, teach, lead, teach again. A man with enemies and a guilty past wants direction more than relief, which is an order of priorities most of us reverse. And the teaching he wants is not information but a path: your ways, your paths, walked rather than learned.

Remember your mercy, O LORD, and your steadfast love, for they have been from of old. Remember not the sins of my youth or my transgressions; according to your steadfast love remember me, for the sake of your goodness, O LORD!

Three times he asks God to remember, and the middle one is a request to forget. The sins of my youth: he is old enough that the worst things he has done are decades behind him and still in the room. Anyone who has lain awake over something from twenty years ago knows this verse from the inside.

And notice what he offers God as grounds. Not the years of service since; not that it was long ago; not that he was young. According to your steadfast love ... for the sake of your goodness. He asks God to consult his own character and leave the record out of it.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 8–15 — He Instructs Sinners in the Way
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Good and upright is the LORD; therefore he instructs sinners in the way, leading and teaching the humble (vv. 8-10). For your name's sake, O LORD, pardon my guilt, for it is great (v. 11). The man who fears the LORD is taught, settled, and given an inheritance, and the friendship of the LORD is for those who fear him (vv. 12-14). My eyes are ever toward the LORD (v. 15).
verseByVerse.theology: God teaches sinners because he is good, not because they are; and the reward for fearing him is being let into his confidence.

verseByVerse.quote: Good and upright is the LORD; therefore he instructs sinners in the way. He leads the humble in what is right, and teaches the humble his way. All the paths of the LORD are steadfast love and faithfulness, for those who keep his covenant and his testimonies. For your name's sake, O LORD, pardon my guilt, for it is great.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Good and upright is the LORD; therefore he instructs sinners in the way. He leads the humble in what is right, and teaches the humble his way. All the paths of the LORD are steadfast love and faithfulness, for those who keep his covenant and his testimonies.

Read verse 8 slowly, because the logic is not what anyone expects. God is good and upright — therefore he teaches sinners. You would expect the opposite: he is upright, therefore he has nothing to say to them. His goodness is the reason he stoops to instruct the very people who have made a mess of the way.

And the people he leads are named twice in one verse: the humble. Not the clever, not the accomplished, not those with a clean record. The single qualification for being taught by God is knowing you need telling.

All the paths of the LORD are steadfast love and faithfulness, for those who keep his covenant and his testimonies. Not some of them. The road God puts a man on is made of two materials the whole way: his covenant love and his reliability. Remember that on the stretch of road that feels like neither, which is the stretch most of us are asking about.

For your name's sake, O LORD, pardon my guilt, for it is great.

One of the boldest sentences in the Bible. He does not minimise the guilt to make the pardon easier; he pleads the size of it as the reason. Great guilt calls for a great pardon, and a great pardon is precisely the thing that makes a great name for God. Moses had argued the same way on Sinai. This is how to pray when the thing you have done feels too big to bring: bring the size of it, and ask for a pardon on that scale.

verseByVerse.quote: Who is the man who fears the LORD? Him will he instruct in the way that he should choose. His soul shall abide in well-being, and his offspring shall inherit the land. The friendship of the LORD is for those who fear him, and he makes known to them his covenant. My eyes are ever toward the LORD, for he will pluck my feet out of the net.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Who is the man who fears the LORD? Him will he instruct in the way that he should choose. His soul shall abide in well-being, and his offspring shall inherit the land.

The question is asked as if scanning a room. And the promise to the man who fears God is instruction in the way that he should choose — not that God chooses for him and hands down a decision, but that God teaches him to choose well. That is a better gift than a series of answers, and it is what most people are actually asking for when they ask for guidance.

And the promise reaches past him: his soul shall abide in well-being, and his offspring shall inherit the land. A man who fears God is not building for himself alone; something of what he receives is still being drawn on by people who come after him. That is the quiet answer to anyone who feels their obedience is going nowhere.

The friendship of the LORD is for those who fear him, and he makes known to them his covenant.

Here is the surprise at the heart of the psalm. The word, as the ESV notes, can be rendered the secret counsel: it is the circle of trusted advisers, the conversation that happens when the door is shut. God said of Abraham, Shall I hide from Abraham what I am about to do? (Gen 18:17), and through Amos, the Lord GOD does nothing without revealing his secret to his servants the prophets (Amos 3:7).

And to people who had followed him three years Jesus said: No longer do I call you servants, for the servant does not know what his master is doing; but I have called you friends, for all that I have heard from my Father I have made known to you (John 15:15). Fear of God is not the opposite of intimacy with him; in this psalm it is the door into it.

My eyes are ever toward the LORD, for he will pluck my feet out of the net. The net is still on his feet while he says it. Looking up is what he does inside the trap, not after.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 16–22 — I Am Lonely and Afflicted
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Turn to me and be gracious to me, for I am lonely and afflicted; his troubles are enlarged, his foes many, their hatred violent (vv. 16-19). Oh, guard my soul, and deliver me! May integrity preserve him, for he waits (vv. 20-21). Redeem Israel, O God, out of all his troubles (v. 22).
verseByVerse.theology: A private prayer that ends by praying for the whole nation.

verseByVerse.quote: Turn to me and be gracious to me, for I am lonely and afflicted. The troubles of my heart are enlarged; bring me out of my distresses. Consider my affliction and my trouble, and forgive all my sins. Consider how many are my foes, and with what violent hatred they hate me. Oh, guard my soul, and deliver me! Let me not be put to shame, for I take refuge in you. May integrity and uprightness preserve me, for I wait for you. Redeem Israel, O God, out of all his troubles.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Turn to me and be gracious to me, for I am lonely and afflicted. The troubles of my heart are enlarged; bring me out of my distresses. Consider my affliction and my trouble, and forgive all my sins.

Now, at last, the trouble itself. Lonely and afflicted — one word for isolation and one for being worn down, which is an honest description of many people's ordinary week and rarely said aloud in church. And his heart's troubles are enlarged: not more numerous, bigger, the way a worry swells overnight.

Then, in the same breath as the request for rescue: forgive all my sins. He does not separate the two. He is not claiming the affliction is deserved, and he is not claiming to be innocent either; he brings both to the same God in the same sentence.

Consider how many are my foes, and with what violent hatred they hate me. Oh, guard my soul, and deliver me! Let me not be put to shame, for I take refuge in you. May integrity and uprightness preserve me, for I wait for you.

The psalm ends its alphabet where it began — waiting, and asking not to be shamed. Nothing has been resolved. The acrostic has run from A to Z and the enemies are still there.

Redeem Israel, O God, out of all his troubles.

And then one more verse, outside the alphabet, which has already finished. A man who has spent twenty-two verses on his own loneliness, guilt and enemies adds a line for the whole nation. It is the right way out of a long season of self-examination: when you have said everything there is to say about your own trouble, pray for somebody else. The psalm's last word is not me.

25.title: Remember Not the Sins of My Youth
25.overview: An acrostic prayer, built to be memorised. David lifts his soul to God, trusts, and asks not to be shamed, for no one who waits is (vv. 1-3). Before any request for rescue he asks to be taught God's ways (vv. 4-5), and asks God to remember his mercy and not the sins of his youth (vv. 6-7). God is good, and therefore instructs sinners and leads the humble (vv. 8-10); so for your name's sake ... pardon my guilt, for it is great (v. 11). The man who fears the LORD is taught to choose well and let into God's confidence (vv. 12-14). Then the trouble itself: lonely, afflicted, hated — guard me, forgive all my sins, let me not be ashamed (vv. 15-21). A final line, outside the alphabet, prays for the whole nation (v. 22).
25.theology:
The soul lifted to God (v. 1) answers 24:4's soul lifted to what is false. Teaching is asked for before rescue (vv. 4-5), and God's instruction is aimed at sinners and the humble because he is good — the qualification is need, not merit (vv. 8-9).

Verse 11 pleads the size of the guilt as the reason for pardon, and grounds it in God's name rather than the sinner's record (cf. vv. 6-7).

Fear of God opens into friendship: the friendship of the LORD — the ESV notes "the secret counsel" — is the circle of those he confides in (v. 14; Gen 18:17; Amos 3:7; John 15:15).

Rescue and forgiveness are asked for in the same breath (v. 18), nothing is resolved by the end, and the psalm's last verse turns from self to the nation (v. 22).
25.examples:
An A-to-Z of what to ask for, built for the memory.

Four requests to be taught before one to be rescued.

Remember, remember not, remember me.

Good and upright — therefore he instructs sinners.

Pardon it because it is great.

The secret counsel: the conversation behind the shut door.

Eyes toward the LORD while the net is still on his feet.

The verse outside the alphabet, for everyone else.

26.text: Of David. 1Vindicate me, O LORD, for I have walked in my integrity, and I have trusted in the LORD without wavering.2Prove me, O LORD, and try me; test my heart and my mind.3For your steadfast love is before my eyes, and I walk in your faithfulness.4I do not sit with men of falsehood, nor do I consort with hypocrites.5I hate the assembly of evildoers, and I will not sit with the wicked.6I wash my hands in innocence and go around your altar, O LORD,7proclaiming thanksgiving aloud, and telling all your wondrous deeds.8O LORD, I love the habitation of your house and the place where your glory dwells.9Do not sweep my soul away with sinners, nor my life with bloodthirsty men,10in whose hands are evil devices, and whose right hands are full of bribes.11But as for me, I shall walk in my integrity; redeem me, and be gracious to me.12My foot stands on level ground; in the great assembly I will bless the LORD.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–8 — Prove Me, O LORD, and Try Me
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Vindicate me, O LORD, for I have walked in my integrity; Prove me, O LORD, and try me; test my heart and my mind (vv. 1-2). God's steadfast love is before his eyes; he does not sit with falsehood, consort with hypocrites, or join the assembly of evildoers (vv. 3-5). I wash my hands in innocence and go around your altar, O LORD, telling his wondrous deeds aloud, and the place where your glory dwells is what he loves (vv. 6-8).
verseByVerse.theology: A man asks to be examined at the deepest level, and offers as evidence the company he keeps and the altar he walks around.

verseByVerse.quote: Vindicate me, O LORD, for I have walked in my integrity, and I have trusted in the LORD without wavering. Prove me, O LORD, and try me; test my heart and my mind. For your steadfast love is before my eyes, and I walk in your faithfulness. I do not sit with men of falsehood, nor do I consort with hypocrites. I hate the assembly of evildoers, and I will not sit with the wicked.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Vindicate me, O LORD, for I have walked in my integrity, and I have trusted in the LORD without wavering. Prove me, O LORD, and try me; test my heart and my mind.

The heading again is bare: Of David. No occasion is given, and the psalm reads like a man preparing to go up to worship while an accusation hangs over him.

Read this immediately after Psalm 25 or it will be misunderstood. One psalm ago the same man asked God to forget the sins of my youth and to pardon his guilt for it is great (25:7, 11). He has not changed his mind between psalms. This is not a claim to be sinless; it is a specific case, brought to a specific court, about a specific accusation — and in that matter he asks to be examined.

Integrity is a word for wholeness: the undivided life, the same man in public and at home. It is the word Job's first sentence uses. And the examination he invites is not of his record but of his interior — the ESV notes the Hebrew is "test my kidneys and my heart", the innermost part a man cannot show anyone. He is asking God to look where nobody else can and see whether it matches.

For your steadfast love is before my eyes, and I walk in your faithfulness. I do not sit with men of falsehood, nor do I consort with hypocrites. I hate the assembly of evildoers, and I will not sit with the wicked.

And here is the evidence he offers, which is not a list of achievements but a list of chairs he has refused to sit in. It is Psalm 1 in the first person: not walking, not standing, not sitting with them. What holds him steady is stated first — God's steadfast love before my eyes, kept in view, the way a man keeps a landmark ahead of him on a walk.

The uncomfortable question this puts to a reader is simple and answerable: where do you sit? Not what you believe about the people around you — whose table you are actually at, whose approval shapes your week. The psalm treats that as evidence in a trial.

verseByVerse.quote: I wash my hands in innocence and go around your altar, O LORD, proclaiming thanksgiving aloud, and telling all your wondrous deeds. O LORD, I love the habitation of your house and the place where your glory dwells.
verseByVerse.commentary:
I wash my hands in innocence and go around your altar, O LORD, proclaiming thanksgiving aloud, and telling all your wondrous deeds.

He is describing a rite. Priests washed at the bronze basin before approaching the altar (Exod 30:17-21), and worshippers washed their hands as a picture of coming clean. The gesture says: I am not bringing my mess in here.

The same gesture can be a lie. A Roman governor took water and washed his hands before the crowd, saying, I am innocent of this man's blood (Matt 27:24), and the washing changed nothing at all — he was using the rite to get out of a decision rather than to bring himself before God. The difference between Psalm 26 and Pilate is not the water. It is whether a man is asking to be examined or trying to close the case.

O LORD, I love the habitation of your house and the place where your glory dwells.

Here is what the psalm is really about. Strip away the legal language and this is a man who loves being where God is, and whose fear is that he will be shut out of it. The evidence he gave in verses 4-5 is all about avoiding one company because he wants another.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 9–12 — I Love the Habitation of Your House
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Do not sweep him away with the bloodthirsty, whose hands hold bribes (vv. 9-10). But as for me, I shall walk in my integrity; redeem me, and be gracious to me. My foot stands on level ground; in the great assembly I will bless the LORD (vv. 11-12).
verseByVerse.theology: The integrity he pleads and the redemption he asks for stand in the same breath, and the psalm ends in church.

verseByVerse.quote: Do not sweep my soul away with sinners, nor my life with bloodthirsty men, in whose hands are evil devices, and whose right hands are full of bribes. But as for me, I shall walk in my integrity; redeem me, and be gracious to me. My foot stands on level ground; in the great assembly I will bless the LORD.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Do not sweep my soul away with sinners, nor my life with bloodthirsty men, in whose hands are evil devices, and whose right hands are full of bribes.

Now the actual fear comes out: being swept away along with people he has spent his life refusing to sit with. It is the anxiety of anyone who has kept his hands clean in a corrupt system and watches the whole thing start to come down. Notice the detail: their right hands are full of bribes, and his own hands have just been washed. The psalm is built on two pairs of hands.

But as for me, I shall walk in my integrity; redeem me, and be gracious to me.

And there, in one verse, is the balance the whole psalm has been holding. I shall walk in my integrity — and in the very next breath, redeem me, and be gracious to me. Redeem is the word for buying someone out; grace is unearned. A man can honestly plead his integrity in a particular matter and still ask, in the same sentence, to be bought out and treated better than he deserves. Anyone who sets those two against each other has misread both.

My foot stands on level ground; in the great assembly I will bless the LORD.

Level ground is what he asked for in the neighbouring psalms (25:15; 27:11): a place where the footing does not slide. He says he has it. And the last line takes this intensely private prayer — kidneys, heart, hidden company, secret fear — and ends it in public: in the great assembly I will bless the LORD. What is settled alone with God gets said out loud among his people.

26.title: I Love the Habitation of Your House
26.overview: David asks God to vindicate him in a particular matter, and invites the deepest examination: Prove me, O LORD, and try me; test my heart and my mind (vv. 1-2). His evidence is the company he has refused — men of falsehood, hypocrites, the assembly of evildoers — and the love of God he keeps in view (vv. 3-5). He washes his hands and walks round the altar, telling God's deeds aloud (vv. 6-7), and says what the psalm is really about: I love the habitation of your house (v. 8). His fear is being swept away with men whose hands are full of bribes (vv. 9-10). So: I shall walk in my integrity; redeem me, and be gracious to me, and the psalm ends on level ground, blessing God in the great assembly (vv. 11-12).
26.theology:
Read beside Psalm 25, where the same man asks pardon for great guilt, this psalm is plainly not a claim to sinlessness but a plea in one case (v. 1). Integrity is wholeness — the same man in public and private — and the examination invited is interior (v. 2).

The evidence offered is company kept and refused (vv. 4-5; cf. 1:1): where a person sits is treated as admissible in a trial.

Washed hands can mean confession or evasion: the rite at the basin (Exod 30:17-21) and Pilate's basin (Matt 27:24) are the same gesture with opposite intent.

Verse 11 holds the two things a believer must hold together: I shall walk in my integrity and redeem me, and be gracious to me — an honest plea in a particular matter alongside a request for unearned mercy. The private prayer ends in the public assembly (v. 12).
26.examples:
Psalm 25 asked pardon for great guilt; this is the same man, one page later.

Test my kidneys and my heart: examine where nobody else can look.

Evidence made of chairs he refused to sit in.

Two pairs of hands: washed, and full of bribes.

Pilate used the same basin to close a case.

I love the habitation of your house — the real subject.

Integrity and "be gracious to me" in one breath.

27.text: Of David. 1The LORD is my light and my salvation; whom shall I fear? The LORD is the stronghold of my life; of whom shall I be afraid?2When evildoers assail me to eat up my flesh, my adversaries and foes, it is they who stumble and fall.3Though an army encamp against me, my heart shall not fear; though war arise against me, yet I will be confident.4One thing have I asked of the LORD, that will I seek after: that I may dwell in the house of the LORD all the days of my life, to gaze upon the beauty of the LORD and to inquire in his temple.5For he will hide me in his shelter in the day of trouble; he will conceal me under the cover of his tent; he will lift me high upon a rock.6And now my head shall be lifted up above my enemies all around me, and I will offer in his tent sacrifices with shouts of joy; I will sing and make melody to the LORD.7Hear, O LORD, when I cry aloud; be gracious to me and answer me!8You have said, "Seek my face." My heart says to you, "Your face, LORD, do I seek."9Hide not your face from me. Turn not your servant away in anger, O you who have been my help. Cast me not off; forsake me not, O God of my salvation!10For my father and my mother have forsaken me, but the LORD will take me in.11Teach me your way, O LORD, and lead me on a level path because of my enemies.12Give me not up to the will of my adversaries; for false witnesses have risen against me, and they breathe out violence.13I believe that I shall look upon the goodness of the LORD in the land of the living!14Wait for the LORD; be strong, and let your heart take courage; wait for the LORD!

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–6 — One Thing Have I Asked
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: The LORD is my light and my salvation; whom shall I fear? Though an army encamp against him his heart will not fear (vv. 1-3). One thing have I asked of the LORD ... that I may dwell in the house of the LORD all the days of my life, to gaze upon the beauty of the LORD and to inquire in his temple (v. 4). God will hide him in his shelter and lift him high on a rock, and he will sacrifice with shouts of joy (vv. 5-6).
verseByVerse.theology: A man surrounded by an army asks for one thing, and it is not the army's defeat.

verseByVerse.quote: The LORD is my light and my salvation; whom shall I fear? The LORD is the stronghold of my life; of whom shall I be afraid? When evildoers assail me to eat up my flesh, my adversaries and foes, it is they who stumble and fall. Though an army encamp against me, my heart shall not fear; though war arise against me, yet I will be confident.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The LORD is my light and my salvation; whom shall I fear? The LORD is the stronghold of my life; of whom shall I be afraid?

Two questions, and both expect the answer nobody. He does not say he has no enemies — verse 3 has an army camped outside. He says the enemies have lost their power to frighten him, which is a different claim and the only one available to most of us.

My light is a rare thing to call God in the Old Testament, and the difference matters: not the one who gives light but light itself, so that a man's ability to see anything at all comes from him. Isaiah promised a city where the sun would be unnecessary because the LORD will be your everlasting light (Isa 60:19). And Jesus said the sentence in the first person: I am the light of the world. Whoever follows me will not walk in darkness (John 8:12).

When evildoers assail me to eat up my flesh, my adversaries and foes, it is they who stumble and fall. Though an army encamp against me, my heart shall not fear; though war arise against me, yet I will be confident.

The picture is of a man standing still while a whole army arranges itself around him. And the confidence is specifically about his heart: it is not a claim that the walls will hold, but that the fear will not get inside him. There is no promise here that the siege will be lifted.

verseByVerse.quote: One thing have I asked of the LORD, that will I seek after: that I may dwell in the house of the LORD all the days of my life, to gaze upon the beauty of the LORD and to inquire in his temple. For he will hide me in his shelter in the day of trouble; he will conceal me under the cover of his tent; he will lift me high upon a rock. And now my head shall be lifted up above my enemies all around me, and I will offer in his tent sacrifices with shouts of joy; I will sing and make melody to the LORD.
verseByVerse.commentary:
One thing have I asked of the LORD, that will I seek after: that I may dwell in the house of the LORD all the days of my life, to gaze upon the beauty of the LORD and to inquire in his temple.

Stop at the arithmetic. A man with an army outside says he has asked God for one thing, and it is not the removal of the army. Most of us, in a crisis, have one thing we want and it is always the crisis ending. His single request is to be somewhere, and the somewhere is where God is.

The one request has three movements, and they are a whole life. Dwell: to live there, not visit — and all the days of my life, not just the frightening ones. Gaze upon the beauty of the LORD: the word is for looking long at something, the way you look at a face rather than glance at a clock. God has beauty, and a man under siege wants to look at it. And inquire in his temple — the ESV notes the word can be rendered meditate — to ask, to seek direction, to keep asking.

Hold that against your own prayer list. If God granted exactly one request this year, and you had to write it now, would it be this? The psalm is not scolding; it is showing what a man wants when he has learned where safety actually is.

For he will hide me in his shelter in the day of trouble; he will conceal me under the cover of his tent; he will lift me high upon a rock. And now my head shall be lifted up above my enemies all around me.

Three pictures of the same protection: hidden, covered, lifted. The tent is God's own — being a guest in someone's tent in that world made you their responsibility to defend. And then the head lifted, which is what God did for the fugitive in Psalm 3. The response is not relief but noise: sacrifices with shouts of joy; I will sing and make melody to the LORD.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 7–14 — Your Face, LORD, Do I Seek
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Hear, O LORD, when I cry aloud: You have said, Seek my face. My heart says to you, Your face, LORD, do I seek. Hide not your face from me (vv. 7-9). For my father and my mother have forsaken me, but the LORD will take me in (v. 10). Teach me, and do not give me up to false witnesses (vv. 11-12). I believe that I shall look upon the goodness of the LORD in the land of the living! Wait for the LORD; be strong, and let your heart take courage; wait for the LORD! (vv. 13-14).
verseByVerse.theology: The confidence of the first half does not save him from having to pray like this, and the psalm ends waiting rather than answered.

verseByVerse.quote: Hear, O LORD, when I cry aloud; be gracious to me and answer me! You have said, "Seek my face." My heart says to you, "Your face, LORD, do I seek." Hide not your face from me. Turn not your servant away in anger, O you who have been my help. Cast me not off; forsake me not, O God of my salvation! For my father and my mother have forsaken me, but the LORD will take me in.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Hear, O LORD, when I cry aloud; be gracious to me and answer me!

The tone changes so sharply here that some have thought this a second psalm. It is better to take the seam seriously and read it as one. The confidence of verses 1-6 did not exempt him from crying aloud in verse 7. A man can mean every word of whom shall I fear? and still, an hour later, be begging God to answer. Anyone who has sung confidently on Sunday and panicked on Tuesday is not a hypocrite; he is in Psalm 27.

You have said, Seek my face. My heart says to you, Your face, LORD, do I seek. Hide not your face from me.

The ESV notes two things here: the command seek is plural, spoken to a congregation, and the Hebrew of the verse is difficult. Both matter. God issued a general invitation to a whole people, and one man overhears it and takes it personally — my heart says to you. That is exactly what should happen when the Bible is read in public: a general summons becomes a private answer.

And what he asks for is a face. Not an outcome, not an explanation: the face of God, which the Aaronic blessing had asked to shine on Israel and which Moses was not allowed to see. He wants the one thing that cannot be arranged.

Turn not your servant away in anger, O you who have been my help. Cast me not off; forsake me not, O God of my salvation! For my father and my mother have forsaken me, but the LORD will take me in.

Verse 10 names the deepest abandonment a human being knows, and it does not soften it: father and mother, the two people who are supposed to be incapable of it. Whether David meant his own family or was speaking of the worst case imaginable, the answer is the same — the LORD will take me in. The verb is the one for gathering someone up off the street and bringing them into the house.

Anyone who was not wanted by the people who should have wanted them is holding the verse this psalm was written for. It does not say God will make up for it. It says God takes you in.

verseByVerse.quote: Teach me your way, O LORD, and lead me on a level path because of my enemies. Give me not up to the will of my adversaries; for false witnesses have risen against me, and they breathe out violence. I believe that I shall look upon the goodness of the LORD in the land of the living! Wait for the LORD; be strong, and let your heart take courage; wait for the LORD!
verseByVerse.commentary:
Teach me your way, O LORD, and lead me on a level path because of my enemies. Give me not up to the will of my adversaries; for false witnesses have risen against me, and they breathe out violence.

Again, under pressure, the request is to be taught (compare 25:4; 26:1-2). Level path is ground you cannot be tripped on, and the reason given is because of my enemies — when people are watching for you to slip, a straight walk is the only defence. Breathe out violence is exact: there are people whose ordinary speech is a threat.
