I believe that I shall look upon the goodness of the LORD in the land of the living!

In Hebrew this verse famously breaks off — the ESV notes other manuscripts read "Oh! Had I not believed that I would look ...", with the sentence left hanging, as if he cannot bring himself to finish the thought of what he would have done without faith. Either way the content is the same: what kept him upright was believing he would yet see God's goodness in the land of the living — not only in some future world, but here, among people still breathing.

Wait for the LORD; be strong, and let your heart take courage; wait for the LORD!

The psalm ends by turning to whoever is listening and saying the hardest thing twice. Not "the LORD has answered"; not "the enemies have gone". Wait. And between the two commands to wait is the only instruction for the interval: be strong, let your heart take courage — which is something done, deliberately, in the waiting rather than after it.

The man who asked for one thing (v. 4) has not been given it yet. He is still looking at an army, still hearing false witnesses, still asking God not to hide. And he tells us to wait, because he knows what he will see: goodness, in the land of the living, from the one who is his light.

27.title: The LORD Is My Light and My Salvation
27.overview: The psalm opens in pure confidence: The LORD is my light and my salvation; whom shall I fear? Even with an army camped around him, the fear will not get inside (vv. 1-3). He has asked God for one thing, and it is not the army's removal: to dwell in God's house all his life, to gaze on his beauty and to keep inquiring there (v. 4) — and he will be hidden, covered, lifted high, and will sacrifice with shouts of joy (vv. 5-6). Then the tone changes completely: hear me, be gracious, answer. You have said, Seek my face. My heart says to you, Your face, LORD, do I seek (vv. 7-9). Though father and mother forsake him, the LORD will take him in (v. 10). Teach me, and do not give me up to false witnesses who breathe out violence (vv. 11-12). He believes he will see God's goodness among the living, and tells whoever is listening to wait for the LORD (vv. 13-14).
27.theology:
The two halves belong together in this order: serene confidence first, urgent pleading second. Meaning every word of whom shall I fear? does not exempt a believer from crying aloud an hour later (vv. 1, 7).

God is called light (v. 1; cf. Isa 60:19; John 8:12), and the confidence claimed is about the heart rather than the walls (v. 3).

The one thing asked by a man under siege is not rescue but presence — to dwell, to gaze on God's beauty, to keep inquiring (v. 4). God's general invitation, Seek my face (plural, as the ESV notes), is taken personally by one heart (v. 8).

The worst human abandonment is named without softening and answered: the LORD will take me in (v. 10). The psalm ends unanswered, with courage commanded between two commands to wait (v. 14).
27.examples:
Not "no enemies" but "no fear of them".

God as light itself, not the one who provides it.

One request, with an army outside, and it is not the army.

Gazing: looking at a face, not glancing at a clock.

Confident on Sunday, begging on Tuesday — both in one psalm.

A plural invitation overheard and answered in the singular.

Taken in off the street when father and mother have gone.

Wait, twice, with courage for the interval.

28.text: Of David. 1To you, O LORD, I call; my rock, be not deaf to me, lest, if you be silent to me, I become like those who go down to the pit.2Hear the voice of my pleas for mercy, when I cry to you for help, when I lift up my hands toward your most holy sanctuary.3Do not drag me off with the wicked, with the workers of evil, who speak peace with their neighbors while evil is in their hearts.4Give to them according to their work and according to the evil of their deeds; give to them according to the work of their hands; render them their due reward.5Because they do not regard the works of the LORD or the work of his hands, he will tear them down and build them up no more.6Blessed be the LORD! For he has heard the voice of my pleas for mercy.7The LORD is my strength and my shield; in him my heart trusts, and I am helped; my heart exults, and with my song I give thanks to him.8The LORD is the strength of his people; he is the saving refuge of his anointed.9Oh, save your people and bless your heritage! Be their shepherd and carry them forever.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–5 — Lest You Be Silent to Me
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: To you, O LORD, I call; my rock, be not deaf to me, lest, if you be silent to me, I become like those who go down to the pit (v. 1). He lifts his hands towards the innermost sanctuary (v. 2). Do not drag him off with men who speak peace with their neighbors while evil is in their hearts; give them what their own work earns, since they pay no attention to what God has done (vv. 3-5).
verseByVerse.theology: The thing he cannot survive is not the enemies but God's silence.

verseByVerse.quote: To you, O LORD, I call; my rock, be not deaf to me, lest, if you be silent to me, I become like those who go down to the pit. Hear the voice of my pleas for mercy, when I cry to you for help, when I lift up my hands toward your most holy sanctuary.
verseByVerse.commentary:
To you, O LORD, I call; my rock, be not deaf to me, lest, if you be silent to me, I become like those who go down to the pit.

Notice precisely what he is afraid of. Not the enemies, who do not appear until verse 3. God's silence. He can survive being opposed; he cannot survive being ignored, and he says so in the first sentence.

Follow the logic of the fear: if God does not answer, he becomes like those who go down to the pit — not merely sad, but indistinguishable from the dead. A living man cut off from God's voice is already, functionally, in the grave. That is a strong thing to say and it is the reason people who pray at all find unanswered prayer so frightening.

Hear the voice of my pleas for mercy, when I cry to you for help, when I lift up my hands toward your most holy sanctuary.

The ESV notes the phrase is literally your innermost sanctuary: the holy of holies, the one room in Israel no ordinary worshipper could ever enter. He stands outside and lifts his hands towards it. The gesture is the whole Old Testament in one picture — a man reaching towards a room with a curtain across it, which is exactly the curtain that tore when Christ died.

verseByVerse.quote: Do not drag me off with the wicked, with the workers of evil, who speak peace with their neighbors while evil is in their hearts. Give to them according to their work and according to the evil of their deeds; give to them according to the work of their hands; render them their due reward. Because they do not regard the works of the LORD or the work of his hands, he will tear them down and build them up no more.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Do not drag me off with the wicked, with the workers of evil, who speak peace with their neighbors while evil is in their hearts.

One line, and it is the most precise description of a particular sin in the Psalter: pleasant to your face, arranging your ruin behind it. Jeremiah said the same of his generation — with his mouth each speaks peace to his neighbor, but in his heart he plans an ambush (Jer 9:8). And it is how the worst betrayal in history was carried out: Greetings, Rabbi! and a kiss (Matt 26:49).

Give to them according to their work and according to the evil of their deeds; give to them according to the work of their hands; render them their due reward.

Three times he asks for the same thing, and notice how limited the request actually is. He does not ask for them to be given more than they have earned, or for anything creative. He asks that their own work come back to them — which is exactly the principle the New Testament states: God will render to each one according to his works (Rom 2:6). Handing a matter to God is not asking for a heavier sentence; it is refusing to set the sentence yourself.

Because they do not regard the works of the LORD or the work of his hands, he will tear them down and build them up no more.

And the root of it all is inattention. They do not regard what God has done — not defiance, indifference. It is the same quiet ruin as the fool of Psalm 14, who simply leaves God out. A man who never looks at what God has made or done ends up speaking peace while planning an ambush, because there is nothing above him to stop it.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 6–9 — Blessed Be the LORD, for He Has Heard
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Blessed be the LORD! For he has heard the voice of my pleas for mercy. The LORD is my strength and my shield; in him my heart trusts, and I am helped (vv. 6-7). He is the strength of his people and the refuge of his anointed (v. 8). Oh, save your people and bless your heritage! Be their shepherd and carry them forever (v. 9).
verseByVerse.theology: Nothing is narrated between the pleading and the blessing, and the answered man immediately prays for everyone else.

verseByVerse.quote: Blessed be the LORD! For he has heard the voice of my pleas for mercy. The LORD is my strength and my shield; in him my heart trusts, and I am helped; my heart exults, and with my song I give thanks to him. The LORD is the strength of his people; he is the saving refuge of his anointed. Oh, save your people and bless your heritage! Be their shepherd and carry them forever.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Blessed be the LORD! For he has heard the voice of my pleas for mercy. The LORD is my strength and my shield; in him my heart trusts, and I am helped; my heart exults, and with my song I give thanks to him.

The turn comes with nothing in between. One verse he is begging not to be ignored, the next he is blessing God for hearing, and the psalm does not tell us what happened. It is the same hinge as Psalm 6 and Psalm 20, and it keeps happening because this is how prayer actually works: the first thing that changes is not the situation but the pray-er's certainty that he has been heard.

Watch the heart in these two verses — in him my heart trusts, and then my heart exults. Trust first, and the leaping comes after. Feelings follow the decision more often than they lead it.

The LORD is the strength of his people; he is the saving refuge of his anointed. The ESV notes a textual difference in the first phrase; either way the psalm has widened from one man to a whole people in a single line.

Oh, save your people and bless your heritage! Be their shepherd and carry them forever.

A man who has just been rescued turns round and prays for everyone else — the same move Psalm 25 made at its last verse. And the words he reaches for are the shepherd's: be their shepherd and carry them. Carrying is what a shepherd does with the lamb that cannot keep up, and it is what he asks God to do with a whole nation, forever. Isaiah would later say it of God to the end of a lifetime: even to your old age ... I will carry and will save (Isa 46:4).

28.title: Be Not Deaf to Me
28.overview: David calls to his rock and asks him not to be deaf, because God's silence would leave him indistinguishable from the dead (v. 1). He lifts his hands towards the innermost sanctuary (v. 2) and asks not to be dragged off with men who speak peace to their neighbours while planning evil; let their own work be given back to them, since they pay no attention to what God has done (vv. 3-5). Then, with nothing narrated in between: Blessed be the LORD! For he has heard — his strength, his shield, his song (vv. 6-7). The LORD is the strength of his whole people (v. 8), and the psalm ends praying for them: save your people ... be their shepherd and carry them forever (v. 9).
28.theology:
The dread in this psalm is God's silence rather than the enemy's success (v. 1): a living man cut off from God's voice is already in the pit.

Hands lifted towards the innermost sanctuary (v. 2) picture the Old Testament's distance from God — the room behind the curtain that tore at the cross.

The imprecation asks only that men receive their own work back (v. 4), the principle of Rom 2:6; handing judgment to God is refusing to set the sentence yourself. The root of their evil is inattention to what God has done (v. 5).

The turn comes by assurance, not by circumstance (v. 6), trust precedes exultation (v. 7), and the rescued man immediately prays for the whole people in the language of the shepherd (v. 9; cf. Ps 23; Isa 46:4).
28.examples:
He can survive opposition; he cannot survive being ignored.

Hands lifted towards a room with a curtain across it.

Speaking peace while the ambush is being arranged.

Asking only that their own work come back to them.

Indifference, not defiance, as the root.

Heart trusts, then heart exults — in that order.

Carry them: what a shepherd does with the lamb that cannot keep up.

29.text: A Psalm of David. 1Ascribe to the LORD, O heavenly beings, ascribe to the LORD glory and strength.2Ascribe to the LORD the glory due his name; worship the LORD in the splendor of holiness.3The voice of the LORD is over the waters; the God of glory thunders, the LORD, over many waters.4The voice of the LORD is powerful; the voice of the LORD is full of majesty.5The voice of the LORD breaks the cedars; the LORD breaks the cedars of Lebanon.6He makes Lebanon to skip like a calf, and Sirion like a young wild ox.7The voice of the LORD flashes forth flames of fire.8The voice of the LORD shakes the wilderness; the LORD shakes the wilderness of Kadesh.9The voice of the LORD makes the deer give birth and strips the forests bare, and in his temple all cry, "Glory!"10The LORD sits enthroned over the flood; the LORD sits enthroned as king forever.11May the LORD give strength to his people! May the LORD bless his people with peace!

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–2 — Ascribe to the LORD Glory
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Ascribe to the LORD, O heavenly beings, ascribe to the LORD glory and strength. Ascribe to the LORD the glory due his name; worship the LORD in the splendor of holiness (vv. 1-2).
verseByVerse.theology: The summons is not addressed to us at all: the angels are told to give God what is already his.

verseByVerse.quote: Ascribe to the LORD, O heavenly beings, ascribe to the LORD glory and strength. Ascribe to the LORD the glory due his name; worship the LORD in the splendor of holiness.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Ascribe to the LORD, O heavenly beings, ascribe to the LORD glory and strength. Ascribe to the LORD the glory due his name; worship the LORD in the splendor of holiness.

The psalm opens by commanding worship, and the ones commanded are not us. The ESV notes the Hebrew is sons of God or sons of might — the heavenly court, the beings around the throne. This is a man on earth telling the angels what to do, which is either presumption or an invitation to join something already in progress.

Ascribe means to give, to hand over. Not to invent praise or to work up a feeling, but to give God what is already due his name. Worship is bookkeeping before it is emotion: putting the glory in the column where it belongs.

And the manner is the splendor of holiness — the ESV notes it may mean in holy attire, dressed for it. Either way it is not casual. Something is happening here that deserves the best clothes a person owns.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 3–9 — The Voice of the LORD Breaks the Cedars
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Seven times the voice of the LORD: over the waters, powerful, full of majesty, breaking the cedars of Lebanon and making the mountains skip like calves, flashing flames of fire, shaking the wilderness, making the deer give birth and stripping the forests — and in his temple all cry, Glory! (vv. 3-9).
verseByVerse.theology: A thunderstorm crosses the whole country, and the psalm hears one thing in it: God speaking.

verseByVerse.quote: The voice of the LORD is over the waters; the God of glory thunders, the LORD, over many waters. The voice of the LORD is powerful; the voice of the LORD is full of majesty. The voice of the LORD breaks the cedars; the LORD breaks the cedars of Lebanon. He makes Lebanon to skip like a calf, and Sirion like a young wild ox. The voice of the LORD flashes forth flames of fire. The voice of the LORD shakes the wilderness; the LORD shakes the wilderness of Kadesh. The voice of the LORD makes the deer give birth and strips the forests bare, and in his temple all cry, "Glory!"
verseByVerse.commentary:
The voice of the LORD is over the waters; the God of glory thunders, the LORD, over many waters. The voice of the LORD is powerful; the voice of the LORD is full of majesty.

Seven times in seven verses: the voice of the LORD. Count them as they come, because the repetition is the poem. What is being described is a thunderstorm, and it is tracked across the map. It builds out at sea (v. 3), comes ashore and hits the northern mountains (vv. 5-6), and rolls south into the desert (v. 8). Anyone who has watched a storm come in off the water knows the sequence.

The voice of the LORD breaks the cedars; the LORD breaks the cedars of Lebanon. He makes Lebanon to skip like a calf, and Sirion like a young wild ox.

The cedars of Lebanon were the strongest timber in the ancient world — the wood kings imported for temples and palaces, the standard picture of what lasts. The storm snaps them. And then the mountains themselves start behaving like livestock: Lebanon and Sirion, which is Mount Hermon, skipping like a calf and a young ox. The most immovable things in the landscape are jumping about.

The voice of the LORD flashes forth flames of fire. The voice of the LORD shakes the wilderness; the LORD shakes the wilderness of Kadesh. The voice of the LORD makes the deer give birth and strips the forests bare, and in his temple all cry, Glory!

Lightning, then the desert shaking, then two things at once: deer dropping their young early with the shock, and whole forests stripped to bare trunks. The ESV notes the first phrase may read that the voice "makes the oaks to shake". Either way the picture is of terror and of birth in the same line, which is what a storm does.

And in the middle of all that noise, one sentence from somewhere else: in his temple all cry, Glory! Outside there is chaos; inside the sanctuary the response is a single word. The creatures who see clearly do not duck — they say what it is.

Scripture is careful to say that God's voice sounds like this to human ears. When the Father spoke audibly over his Son, the crowd that stood there and heard it said that it had thundered (John 12:29). The voice that breaks cedars is the voice that said I have glorified it, and I will glorify it again.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: The LORD sits enthroned over the flood; the LORD sits enthroned as king forever. May the LORD give strength to his people! May the LORD bless his people with peace! (vv. 10-11).
verseByVerse.theology: The storm ends with God seated, and the last word of the psalm is peace.

verseByVerse.quote: The LORD sits enthroned over the flood; the LORD sits enthroned as king forever. May the LORD give strength to his people! May the LORD bless his people with peace!
verseByVerse.commentary:
The LORD sits enthroned over the flood; the LORD sits enthroned as king forever.

After nine verses of noise, a man sitting down. And the word for flood is the one Genesis uses for Noah's flood and hardly anywhere else — the deluge, the moment the world came apart. The psalm says God was seated over that. Not surviving it, not reacting to it: enthroned, in the posture of a king holding court, while the waters that undid the world went over the top of the mountains.

Which means the storm in verses 3-9 was never a rival power. The cedars break, the mountains skip, the desert shakes — and the one whose voice does it has not stood up.

May the LORD give strength to his people! May the LORD bless his people with peace!

And here is the last thing anyone would predict at the end of this psalm. Eleven verses of thunder, and the final word is peace — shalom, wholeness, everything in its place. The ESV notes the lines can be read as statements: the LORD will give, the LORD will bless.

The two gifts belong together and in that order. Strength for his people, because the storm is real and they are in it; and peace, because the one whose voice is in the storm is on their side. Whatever is breaking your cedars this month is being done by a voice, and the owner of the voice is seated, and what he intends for his people at the end of it is peace.

29.title: The Voice of the LORD
29.overview: The angels are ordered to give God the glory that is already his, and to worship in holy splendour (vv. 1-2). Then a thunderstorm crosses the land, and seven times the psalm names what it is hearing: the voice of the LORD — over the sea, powerful, majestic, breaking the cedars of Lebanon, making the mountains skip like calves, flashing fire, shaking the southern wilderness, making the deer give birth and stripping the forests bare — while in the temple everyone cries Glory! (vv. 3-9). The LORD sits enthroned over the flood, king forever, and the psalm ends asking strength and peace for his people (vv. 10-11).
29.theology:
Worship is ascribing — handing over what is already due (vv. 1-2) — and the summons is issued first to the heavenly court, so human praise joins something already going on.

The sevenfold voice of the LORD reads a storm as speech: the strongest timber snaps and the most immovable mountains skip (vv. 5-6). Scripture elsewhere records that God's audible voice sounded like thunder to those standing nearby (John 12:29).

Inside the temple the response to all that terror is one word, Glory (v. 9): those who see clearly name it rather than flinch.

God was enthroned over the deluge itself (v. 10) — the Genesis word — so the storm is never a rival power; the King never stands up. And the psalm of thunder ends in peace (v. 11), with strength given for the storm his people are actually in.
29.examples:
A man on earth telling the angels what to do.

Worship as bookkeeping before it is emotion.

Seven voices: a storm tracked from the sea to the desert.

The timber kings imported, snapped.

Mountains behaving like calves.

Terror and birth in the same line.

Inside the temple, one word: Glory.

Enthroned over the deluge — and the last word is peace.

30.text: A Psalm of David. A song at the dedication of the temple. 1I will extol you, O LORD, for you have drawn me up and have not let my foes rejoice over me.2O LORD my God, I cried to you for help, and you have healed me.3O LORD, you have brought up my soul from Sheol; you restored me to life from among those who go down to the pit.4Sing praises to the LORD, O you his saints, and give thanks to his holy name.5For his anger is but for a moment, and his favor is for a lifetime. Weeping may tarry for the night, but joy comes with the morning.6As for me, I said in my prosperity, "I shall never be moved."7By your favor, O LORD, you made my mountain stand strong; you hid your face; I was dismayed.8To you, O LORD, I cry, and to the Lord I plead for mercy:9"What profit is there in my death, if I go down to the pit? Will the dust praise you? Will it tell of your faithfulness?10Hear, O LORD, and be merciful to me! O LORD, be my helper!"11You have turned for me my mourning into dancing; you have loosed my sackcloth and clothed me with gladness,12that my glory may sing your praise and not be silent. O LORD my God, I will give thanks to you forever!

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–5 — Weeping May Tarry for the Night
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: I will extol you, O LORD, for you have drawn me up; God healed him and brought his soul up from Sheol (vv. 1-3). Let the saints sing, for his anger is but for a moment, and his favor is for a lifetime. Weeping may tarry for the night, but joy comes with the morning (vv. 4-5).
verseByVerse.theology: A rescued man does the arithmetic of God's dealings: a moment of anger against a lifetime of favour.

verseByVerse.quote: I will extol you, O LORD, for you have drawn me up and have not let my foes rejoice over me. O LORD my God, I cried to you for help, and you have healed me. O LORD, you have brought up my soul from Sheol; you restored me to life from among those who go down to the pit.
verseByVerse.commentary:
A Psalm of David. A song at the dedication of the temple.

The heading raises a question, and it should be stated plainly rather than smoothed over: David did not live to see the temple built. The psalm is his; the occasion named is later. Most likely his song of personal rescue was taken up and sung when the house was dedicated, which is exactly what congregations have done with it ever since — one man's recovery becomes everybody's hymn.

I will extol you, O LORD, for you have drawn me up and have not let my foes rejoice over me. O LORD my God, I cried to you for help, and you have healed me. O LORD, you have brought up my soul from Sheol; you restored me to life from among those who go down to the pit.

Drawn me up is the word for hauling a bucket out of a well: dropped down out of sight into the dark, and pulled back up on a rope. Three times in three verses the movement is upward — drawn up, healed, brought up from Sheol. Whatever the illness was, he had been close enough to death to use the language of the grave, and the ESV notes an alternative reading in verse 3 which makes it "to life, that I should not go down to the pit".

verseByVerse.quote: Sing praises to the LORD, O you his saints, and give thanks to his holy name. For his anger is but for a moment, and his favor is for a lifetime. Weeping may tarry for the night, but joy comes with the morning.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Sing praises to the LORD, O you his saints, and give thanks to his holy name.

He cannot keep it to himself; he wants a choir. The ESV notes the last phrase is literally "to the memorial of his holiness", pointing back to the name God gave Moses at the bush to be remembered through all generations (Exod 3:15). What he wants sung is not his own recovery but the character of the God who did it.

For his anger is but for a moment, and his favor is for a lifetime. Weeping may tarry for the night, but joy comes with the morning.

Two comparisons, and both are about proportion. A moment against a lifetime; a night against a morning. Notice that the psalm does not deny either half — the anger was real and the weeping lasted all night. It is measuring them against each other, which is the thing nobody can do at three in the morning without help.

Tarry is a gentle word: weeping is a guest who stays the night, not a resident. And joy comes with the morning does not promise that every trouble ends by breakfast; the psalm has just described an illness that took a man to the edge of the grave. It promises that in God's dealings with his people, the night has a morning attached to it. For the Christian that is not optimism but arithmetic: this light momentary affliction against an eternal weight of glory, as Paul does the same sum.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 6–12 — You Have Turned My Mourning into Dancing
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: As for me, I said in my prosperity, I shall never be moved — then God hid his face and he was dismayed (vv. 6-7). He pleaded: what profit is there in my death? Will the dust praise you (vv. 8-10)? You have turned for me my mourning into dancing; you have loosed my sackcloth and clothed me with gladness, that my glory may sing your praise and not be silent (vv. 11-12).
verseByVerse.theology: The confession at the centre of the psalm is that comfort had made a believer talk like a fool.

verseByVerse.quote: As for me, I said in my prosperity, "I shall never be moved." By your favor, O LORD, you made my mountain stand strong; you hid your face; I was dismayed. To you, O LORD, I cry, and to the Lord I plead for mercy: "What profit is there in my death, if I go down to the pit? Will the dust praise you? Will it tell of your faithfulness? Hear, O LORD, and be merciful to me! O LORD, be my helper!"
verseByVerse.commentary:
As for me, I said in my prosperity, I shall never be moved. By your favor, O LORD, you made my mountain stand strong; you hid your face; I was dismayed.

Here is the confession at the heart of the psalm, and it is unusually honest. When everything was going well he said, I shall never be moved — and the wicked man of Psalm 10 says almost exactly that, "I shall not be moved", as the creed of a man who has decided God will never call him to account (10:6). Comfort had quietly turned a believer into someone who talked like a fool.

And he is careful about the credit even as he confesses. It was by your favor that the mountain stood strong in the first place. That is exactly what he had forgotten: the very stability he was boasting about had been a gift, and he had begun to hold it as a possession.

Then five words that explain the whole illness: you hid your face; I was dismayed. God withdrew the sense of his presence, and the man who could not be moved collapsed immediately. If you are in a season of feeling God has gone quiet after a stretch of things going well, this psalm has been there and does not think it is an accident.

To you, O LORD, I cry, and to the Lord I plead for mercy: What profit is there in my death, if I go down to the pit? Will the dust praise you? Will it tell of your faithfulness?

His argument is the one from Psalm 6: a dead man is one voice fewer in the choir. The ESV notes the first phrase is literally "in my blood", and that the pit may be rendered "corruption". It is a bold way to pray — what do you gain from this? — and God does not rebuke it. He answers it.

verseByVerse.quote: You have turned for me my mourning into dancing; you have loosed my sackcloth and clothed me with gladness, that my glory may sing your praise and not be silent. O LORD my God, I will give thanks to you forever!
verseByVerse.commentary:
You have turned for me my mourning into dancing; you have loosed my sackcloth and clothed me with gladness.

Two pictures, and both are physical. Mourning turned to dancing: the same body, doing the opposite thing. And the sackcloth — the rough, deliberately uncomfortable cloth of grief — untied, taken off him like a coat, and gladness put on instead. He did not dress himself. Isaiah promised the same wardrobe change to people in ashes: a beautiful headdress instead of ashes, the oil of gladness instead of mourning (Isa 61:3), which is the passage Jesus read in Nazareth and said was fulfilled that day.

That my glory may sing your praise and not be silent. O LORD my God, I will give thanks to you forever!

The purpose clause matters: the rescue was for the singing. He asked in verse 9 whether dust could praise God, and the answer he has been given is a voice that will not shut up. Not be silent, and then forever — a word a man in a sickbed has no right to use, unless the God who hauled him up out of the well intends to keep him.

30.title: Joy Comes with the Morning
30.overview: A psalm of David sung at the dedication of the temple. He extols God for hauling him up like a bucket from a well: he cried, and was healed, and his soul was brought up from Sheol (vv. 1-3). Let the saints sing, because his anger is but for a moment, and his favor is for a lifetime. Weeping may tarry for the night, but joy comes with the morning (vv. 4-5). Then the confession: in prosperity he had said I shall never be moved; God hid his face and he was dismayed, and he pleaded that the dust cannot praise God (vv. 6-10). You have turned for me my mourning into dancing; you have loosed my sackcloth and clothed me with gladness — and the purpose is a voice that will not be silent (vv. 11-12).
30.theology:
Rescue is described as being drawn up (v. 1), and the psalm measures God's dealings by proportion: a moment of anger against a lifetime of favour, one night's weeping against the morning (v. 5). Neither half is denied; they are weighed.

The confession at the centre is that prosperity had made a believer speak the wicked man's line — I shall never be moved (v. 6; cf. 10:6) — while forgetting that the mountain stood by your favor (v. 7). The hidden face brought immediate collapse.

He argues for rescue on the ground that the dead do not praise (v. 9; cf. 6:5), and God answers rather than rebukes.

The change of clothes is God's doing (v. 11; cf. Isa 61:3), and its purpose is praise that does not fall silent (v. 12).
30.examples:
A bucket hauled up out of a well.

A moment against a lifetime; a night against a morning.

Weeping as a guest who stays the night, not a resident.

I shall never be moved — the fool's line, in a believer's mouth.

The mountain that stood by favour and was held as a possession.

Sackcloth untied; gladness put on him.

The rescue was for the singing.

31.text: To the choirmaster. A Psalm of David. 1In you, O LORD, do I take refuge; let me never be put to shame; in your righteousness deliver me!2Incline your ear to me; rescue me speedily! Be a rock of refuge for me, a strong fortress to save me!3For you are my rock and my fortress; and for your name's sake you lead me and guide me;4you take me out of the net they have hidden for me, for you are my refuge.5Into your hand I commit my spirit; you have redeemed me, O LORD, faithful God.6I hate those who pay regard to worthless idols, but I trust in the LORD.7I will rejoice and be glad in your steadfast love, because you have seen my affliction; you have known the distress of my soul,8and you have not delivered me into the hand of the enemy; you have set my feet in a broad place.9Be gracious to me, O LORD, for I am in distress; my eye is wasted from grief; my soul and my body also.10For my life is spent with sorrow, and my years with sighing; my strength fails because of my iniquity, and my bones waste away.11Because of all my adversaries I have become a reproach, especially to my neighbors, and an object of dread to my acquaintances; those who see me in the street flee from me.12I have been forgotten like one who is dead; I have become like a broken vessel.13For I hear the whispering of many— terror on every side!— as they scheme together against me, as they plot to take my life.14But I trust in you, O LORD; I say, "You are my God."15My times are in your hand; rescue me from the hand of my enemies and from my persecutors!16Make your face shine on your servant; save me in your steadfast love!17O LORD, let me not be put to shame, for I call upon you; let the wicked be put to shame; let them go silently to Sheol.18Let the lying lips be mute, which speak insolently against the righteous in pride and contempt.19Oh, how abundant is your goodness, which you have stored up for those who fear you and worked for those who take refuge in you, in the sight of the children of mankind!20In the cover of your presence you hide them from the plots of men; you store them in your shelter from the strife of tongues.21Blessed be the LORD, for he has wondrously shown his steadfast love to me when I was in a besieged city.22I had said in my alarm, "I am cut off from your sight." But you heard the voice of my pleas for mercy when I cried to you for help.23Love the LORD, all you his saints! The LORD preserves the faithful but abundantly repays the one who acts in pride.24Be strong, and let your heart take courage, all you who wait for the LORD!

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–8 — Into Your Hand I Commit My Spirit
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: In you, O LORD, do I take refuge — be a rock, a fortress, take me out of the hidden net (vv. 1-4). Into your hand I commit my spirit; you have redeemed me, O LORD, faithful God (v. 5). He will rejoice in God's steadfast love, because you have seen my affliction; you have known the distress of my soul, and set his feet in a broad place (vv. 6-8).
verseByVerse.theology: The verse Jesus died saying is, in its own psalm, a living man's daily act of handing himself over.

verseByVerse.quote: In you, O LORD, do I take refuge; let me never be put to shame; in your righteousness deliver me! Incline your ear to me; rescue me speedily! Be a rock of refuge for me, a strong fortress to save me! For you are my rock and my fortress; and for your name's sake you lead me and guide me; you take me out of the net they have hidden for me, for you are my refuge. Into your hand I commit my spirit; you have redeemed me, O LORD, faithful God.
verseByVerse.commentary:
In you, O LORD, do I take refuge; let me never be put to shame; in your righteousness deliver me! Incline your ear to me; rescue me speedily! Be a rock of refuge for me, a strong fortress to save me!

The opening is all stone: rock, refuge, fortress. And in the middle of it, one word that tells you how bad things are — speedily. He is not asking for eventual help.

You take me out of the net they have hidden for me, for you are my refuge. Into your hand I commit my spirit; you have redeemed me, O LORD, faithful God.

Verse 5 is the sentence the world knows, because it is the last thing Jesus said before he died: Father, into your hands I commit my spirit! (Luke 23:46). He added one word — Father — and said the rest exactly as it stands here. Stephen, being stoned, prayed it to Jesus himself: Lord Jesus, receive my spirit (Acts 7:59).

But read it where it sits. This is not a dying man's line in its own psalm; the writer goes on living for nineteen more verses, and the next thing he says is that God has redeemed him — past tense, already done. Commit is the word for depositing something valuable with someone you trust: handing over a purse for safekeeping. So the verse is first a living act — I put my life in your hands this morning — and only then a way to die. Peter tells suffering Christians to do exactly this: let those who suffer according to God's will entrust their souls to a faithful Creator while doing good (1 Pet 4:19). Learning the sentence now is how it comes to hand at the end.

verseByVerse.quote: I hate those who pay regard to worthless idols, but I trust in the LORD. I will rejoice and be glad in your steadfast love, because you have seen my affliction; you have known the distress of my soul, and you have not delivered me into the hand of the enemy; you have set my feet in a broad place.
verseByVerse.commentary:
I hate those who pay regard to worthless idols, but I trust in the LORD. I will rejoice and be glad in your steadfast love, because you have seen my affliction; you have known the distress of my soul.

The ESV notes a textual question in the first line: most Hebrew manuscripts have I hate, while one manuscript and the ancient versions read You hate. Either the man is stating his own settled opposition to idolatry, or he is contrasting God's attitude with his own trust. The contrast in the verse is the same either way: worthless things on one side, the LORD on the other.

And then two verbs that are the reason he can be glad in the middle of trouble: you have seen, you have known. Not fixed, not yet — seen and known. A great deal of what a suffering person actually wants is contained in those two words, and they are given before any rescue is.

You have set my feet in a broad place. The opposite of the tight spot of 4:1 and the caves of Psalm 18. Room to stand.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 9–18 — I Have Become Like a Broken Vessel
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Be gracious to me, O LORD, for I am in distress: eye wasted with grief, years spent sighing, a reproach to neighbours, dreaded by acquaintances, avoided in the street, forgotten like one who is dead ... like a broken vessel, with terror on every side (vv. 9-13). But I trust in you, O LORD; I say, You are my God. My times are in your hand (vv. 14-15). Make your face shine; silence the lying lips (vv. 16-18).
verseByVerse.theology: The most complete description of social shame in the Psalter, answered by five words about whose hand holds the clock.

verseByVerse.quote: Be gracious to me, O LORD, for I am in distress; my eye is wasted from grief; my soul and my body also. For my life is spent with sorrow, and my years with sighing; my strength fails because of my iniquity, and my bones waste away. Because of all my adversaries I have become a reproach, especially to my neighbors, and an object of dread to my acquaintances; those who see me in the street flee from me. I have been forgotten like one who is dead; I have become like a broken vessel. For I hear the whispering of many— terror on every side!— as they scheme together against me, as they plot to take my life.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Be gracious to me, O LORD, for I am in distress; my eye is wasted from grief; my soul and my body also. For my life is spent with sorrow, and my years with sighing; my strength fails because of my iniquity, and my bones waste away.

This is the fullest description in the Psalter of what long trouble does to a person, and it does not separate body from soul. The eye goes first — grief shows there before anywhere else — then the whole frame. Years, not days: this has been going on. And he does not tidy up the cause, either: my strength fails because of my iniquity. Some of what is crushing him is his own doing, and he says so without collapsing into it.

Because of all my adversaries I have become a reproach, especially to my neighbors, and an object of dread to my acquaintances; those who see me in the street flee from me. I have been forgotten like one who is dead; I have become like a broken vessel.

Now the social pain, which Scripture takes as seriously as the physical. He has become an embarrassment. The worst of it is especially to my neighbors — the people closest in, the ones whose doors he passes every day. Acquaintances cross the road. And two images finish it: forgotten like one who is dead, which is what it feels like when people stop asking how you are; and like a broken vessel, a pot with a crack in it, no longer good for anything, swept up and thrown out.

Anyone who has been through a public disgrace, a long illness, a divorce, a scandal true or false, knows these three verses from the inside. It matters enormously that they are in the Bible, in a hymnbook, unresolved.

For I hear the whispering of many — terror on every side! — as they scheme together against me, as they plot to take my life. Jeremiah would use that exact phrase, Terror is on every side!, about the men waiting for him to stumble (Jer 20:10). The whispering is the thing: not a public accusation he could answer, a murmur he can hear and cannot address.

verseByVerse.quote: But I trust in you, O LORD; I say, "You are my God." My times are in your hand; rescue me from the hand of my enemies and from my persecutors! Make your face shine on your servant; save me in your steadfast love! O LORD, let me not be put to shame, for I call upon you; let the wicked be put to shame; let them go silently to Sheol. Let the lying lips be mute, which speak insolently against the righteous in pride and contempt.
verseByVerse.commentary:
But I trust in you, O LORD; I say, You are my God. My times are in your hand; rescue me from the hand of my enemies and from my persecutors!

But I trust in you — said immediately after the whispering, not after it stopped. And then five words that have carried more people through more than almost any others in the book: My times are in your hand.

Not my life in general: my times. The plural is the point — this stretch and the next, the waiting and the ending of it, the years of sighing in verse 10 and whatever comes after. All of it is held, and held by the same hand he put his spirit into in verse 5. The hand that has his spirit also has his calendar.

Notice too that trusting God with his times does not stop him asking for a change in them. The very next clause is rescue me. Submission and petition are not rivals.

Make your face shine on your servant; save me in your steadfast love! O LORD, let me not be put to shame, for I call upon you; let the wicked be put to shame; let them go silently to Sheol. Let the lying lips be mute, which speak insolently against the righteous in pride and contempt.

The prayer against the enemies is aimed at their mouths. He asks that the lying lips be mute — the whispering campaign of verse 13 silenced — and that the shame he is carrying be transferred to where it belongs. That is a reasonable thing to ask of a just God, and it is asked of him rather than arranged by hand.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 19–24 — How Abundant Is Your Goodness
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Oh, how abundant is your goodness, which you have stored up for those who fear you; he hides them in the cover of his presence from the strife of tongues (vv. 19-20). God showed steadfast love to him in a besieged city, and heard him even when he had said in alarm, I am cut off from your sight (vv. 21-22). Love the LORD, all you his saints! ... Be strong, and let your heart take courage, all you who wait for the LORD! (vv. 23-24).
verseByVerse.theology: God had already heard the prayer the man thought was wasted.

verseByVerse.quote: Oh, how abundant is your goodness, which you have stored up for those who fear you and worked for those who take refuge in you, in the sight of the children of mankind! In the cover of your presence you hide them from the plots of men; you store them in your shelter from the strife of tongues. Blessed be the LORD, for he has wondrously shown his steadfast love to me when I was in a besieged city. I had said in my alarm, "I am cut off from your sight." But you heard the voice of my pleas for mercy when I cried to you for help. Love the LORD, all you his saints! The LORD preserves the faithful but abundantly repays the one who acts in pride. Be strong, and let your heart take courage, all you who wait for the LORD!
verseByVerse.commentary:
Oh, how abundant is your goodness, which you have stored up for those who fear you and worked for those who take refuge in you, in the sight of the children of mankind! In the cover of your presence you hide them from the plots of men; you store them in your shelter from the strife of tongues.

Two kinds of storing. God has stored up goodness — a reserve laid by, not all of it issued yet — and he stores his people, the same word, in a shelter. The goodness is in store and so are the people, which is a good thing to know in a season when neither seems to be in evidence.

And do not miss the last clause of verse 19: the goodness is worked for them in the sight of the children of mankind. God does not only do good to his people; at some point he does it where everyone can see. The man whose neighbours crossed the street in verse 11 is promised a public reckoning of a different kind — not his enemies shamed in private, but God's kindness to him done in daylight.

The strife of tongues is one of the exact phrases of the Bible. Not the strife of armies: tongues. The damage that is done in conversations you are not present at. And the shelter from it is the cover of your presence — not a defence you mount but a place you are put.

Blessed be the LORD, for he has wondrously shown his steadfast love to me when I was in a besieged city. I had said in my alarm, I am cut off from your sight. But you heard the voice of my pleas for mercy when I cried to you for help.

Here is the confession, and it is one of the most reassuring sentences in the Psalter. In his panic — the ESV notes it may be in my haste — he said the worst thing: I am cut off, he is not looking at me any more. He was wrong. But you heard. God was listening to the very prayer the man had decided was not being heard.

Anyone who has prayed while convinced it was pointless should stop on that verse. Being sure you are unheard is not evidence that you are.

Love the LORD, all you his saints! The LORD preserves the faithful but abundantly repays the one who acts in pride. Be strong, and let your heart take courage, all you who wait for the LORD!

And the reason given is a pair: God preserves the faithful and abundantly repays the one who acts in pride. Both halves are needed. Without the first, faithfulness looks pointless; without the second, arrogance looks like it works. The psalm has had both in view since verse 13.

The psalm ends where Psalm 27 ended, word for word in its last line, and it ends by turning outwards. A man who has been avoided in the street tells the whole congregation to love God and take courage. The command is the same one he has just obeyed himself, which is the only kind that carries.

31.title: My Times Are in Your Hand
31.overview: David takes refuge in God — rock, fortress, refuge — and asks to be rescued speedily and taken out of a hidden net (vv. 1-4). Into your hand I commit my spirit (v. 5). He will be glad in God's steadfast love, because God has seen his affliction and known his distress (vv. 6-8). Then the full account of his trouble: eye wasted with grief, years of sighing, strength failing, a reproach to neighbours, dreaded by acquaintances, avoided in the street, forgotten like the dead, like a broken pot, with terror on every side and whispering he cannot answer (vv. 9-13). But I trust in you ... My times are in your hand (vv. 14-15); let the lying lips be silenced (vv. 16-18). God's goodness is stored up, and his people stored in a shelter from the strife of tongues (vv. 19-20). He had said in panic that he was cut off, and God heard him anyway (vv. 21-22). So: love the LORD, be strong, and wait (vv. 23-24).
31.theology:
Verse 5 is a living man's daily deposit before it is a dying man's last word: Jesus added only Father (Luke 23:46), Stephen prayed it to Jesus (Acts 7:59), and Peter tells sufferers to entrust their souls to a faithful Creator (1 Pet 4:19).

God's seeing and knowing (v. 7) are given before any rescue, and much of what a suffering person wants is in those two words.

Social shame is treated as seriously as bodily pain (vv. 9-13), including the part caused by his own iniquity, which is admitted without collapse (v. 10).

My times are in your hand (v. 15) puts the calendar in the same hand as the spirit (v. 5), and it does not cancel the request for change in the next clause: submission and petition are not rivals.

God heard the prayer the man had already written off as unheard (v. 22): the conviction of being cut off is not evidence of being cut off.
31.examples:
All stone — rock, refuge, fortress — and one word: speedily.

Commit: depositing a purse with someone you trust.

Seen and known, before anything is fixed.

Grief shows in the eye first.

Forgotten like the dead; a pot with a crack in it.

The whisper you can hear and cannot answer.

The hand that holds his spirit holds his calendar.

The strife of tongues: damage done in rooms you are not in.

"I am cut off" — said by a man God was listening to.

32.text: A Maskil of David. 1Blessed is the one whose transgression is forgiven, whose sin is covered.2Blessed is the man against whom the LORD counts no iniquity, and in whose spirit there is no deceit.3For when I kept silent, my bones wasted away through my groaning all day long.4For day and night your hand was heavy upon me; my strength was dried up as by the heat of summer. Selah5I acknowledged my sin to you, and I did not cover my iniquity; I said, "I will confess my transgressions to the LORD," and you forgave the iniquity of my sin. Selah6Therefore let everyone who is godly offer prayer to you at a time when you may be found; surely in the rush of great waters, they shall not reach him.7You are a hiding place for me; you preserve me from trouble; you surround me with shouts of deliverance. Selah8I will instruct you and teach you in the way you should go; I will counsel you with my eye upon you.9Be not like a horse or a mule, without understanding, which must be curbed with bit and bridle, or it will not stay near you.10Many are the sorrows of the wicked, but steadfast love surrounds the one who trusts in the LORD.11Be glad in the LORD, and rejoice, O righteous, and shout for joy, all you upright in heart!

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Blessed is the one whose transgression is forgiven, whose sin is covered. Blessed is the man against whom the LORD counts no iniquity (vv. 1-2). While he kept silent his bones wasted away and God's hand was heavy on him day and night (vv. 3-4). I acknowledged my sin to you, and I did not cover my iniquity; I said, I will confess my transgressions to the LORD, and you forgave the iniquity of my sin (v. 5).
verseByVerse.theology: Two ways to deal with sin — cover it yourself, or let God cover it — and the psalm has tried both.

verseByVerse.quote: Blessed is the one whose transgression is forgiven, whose sin is covered. Blessed is the man against whom the LORD counts no iniquity, and in whose spirit there is no deceit.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Blessed is the one whose transgression is forgiven, whose sin is covered. Blessed is the man against whom the LORD counts no iniquity, and in whose spirit there is no deceit.

The Psalter's first word was blessed, of the man who walks with God and delights in his law. Here is the other blessedness, and it is the one most of us need first: not the happiness of the man who has kept the rules but of the man who has broken them and been forgiven.

Three words for what is wrong, and they cover the ground between them. Transgression is rebellion, crossing a line on purpose. Sin is missing the mark, falling short of what you were made for. Iniquity is the crookedness in a man, the bend in the timber. Nobody gets to say his problem is only one of the three.

And three words for the remedy, which are better still. Forgiven is a word for lifting a weight off and carrying it away. Covered — put out of sight, and notice who does the covering, because verse 5 will say what happens when a man covers his own. And counts no iniquity is an accountant's word: the debt is not entered in the column.

Paul builds an argument on these two verses. Having said that God justifies the ungodly, he calls David as his witness: Blessed are those whose lawless deeds are forgiven, and whose sins are covered; blessed is the man against whom the Lord will not count his sin (Rom 4:7-8). The point he draws out is the silence in the verses — nothing at all is said about what the man did to deserve it. Justification by faith is not a doctrine the church invented late; it is what the Old Testament sings.

The last clause adds the one thing required: in whose spirit there is no deceit. Not sinlessness — there is none of that in this psalm — but the end of pretending.

verseByVerse.quote: For when I kept silent, my bones wasted away through my groaning all day long. For day and night your hand was heavy upon me; my strength was dried up as by the heat of summer. Selah I acknowledged my sin to you, and I did not cover my iniquity; I said, "I will confess my transgressions to the LORD," and you forgave the iniquity of my sin. Selah
verseByVerse.commentary:
For when I kept silent, my bones wasted away through my groaning all day long. For day and night your hand was heavy upon me; my strength was dried up as by the heat of summer.

This is the other half of the first two verses, and it is autobiography. He knows what unconfessed sin costs because he paid it, probably for the best part of a year while the Bathsheba business sat unspoken.

Notice that the silence was not peaceful. Groaning all day long: he was making plenty of noise, just not the one sentence that would have helped. The body took it — bones wasting, strength dried out like a puddle in August; the ESV notes the Hebrew is that his vitality was changed. And the pressure is named without flinching: your hand was heavy upon me. That weight was mercy in disguise, and he only calls it God's hand after it lifted.

I acknowledged my sin to you, and I did not cover my iniquity; I said, I will confess my transgressions to the LORD, and you forgave the iniquity of my sin.

Read the verse slowly and watch where the pardon arrives. I said, I will confess — and the sentence does not even finish before the forgiveness comes. God does not wait for the full account, the adequate remorse, the demonstrated improvement. The turn of intention is met at once.

And see the contrast the psalm is built on. He had been covering his own iniquity; he stopped, and discovered that God had covered it (v. 1). Those are the only two options with sin, and they are mutually exclusive: what you cover, God exposes; what you uncover, God covers. If we confess our sins, he is faithful and just to forgive us our sins and to cleanse us from all unrighteousness (1 John 1:9).

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 6–11 — You Are a Hiding Place for Me
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Let everyone godly pray while God may be found; the great waters will not reach him (v. 6). You are a hiding place for me; you preserve me from trouble; you surround me with shouts of deliverance (v. 7). God speaks: I will instruct you and teach you in the way you should go; I will counsel you with my eye upon you — do not be like a horse or mule needing bit and bridle (vv. 8-9). Steadfast love surrounds the one who trusts; be glad and shout for joy (vv. 10-11).
verseByVerse.theology: The forgiven man is taught by a glance rather than a bridle, and the psalm ends in shouting.

verseByVerse.quote: Therefore let everyone who is godly offer prayer to you at a time when you may be found; surely in the rush of great waters, they shall not reach him. You are a hiding place for me; you preserve me from trouble; you surround me with shouts of deliverance. Selah
verseByVerse.commentary:
Therefore let everyone who is godly offer prayer to you at a time when you may be found; surely in the rush of great waters, they shall not reach him.

Therefore: this is what the testimony is for. He has been through it and now tells everyone else to do the thing he delayed. And there is an urgency in it — at a time when you may be found. Confession has a season. Not because God tires of waiting, but because a man who puts it off learns to live with the weight, and the longer the silence the more natural it feels.

You are a hiding place for me; you preserve me from trouble; you surround me with shouts of deliverance.

He had been hiding from God; now God is his hiding place. That is the whole movement of the psalm in one sentence. And what surrounds him is noise — shouts of deliverance, the sound of people celebrating a rescue, ringing him about where the guilt used to be.

verseByVerse.quote: I will instruct you and teach you in the way you should go; I will counsel you with my eye upon you. Be not like a horse or a mule, without understanding, which must be curbed with bit and bridle, or it will not stay near you. Many are the sorrows of the wicked, but steadfast love surrounds the one who trusts in the LORD. Be glad in the LORD, and rejoice, O righteous, and shout for joy, all you upright in heart!
verseByVerse.commentary:
I will instruct you and teach you in the way you should go; I will counsel you with my eye upon you.

The voice changes, and it is now God speaking to the forgiven man. Three verbs of teaching, and then a picture to sit with: with my eye upon you. Guidance by a look. That is how you direct someone who is close to you and paying attention — a glance across a room is enough.

Be not like a horse or a mule, without understanding, which must be curbed with bit and bridle, or it will not stay near you.

The alternative is an animal that has to be hauled about by the mouth. The difference is not obedience — the horse ends up going the right way too — but understanding. God can guide a responsive man with a look and a stubborn one with a bit, and it is entirely up to us which kind of dealing we get. The heavy hand of verse 4 was the bridle. The eye in verse 8 is the better way, and it is offered only to a man who has stopped pretending.

Many are the sorrows of the wicked, but steadfast love surrounds the one who trusts in the LORD. Be glad in the LORD, and rejoice, O righteous, and shout for joy, all you upright in heart!

Two things surround a man in this psalm: shouts of deliverance (v. 7) and steadfast love (v. 10). Both replaced a year of groaning.

And it ends loudly. A psalm about confession finishes with a shout — not a whisper of relief but the noise of people who have been let off. Anyone who thinks repentance is a gloomy business has not read to the end of this one. The blessedness announced in verse 1 turns out to sound like a crowd cheering.

32.title: Blessed Is the One Whose Transgression Is Forgiven
32.overview: Blessed is the man whose transgression is lifted off, whose sin is covered, whose iniquity God does not enter in the ledger — and in whose spirit there is no deceit (vv. 1-2). While he kept silent, his bones wasted and God's hand lay heavy on him day and night (vv. 3-4). Then he stopped covering it: I said, I will confess my transgressions to the LORD, and you forgave the iniquity of my sin (v. 5). So let everyone godly pray while God may be found (v. 6); God is a hiding place, surrounding him with shouts of deliverance (v. 7). God himself speaks: I will instruct you and counsel you with my eye upon you — do not be a horse or mule that needs a bridle (vv. 8-9). Steadfast love surrounds the one who trusts, and the psalm ends in a shout (vv. 10-11).
32.theology:
Three words for sin and three for pardon (vv. 1-2): rebellion, falling short and crookedness, met by a weight lifted, a thing covered, and a debt not entered. Paul quotes both verses to prove that God credits righteousness apart from works (Rom 4:7-8) — the silence about merit is the argument.

Unconfessed sin is described physically and honestly (vv. 3-4); the heavy hand was mercy, recognised only afterwards.

Pardon arrives before the sentence of confession is finished (v. 5; cf. 1 John 1:9), and the psalm's governing contrast is the two coverings: what a man covers, God exposes; what he uncovers, God covers.

The forgiven are guided by a look rather than a bridle (vv. 8-9), and repentance ends in shouting (v. 11).
32.examples:
The second blessedness — the one for people who have broken the rules.

Rebellion, missing the mark, the bend in the timber.

Lifted off, covered, not entered in the column.

Groaning all day and never saying the one sentence.

Forgiven before the confession is finished.

Hiding from God, then hiding in him.

Guidance by a glance, or by a bit in the mouth.

A psalm about repentance that ends in a shout.

33.text: <sup>1</sup>Shout for joy in the LORD, O you righteous! Praise befits the upright.<sup>2</sup>Give thanks to the LORD with the lyre; make melody to him with the harp of ten strings!<sup>3</sup>Sing to him a new song; play skillfully on the strings, with loud shouts.<sup>4</sup>For the word of the LORD is upright, and all his work is done in faithfulness.<sup>5</sup>He loves righteousness and justice; the earth is full of the steadfast love of the LORD.<sup>6</sup>By the word of the LORD the heavens were made, and by the breath of his mouth all their host.<sup>7</sup>He gathers the waters of the sea as a heap; he puts the deeps in storehouses.<sup>8</sup>Let all the earth fear the LORD; let all the inhabitants of the world stand in awe of him!<sup>9</sup>For he spoke, and it came to be; he commanded, and it stood firm.<sup>10</sup>The LORD brings the counsel of the nations to nothing; he frustrates the plans of the peoples.<sup>11</sup>The counsel of the LORD stands forever, the plans of his heart to all generations.<sup>12</sup>Blessed is the nation whose God is the LORD, the people whom he has chosen as his heritage!<sup>13</sup>The LORD looks down from heaven; he sees all the children of man;<sup>14</sup>from where he sits enthroned he looks out on all the inhabitants of the earth,<sup>15</sup>he who fashions the hearts of them all and observes all their deeds.<sup>16</sup>The king is not saved by his great army; a warrior is not delivered by his great strength.<sup>17</sup>The war horse is a false hope for salvation, and by its great might it cannot rescue.<sup>18</sup>Behold, the eye of the LORD is on those who fear him, on those who hope in his steadfast love,<sup>19</sup>that he may deliver their soul from death and keep them alive in famine.<sup>20</sup>Our soul waits for the LORD; he is our help and our shield.<sup>21</sup>For our heart is glad in him, because we trust in his holy name.<sup>22</sup>Let your steadfast love, O LORD, be upon us, even as we hope in you.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–9 — For He Spoke, and It Came to Be
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Shout for joy in the LORD, O you righteous! — with lyre, harp, a new song, skilled playing and loud shouts (vv. 1-3), because God's word is upright, his work faithful, and the earth is full of the steadfast love of the LORD (vv. 4-5). By the word of the LORD the heavens were made; he gathers the sea as a heap and stores the deeps, for he spoke, and it came to be; he commanded, and it stood firm (vv. 6-9).
verseByVerse.theology: The praise is skilled and loud, and its reason is that the universe came out of a sentence.

verseByVerse.quote: Shout for joy in the LORD, O you righteous! Praise befits the upright. Give thanks to the LORD with the lyre; make melody to him with the harp of ten strings! Sing to him a new song; play skillfully on the strings, with loud shouts. For the word of the LORD is upright, and all his work is done in faithfulness. He loves righteousness and justice; the earth is full of the steadfast love of the LORD.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Shout for joy in the LORD, O you righteous! Praise befits the upright. Give thanks to the LORD with the lyre; make melody to him with the harp of ten strings! Sing to him a new song; play skillfully on the strings, with loud shouts.

This psalm has no heading, and it begins with the word Psalm 32 ended on: shout for joy. Read them together and the joining makes sense — the forgiven man of Psalm 32 leads the congregation into the praise of Psalm 33.

Three things are asked of the musicians, and they settle most church arguments about worship. It is to be new — fresh composition, not only the old repertoire. It is to be skilful: God is not honoured by slapdash playing, and rehearsal is a spiritual activity. And it is to be loud. Anyone who wants their worship to be only one of these three is arguing with the verse.

For the word of the LORD is upright, and all his work is done in faithfulness. He loves righteousness and justice; the earth is full of the steadfast love of the LORD.

The reason for the noise is character: what God says is straight, what he does is reliable, what he loves is right. And then a line to lift your head at — the earth is full of the steadfast love of the LORD. Not will be full; is. The same world that is full of trouble in the rest of this book is full of covenant love now, and the psalm assumes a person could look out of a window and see it.

verseByVerse.quote: By the word of the LORD the heavens were made, and by the breath of his mouth all their host. He gathers the waters of the sea as a heap; he puts the deeps in storehouses. Let all the earth fear the LORD; let all the inhabitants of the world stand in awe of him! For he spoke, and it came to be; he commanded, and it stood firm.
verseByVerse.commentary:
By the word of the LORD the heavens were made, and by the breath of his mouth all their host. He gathers the waters of the sea as a heap; he puts the deeps in storehouses.

Genesis in one line. God did not assemble the universe or wrestle it out of something; he said it. The stars are the breath of his mouth — what it costs him to make a galaxy is a breath. And the sea, which every ancient people treated as the great untameable thing, is handled like a farmer's produce: gathered up as a heap and put away in storehouses, the way you would store grain.

Let all the earth fear the LORD; let all the inhabitants of the world stand in awe of him! For he spoke, and it came to be; he commanded, and it stood firm.

The proper response to a spoken universe is fear — not fright, but the awe of a creature who has understood what he is standing on. He spoke, and it came to be: there is no gap between God's word and the fact. The New Testament makes this a matter of faith rather than observation — By faith we understand that the universe was created by the word of God (Heb 11:3) — and draws the obvious conclusion for prayer. The God who called the light out of nothing is being asked, in the next psalm and the next, for bread and rescue. He is not stretched by either.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 10–19 — The Counsel of the LORD Stands Forever
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: God brings the counsel of the nations to nothing, while the counsel of the LORD stands forever (vv. 10-11). Blessed is the nation whose God is the LORD (v. 12). He looks down on everyone, he who fashions the hearts of them all (vv. 13-15). No king is saved by his army and the war horse is a false hope for salvation (vv. 16-17); God's eye is on those who fear him, to deliver them from death and keep them alive in famine (vv. 18-19).
verseByVerse.theology: Two kinds of plan and two kinds of security, with the world's best version of each dismissed in a line.

verseByVerse.quote: The LORD brings the counsel of the nations to nothing; he frustrates the plans of the peoples. The counsel of the LORD stands forever, the plans of his heart to all generations. Blessed is the nation whose God is the LORD, the people whom he has chosen as his heritage! The LORD looks down from heaven; he sees all the children of man; from where he sits enthroned he looks out on all the inhabitants of the earth, he who fashions the hearts of them all and observes all their deeds.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The LORD brings the counsel of the nations to nothing; he frustrates the plans of the peoples. The counsel of the LORD stands forever, the plans of his heart to all generations.

Two councils are in session: the nations', and God's. One is brought to nothing; the other stands. That is not a claim that human planning is worthless — Scripture is full of good planning — but that no plan can outrank his. Isaiah says it as God's own boast: My counsel shall stand, and I will accomplish all my purpose (Isa 46:10).

And notice the tenderness in the second half: the plans of his heart. God's purposes are not policy; they are what he has set his heart on, and they last to all generations, which means the thing he intended for your grandmother and intends for your grandchildren is one continuous purpose.

And there is comfort in the first half for anyone whose own plan has just been brought to nothing. The verse is about nations and their councils, but the principle reaches down: the plans that collapse are not always a disaster, because there is a counsel underneath them that does not. What frustrates the peoples protects the people.

Blessed is the nation whose God is the LORD, the people whom he has chosen as his heritage! A line that has been claimed by a great many countries and belongs first to the people God chose, and now to the church gathered from every tribe and language — a nation not marked on any map.

The LORD looks down from heaven; he sees all the children of man; from where he sits enthroned he looks out on all the inhabitants of the earth, he who fashions the hearts of them all and observes all their deeds.

God looked down in Psalm 14 and found no one who sought him. He looks down here as the one who fashions the hearts of them all — the verb is a potter's, used of forming clay, and it is singular work done to each one. He is not scanning a crowd. He made every heart in it individually and knows what is in it, which is the most comforting and the most exposing fact available to a human being.

verseByVerse.quote: The king is not saved by his great army; a warrior is not delivered by his great strength. The war horse is a false hope for salvation, and by its great might it cannot rescue. Behold, the eye of the LORD is on those who fear him, on those who hope in his steadfast love, that he may deliver their soul from death and keep them alive in famine.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The king is not saved by his great army; a warrior is not delivered by his great strength. The war horse is a false hope for salvation, and by its great might it cannot rescue.

Psalm 20 shouted this before a battle; here it is stated calmly as doctrine. Three of the strongest things in that world — a standing army, a champion, a war horse — and each is dismissed with the same verdict. The phrase is exact: not a weak hope, a false one. It is not that the horse helps a little and God helps more. The horse is in the wrong category altogether.

Every generation keeps its own horses, and they are usually the things we are proud of and would be ashamed to name in a prayer: the savings, the qualifications, the contacts, the plan B. The psalm is not telling anyone to sell the horse. It is telling them what the horse can and cannot do.

Behold, the eye of the LORD is on those who fear him, on those who hope in his steadfast love, that he may deliver their soul from death and keep them alive in famine.

Against the armies and the horses: an eye. That is the whole of the security offered, and it is set on a particular group — those who fear him and hope in his love. And the two things promised are deliverance from death and being kept alive in famine, not out of it. God's people are not exempted from the hungry year; they are kept through it.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 20–22 — Our Soul Waits for the LORD
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Our soul waits for the LORD; he is our help and our shield. For our heart is glad in him, because we trust in his holy name. Let your steadfast love, O LORD, be upon us, even as we hope in you (vv. 20-22).
verseByVerse.theology: The psalm of the spoken universe ends with a congregation waiting.

verseByVerse.quote: Our soul waits for the LORD; he is our help and our shield. For our heart is glad in him, because we trust in his holy name. Let your steadfast love, O LORD, be upon us, even as we hope in you.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Our soul waits for the LORD; he is our help and our shield. For our heart is glad in him, because we trust in his holy name. Let your steadfast love, O LORD, be upon us, even as we hope in you.

After a universe made by a word, after nations frustrated and armies dismissed, the psalm ends with a congregation standing still. Our soul waits — the same verb the last three psalms have ended on. It is the posture of people who know exactly how strong God is and are still in the middle of their own story.

Notice what the gladness rests on: because we trust in his holy name. Not because the waiting is over. The heart is glad in the middle of the wait, and what makes it glad is a name — everything God has revealed himself to be, which does not alter while they wait.

And the last line is a beautiful piece of logic. Let your steadfast love, O LORD, be upon us, even as we hope in you. He does not ask for love in proportion to their obedience, or their gifts, or their record. In proportion to their hope. Which means the poorest believer in the room, who has nothing to bring but expectation, is asking for the full measure.

33.title: He Spoke, and It Came to Be
33.overview: A call to loud, skilful, new praise, because God's word is upright, his work faithful, and the earth is full of his steadfast love (vv. 1-5). The heavens were made by his word and the stars by the breath of his mouth; he stores the sea like grain, and he spoke, and it came to be (vv. 6-9). The plans of the nations come to nothing while the counsel of the LORD stands forever (vv. 10-12); he looks down on everyone and fashions each heart himself (vv. 13-15). No army, warrior or war horse can save; God's eye is on those who fear him, to keep them alive in famine (vv. 16-19). The psalm ends with a congregation waiting, asking for steadfast love in proportion to their hope (vv. 20-22).
33.theology:
Worship here is new, skilful and loud (vv. 1-3) and grounded in God's character rather than the worshippers' mood (vv. 4-5).

Creation is by speech (vv. 6, 9; Gen 1; Heb 11:3): there is no gap between God's word and the fact, and the sea that terrified the nations is stored like produce (v. 7).

Two councils sit; only one stands (vv. 10-11; cf. Isa 46:10), and God's purposes are the plans of his heart, running through all generations.

God fashions each heart individually, as a potter (v. 15) — at once the most comforting and most exposing fact about a person.

The war horse is not a weak hope but a false one (v. 17; cf. 20:7), and what is promised instead is God's eye, and life kept in famine rather than out of it (vv. 18-19). The closing prayer asks for love in proportion to hope, not to merit (v. 22).
33.examples:
No heading: it begins on the word Psalm 32 ended on.

New, skilful and loud — all three, in one verse.

What it costs God to make a galaxy: a breath.

The untameable sea, stored like grain.

The plans of his heart, running through all generations.

Each heart made individually by a potter's hand.

Everyone keeps a war horse; the psalm says what it cannot do.

Kept alive in famine, not out of it.

34.text: Of David, when he changed his behavior before Abimelech, so that he drove him out, and he went away. 1I will bless the LORD at all times; his praise shall continually be in my mouth.2My soul makes its boast in the LORD; let the humble hear and be glad.3Oh, magnify the LORD with me, and let us exalt his name together!4I sought the LORD, and he answered me and delivered me from all my fears.5Those who look to him are radiant, and their faces shall never be ashamed.6This poor man cried, and the LORD heard him and saved him out of all his troubles.7The angel of the LORD encamps around those who fear him, and delivers them.8Oh, taste and see that the LORD is good! Blessed is the man who takes refuge in him!9Oh, fear the LORD, you his saints, for those who fear him have no lack!10The young lions suffer want and hunger; but those who seek the LORD lack no good thing.11Come, O children, listen to me; I will teach you the fear of the LORD.12What man is there who desires life and loves many days, that he may see good?13Keep your tongue from evil and your lips from speaking deceit.14Turn away from evil and do good; seek peace and pursue it.15The eyes of the LORD are toward the righteous and his ears toward their cry.16The face of the LORD is against those who do evil, to cut off the memory of them from the earth.17When the righteous cry for help, the LORD hears and delivers them out of all their troubles.18The LORD is near to the brokenhearted and saves the crushed in spirit.19Many are the afflictions of the righteous, but the LORD delivers him out of them all.20He keeps all his bones; not one of them is broken.21Affliction will slay the wicked, and those who hate the righteous will be condemned.22The LORD redeems the life of his servants; none of those who take refuge in him will be condemned.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: I will bless the LORD at all times; let the humble hear and be glad, and let us magnify him together (vv. 1-3). I sought the LORD, and he answered me and delivered me from all my fears; those who look to him are radiant, and this poor man cried and was heard (vv. 4-6). The angel of the LORD encamps around those who fear him (v. 7). Oh, taste and see that the LORD is good! Those who fear him lack nothing, while young lions go hungry (vv. 8-10).
