verseByVerse.theology: A psalm written after a humiliating escape, inviting everyone to try God for themselves.

verseByVerse.quote: I will bless the LORD at all times; his praise shall continually be in my mouth. My soul makes its boast in the LORD; let the humble hear and be glad. Oh, magnify the LORD with me, and let us exalt his name together!
verseByVerse.commentary:
Of David, when he changed his behavior before Abimelech, so that he drove him out, and he went away.

The heading sends us to one of the least dignified pages in David's life. On the run from Saul he fled to Gath, a Philistine city, and was recognised as the man who had killed their champion. So he saved himself by pretending to be insane: he changed his behavior before them and pretended to be insane in their hands and made marks on the doors of the gate and let his spittle run down his beard (1 Sam 21:13). The king threw him out as a nuisance. (The king is called Achish there and Abimelech here, which appears to have been a Philistine royal title rather than a different man.)

That is the occasion of taste and see that the LORD is good. Not a coronation; an escape by humiliation, from a mess he had walked into himself. Keep that in view for the whole psalm.

I will bless the LORD at all times; his praise shall continually be in my mouth. My soul makes its boast in the LORD; let the humble hear and be glad. Oh, magnify the LORD with me, and let us exalt his name together!

At all times and continually are large words from a man who has just been scrabbling at a gate. And notice who he expects to enjoy his testimony: let the humble hear and be glad. A story about God rescuing a man who had made a fool of himself is no use to the self-assured and food and drink to everyone else.

Magnify does not mean make God bigger; nothing can. It means make him look as big as he is — the work of a lens, not of a fable. And he will not do it alone: with me ... together.

verseByVerse.quote: I sought the LORD, and he answered me and delivered me from all my fears. Those who look to him are radiant, and their faces shall never be ashamed. This poor man cried, and the LORD heard him and saved him out of all his troubles. The angel of the LORD encamps around those who fear him, and delivers them. Oh, taste and see that the LORD is good! Blessed is the man who takes refuge in him! Oh, fear the LORD, you his saints, for those who fear him have no lack! The young lions suffer want and hunger; but those who seek the LORD lack no good thing.
verseByVerse.commentary:
I sought the LORD, and he answered me and delivered me from all my fears. Those who look to him are radiant, and their faces shall never be ashamed. This poor man cried, and the LORD heard him and saved him out of all his troubles.

Three testimonies in three verses, and the middle one is about faces. Those who look to him are radiant — the word is used of dawn breaking. A face that has been turned towards God catches the light, and the psalm sets that against the shame of the man dribbling at the gate of Gath. He was ashamed there; he says here that those who look to God shall never be ashamed.

This poor man cried is how he now describes himself. Not the giant-killer, not the anointed king: this poor man. It is the right way to remember your own rescue.

The angel of the LORD encamps around those who fear him, and delivers them. One angel, and the verb is an army's: he camps. Elisha's servant would one day have his eyes opened to see what that looks like.

Oh, taste and see that the LORD is good! Blessed is the man who takes refuge in him! Oh, fear the LORD, you his saints, for those who fear him have no lack! The young lions suffer want and hunger; but those who seek the LORD lack no good thing.

Taste is the invitation of a man handing you a spoon. You cannot know what something is like by being told; at some point you have to try it. Peter quotes this line to young Christians and treats it as already happening to them: if indeed you have tasted that the Lord is good (1 Pet 2:3).

And then the lions. The strongest hunters in the region go hungry, and people who seek God lack no good thing. Not lack nothing they want — no good thing, which leaves God the judgment of what counts. Strength is not the same as provision, and a man who has just escaped a city by drooling is the right person to say so.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 11–22 — The LORD Is Near to the Brokenhearted
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Come, O children, listen to me; I will teach you the fear of the LORD: keep your tongue from evil, turn from evil and do good, seek peace and pursue it (vv. 11-14). God's eyes and ears are toward the righteous, his face against evildoers (vv. 15-16). The LORD is near to the brokenhearted and saves the crushed in spirit (vv. 17-18). Many are the afflictions of the righteous, but the LORD delivers him out of them all. He keeps all his bones; not one of them is broken (vv. 19-22).
verseByVerse.theology: The fear of the LORD is taught as a set of habits, and the promise is not exemption from affliction but rescue through it.

verseByVerse.quote: Come, O children, listen to me; I will teach you the fear of the LORD. What man is there who desires life and loves many days, that he may see good? Keep your tongue from evil and your lips from speaking deceit. Turn away from evil and do good; seek peace and pursue it. The eyes of the LORD are toward the righteous and his ears toward their cry. The face of the LORD is against those who do evil, to cut off the memory of them from the earth.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Come, O children, listen to me; I will teach you the fear of the LORD. What man is there who desires life and loves many days, that he may see good? Keep your tongue from evil and your lips from speaking deceit. Turn away from evil and do good; seek peace and pursue it.

Now he turns teacher, and the fear of the LORD — which sounds abstract — is handed over as four ordinary habits. Control your tongue. Stop lying. Leave off evil. Do good. And then a fifth that will not sit still: seek peace and pursue it. Peace does not stay where you put it; you have to go after it, which is exactly what anyone who has tried to mend a quarrel discovers.

Peter takes these verses and hands them to Christians facing hostility, word for word: Whoever desires to love life and see good days, let him keep his tongue from evil and his lips from speaking deceit; let him turn away from evil and do good; let him seek peace and pursue it (1 Pet 3:10-11). Written by a man who escaped by his wits, quoted to people who must not.

The eyes of the LORD are toward the righteous and his ears toward their cry. The face of the LORD is against those who do evil, to cut off the memory of them from the earth.

Eyes, ears, face. Attention in three organs, and the third is the frightening one: the same face that shines on the righteous is set against the evildoer. God is not neutral, and the psalm is comfortable saying so.

verseByVerse.quote: When the righteous cry for help, the LORD hears and delivers them out of all their troubles. The LORD is near to the brokenhearted and saves the crushed in spirit. Many are the afflictions of the righteous, but the LORD delivers him out of them all. He keeps all his bones; not one of them is broken. Affliction will slay the wicked, and those who hate the righteous will be condemned. The LORD redeems the life of his servants; none of those who take refuge in him will be condemned.
verseByVerse.commentary:
When the righteous cry for help, the LORD hears and delivers them out of all their troubles. The LORD is near to the brokenhearted and saves the crushed in spirit.

Verse 18 is the pastoral centre of the psalm and one of the great sentences of the Bible. Not: the LORD is near to the cheerful; not: he waits until you have pulled yourself together. Near to the brokenhearted, and the second half goes further — crushed in spirit, ground down, the way grain is crushed.

Most religions locate God at the top of the ladder. This verse puts him at the bottom of the stairs, standing close to the person who cannot get up. If you are reading this from inside that condition, the psalm does not explain it and does not ask you to feel better about it. It tells you where God is standing.

Many are the afflictions of the righteous, but the LORD delivers him out of them all.

Hold both halves. Many — the psalm has no interest in pretending faith reduces the number of afflictions, and has just spent six verses on the brokenhearted. And out of them all: not round them, through them. Every affliction the righteous man has ever had has been one he was brought out of; the last one will be no different, though it will take a resurrection.

He keeps all his bones; not one of them is broken.

Which, said of an ordinary righteous man, is a promise about God's carefulness. And then it happened literally, once. When the soldiers came to break the legs of the crucified men to hasten their deaths, when they came to Jesus and saw that he was already dead, they did not break his legs — and John writes, For these things took place that the Scripture might be fulfilled: Not one of his bones will be broken (John 19:33, 36). The Passover lamb was protected by the same rule. God's care for the bones of his righteous one was exact to the inch on the day it mattered most.

Affliction will slay the wicked, and those who hate the righteous will be condemned. The LORD redeems the life of his servants; none of those who take refuge in him will be condemned.

The acrostic ends on the word condemned, used twice: the haters will be, and those who take refuge will not. A man who once escaped a king by pretending to be mad ends his alphabet by saying that the only refuge that ever really worked was God — and that the verdict on everyone who runs there is settled.

34.title: Taste and See That the LORD Is Good
34.overview: Written after David escaped a Philistine king by pretending to be insane. He blesses the LORD at all times and calls the humble to magnify God with him (vv. 1-3). He sought God and was answered and delivered from all his fears; those who look to God are radiant, and this poor man cried and was heard (vv. 4-7). Oh, taste and see that the LORD is good! Those who fear him lack no good thing, while young lions go hungry (vv. 8-10). Then he teaches the fear of the LORD as ordinary habits: guard the tongue, turn from evil, do good, seek peace and pursue it (vv. 11-14). God's eyes and ears are toward the righteous and his face against evildoers (vv. 15-16). The LORD is near to the brokenhearted and saves the crushed in spirit (vv. 17-18). Many are the afflictions of the righteous, and he is delivered out of them all; not one of his bones is broken; those who take refuge in God are not condemned (vv. 19-22).
34.theology:
The invitation to taste and see (v. 8; 1 Pet 2:3) comes from a man whose most recent experience of God was a humiliating escape, which is why the humble are the ones told to listen (v. 2).

The fear of the LORD is taught as habits, not as mood (vv. 11-14), and Peter hands the same verses to Christians under hostility (1 Pet 3:10-12).

God's nearness is located precisely: near to the brokenhearted ... saves the crushed in spirit (v. 18). The promise to the righteous is not fewer afflictions but rescue out of all of them (v. 19), which for the last one requires resurrection.

Not one of them is broken (v. 20) was fulfilled to the letter at the cross, under the Passover rule (John 19:36; Exod 12:46), and the psalm closes on the verdict: those who take refuge in him are not condemned (v. 22).
34.examples:
The psalm of "taste and see" was written after an escape by drooling.

Magnify: the work of a lens, not a fable.

Faces catching the light, set against a face that had been shamed.

This poor man cried — the right way to remember a rescue.

Young lions hungry; seekers lacking no good thing.

Peace will not stay put: pursue it.

God at the bottom of the stairs, near the crushed.

Bones kept exactly, on the day it mattered most.

35.text: Of David. 1Contend, O LORD, with those who contend with me; fight against those who fight against me!2Take hold of shield and buckler and rise for my help!3Draw the spear and javelin against my pursuers! Say to my soul, "I am your salvation!"4Let them be put to shame and dishonor who seek after my life! Let them be turned back and disappointed who devise evil against me!5Let them be like chaff before the wind, with the angel of the LORD driving them away!6Let their way be dark and slippery, with the angel of the LORD pursuing them!7For without cause they hid their net for me; without cause they dug a pit for my life.8Let destruction come upon him when he does not know it! And let the net that he hid ensnare him; let him fall into it—to his destruction!9Then my soul will rejoice in the LORD, exulting in his salvation.10All my bones shall say, "O LORD, who is like you, delivering the poor from him who is too strong for him, the poor and needy from him who robs him?"11Malicious witnesses rise up; they ask me of things that I do not know.12They repay me evil for good; my soul is bereft.13But I, when they were sick— I wore sackcloth; I afflicted myself with fasting; I prayed with head bowed on my chest.14I went about as though I grieved for my friend or my brother; as one who laments his mother, I bowed down in mourning.15But at my stumbling they rejoiced and gathered; they gathered together against me; wretches whom I did not know tore at me without ceasing;16like profane mockers at a feast, they gnash at me with their teeth.17How long, O Lord, will you look on? Rescue me from their destruction, my precious life from the lions!18I will thank you in the great congregation; in the mighty throng I will praise you.19Let not those rejoice over me who are wrongfully my foes, and let not those wink the eye who hate me without cause.20For they do not speak peace, but against those who are quiet in the land they devise words of deceit.21They open wide their mouths against me; they say, "Aha, Aha! Our eyes have seen it!"22You have seen, O LORD; be not silent! O Lord, be not far from me!23Awake and rouse yourself for my vindication, for my cause, my God and my Lord!24Vindicate me, O LORD, my God, according to your righteousness, and let them not rejoice over me!25Let them not say in their hearts, "Aha, our heart's desire!" Let them not say, "We have swallowed him up."26Let them be put to shame and disappointed altogether who rejoice at my calamity! Let them be clothed with shame and dishonor who magnify themselves against me!27Let those who delight in my righteousness shout for joy and be glad and say evermore, "Great is the LORD, who delights in the welfare of his servant!"28Then my tongue shall tell of your righteousness and of your praise all the day long.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–8 — Say to My Soul, I Am Your Salvation
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Contend, O LORD, with those who contend with me — take shield and buckler, draw the spear, and say to my soul, I am your salvation! (vv. 1-3). Let his pursuers be shamed, driven like chaff by the angel of the LORD, caught in the net they hid (vv. 4-8).
verseByVerse.theology: Every request is handed to God, and the one thing he asks for himself is a word.

verseByVerse.quote: Contend, O LORD, with those who contend with me; fight against those who fight against me! Take hold of shield and buckler and rise for my help! Draw the spear and javelin against my pursuers! Say to my soul, "I am your salvation!" Let them be put to shame and dishonor who seek after my life! Let them be turned back and disappointed who devise evil against me! Let them be like chaff before the wind, with the angel of the LORD driving them away! Let their way be dark and slippery, with the angel of the LORD pursuing them! For without cause they hid their net for me; without cause they dug a pit for my life. Let destruction come upon him when he does not know it! And let the net that he hid ensnare him; let him fall into it—to his destruction!
verseByVerse.commentary:
Contend, O LORD, with those who contend with me; fight against those who fight against me! Take hold of shield and buckler and rise for my help! Draw the spear and javelin against my pursuers! Say to my soul, I am your salvation!

This is the first sustained prayer against enemies in the Psalter, and there is no point softening it. But read what is actually being asked. Every verb is God's: you contend, you fight, you take the shield, you draw the spear. David has a sword and does not mention it. The whole psalm is a man handing over a case he could have prosecuted himself, which is precisely what the New Testament tells Christians to do: Beloved, never avenge yourselves, but leave it to the wrath of God (Rom 12:19). An imprecatory psalm is not the opposite of loving your enemies; it is what stops you from becoming one.

And notice the one thing he asks for himself: Say to my soul, I am your salvation. Not "destroy them and I will be content" — a word, spoken inwardly, to steady a frightened man. Everything else in the list is about his opponents; the only personal request is for God's voice.

Let them be put to shame and dishonor who seek after my life! ... Let them be like chaff before the wind, with the angel of the LORD driving them away! Let their way be dark and slippery, with the angel of the LORD pursuing them!

The images are borrowed from earlier psalms and turned around. The wicked were chaff in Psalm 1; the angel of the LORD camped protectively round the godly in Psalm 34, and here the same angel is doing the chasing. A dark, slippery road is the exact reverse of the level path he asked for in 26:12 and 27:11.

For without cause they hid their net for me; without cause they dug a pit for my life. Twice without cause — the phrase the psalm will come back to at verse 19, and the phrase Jesus took onto his own lips. The ESV notes that the word pit has been moved between the lines to make sense of a difficult Hebrew text.

Let destruction come upon him when he does not know it! And let the net that he hid ensnare him; let him fall into it — to his destruction! The request is the oldest justice in the Psalter: let the trap work as designed, on the man who set it (7:15; 9:15). He is not asking for a punishment he has invented.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 9–16 — They Repay Me Evil for Good
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: His soul will rejoice and all his bones say, O LORD, who is like you, delivering the poor from him who is too strong for him? (vv. 9-10). Malicious witnesses ask him of things he does not know; they repay me evil for good (vv. 11-12). When they were ill he wore sackcloth, fasted and prayed with his head bowed, mourning as for a brother (vv. 13-14). But at my stumbling they rejoiced and gathered, tearing at him, gnashing their teeth (vv. 15-16). How long, O Lord, will you look on? — and he promises thanks in the great congregation (vv. 17-18).
verseByVerse.theology: The injury is not from strangers: he had nursed these people, and they gathered when he fell.

verseByVerse.quote: Then my soul will rejoice in the LORD, exulting in his salvation. All my bones shall say, "O LORD, who is like you, delivering the poor from him who is too strong for him, the poor and needy from him who robs him?" Malicious witnesses rise up; they ask me of things that I do not know. They repay me evil for good; my soul is bereft. But I, when they were sick— I wore sackcloth; I afflicted myself with fasting; I prayed with head bowed on my chest. I went about as though I grieved for my friend or my brother; as one who laments his mother, I bowed down in mourning. But at my stumbling they rejoiced and gathered; they gathered together against me; wretches whom I did not know tore at me without ceasing; like profane mockers at a feast, they gnash at me with their teeth.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Then my soul will rejoice in the LORD, exulting in his salvation. All my bones shall say, O LORD, who is like you, delivering the poor from him who is too strong for him, the poor and needy from him who robs him?

The purpose of the rescue is worship, and the worship is physical: all my bones shall say. The frame that has been aching with fear will do the praising. And the title he gives God is the one this psalm exists for: the deliverer of people from someone too strong for him. That is the definition of the situation — not an even fight.

Malicious witnesses rise up; they ask me of things that I do not know. They repay me evil for good; my soul is bereft.

The ESV notes the last phrase is literally "it is bereavement to my soul" — he is grieving, as for a death. And now the psalm turns from the general to the wound underneath it, which is not that he is opposed but that he is betrayed.

But I, when they were sick — I wore sackcloth; I afflicted myself with fasting; I prayed with head bowed on my chest. I went about as though I grieved for my friend or my brother; as one who laments his mother, I bowed down in mourning.

Read that slowly. When these people were ill, he fasted for them. He put on mourning clothes and prayed with his head on his chest, and walked around as if the sick man were his own brother, his own mother. The ESV notes that verse 13 may end "my prayer shall turn back" — prayer returning to his own chest unanswered.

But at my stumbling they rejoiced and gathered; they gathered together against me; wretches whom I did not know tore at me without ceasing; like profane mockers at a feast, they gnash at me with their teeth.

And when he stumbled, they threw a party. The word for their gathering is used twice, the way a crowd forms quickly around an accident; people he had never met joined in. The ESV notes the phrase in verse 16 is obscure in Hebrew, but the picture is clear enough: mockery with a festive air.

Anyone who has fasted for someone who later led the campaign against them is holding this psalm by the right handle. The bitterness in it is not petty. It is the specific ache of kindness repaid with pleasure at your fall.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 17–28 — You Have Seen, O LORD
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: How long, O Lord, will you look on? — and he vows thanks in the great congregation (vv. 17-18). Let them not wink the eye who hate me without cause, who devise words of deceit against those who are quiet in the land and cry Aha, Aha! Our eyes have seen it! (vv. 19-21). You have seen, O LORD; be not silent! Vindicate me, and let them not say We have swallowed him up (vv. 22-26). Let those who delight in his righteousness shout, Great is the LORD, who delights in the welfare of his servant! (vv. 27-28).
verseByVerse.theology: Their eyes have seen; God's eyes have seen; the psalm asks the one who sees to speak.

verseByVerse.quote: How long, O Lord, will you look on? Rescue me from their destruction, my precious life from the lions! I will thank you in the great congregation; in the mighty throng I will praise you. Let not those rejoice over me who are wrongfully my foes, and let not those wink the eye who hate me without cause. For they do not speak peace, but against those who are quiet in the land they devise words of deceit. They open wide their mouths against me; they say, "Aha, Aha! Our eyes have seen it!"
verseByVerse.commentary:
How long, O Lord, will you look on? Rescue me from their destruction, my precious life from the lions! I will thank you in the great congregation; in the mighty throng I will praise you.

How long, O Lord, will you look on? is a hard thing to say to God and an honest one: you are watching this. It is the same complaint as 10:1 and 13:1, and the psalm will answer it in verse 22 with the same verb turned into comfort.

And in the middle of the fear, a vow about the future tense: I will thank you in the great congregation. He is planning the testimony before the rescue. Copy that: decide in advance where the story will be told.

Let not those rejoice over me who are wrongfully my foes, and let not those wink the eye who hate me without cause. For they do not speak peace, but against those who are quiet in the land they devise words of deceit. They open wide their mouths against me; they say, Aha, Aha! Our eyes have seen it!

Hate me without cause is the phrase Jesus quoted from this psalm and Psalm 69 about the world's hatred of himself: But the word that is written in their Law must be fulfilled: They hated me without a cause (John 15:25). He said it to prepare his followers for the same treatment. When hostility has no rational cause, it is not a sign that something has gone wrong with your discipleship.

Those who are quiet in the land is a lovely phrase for the people being targeted: not activists or combatants, people going about their business. And Aha, Aha! Our eyes have seen it! is the sound of someone enjoying your disgrace, which the psalm records because God is not squeamish about how ugly this is.

verseByVerse.quote: You have seen, O LORD; be not silent! O Lord, be not far from me! Awake and rouse yourself for my vindication, for my cause, my God and my Lord! Vindicate me, O LORD, my God, according to your righteousness, and let them not rejoice over me! Let them not say in their hearts, "Aha, our heart's desire!" Let them not say, "We have swallowed him up." Let them be put to shame and disappointed altogether who rejoice at my calamity! Let them be clothed with shame and dishonor who magnify themselves against me! Let those who delight in my righteousness shout for joy and be glad and say evermore, "Great is the LORD, who delights in the welfare of his servant!" Then my tongue shall tell of your righteousness and of your praise all the day long.
verseByVerse.commentary:
You have seen, O LORD; be not silent! O Lord, be not far from me! Awake and rouse yourself for my vindication, for my cause, my God and my Lord!

There is the answer to verse 17. They said our eyes have seen it; the psalmist says to God, You have seen. The same seeing, from a different height. Their eyes saw an opportunity; his sees a case.

And the complaint of verse 17 — you are only looking on — has become the ground of the appeal: because you have seen, do not stay silent. Faith does not always resolve the tension between God's watching and God's acting. It leans on the first while asking for the second.

Vindicate me, O LORD, my God, according to your righteousness, and let them not rejoice over me! Let them not say in their hearts, Aha, our heart's desire! Let them not say, We have swallowed him up.

What he cannot bear is the sentence we have swallowed him up — their triumph made permanent, with God seeming to have agreed. And he asks for vindication according to your righteousness, which is to say: judge it properly, not in my favour merely because I am the one praying.

Let those who delight in my righteousness shout for joy and be glad and say evermore, Great is the LORD, who delights in the welfare of his servant! Then my tongue shall tell of your righteousness and of your praise all the day long.

The psalm ends with a sentence it wants shouted, and it is not about David at all: Great is the LORD, who delights in the welfare of his servant. That is what he wants the outcome to prove — not that he was right, but that God takes pleasure in the good of the people who belong to him.

And that is the honest Christian use of a psalm like this. Pray it as it is written: hand the case over, ask God to act and not yourself, ask that the verdict be righteous, and want the result to be a reputation for God rather than a scalp for you. The cross is where hatred without cause did its worst, and where the man praying this kind of prayer said, Father, forgive them.

35.title: Contend with Those Who Contend with Me
35.overview: David asks God to take up his case: contend, fight, take the shield, draw the spear, and say to my soul, I am your salvation (vv. 1-3). Let his pursuers be shamed and driven like chaff, caught in their own net (vv. 4-8), so that his whole body praises the God who delivers the poor from those too strong for them (vv. 9-10). Then the wound underneath: malicious witnesses, evil repaid for good — when they were sick he fasted and mourned for them as for a brother, and when he stumbled they gathered and mocked (vv. 11-16). How long, O Lord, will you look on? (v. 17). They hate him without cause and gloat, Aha! Our eyes have seen it! (vv. 19-21). You have seen, O LORD; be not silent! Vindicate me according to your righteousness (vv. 22-26), and let the end of it be a shout: Great is the LORD, who delights in the welfare of his servant! (vv. 27-28).
35.theology:
Every petition in this imprecation is addressed to God and asks God to act (vv. 1-8, 22-26); the psalmist never lifts a hand. That is exactly the handover the New Testament commands (Rom 12:19), which makes such a psalm the opposite of private revenge.

The only thing he asks for himself is a word: say to my soul, I am your salvation (v. 3).

The injury is betrayal by people he had nursed in their illness (vv. 13-14) — kindness repaid with pleasure at his fall.

Hated without cause (v. 19) is applied by Jesus to himself and used to prepare his followers for groundless hostility (John 15:25).

The complaint that God is merely looking on (v. 17) becomes the ground of the appeal: You have seen ... be not silent (v. 22). And the desired outcome is God's reputation, not the psalmist's: Great is the LORD, who delights in the welfare of his servant (v. 27).
35.examples:
Every verb belongs to God; David's sword is never mentioned.

The one personal request: a word, spoken inwardly.

The angel who camps in Psalm 34 does the chasing here.

He fasted for the people who later gathered to watch him fall.

Grief described as bereavement, because that is what betrayal is.

Their eyes saw an opportunity; God's eyes saw a case.

What he cannot bear: We have swallowed him up.

The shout he wants at the end is about God, not about him.

36.text: To the choirmaster. Of David, the servant of the LORD. 1Transgression speaks to the wicked deep in his heart; there is no fear of God before his eyes.2For he flatters himself in his own eyes that his iniquity cannot be found out and hated.3The words of his mouth are trouble and deceit; he has ceased to act wisely and do good.4He plots trouble while on his bed; he sets himself in a way that is not good; he does not reject evil.5Your steadfast love, O LORD, extends to the heavens, your faithfulness to the clouds.6Your righteousness is like the mountains of God; your judgments are like the great deep; man and beast you save, O LORD.7How precious is your steadfast love, O God! The children of mankind take refuge in the shadow of your wings.8They feast on the abundance of your house, and you give them drink from the river of your delights.9For with you is the fountain of life; in your light do we see light.10Oh, continue your steadfast love to those who know you, and your righteousness to the upright of heart!11Let not the foot of arrogance come upon me, nor the hand of the wicked drive me away.12There the evildoers lie fallen; they are thrust down, unable to rise.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–4 — No Fear of God Before His Eyes
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Transgression speaks to the wicked deep in his heart; there is no fear of God before his eyes (v. 1). He flatters himself that his iniquity will not be found out; his words are trouble and deceit; he has given up doing good, plots trouble on his bed, and does not reject evil (vv. 2-4).
verseByVerse.theology: Four verses inside a man who has stopped fearing God, ending with him lying awake planning.

verseByVerse.quote: Transgression speaks to the wicked deep in his heart; there is no fear of God before his eyes. For he flatters himself in his own eyes that his iniquity cannot be found out and hated. The words of his mouth are trouble and deceit; he has ceased to act wisely and do good. He plots trouble while on his bed; he sets himself in a way that is not good; he does not reject evil.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Transgression speaks to the wicked deep in his heart; there is no fear of God before his eyes.

Sin is given a voice here, and a listener. It speaks, deep down, where nobody else can hear the conversation, and the man has learned to take its advice. (The ESV notes a textual difference: most Hebrew manuscripts read in my heart, which would make it the psalmist reporting an oracle he has received about the wicked. Either way the anatomy is the same.)

The diagnosis is in the second line, and Paul thought it the last word on the human race. He ends his long chain of Old Testament quotations about sin — throats like open graves, feet swift to shed blood — with this verse: There is no fear of God before their eyes (Rom 3:18). Everything else in the list grows out of that one absence. Not hatred of God: no fear of him, in the sense of no reckoning with him, nothing above eye level.

For he flatters himself in his own eyes that his iniquity cannot be found out and hated.

Here is the mechanism. He flatters himself — runs a private public-relations operation in which he always comes out well. And the consequence is that he cannot see his own iniquity clearly enough to hate it. That is the real damage of self-flattery: not that it makes a man vain, but that it blinds him at exactly the point where he would need to see in order to repent.

The words of his mouth are trouble and deceit; he has ceased to act wisely and do good. He plots trouble while on his bed; he sets himself in a way that is not good; he does not reject evil.

Watch the progression, because it is a route more than a character sketch. First the speech goes. Then he ceases to do good — he does not become a monster, he stops doing what he used to do. Then the planning, in bed, in the dark, where a man is alone with his own mind. And finally the settled position: he does not reject evil. Not that he loves it; he has simply stopped saying no to it.

Sixteen psalms ago the same bed was the place a believer was told to lie and be silent before God (4:4). One man lies awake pondering and repents; the other lies awake plotting. The night does not make the difference; what is already in the heart does.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Your steadfast love, O LORD, extends to the heavens, your faithfulness to the clouds. Your righteousness is like the mountains of God; your judgments are like the great deep; man and beast you save, O LORD (vv. 5-6). People take refuge in the shadow of his wings, feast on the abundance of his house and drink from the river of your delights, for with you is the fountain of life; in your light do we see light (vv. 7-9). Continue that love; let no arrogant foot drive him away; the evildoers lie fallen (vv. 10-12).
verseByVerse.theology: Against four verses of a closed heart, five verses of a God whose love has no ceiling.

verseByVerse.quote: Your steadfast love, O LORD, extends to the heavens, your faithfulness to the clouds. Your righteousness is like the mountains of God; your judgments are like the great deep; man and beast you save, O LORD.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Your steadfast love, O LORD, extends to the heavens, your faithfulness to the clouds. Your righteousness is like the mountains of God; your judgments are like the great deep; man and beast you save, O LORD.

The psalm turns without warning, and the effect is deliberate: four verses of a man's cramped interior, and then the sky. Four of God's attributes are measured against the biggest things there are. His covenant love goes up as far as the heavens; his faithfulness reaches the clouds. His righteousness is like the great mountains — immovable, visible from a long way off, older than anyone looking at them. His judgments are like the great deep: unfathomable, and not always comfortable to sail over.

Notice the pairing. Righteousness that you can see and climb; judgments you cannot see the bottom of. Both are God. A believer who only has the mountains will be shocked by the sea, and one who only has the sea will think God arbitrary.

And then the line nobody expects: man and beast you save, O LORD. In the middle of a psalm about human wickedness, God's care takes in the animals. He saves creatures who cannot sin, cannot praise him in words, and will never read this psalm. That single clause tells you something about the reach of his kindness that the four grand comparisons do not.

verseByVerse.quote: How precious is your steadfast love, O God! The children of mankind take refuge in the shadow of your wings. They feast on the abundance of your house, and you give them drink from the river of your delights. For with you is the fountain of life; in your light do we see light.
verseByVerse.commentary:
How precious is your steadfast love, O God! The children of mankind take refuge in the shadow of your wings. They feast on the abundance of your house, and you give them drink from the river of your delights.

The shadow of the wings is the image from Psalm 17, and here the whole human race is invited under them — the children of mankind, not only Israel. And once under there they are not merely safe, they are fed. Feast is a strong word: the same root as the fat portion of a sacrifice. God's hospitality is not rationing.

The river of your delights uses the word Eden — delights, pleasures. There was a river in that garden and there is one at the end of the Bible, the river of the water of life, bright as crystal, flowing from the throne of God and of the Lamb (Rev 22:1). The psalm puts believers drinking from it now.

For with you is the fountain of life; in your light do we see light.

Two of the most quoted phrases in the Psalter, and both are about source rather than supply. God does not have life on hand; he is the fountain of it — the spring, where it comes out of the ground. John writes of the Word, In him was life, and the life was the light of men (John 1:4), and of Jesus, I am the light of the world (John 8:12).

And in your light do we see light is the epistemology of the whole Bible in six words. You do not examine God by some other light and reach a verdict; you see everything else, including yourself, by his. That is exactly what the man in verses 1-4 has lost. He flatters himself in his own eyes because he is looking by his own light, and in that light his iniquity cannot be found. Bring the same man into God's light and he would see it at once.

verseByVerse.quote: Oh, continue your steadfast love to those who know you, and your righteousness to the upright of heart! Let not the foot of arrogance come upon me, nor the hand of the wicked drive me away. There the evildoers lie fallen; they are thrust down, unable to rise.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Oh, continue your steadfast love to those who know you, and your righteousness to the upright of heart! Let not the foot of arrogance come upon me, nor the hand of the wicked drive me away.

After the mountains and the deep, a small and very human request: keep it coming. Continue — he is not asking for a new experience but for the same one tomorrow. And the fear is concrete: a foot on him, a hand shoving him out. Arrogance has a foot in this psalm and a voice in verse 1.

There the evildoers lie fallen; they are thrust down, unable to rise.

The psalm ends abruptly, and in the past tense, as though the psalmist has been shown the end of the story and is pointing at it: there — look, over there, it is done. The man whose sin talked to him in the dark, who flattered himself, who plotted in bed and would not reject evil, is on the ground and cannot get up.

That is the answer to the first four verses, and it is not an argument. It is an outcome. Which is why the middle of the psalm matters most: the difference between the two men is not intelligence or luck but which light they see by, and whose wings they are under.

36.title: In Your Light Do We See Light
36.overview: Sin speaks to the wicked man deep in his heart, and the root of it is that there is no fear of God before his eyes: he flatters himself so that he cannot see his iniquity to hate it, his speech goes bad, he stops doing good, he plots on his bed and refuses to reject evil (vv. 1-4). Then the psalm lifts: God's steadfast love reaches the heavens, his faithfulness the clouds, his righteousness stands like great mountains, his judgments run deep as the sea — man and beast you save, O LORD (vv. 5-6). People shelter under his wings, feast at his house, and drink from the river of his delights, for with you is the fountain of life; in your light do we see light (vv. 7-9). Continue that love, and keep the foot of arrogance off me — there the evildoers lie fallen, unable to rise (vv. 10-12).
36.theology:
The anatomy of a hardened man: sin as a voice he has learned to heed, self-flattery that blinds him to his own iniquity, and a slide from speech to omission to planning to settled acceptance (vv. 1-4). Paul makes v. 1b the conclusion of his case against the race (Rom 3:18) — everything else grows from the absence of the fear of God.

God's attributes are measured against sky, cloud, mountain and sea (vv. 5-6), holding together a righteousness that can be seen and judgments that cannot be fathomed; and his saving care reaches man and beast.

Under his wings the whole human race is offered shelter, feasting and the river of Eden's delights (vv. 7-8; cf. Rev 22:1). He is the fountain of life, not its supplier (John 1:4), and in your light do we see light (v. 9) is the answer to the self-flattery of v. 2: a man who looks by his own light can never find his own sin.
36.examples:
Sin with a voice, and a listener who takes its advice.

Self-flattery's real damage: it blinds you where you would need to see.

He does not turn monstrous; he ceases to do good.

Two men awake in bed — one repenting (4:4), one plotting.

Mountains you can see; a sea you cannot sound.

Man and beast you save — in a psalm about human evil.

The river of Eden's delights, drunk from now.

Six words of epistemology: in your light do we see light.

37.text: Of David. 1Fret not yourself because of evildoers; be not envious of wrongdoers!2For they will soon fade like the grass and wither like the green herb.3Trust in the LORD, and do good; dwell in the land and befriend faithfulness.4Delight yourself in the LORD, and he will give you the desires of your heart.5Commit your way to the LORD; trust in him, and he will act.6He will bring forth your righteousness as the light, and your justice as the noonday.7Be still before the LORD and wait patiently for him; fret not yourself over the one who prospers in his way, over the man who carries out evil devices!8Refrain from anger, and forsake wrath! Fret not yourself; it tends only to evil.9For the evildoers shall be cut off, but those who wait for the LORD shall inherit the land.10In just a little while, the wicked will be no more; though you look carefully at his place, he will not be there.11But the meek shall inherit the land and delight themselves in abundant peace.12The wicked plots against the righteous and gnashes his teeth at him,13but the Lord laughs at the wicked, for he sees that his day is coming.14The wicked draw the sword and bend their bows to bring down the poor and needy, to slay those whose way is upright;15their sword shall enter their own heart, and their bows shall be broken.16Better is the little that the righteous has than the abundance of many wicked.17For the arms of the wicked shall be broken, but the LORD upholds the righteous.18The LORD knows the days of the blameless, and their heritage will remain forever;19they are not put to shame in evil times; in the days of famine they have abundance.20But the wicked will perish; the enemies of the LORD are like the glory of the pastures; they vanish—like smoke they vanish away.21The wicked borrows but does not pay back, but the righteous is generous and gives;22for those blessed by the LORD shall inherit the land, but those cursed by him shall be cut off.23The steps of a man are established by the LORD, when he delights in his way;24though he fall, he shall not be cast headlong, for the LORD upholds his hand.25I have been young, and now am old, yet I have not seen the righteous forsaken or his children begging for bread.26He is ever lending generously, and his children become a blessing.27Turn away from evil and do good; so shall you dwell forever.28For the LORD loves justice; he will not forsake his saints. They are preserved forever, but the children of the wicked shall be cut off.29The righteous shall inherit the land and dwell upon it forever.30The mouth of the righteous utters wisdom, and his tongue speaks justice.31The law of his God is in his heart; his steps do not slip.32The wicked watches for the righteous and seeks to put him to death.33The LORD will not abandon him to his power or let him be condemned when he is brought to trial.34Wait for the LORD and keep his way, and he will exalt you to inherit the land; you will look on when the wicked are cut off.35I have seen a wicked, ruthless man, spreading himself like a green laurel tree.36But he passed away, and behold, he was no more; though I sought him, he could not be found.37Mark the blameless and behold the upright, for there is a future for the man of peace.38But transgressors shall be altogether destroyed; the future of the wicked shall be cut off.39The salvation of the righteous is from the LORD; he is their stronghold in the time of trouble.40The LORD helps them and delivers them; he delivers them from the wicked and saves them, because they take refuge in him.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–11 — Delight Yourself in the LORD
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Fret not yourself because of evildoers; they fade like grass (vv. 1-2). Trust in the LORD, and do good ... Delight yourself in the LORD, and he will give you the desires of your heart. Commit your way to the LORD; trust in him, and he will act (vv. 3-6). Be still before the LORD and wait patiently for him; refrain from anger, for fretting tends only to evil (vv. 7-8). The evildoers will be cut off, but the meek shall inherit the land (vv. 9-11).
verseByVerse.theology: Five commands for a believer watching the wrong people win, and every one of them is about where he puts his attention.

verseByVerse.quote: Fret not yourself because of evildoers; be not envious of wrongdoers! For they will soon fade like the grass and wither like the green herb. Trust in the LORD, and do good; dwell in the land and befriend faithfulness. Delight yourself in the LORD, and he will give you the desires of your heart. Commit your way to the LORD; trust in him, and he will act. He will bring forth your righteousness as the light, and your justice as the noonday.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Fret not yourself because of evildoers; be not envious of wrongdoers! For they will soon fade like the grass and wither like the green herb.

The psalm names the feeling exactly, and it is not anger first — it is envy. Watching people who cut corners do well produces a particular heat in a decent person, and the Hebrew word for fret means precisely that: to get hot. Proverbs gives the same instruction in the same words (Prov 24:19), which is a sign of how universal the problem is.

And the ESV notes the psalm is an acrostic, running through the alphabet by stanzas. This is a poem written to be memorised, because the problem it treats does not go away after one reading.

Trust in the LORD, and do good; dwell in the land and befriend faithfulness. Delight yourself in the LORD, and he will give you the desires of your heart. Commit your way to the LORD; trust in him, and he will act.

Four imperatives, and they are all pointed away from the problem. Trust. Do good. Stay where God has put you — the ESV notes the last phrase may be feed on faithfulness or find safe pasture; graze where it is safe rather than chewing over what the wicked are getting.

Delight yourself in the LORD, and he will give you the desires of your heart is one of the most misquoted verses in the Bible. It is not a promise that God will hand over whatever you want if you are sufficiently religious about asking. Read it as it stands: the delight comes first, and it does something to the desires. A man who delights in God starts wanting different things, and those are the things he is given. That is why the promise is safe to make.

Commit your way is literally to roll it onto him, the way a load is rolled off your own back onto someone stronger. Peter says the same: casting all your anxieties on him, because he cares for you (1 Pet 5:7). And then five words that settle the matter for anyone who has been trying to arrange their own vindication: he will act.

He will bring forth your righteousness as the light, and your justice as the noonday. Not a whispered verdict but daylight. The man who has been misrepresented does not have to publish his own defence; God does the publishing, and he does it at noon.

verseByVerse.quote: Be still before the LORD and wait patiently for him; fret not yourself over the one who prospers in his way, over the man who carries out evil devices! Refrain from anger, and forsake wrath! Fret not yourself; it tends only to evil. For the evildoers shall be cut off, but those who wait for the LORD shall inherit the land. In just a little while, the wicked will be no more; though you look carefully at his place, he will not be there. But the meek shall inherit the land and delight themselves in abundant peace.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Be still before the LORD and wait patiently for him; fret not yourself over the one who prospers in his way, over the man who carries out evil devices! Refrain from anger, and forsake wrath! Fret not yourself; it tends only to evil.

Fret not a second and a third time, and now with a diagnosis attached: it tends only to evil. Fretting does not stay a private discomfort. It sours a man, and then it recruits him — the person most likely to adopt the methods of the wicked is the one who has spent a year seething about how well they work.

And what is prescribed instead is stillness. Be still before the LORD and wait patiently: two of the hardest things asked of anyone in Scripture, and there is no hint that they are passive. Staying still while someone else is being rewarded for dishonesty takes more strength than acting.

For the evildoers shall be cut off, but those who wait for the LORD shall inherit the land. In just a little while, the wicked will be no more; though you look carefully at his place, he will not be there. But the meek shall inherit the land and delight themselves in abundant peace.

Here is the psalm's whole answer, and it is time. In just a little while — not immediately, and not never. The picture in verse 10 is exact and slightly eerie: you will go and look at the place where he was, carefully, and he will not be there. Everyone who lives long enough sees this happen to someone.

And the meek shall inherit the land is the verse Jesus lifted into the Beatitudes, widening the boundary as he did it: Blessed are the meek, for they shall inherit the earth (Matt 5:5). The meek are not the spineless; the word describes people who have stopped grabbing. In the world's accounting they are precisely the ones who will inherit nothing, which is why both the psalm and the sermon have to say it out loud.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 12–26 — Better Is the Little That the Righteous Has
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: The wicked plots and gnashes his teeth, but the Lord laughs at the wicked, for he sees that his day is coming; the sword he drew enters his own heart (vv. 12-15). Better is the little that the righteous has than the abundance of many wicked (v. 16). God knows the days of the blameless and feeds them in famine, while the wicked vanish like smoke (vv. 17-20). The steps of a man are established by the LORD ... though he fall, he shall not be cast headlong (vv. 21-26).
verseByVerse.theology: The comparison is not between two amounts but between two futures.

verseByVerse.quote: The wicked plots against the righteous and gnashes his teeth at him, but the Lord laughs at the wicked, for he sees that his day is coming. The wicked draw the sword and bend their bows to bring down the poor and needy, to slay those whose way is upright; their sword shall enter their own heart, and their bows shall be broken. Better is the little that the righteous has than the abundance of many wicked. For the arms of the wicked shall be broken, but the LORD upholds the righteous. The LORD knows the days of the blameless, and their heritage will remain forever; they are not put to shame in evil times; in the days of famine they have abundance. But the wicked will perish; the enemies of the LORD are like the glory of the pastures; they vanish—like smoke they vanish away.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The wicked plots against the righteous and gnashes his teeth at him, but the Lord laughs at the wicked, for he sees that his day is coming.

The second laugh in the Psalter (see 2:4), and it is not cruelty. God laughs because he can see the calendar. The plotter is working hard on a scheme whose expiry date is already fixed, which from a great enough height is genuinely absurd.

The wicked draw the sword and bend their bows to bring down the poor and needy, to slay those whose way is upright; their sword shall enter their own heart, and their bows shall be broken.

The pit-digger of Psalm 7 again, armed this time. Note who the targets are: the poor and needy. That is almost always who suffers when the unscrupulous do well — not their rivals, the people with the least protection.

Better is the little that the righteous has than the abundance of many wicked. For the arms of the wicked shall be broken, but the LORD upholds the righteous.

The comparison is not between two bank balances. A little with God's upholding is better than an abundance with arms about to break, because the psalm is comparing futures rather than amounts. That is the only honest way this sum works, and the psalm is perfectly aware that today the abundance looks better.

The LORD knows the days of the blameless, and their heritage will remain forever; they are not put to shame in evil times; in the days of famine they have abundance. But the wicked will perish ... they vanish — like smoke they vanish away.

The LORD knows the days: every one of them is on a list he keeps. And again the promise is provision in the famine rather than exemption from it (as at 33:19). Against that, the enemies of God are like smoke — visible, rising, filling the sky, and gone with the first wind.

verseByVerse.quote: The wicked borrows but does not pay back, but the righteous is generous and gives; for those blessed by the LORD shall inherit the land, but those cursed by him shall be cut off. The steps of a man are established by the LORD, when he delights in his way; though he fall, he shall not be cast headlong, for the LORD upholds his hand. I have been young, and now am old, yet I have not seen the righteous forsaken or his children begging for bread. He is ever lending generously, and his children become a blessing.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The wicked borrows but does not pay back, but the righteous is generous and gives ... The steps of a man are established by the LORD, when he delights in his way; though he fall, he shall not be cast headlong, for the LORD upholds his hand.

Two ways with money in one verse, and the contrast is not rich against poor: it is the man who takes and does not return against the man who gives without being asked. Generosity is treated here as evidence of which side of the psalm you are on.

And then a promise for people who are not managing very well. Though he fall — it is assumed he will — he shall not be cast headlong. The picture is of someone stumbling while a stronger hand keeps hold of his: he goes down, and he does not go down face first, because he was never holding himself up in the first place.

I have been young, and now am old, yet I have not seen the righteous forsaken or his children begging for bread. He is ever lending generously, and his children become a blessing.

This verse must be handled honestly or it will wound someone. It is an old man's testimony, not a universal law, and the Bible itself supplies the exceptions: Job on his ash heap, and the believers of Hebrews 11 who were destitute and sawn in two. Scripture does not promise that a godly family never goes hungry.

What David is reporting is the long pattern he has actually watched over a lifetime — that God does not abandon his people, and that generous households tend to be sustained in ways that are hard to explain from the accounts. Taken as a guarantee, the verse is cruel to the faithful poor. Taken as a witness statement from a man with grey hair, it is worth a great deal.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 27–40 — There Is a Future for the Man of Peace
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Turn away from evil and do good, for the LORD loves justice and will not forsake his saints (vv. 27-29). The righteous man's mouth utters wisdom and the law of his God is in his heart (vv. 30-31). Though the wicked watches for him, God will not abandon him at his trial (vv. 32-33). Wait for the LORD and keep his way (v. 34). He saw a ruthless man spreading like a green tree, and then he was gone (vv. 35-36). Mark the blameless ... for there is a future for the man of peace, and the salvation of the righteous is from the LORD (vv. 37-40).
verseByVerse.theology: An old man reports what he has watched happen, twice: the tree that vanished and the righteous who were never abandoned.

verseByVerse.quote: Turn away from evil and do good; so shall you dwell forever. For the LORD loves justice; he will not forsake his saints. They are preserved forever, but the children of the wicked shall be cut off. The righteous shall inherit the land and dwell upon it forever. The mouth of the righteous utters wisdom, and his tongue speaks justice. The law of his God is in his heart; his steps do not slip. The wicked watches for the righteous and seeks to put him to death. The LORD will not abandon him to his power or let him be condemned when he is brought to trial.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Turn away from evil and do good; so shall you dwell forever. For the LORD loves justice; he will not forsake his saints. They are preserved forever, but the children of the wicked shall be cut off.

The command is the same one Psalm 34 gave (34:14), and the reason offered is God's own taste: the LORD loves justice. He is not merely committed to it as a policy; he likes it. That is why injustice will not be allowed to stand, and why the people who practise it are not forsaken.

The mouth of the righteous utters wisdom, and his tongue speaks justice. The law of his God is in his heart; his steps do not slip.

The order runs inward to outward: the law in the heart, and therefore wisdom in the mouth, and therefore steps that hold. The first psalm said the blessed man murmurs God's law day and night; here is what that produces after some years. What a man says under pressure comes out of what he has been storing.

The wicked watches for the righteous and seeks to put him to death. The LORD will not abandon him to his power or let him be condemned when he is brought to trial.

The watching is patient and the intent is lethal, and the psalm does not pretend the trial will not happen. It says the verdict is not theirs to give. When he is brought to trial — so he will be — God will not let the court's word be the last one. Paul asks the same question in a sharper form: Who shall bring any charge against God's elect? It is God who justifies (Rom 8:33).

verseByVerse.quote: Wait for the LORD and keep his way, and he will exalt you to inherit the land; you will look on when the wicked are cut off. I have seen a wicked, ruthless man, spreading himself like a green laurel tree. But he passed away, and behold, he was no more; though I sought him, he could not be found. Mark the blameless and behold the upright, for there is a future for the man of peace. But transgressors shall be altogether destroyed; the future of the wicked shall be cut off. The salvation of the righteous is from the LORD; he is their stronghold in the time of trouble. The LORD helps them and delivers them; he delivers them from the wicked and saves them, because they take refuge in him.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Wait for the LORD and keep his way, and he will exalt you to inherit the land; you will look on when the wicked are cut off.

Waiting again, and paired with activity: keep his way. The waiting is never idleness in this psalm; it is doing the next right thing while the outcome is delayed.

I have seen a wicked, ruthless man, spreading himself like a green laurel tree. But he passed away, and behold, he was no more; though I sought him, he could not be found.

The second thing the old man has watched. The image is of a tree in its own soil, leafy and spreading, obviously thriving — the ESV notes the species is uncertain, which does not matter; what matters is that it was green and it was everywhere. And then the two clauses that are the psalm in miniature: he passed by again, and there was nothing there. He went looking, and could not find him.

Mark the blameless and behold the upright, for there is a future for the man of peace. But transgressors shall be altogether destroyed; the future of the wicked shall be cut off.

The word that carries the ending is future. It is not that the righteous man has a better present — the psalm has admitted all along that he often does not. He has an after. And the thing the wicked man lacks is not comfort or success but a tomorrow that belongs to him.

The salvation of the righteous is from the LORD; he is their stronghold in the time of trouble. The LORD helps them and delivers them; he delivers them from the wicked and saves them, because they take refuge in him.

The last verse gives the only qualification in forty verses of instruction: because they take refuge in him. Not because they managed not to fret, or waited well, or never envied anyone. The psalm's commands are real and none of them is the ground of the rescue. Refuge is.

37.title: Fret Not Yourself
37.overview: An acrostic wisdom poem for the believer watching dishonest people do well. Three times: fret not yourself — they fade like grass (vv. 1-2, 7-8). Instead: trust, do good, stay put, delight yourself in the LORD, roll your way onto him, and he will act and bring your righteousness out like noonday (vv. 3-6). In a little while the wicked will not be there, and the meek shall inherit the land (vv. 9-11). God laughs at the plotter because he can see his day coming; the drawn sword enters his own heart (vv. 12-15). Better a little with God than abundance without him (vv. 16-20). The righteous give, their steps are established, and though they fall they are not cast headlong (vv. 21-26). An old man testifies that he has not seen the righteous forsaken (v. 25), and that he watched a ruthless man spread like a green tree and then vanish (vv. 35-36). There is a future for the man of peace, and salvation comes from the LORD, to those who take refuge in him (vv. 27-40).
37.theology:
The answer to prospering wickedness is time: in just a little while (v. 10), and there is a future for the man of peace (v. 37). The righteous man is not promised a better present; he is promised an after.

Fretting is diagnosed as dangerous, not merely unpleasant — it tends only to evil (v. 8): envy of the wicked eventually recruits.

Verse 4 is not a promise that God grants wishes; delight in God reshapes the desires he then satisfies. Commit your way (v. 5) is to roll a load onto someone stronger (cf. 1 Pet 5:7), and vindication is God's to publish (v. 6).

Jesus took the meek shall inherit the land into the Beatitudes and widened it to the earth (v. 11; Matt 5:5).

Verse 25 is an old man's testimony, not a universal law — Job and Heb 11:37 stand beside it — and the psalm's own last word gives the ground of rescue: because they take refuge in him (v. 40).
37.examples:
Fret: a word for heating yourself up.

Envy of the cheerful cheat, named before anger.

Delight first, and the desires change.

Rolling the load onto someone stronger.

Your righteousness published at noon.

Go and look at his place carefully: he is not there.

He falls, and does not fall face first.

The green tree that could not be found again.

38.text: A Psalm of David, for the memorial offering. 1O LORD, rebuke me not in your anger, nor discipline me in your wrath!2For your arrows have sunk into me, and your hand has come down on me.3There is no soundness in my flesh because of your indignation; there is no health in my bones because of my sin.4For my iniquities have gone over my head; like a heavy burden, they are too heavy for me.5My wounds stink and fester because of my foolishness,6I am utterly bowed down and prostrate; all the day I go about mourning.7For my sides are filled with burning, and there is no soundness in my flesh.8I am feeble and crushed; I groan because of the tumult of my heart.9O Lord, all my longing is before you; my sighing is not hidden from you.10My heart throbs; my strength fails me, and the light of my eyes—it also has gone from me.11My friends and companions stand aloof from my plague, and my nearest kin stand far off.12Those who seek my life lay their snares; those who seek my hurt speak of ruin and meditate treachery all day long.13But I am like a deaf man; I do not hear, like a mute man who does not open his mouth.14I have become like a man who does not hear, and in whose mouth are no rebukes.15But for you, O LORD, do I wait; it is you, O Lord my God, who will answer.16For I said, "Only let them not rejoice over me, who boast against me when my foot slips!"17For I am ready to fall, and my pain is ever before me.18I confess my iniquity; I am sorry for my sin.19But my foes are vigorous, they are mighty, and many are those who hate me wrongfully.20Those who render me evil for good accuse me because I follow after good.21Do not forsake me, O LORD! O my God, be not far from me!22Make haste to help me, O Lord, my salvation!

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–8 — No Soundness in My Flesh
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: O LORD, rebuke me not in your anger: God's arrows have sunk in and his hand has come down (vv. 1-2). There is no soundness in my flesh ... no health in my bones because of my sin; his iniquities have gone over his head like a load too heavy to lift, his wounds stink and fester, he is bowed down and mourning all day (vv. 3-8).
verseByVerse.theology: Sickness, guilt and grief described together, with nothing tidied up and nothing hidden from God.

verseByVerse.quote: O LORD, rebuke me not in your anger, nor discipline me in your wrath! For your arrows have sunk into me, and your hand has come down on me. There is no soundness in my flesh because of your indignation; there is no health in my bones because of my sin. For my iniquities have gone over my head; like a heavy burden, they are too heavy for me. My wounds stink and fester because of my foolishness, I am utterly bowed down and prostrate; all the day I go about mourning. For my sides are filled with burning, and there is no soundness in my flesh. I am feeble and crushed; I groan because of the tumult of my heart.
verseByVerse.commentary:
A Psalm of David, for the memorial offering.

The heading points to a particular rite: a handful of the grain offering was burned as a memorial portion, to bring the worshipper to God's remembrance (Lev 2:2). This psalm is that handful, put into words. A man who cannot get to the altar sends up his condition instead.

O LORD, rebuke me not in your anger, nor discipline me in your wrath! For your arrows have sunk into me, and your hand has come down on me.

The opening line is word for word the opening of Psalm 6. Again he does not ask to be let off the correction, only that it not come in anger. And he does not pretend about the source: God's arrows, God's hand. It is a braver theology than blaming circumstances.

There is no soundness in my flesh because of your indignation; there is no health in my bones because of my sin. For my iniquities have gone over my head; like a heavy burden, they are too heavy for me. My wounds stink and fester because of my foolishness.

The psalm makes a connection modern readers flinch at, and it should be handled carefully. It does not teach that every illness is punishment for a particular sin — Job settles that, and so does Jesus at John 9:3. But it does insist that this man's own sin and this man's own state are connected, and he is the one saying so. There is a kind of suffering that we bring on ourselves, and pretending otherwise helps nobody.

Two images carry the guilt. It has gone over my head, like water closing above a man who cannot touch the bottom. And it is a heavy burden ... too heavy for me: guilt as freight. Anyone who has carried something unconfessed knows both sensations, the drowning and the weight.

I am utterly bowed down and prostrate; all the day I go about mourning. For my sides are filled with burning ... I am feeble and crushed; I groan because of the tumult of my heart.

This is the most unsparing description of a body in the Psalter — infected wounds, fever, exhaustion, a heart in uproar. Scripture is not squeamish, and it does not require a sufferer to be presentable before praying.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 9–22 — But for You, O LORD, Do I Wait
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: All my longing is before you; my sighing is not hidden from you, though his heart throbs and the light of his eyes has gone (vv. 9-10). His friends stand aloof from his plague and his family at a distance, while his enemies lay snares and plot all day (vv. 11-12). But I am like a deaf man; I do not hear, like a mute man who does not open his mouth (vv. 13-14). But for you, O LORD, do I wait; it is you, O Lord my God, who will answer (vv. 15-17). I confess my iniquity; I am sorry for my sin, while strong enemies hate him for following good (vv. 18-20). Do not forsake me ... Make haste to help me, O Lord, my salvation! (vv. 21-22).
verseByVerse.theology: He will not defend himself, confesses what is true, and ends still waiting.

verseByVerse.quote: O Lord, all my longing is before you; my sighing is not hidden from you. My heart throbs; my strength fails me, and the light of my eyes—it also has gone from me. My friends and companions stand aloof from my plague, and my nearest kin stand far off. Those who seek my life lay their snares; those who seek my hurt speak of ruin and meditate treachery all day long. But I am like a deaf man; I do not hear, like a mute man who does not open his mouth. I have become like a man who does not hear, and in whose mouth are no rebukes.
verseByVerse.commentary:
O Lord, all my longing is before you; my sighing is not hidden from you. My heart throbs; my strength fails me, and the light of my eyes — it also has gone from me.

In the middle of the catalogue, one restful sentence. He cannot explain himself; he does not have to. All my longing is before you — the wanting he cannot put into a request is already laid out in God's sight, and the sighing that is not even words has been heard. For anyone too ill or too low to pray properly, this verse is the whole permission slip.

My friends and companions stand aloof from my plague, and my nearest kin stand far off. Those who seek my life lay their snares; those who seek my hurt speak of ruin and meditate treachery all day long.

Two circles, and both fail him. The people who love him keep their distance — from my plague, which is honest about why: illness frightens people, and the visibly sick are left alone in every century. And the people who hate him move closer, because a man who is down is easier to finish.

But I am like a deaf man; I do not hear, like a mute man who does not open his mouth. I have become like a man who does not hear, and in whose mouth are no rebukes.

And here is his response to the whispering: nothing. He does not answer, does not defend himself, does not return the rebukes he could easily make. Isaiah described the Servant the same way — like a lamb that is led to the slaughter ... so he opened not his mouth (Isa 53:7) — and at the trial, questioned at length by Herod, Jesus made no answer (Luke 23:9), so that Peter could tell suffering Christians that when he was reviled, he did not revile in return (1 Pet 2:23).

Silence under accusation is not weakness. It is what a man can afford when he has handed the case to someone else.

verseByVerse.quote: But for you, O LORD, do I wait; it is you, O Lord my God, who will answer. For I said, "Only let them not rejoice over me, who boast against me when my foot slips!" For I am ready to fall, and my pain is ever before me. I confess my iniquity; I am sorry for my sin. But my foes are vigorous, they are mighty, and many are those who hate me wrongfully. Those who render me evil for good accuse me because I follow after good. Do not forsake me, O LORD! O my God, be not far from me! Make haste to help me, O Lord, my salvation!
verseByVerse.commentary:
But for you, O LORD, do I wait; it is you, O Lord my God, who will answer.

There is the reason for the silence. He is not answering them because he is waiting for someone else to answer — and notice the confidence: not might answer. God will speak, and until he does, the psalmist has nothing to add.

For I said, Only let them not rejoice over me, who boast against me when my foot slips! For I am ready to fall, and my pain is ever before me.

I am ready to fall is a candid thing for a king to write. He is not steady, he knows it, and his pain never leaves the front of his mind. And his one fear about it is that his fall would give his enemies a celebration.

I confess my iniquity; I am sorry for my sin.

Eight words, with no excuses attached, no explanation of circumstances, no comparison with anyone worse. This is the sentence Psalm 32 spent four verses avoiding before it was finally said. Everything else in the psalm is description; this is the turn.

But my foes are vigorous, they are mighty, and many are those who hate me wrongfully. Those who render me evil for good accuse me because I follow after good.

Two things are true at once, and the psalm holds them without blending them. He is genuinely guilty before God (v. 18) and genuinely wronged by men (vv. 19-20). Confession does not oblige a man to accept every accusation, and being sinned against does not cancel his own sin. Most real situations are exactly this mixed.

Do not forsake me, O LORD! O my God, be not far from me! Make haste to help me, O Lord, my salvation!

The psalm ends there. No rescue is reported, no health returns, the friends are still at a distance. The last three lines are pure asking — do not leave, do not stay far off, hurry — and the final word is the one thing he is sure of: my salvation. Some prayers end without answers, and are still prayed by people who know whose they are.

38.title: I Confess My Iniquity
38.overview: A psalm for the memorial offering. God's arrows have sunk into him and his hand has come down: there is no soundness in his flesh or health in his bones, his iniquities have gone over his head like water and weigh on him like freight, his wounds stink and fester, he is bowed down and mourning all day (vv. 1-8). All his longing is before God and his sighing is not hidden (vv. 9-10). His friends stand aloof from his plague and his family at a distance, while his enemies lay snares (vv. 11-12). He answers nothing, like a deaf and mute man, because for you, O LORD, do I wait (vv. 13-15). I confess my iniquity; I am sorry for my sin — and yet his foes hate him wrongfully (vv. 16-20). The psalm ends still asking: do not forsake me, do not be far, make haste (vv. 21-22).
38.theology:
The psalm ties this man's illness to his own sin (vv. 3, 5, 18) without teaching that all sickness is punishment — Job and John 9:3 forbid the generalisation — and without pretending that self-inflicted suffering is anything else.

Guilt is pictured as water over the head and as a load too heavy to lift (v. 4).

Prayer does not require composure: all my longing is before you; my sighing is not hidden from you (v. 9).

His silence under accusation (vv. 13-14) is possible because the case is in other hands (v. 15), and it prefigures the Servant who opened not his mouth (Isa 53:7; Luke 23:9; 1 Pet 2:23).

Real guilt before God and real injury from men stand side by side without cancelling each other (vv. 18-20), and the psalm closes unanswered, holding on to my salvation (v. 22).
38.examples:
A handful of grain burned to bring a man to remembrance — here, in words.

God's arrows named as God's, not blamed on circumstances.

Guilt as water closing over the head, and as freight.

Friends keeping their distance from my plague.

The sighing that is not words, already heard.

Deaf and mute under accusation — and why he can afford it.

Eight words of confession with nothing attached.

A prayer that ends without an answer.

39.text: To the choirmaster: to Jeduthun. A Psalm of David. 1I said, "I will guard my ways, that I may not sin with my tongue; I will guard my mouth with a muzzle, so long as the wicked are in my presence."2I was mute and silent; I held my peace to no avail, and my distress grew worse.3My heart became hot within me. As I mused, the fire burned; then I spoke with my tongue:4"O LORD, make me know my end and what is the measure of my days; let me know how fleeting I am!5Behold, you have made my days a few handbreadths, and my lifetime is as nothing before you. Surely all mankind stands as a mere breath! Selah6Surely a man goes about as a shadow! Surely for nothing they are in turmoil; man heaps up wealth and does not know who will gather!7"And now, O Lord, for what do I wait? My hope is in you.8Deliver me from all my transgressions. Do not make me the scorn of the fool!9I am mute; I do not open my mouth, for it is you who have done it.10Remove your stroke from me; I am spent by the hostility of your hand.11When you discipline a man with rebukes for sin, you consume like a moth what is dear to him; surely all mankind is a mere breath! Selah12"Hear my prayer, O LORD, and give ear to my cry; hold not your peace at my tears! For I am a sojourner with you, a guest, like all my fathers.13Look away from me, that I may smile again, before I depart and am no more!"

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–6 — Let Me Know How Fleeting I Am
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: I will guard my ways, that I may not sin with my tongue; I will guard my mouth with a muzzle — but the silence made his distress worse until the fire burned and he spoke (vv. 1-3). O LORD, make me know my end and what is the measure of my days; let me know how fleeting I am! His days are a few handbreadths, all mankind a mere breath, a man going about as a shadow, heaping up wealth without knowing who will gather it (vv. 4-6).
verseByVerse.theology: A man who muzzles himself and boils over, and whose first request when he speaks is to be told how short his life is.

verseByVerse.quote: I said, "I will guard my ways, that I may not sin with my tongue; I will guard my mouth with a muzzle, so long as the wicked are in my presence." I was mute and silent; I held my peace to no avail, and my distress grew worse. My heart became hot within me. As I mused, the fire burned; then I spoke with my tongue:
verseByVerse.commentary:
