I said, I will guard my ways, that I may not sin with my tongue; I will guard my mouth with a muzzle, so long as the wicked are in my presence. I was mute and silent; I held my peace to no avail, and my distress grew worse. My heart became hot within me. As I mused, the fire burned; then I spoke with my tongue.

The resolution is a good one and it fails. He decided not to complain in front of people who would make something of it — a wise instinct, and one many believers have adopted in a hostile workplace or family. He put a muzzle on his mouth, which is the word for the strap over an animal's jaws.

And what happened was not peace. My distress grew worse. The heat built up with nowhere to go until it caught fire, and then he spoke anyway. The psalm is honest about something religious people rarely admit: bottling it up is not the same as trusting God, and silence that is only suppression eventually blows.

What matters is who he finally speaks to. He does not turn on the wicked; he turns to God, which is what he should have done in verse 1.

verseByVerse.quote: "O LORD, make me know my end and what is the measure of my days; let me know how fleeting I am! Behold, you have made my days a few handbreadths, and my lifetime is as nothing before you. Surely all mankind stands as a mere breath! Selah Surely a man goes about as a shadow! Surely for nothing they are in turmoil; man heaps up wealth and does not know who will gather!
verseByVerse.commentary:
O LORD, make me know my end and what is the measure of my days; let me know how fleeting I am!

Of all the things a man might ask for after months of pent-up frustration, this is not the obvious one. He asks to be shown how short his life is — and he asks for it as a favour. Most of us spend real effort not thinking about this. He wants it put in front of him, because a man who knows the length of his life stops taking certain things so seriously, including the prosperity of the wicked that had him fuming in verse 1.

Behold, you have made my days a few handbreadths, and my lifetime is as nothing before you. Surely all mankind stands as a mere breath!

A handbreadth is the width of four fingers — the shortest measure they had. Hold up your hand: that is the scale. And a mere breath is the word Ecclesiastes repeats, a puff of vapour on a cold morning, there and gone. James says the same to people planning next year's business: What is your life? For you are a mist that appears for a little time and then vanishes (Jas 4:14).

Surely a man goes about as a shadow! Surely for nothing they are in turmoil; man heaps up wealth and does not know who will gather!

Two pictures of futility, and the second has teeth. A man spends decades accumulating and has no idea whose hands it will end up in. Jesus told a story about exactly that — the barn-builder whose soul was required that night, and the question the things you have prepared, whose will they be? (Luke 12:20). The psalm is not saying work is pointless. It is saying that turmoil over possessions is, when the possessor lasts a handbreadth.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 7–13 — For What Do I Wait?
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: And now, O Lord, for what do I wait? My hope is in you (v. 7). Deliver me, and do not make me the fool's joke (v. 8). I am mute; I do not open my mouth, for it is you who have done it; remove your stroke (vv. 9-11). Hear my prayer, O LORD ... For I am a sojourner with you, a guest, like all my fathers (v. 12). Look away from me, that I may smile again, before I depart and am no more! (v. 13).
verseByVerse.theology: The second silence is submission, not suppression — and the psalm ends by asking God to look somewhere else.

verseByVerse.quote: "And now, O Lord, for what do I wait? My hope is in you. Deliver me from all my transgressions. Do not make me the scorn of the fool! I am mute; I do not open my mouth, for it is you who have done it. Remove your stroke from me; I am spent by the hostility of your hand. When you discipline a man with rebukes for sin, you consume like a moth what is dear to him; surely all mankind is a mere breath! Selah
verseByVerse.commentary:
And now, O Lord, for what do I wait? My hope is in you.

The question is asked and answered in the same breath, and it is the turn of the psalm. If life is that short and wealth that uncertain, what is left to hope in? Nothing that can be heaped up. My hope is in you is not a pious add-on here; it is the only surviving option after verses 4-6.

Deliver me from all my transgressions. Do not make me the scorn of the fool! He takes his own sin to God first, before his circumstances — and then admits an ordinary fear: being laughed at by people whose opinion he does not even respect.

I am mute; I do not open my mouth, for it is you who have done it.

He is silent again, and this time it is a different silence. In verse 2 he was muzzled and boiling; here he is quiet because he has seen God's hand in what has happened. The first silence was suppression and it failed. The second is submission, and it holds. That is the difference between not saying something because you dare not and not saying it because you have understood who is at work.

Remove your stroke from me; I am spent by the hostility of your hand. When you discipline a man with rebukes for sin, you consume like a moth what is dear to him.

Submission does not stop him asking for the discipline to end. And the image of the moth is dreadfully exact: not a fire that destroys everything at once, but something small working quietly in the dark on the things a man values, until he takes the coat out of the cupboard and finds it ruined.

verseByVerse.quote: "Hear my prayer, O LORD, and give ear to my cry; hold not your peace at my tears! For I am a sojourner with you, a guest, like all my fathers. Look away from me, that I may smile again, before I depart and am no more!"
verseByVerse.commentary:
Hear my prayer, O LORD, and give ear to my cry; hold not your peace at my tears! For I am a sojourner with you, a guest, like all my fathers.

He asks God not to be silent, having just been silent himself, and gives a reason to stop on: I am a sojourner with you, a guest. Jacob said the same to Pharaoh — the days of the years of my sojourning (Gen 47:9) — and Hebrews says of all the patriarchs that they acknowledged that they were strangers and exiles on the earth (Heb 11:13).

In that world a resident alien had no land and no standing, and depended entirely on a host's protection. That is his argument: I am your guest, and a guest is the host's responsibility. The man who has just measured his life in handbreadths is claiming the one status that gives a temporary creature a permanent claim on a permanent God.

Look away from me, that I may smile again, before I depart and am no more!

And the psalm ends there — with the strangest request in the Psalter. Everyone else asks God to turn his face towards them. This man asks him to look away, because at present God's gaze is the pressure that is crushing him. Job said it twice in the same mood (Job 7:19; 14:6).

Scripture prints it without comment, which is itself a mercy. There are seasons when a believer's honest prayer is not draw near but ease off, and the Bible does not edit them out or scold the man who prays that way. He is still praying, still calling God his host, still hoping in him (v. 7). And the God who was asked to look away is the one who, in the end, looked at his own Son instead.

39.title: A Sojourner with You
39.overview: David muzzles his mouth in front of the wicked, and the silence makes things worse until the fire burns and he speaks (vv. 1-3). What he asks for is startling: let me know how fleeting I am — days a few handbreadths wide, all mankind a mere breath, a man walking about as a shadow and heaping up wealth without knowing who will get it (vv. 4-6). And now, O Lord, for what do I wait? My hope is in you (v. 7). He asks deliverance from his transgressions, is silent again — this time because God has done it — and asks that the stroke be lifted, since God consumes like a moth what a man treasures (vv. 8-11). I am a sojourner with you, a guest, like all my fathers (v. 12). And it ends: Look away from me, that I may smile again, before I depart and am no more! (v. 13).
39.theology:
Suppressed silence is not the same as trust: the muzzle made the distress worse (vv. 1-3). The second silence, in v. 9, is different — submission to a hand he has recognised — and it holds.

Mortality is requested as a mercy (v. 4; cf. 90:12): a man who knows his life is four fingers wide stops fretting over the prosperity that had him boiling in v. 1. Wealth outlives the one who heaps it (v. 6; Luke 12:20; Jas 4:14).

Submission and petition coexist: he still asks for the discipline to end (v. 10), and God's dealing is pictured as a moth quietly ruining what is dear (v. 11).

His claim on God is guest-right: a sojourner has no standing except his host's (v. 12; Gen 47:9; Heb 11:13). And Scripture prints his last request — look away from me — without rebuke (v. 13; cf. Job 7:19).
39.examples:
A muzzle, and the fire it fed.

Asking to be shown the length of your own life, as a favour.

Four fingers wide: hold up your hand.

Heaping up what somebody else will gather.

Two silences: one that blew, one that held.

God as a moth in the wardrobe.

Guest-right: the temporary creature's claim on a permanent host.

The prayer that asks God to look somewhere else.

40.text: To the choirmaster. A Psalm of David. 1I waited patiently for the LORD; he inclined to me and heard my cry.2He drew me up from the pit of destruction, out of the miry bog, and set my feet upon a rock, making my steps secure.3He put a new song in my mouth, a song of praise to our God. Many will see and fear, and put their trust in the LORD.4Blessed is the man who makes the LORD his trust, who does not turn to the proud, to those who go astray after a lie!5You have multiplied, O LORD my God, your wondrous deeds and your thoughts toward us; none can compare with you! I will proclaim and tell of them, yet they are more than can be told.6In sacrifice and offering you have not delighted, but you have given me an open ear. Burnt offering and sin offering you have not required.7Then I said, "Behold, I have come; in the scroll of the book it is written of me:8I delight to do your will, O my God; your law is within my heart."9I have told the glad news of deliverance in the great congregation; behold, I have not restrained my lips, as you know, O LORD.10I have not hidden your deliverance within my heart; I have spoken of your faithfulness and your salvation; I have not concealed your steadfast love and your faithfulness from the great congregation.11As for you, O LORD, you will not restrain your mercy from me; your steadfast love and your faithfulness will ever preserve me!12For evils have encompassed me beyond number; my iniquities have overtaken me, and I cannot see; they are more than the hairs of my head; my heart fails me.13Be pleased, O LORD, to deliver me! O LORD, make haste to help me!14Let those be put to shame and disappointed altogether who seek to snatch away my life; let those be turned back and brought to dishonor who delight in my hurt!15Let those be appalled because of their shame who say to me, "Aha, Aha!"16But may all who seek you rejoice and be glad in you; may those who love your salvation say continually, "Great is the LORD!"17As for me, I am poor and needy, but the Lord takes thought for me. You are my help and my deliverer; do not delay, O my God!

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–5 — He Drew Me Up from the Pit
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: I waited patiently for the LORD; he inclined to me and heard my cry. He drew me up from the pit of destruction, out of the miry bog, and set my feet upon a rock, making my steps secure. He put a new song in my mouth, so that many will see and trust him (vv. 1-3). Blessed is the man who makes the LORD his trust; God's wondrous deeds are more than can be told (vv. 4-5).
verseByVerse.theology: A man hauled out of mud onto rock, given a song that turns out to be for other people.

verseByVerse.quote: I waited patiently for the LORD; he inclined to me and heard my cry. He drew me up from the pit of destruction, out of the miry bog, and set my feet upon a rock, making my steps secure. He put a new song in my mouth, a song of praise to our God. Many will see and fear, and put their trust in the LORD. Blessed is the man who makes the LORD his trust, who does not turn to the proud, to those who go astray after a lie! You have multiplied, O LORD my God, your wondrous deeds and your thoughts toward us; none can compare with you! I will proclaim and tell of them, yet they are more than can be told.
verseByVerse.commentary:
I waited patiently for the LORD; he inclined to me and heard my cry. He drew me up from the pit of destruction, out of the miry bog, and set my feet upon a rock, making my steps secure.

Everything is in the mud. He is not in a prison or a battle but a miry bog — the particular horror of which is that there is nothing to push against. A man in mud who struggles goes down faster. That is why the psalm opens with waiting: not because waiting is noble, but because it was the only thing left to do.

And the rescue is entirely God's: he inclined, he heard, he drew up, he set, he made secure. Five verbs, none of them the psalmist's. From mud that gives way to rock that does not — and then, precisely, making my steps secure: not carried, walking.

He put a new song in my mouth, a song of praise to our God. Many will see and fear, and put their trust in the LORD.

A new rescue calls for new words; the old repertoire will not carry what he now knows. And notice what the song is for. Many will see — they watch a man who was in the bog standing on rock and singing, and the result is that they trust God. Your testimony is not only yours.

Blessed is the man who makes the LORD his trust, who does not turn to the proud, to those who go astray after a lie! You have multiplied, O LORD my God, your wondrous deeds and your thoughts toward us; none can compare with you! I will proclaim and tell of them, yet they are more than can be told.

Two things God has multiplied: his deeds, and his thoughts toward us. The first is history; the second is attention. And the man who has just been given a song admits he cannot finish it — there is more material than he can get through, which is the happiest defeat in the Psalter.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: In sacrifice and offering you have not delighted, but you have given me an open ear (v. 6). Then I said, Behold, I have come; in the scroll of the book it is written of me: I delight to do your will, O my God; your law is within my heart (vv. 7-8). He has told the glad news in the great congregation and has not concealed God's steadfast love (vv. 9-10).
verseByVerse.theology: The verses Hebrews puts in the mouth of Christ as he comes into the world.

verseByVerse.quote: In sacrifice and offering you have not delighted, but you have given me an open ear. Burnt offering and sin offering you have not required. Then I said, "Behold, I have come; in the scroll of the book it is written of me: I delight to do your will, O my God; your law is within my heart."
verseByVerse.commentary:
In sacrifice and offering you have not delighted, but you have given me an open ear. Burnt offering and sin offering you have not required.

This is not an attack on the sacrificial system God himself commanded. It is the prophets' point: God never wanted the animals for their own sake. To obey is better than sacrifice, Samuel told Saul (1 Sam 15:22). What he wants is the man.

And the middle phrase is remarkable. The ESV notes the Hebrew is "ears you have dug for me" — hollowed out, opened, the way you would dig a channel. God does not merely ask for obedience; he excavates the hearing that makes obedience possible.

When this verse was translated into Greek, some centuries before Christ, it came out as a body have you prepared for me — an interpretation rather than a word-for-word rendering, taking the part for the whole: the opened ear stands for the whole prepared person. And that is the form the letter to the Hebrews quotes.

Then I said, Behold, I have come; in the scroll of the book it is written of me: I delight to do your will, O my God; your law is within my heart.

Hebrews puts these words into the mouth of Christ at the incarnation: Consequently, when Christ came into the world, he said, Sacrifices and offerings you have not desired, but a body have you prepared for me ... Behold, I have come to do your will, O God, as it is written of me in the scroll of the book (Heb 10:5-7). And it draws the conclusion: He does away with the first in order to establish the second. And by that will we have been sanctified through the offering of the body of Jesus Christ once for all (Heb 10:9-10).

So the psalm's I delight to do your will — true enough of David, and truer of nobody else who ever said it — becomes the sentence that ends the animals. The body prepared was offered, once, and the thing all those sacrifices pointed at arrived. In the scroll of the book it is written of me: Jesus told his disciples the same on the Emmaus road, that everything written about him in the Law and the Prophets and the Psalms had to be fulfilled (Luke 24:44).

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 9–17 — I Am Poor and Needy
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: He has told the glad news in the great congregation and has not concealed God's steadfast love (vv. 9-10). God's mercy, steadfast love and faithfulness preserve him — and yet my iniquities have overtaken me ... they are more than the hairs of my head (vv. 11-12). Be pleased, O LORD, to deliver me! Let those who seek his life be shamed and those who seek God rejoice (vv. 13-16). As for me, I am poor and needy, but the Lord takes thought for me (v. 17).
verseByVerse.theology: The psalm of the new song ends in the mud again, and the last word is that God is thinking about him.

verseByVerse.quote: I have told the glad news of deliverance in the great congregation; behold, I have not restrained my lips, as you know, O LORD. I have not hidden your deliverance within my heart; I have spoken of your faithfulness and your salvation; I have not concealed your steadfast love and your faithfulness from the great congregation. As for you, O LORD, you will not restrain your mercy from me; your steadfast love and your faithfulness will ever preserve me! For evils have encompassed me beyond number; my iniquities have overtaken me, and I cannot see; they are more than the hairs of my head; my heart fails me.
verseByVerse.commentary:
I have told the glad news of deliverance in the great congregation; behold, I have not restrained my lips, as you know, O LORD. I have not hidden your deliverance within my heart; I have spoken of your faithfulness and your salvation; I have not concealed your steadfast love and your faithfulness from the great congregation.

Four times he says what he has not done: not restrained, not hidden, not concealed. The repetition is the point — his temptation was to keep it in, and he names the refusal four ways. The ESV notes that deliverance here is literally righteousness: what he has been publishing is not merely that he got out of the bog but that God is right.

As for you, O LORD, you will not restrain your mercy from me; your steadfast love and your faithfulness will ever preserve me! He has not restrained his lips; God will not restrain his mercy. The same verb, turned round.

For evils have encompassed me beyond number; my iniquities have overtaken me, and I cannot see; they are more than the hairs of my head; my heart fails me.

And then, in the middle of a thanksgiving psalm, the ground opens again. This is not a different psalm badly joined on; it is what actually happens. A man can be genuinely rescued, genuinely singing the new song in public, and find his sins catching up with him so that he cannot see straight.

My iniquities have overtaken me — they ran after him and caught him. He counts them the way Psalm 139 counts God's thoughts, and finds they outnumber the hairs on his head. Whoever thought that being rescued once settles the question of sin has not read verse 12.

verseByVerse.quote: Be pleased, O LORD, to deliver me! O LORD, make haste to help me! Let those be put to shame and disappointed altogether who seek to snatch away my life; let those be turned back and brought to dishonor who delight in my hurt! Let those be appalled because of their shame who say to me, "Aha, Aha!" But may all who seek you rejoice and be glad in you; may those who love your salvation say continually, "Great is the LORD!" As for me, I am poor and needy, but the Lord takes thought for me. You are my help and my deliverer; do not delay, O my God!
verseByVerse.commentary:
Be pleased, O LORD, to deliver me! O LORD, make haste to help me! Let those be put to shame and disappointed altogether who seek to snatch away my life ... But may all who seek you rejoice and be glad in you; may those who love your salvation say continually, Great is the LORD!

These five verses appear again, almost word for word, as Psalm 70. The Psalter is happy to print the same prayer twice, in different settings — here as the last movement of a thanksgiving, there on its own as an emergency call. A prayer that worked once deserves to be known by heart.

And the request is even-handed: shame for those hunting him, gladness for everyone seeking God. He is not asking for a private rescue but for the right outcome all round, and what he wants people saying is not his name but Great is the LORD!

As for me, I am poor and needy, but the Lord takes thought for me. You are my help and my deliverer; do not delay, O my God!

The psalm that began with a man being hauled out of a bog ends with him poor and needy and still asking. The middle of it holds the words Christ said when he came into the world. That is the shape of the Christian life: a rescue behind you, a Saviour who delighted to do God's will in your place, and a present condition that still requires the sentence do not delay.

And the best five words in the psalm are the quietest: the Lord takes thought for me. Not only acts for — thinks about. The God whose thoughts toward us were multiplied beyond counting in verse 5 is, at this moment, thinking about a poor and needy man.

40.title: I Delight to Do Your Will
40.overview: He waited, and God drew him up out of a miry bog onto rock and put a new song in his mouth, so that many would see and trust (vv. 1-3); God's deeds and his thoughts toward us are past counting (vv. 4-5). Sacrifice was never what God wanted — you have given me an open ear — and so: Behold, I have come; in the scroll of the book it is written of me: I delight to do your will, O my God (vv. 6-8). He has not restrained his lips or hidden God's deliverance from the congregation (vv. 9-10). Then the ground opens again: his iniquities have overtaken him and outnumber the hairs of his head (vv. 11-12). Deliver me, shame those who hunt me, and let all who seek God say Great is the LORD! (vv. 13-16). As for me, I am poor and needy, but the Lord takes thought for me (v. 17).
40.theology:
The rescue is wholly God's — five verbs, none of them the psalmist's (vv. 1-2) — and the new song is evangelistic by design: others see and trust (v. 3).

Verses 6-8 are quoted in Heb 10:5-10 of Christ entering the world, following the Greek Old Testament's a body have you prepared for me where the Hebrew has "ears you have dug for me" (see the ESV's note): the opened ear stands for the whole prepared person. Hebrews concludes that this will abolishes the sacrificial system and sanctifies us through the offering of Christ's body once for all.

Rescue does not end the problem of sin: in the middle of a thanksgiving, iniquities overtake him and outnumber his hairs (v. 12).

Verses 13-17 stand again as Psalm 70. The psalm ends poor, needy and still asking, on the quietest comfort in it: the Lord takes thought for me (v. 17).
40.examples:
Mud gives nothing to push against; struggling makes it worse.

Five verbs of rescue, none of them his.

A new song, because the old repertoire will not carry it.

Ears dug out, the way you dig a channel.

The body prepared, and the sacrifices ended.

Four ways of saying he refused to keep quiet.

Sins that ran after him and caught him.

Not only acts for — takes thought for.

41.text: To the choirmaster. A Psalm of David. 1Blessed is the one who considers the poor! In the day of trouble the LORD delivers him;2the LORD protects him and keeps him alive; he is called blessed in the land; you do not give him up to the will of his enemies.3The LORD sustains him on his sickbed; in his illness you restore him to full health.4As for me, I said, "O LORD, be gracious to me; heal me, for I have sinned against you!"5My enemies say of me in malice, "When will he die, and his name perish?"6And when one comes to see me, he utters empty words, while his heart gathers iniquity; when he goes out, he tells it abroad.7All who hate me whisper together about me; they imagine the worst for me.8They say, "A deadly thing is poured out on him; he will not rise again from where he lies."9Even my close friend in whom I trusted, who ate my bread, has lifted his heel against me.10But you, O LORD, be gracious to me, and raise me up, that I may repay them!11By this I know that you delight in me: my enemy will not shout in triumph over me.12But you have upheld me because of my integrity, and set me in your presence forever.13Blessed be the LORD, the God of Israel, from everlasting to everlasting! Amen and Amen.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–4 — The LORD Sustains Him on His Sickbed
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Blessed is the one who considers the poor! In the day of trouble the LORD delivers him, protects and keeps him alive (vv. 1-2). The LORD sustains him on his sickbed; in his illness you restore him to full health (v. 3). O LORD, be gracious to me; heal me, for I have sinned against you! (v. 4).
verseByVerse.theology: The man who has thought carefully about the poor is the man God thinks carefully about when he is ill.

verseByVerse.quote: Blessed is the one who considers the poor! In the day of trouble the LORD delivers him; the LORD protects him and keeps him alive; he is called blessed in the land; you do not give him up to the will of his enemies. The LORD sustains him on his sickbed; in his illness you restore him to full health. As for me, I said, "O LORD, be gracious to me; heal me, for I have sinned against you!"
verseByVerse.commentary:
Blessed is the one who considers the poor! In the day of trouble the LORD delivers him; the LORD protects him and keeps him alive; he is called blessed in the land; you do not give him up to the will of his enemies.

The verb matters. Considers is not the word for giving; it is the word for giving thought — weighing a situation, working out what would actually help. The ESV notes the object may be rendered the weak. Anyone can drop a coin in a tin without considering anybody. This blessing is on the person who has thought carefully about someone with nothing.

And the promise is symmetrical: the man who gives attention to the helpless gets attention when he is helpless. God treats him the way he treated others. Jesus put the same principle in a beatitude: Blessed are the merciful, for they shall receive mercy (Matt 5:7).

The LORD sustains him on his sickbed; in his illness you restore him to full health.

Two lines about God in a sickroom, and the ESV notes the second is literally "you turn all his bed" — the picture of a nurse straightening the sheets and turning a patient who cannot turn himself. That is God at the bedside, doing the intimate, undignified work of care. Anyone who has done it for a parent knows exactly what kind of love is being described.

As for me, I said, O LORD, be gracious to me; heal me, for I have sinned against you!

He asks for healing and confesses sin in the same breath, without making one the price of the other. He does not say his illness is punishment; he does say that a sick man before God is still a sinner before God, and he would rather have both dealt with. Compare Jesus with the paralysed man: forgiveness first, then the mat.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: His enemies ask when he will die and his name perish; a visitor comes with empty words, gathers material and spreads it outside; they whisper that a deadly thing has fastened on him and he will not get up (vv. 5-8). Even my close friend in whom I trusted, who ate my bread, has lifted his heel against me (v. 9).
verseByVerse.theology: The sickroom as a place to collect gossip, and at the end of the list the friend who shared his table.

verseByVerse.quote: My enemies say of me in malice, "When will he die, and his name perish?" And when one comes to see me, he utters empty words, while his heart gathers iniquity; when he goes out, he tells it abroad. All who hate me whisper together about me; they imagine the worst for me. They say, "A deadly thing is poured out on him; he will not rise again from where he lies." Even my close friend in whom I trusted, who ate my bread, has lifted his heel against me.
verseByVerse.commentary:
My enemies say of me in malice, When will he die, and his name perish? And when one comes to see me, he utters empty words, while his heart gathers iniquity; when he goes out, he tells it abroad.

Here is one of the ugliest scenes in Scripture, and it is instantly recognisable. Someone visits the sickbed. He says the right things — empty words, the usual noises — while his real business is collecting. Then he gets outside and tells everyone how bad it looked.

The question in verse 5 is worse than the visit: When will he die, and his name perish? They are not merely waiting for him to go; they want the memory of him gone too.

All who hate me whisper together about me; they imagine the worst for me. They say, A deadly thing is poured out on him; he will not rise again from where he lies.

The whispering is a diagnosis he is not present for, delivered with satisfaction. The ESV notes alternative readings in both verses — "they devise evil against me", and that the deadly thing "has fastened" on him. Either way they have decided he is finished, and they are pleased.

Even my close friend in whom I trusted, who ate my bread, has lifted his heel against me.

And then the worst of it, kept for last. Not an enemy: the man who ate at his table. In that world sharing bread was a covenant of sorts — you did not eat a man's food and then move against him.

On the last night of his life, Jesus quoted this verse. I am not speaking of all of you; I know whom I have chosen. But the Scripture will be fulfilled: He who ate my bread has lifted his heel against me (John 13:18). He said it with the bread in his hand and Judas at the table. Every betrayed believer since has had this verse and the knowledge that the Lord used it first about himself.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: But you, O LORD, be gracious to me, and raise me up, that I may repay them! (v. 10). By this I know that you delight in me: my enemy will not shout in triumph over me; God upholds him and sets him in his presence forever (vv. 11-12). Blessed be the LORD, the God of Israel, from everlasting to everlasting! Amen and Amen (v. 13).
verseByVerse.theology: The last verse is not the psalm's ending but Book One's: a doxology sealing forty-one psalms.

verseByVerse.quote: But you, O LORD, be gracious to me, and raise me up, that I may repay them! By this I know that you delight in me: my enemy will not shout in triumph over me. But you have upheld me because of my integrity, and set me in your presence forever. Blessed be the LORD, the God of Israel, from everlasting to everlasting! Amen and Amen.
verseByVerse.commentary:
But you, O LORD, be gracious to me, and raise me up, that I may repay them!

David wants to get up off the bed in order to settle accounts, and the psalm does not hide it. He is a king, and repayment was part of the office; but look at what happened when a greater Son of David quoted this psalm. He took verse 9 and stopped. He did not pray verse 10. He was raised up, and he did not repay them; he prayed for their forgiveness and sent his apostles to preach to the city that killed him.

By this I know that you delight in me: my enemy will not shout in triumph over me. But you have upheld me because of my integrity, and set me in your presence forever.

His evidence that God is pleased with him is not his recovery — the psalm never says he got better — but that the enemy does not get the last word. And the ending is larger than the sickroom: set me in your presence forever. A man who was being written off as finished says he has been placed in God's presence permanently. That is a hope no diagnosis can revise.

Blessed be the LORD, the God of Israel, from everlasting to everlasting! Amen and Amen.

This last verse is not really the end of Psalm 41. It is the end of Book One. The Psalter is arranged in five books, and each is sealed with a doxology like this one (72:18-19; 89:52; 106:48), with the whole of Psalm 150 closing the fifth and the collection.

So stop here and look back over forty-one psalms. They began with a man delighting in God's law and a King installed on Zion; they have been through caves, sickbeds, betrayal, guilt, silence, slander, and the cry of dereliction; and the book closes not with a resolution but with a blessing that runs from everlasting to everlasting. The trouble is not over. The doxology is said anyway, and doubled: Amen and Amen.

41.title: Blessed Is the One Who Considers the Poor
41.overview: Blessed is the one who gives careful thought to the poor: God delivers, protects and keeps him, sustains him on his sickbed and turns his bed for him (vv. 1-3). O LORD, be gracious to me; heal me, for I have sinned against you (v. 4). His enemies ask when he will die and his name perish; a visitor comes with empty words while his heart gathers material, and spreads it outside; they whisper that he will never get up (vv. 5-8). Even my close friend in whom I trusted, who ate my bread, has lifted his heel against me (v. 9). He asks to be raised up to repay them (v. 10), and knows God delights in him because the enemy will not triumph; God upholds him and sets him in his presence forever (vv. 11-12). The last verse is Book One's doxology: Blessed be the LORD, the God of Israel, from everlasting to everlasting! Amen and Amen (v. 13).
41.theology:
The blessing of v. 1 is on thought given to the helpless, not on casual charity, and the promise is symmetrical — the man who attends to others is attended to (cf. Matt 5:7). God's care is domestic: the Hebrew of v. 3 is "you turn all his bed".

Healing and forgiveness are asked for together without making illness a punishment (v. 4).

Jesus quoted v. 9 of Judas at the table (John 13:18) and stopped there: he did not pray v. 10's that I may repay them. Raised up, he prayed for his betrayers instead.

The evidence of God's delight is not recovery but that the enemy gets no final shout (v. 11), and the hope reaches past the sickbed: set me in your presence forever (v. 12).

Verse 13 is the doxology closing Book One of the Psalter (cf. 72:18-19; 89:52; 106:48; Ps 150) — a blessing said while the trouble is unresolved.
41.examples:
Considers: thinking carefully, not tossing a coin.

God turning the sheets of a man who cannot turn himself.

Healing and forgiveness asked for in one breath.

The visitor whose real business is collecting.

Not just his death — his name gone too.

The friend who ate his bread, quoted with bread in hand.

Verse 10 is the verse Jesus did not pray.

Book One ends with a doxology, and the trouble is still there.

42.text: To the choirmaster. A Maskil of the Sons of Korah. 1As a deer pants for flowing streams, so pants my soul for you, O God.2My soul thirsts for God, for the living God. When shall I come and appear before God?3My tears have been my food day and night, while they say to me all the day long, "Where is your God?"4These things I remember, as I pour out my soul: how I would go with the throng and lead them in procession to the house of God with glad shouts and songs of praise, a multitude keeping festival.5Why are you cast down, O my soul, and why are you in turmoil within me? Hope in God; for I shall again praise him, my salvation6and my God. My soul is cast down within me; therefore I remember you from the land of Jordan and of Hermon, from Mount Mizar.7Deep calls to deep at the roar of your waterfalls; all your breakers and your waves have gone over me.8By day the LORD commands his steadfast love, and at night his song is with me, a prayer to the God of my life.9I say to God, my rock: "Why have you forgotten me? Why do I go mourning because of the oppression of the enemy?"10As with a deadly wound in my bones, my adversaries taunt me, while they say to me all the day long, "Where is your God?"11Why are you cast down, O my soul, and why are you in turmoil within me? Hope in God; for I shall again praise him, my salvation and my God.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: As a deer pants for flowing streams, so pants my soul for you, O God. My soul thirsts for God, for the living God (vv. 1-2). My tears have been my food day and night, while they say to me all the day long, Where is your God? (v. 3). He remembers leading the festival procession to God's house (v. 4). Why are you cast down, O my soul ... Hope in God; for I shall again praise him (v. 5).
verseByVerse.theology: Thirst, tears, a taunt, and a man who turns round and speaks to his own soul instead of listening to it.

verseByVerse.quote: As a deer pants for flowing streams, so pants my soul for you, O God. My soul thirsts for God, for the living God. When shall I come and appear before God? My tears have been my food day and night, while they say to me all the day long, "Where is your God?" These things I remember, as I pour out my soul: how I would go with the throng and lead them in procession to the house of God with glad shouts and songs of praise, a multitude keeping festival.
verseByVerse.commentary:
To the choirmaster. A Maskil of the Sons of Korah.

Book Two of the Psalter begins here, and it begins with a family whose name is a warning. Korah led the rebellion in the wilderness and the ground opened under him — and yet his line survived, and centuries later the sons of Korah are the temple singers. The family of the great rebellion became the family of the choir. Whoever thinks their ancestry disqualifies them should notice whose name is at the top of this psalm.

As a deer pants for flowing streams, so pants my soul for you, O God. My soul thirsts for God, for the living God. When shall I come and appear before God?

The image is a body in distress, not a soul at leisure. A deer panting for water is not enjoying a spiritual mood; it is in trouble, and will die without the thing it is looking for. That is the level at which this man wants God.

And what he wants is specific: the living God, and to appear before him — the ESV notes the line can be read "and see the face of God". He is far from the sanctuary and cannot get to the place where God met his people. Anyone cut off from church by illness, distance or disgrace knows this particular thirst.

My tears have been my food day and night, while they say to me all the day long, Where is your God?

Two griefs. The tears, which have replaced his meals — and the question, which arrives all the day long. Where is your God? is the cruellest thing anyone can ask a believer in trouble, and the psalm does not pretend it has an easy answer; it repeats the taunt again at verse 10.

These things I remember, as I pour out my soul: how I would go with the throng and lead them in procession to the house of God with glad shouts and songs of praise, a multitude keeping festival.

And here is the memory that hurts most: he used to lead the singing. The crowd, the shouting, the festival — he was at the front of it. Remembering good days in a bad season can be medicine or poison, and in this verse it is both; he is pouring his soul out over it.

verseByVerse.quote: Why are you cast down, O my soul, and why are you in turmoil within me? Hope in God; for I shall again praise him, my salvation
verseByVerse.commentary:
Why are you cast down, O my soul, and why are you in turmoil within me? Hope in God; for I shall again praise him, my salvation and my God.

The refrain of this poem, which will come three times in all (42:5, 42:11, 43:5). And what is happening in it is the most practical thing in the psalm: he is talking to himself.

Most of us listen to ourselves instead. The soul reports that everything is hopeless, and we take the report as news. Here a man interrupts, asks his own soul two questions — why are you cast down, why this turmoil — and then gives it an order: hope in God. Faith is not the absence of the downcast feeling; it is what you say to the feeling.

Notice that he does not tell himself the trouble is small or that things will improve. He says I shall again praise him. The ground of the command is the future: a day is coming when this same mouth will be singing, so hold on. The ESV notes that my salvation is literally "the salvation of my face" — the countenance that is fallen now will be lifted by God himself.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: He remembers God from the far north, from Jordan and Hermon and Mount Mizar (v. 6). Deep calls to deep at the roar of your waterfalls; all your breakers and your waves have gone over me (v. 7). By day the LORD commands his steadfast love, and at night his song is with me (v. 8). Why have you forgotten me? — and the taunt again (vv. 9-10), and the refrain again (v. 11).
verseByVerse.theology: The waves are called God's own, and the song in the night is given by the one who sent them.

verseByVerse.quote: and my God. My soul is cast down within me; therefore I remember you from the land of Jordan and of Hermon, from Mount Mizar. Deep calls to deep at the roar of your waterfalls; all your breakers and your waves have gone over me. By day the LORD commands his steadfast love, and at night his song is with me, a prayer to the God of my life.
verseByVerse.commentary:
My soul is cast down within me; therefore I remember you from the land of Jordan and of Hermon, from Mount Mizar.

He tells us where he is: the far north, the headwaters of the Jordan under Mount Hermon, a long way from Jerusalem. And the therefore is the discipline of the whole psalm — because I am cast down, I remember you. The downcast feeling becomes the reason to turn towards God rather than away.

Deep calls to deep at the roar of your waterfalls; all your breakers and your waves have gone over me.

He is standing where the streams come crashing off Hermon, and the noise of the water becomes the sound of his own trouble: one depth shouting to another, wave after wave going over his head. Jonah used the identical line from inside the fish — all your breakers and your waves passed over me (Jonah 2:3).

And the pronoun is the thing to notice: your waterfalls, your breakers, your waves. He does not say the trouble is random or that it came from his enemies. He says it is God's, which is either the worst thing about it or the only comfort in it, depending on what you believe about God.

By day the LORD commands his steadfast love, and at night his song is with me, a prayer to the God of my life.

This is the one place in the psalm where the covenant name appears, and it appears in the dark. God commands his steadfast love — it is dispatched on orders, like a soldier sent out — and at night there is a song. The same one whose breakers went over him in verse 7 is the one who gives a song in verse 8. Both are his, on the same day.

verseByVerse.quote: I say to God, my rock: "Why have you forgotten me? Why do I go mourning because of the oppression of the enemy?" As with a deadly wound in my bones, my adversaries taunt me, while they say to me all the day long, "Where is your God?" Why are you cast down, O my soul, and why are you in turmoil within me? Hope in God; for I shall again praise him, my salvation and my God.
verseByVerse.commentary:
I say to God, my rock: Why have you forgotten me? Why do I go mourning because of the oppression of the enemy? As with a deadly wound in my bones, my adversaries taunt me, while they say to me all the day long, Where is your God?

He calls God my rock in the same breath as asking why he has been forgotten — and both are honest. The taunt returns word for word from verse 3, because that is how taunts work: they do not arrive once and leave. He calls it a wound in the bones, which is where you feel something that will not stop.

Why are you cast down, O my soul, and why are you in turmoil within me? Hope in God; for I shall again praise him, my salvation and my God.

And the refrain a second time, in exactly the same words. He has not talked himself out of anything; the situation has not changed between verse 5 and verse 11. He simply says it again.

That is the honest pattern of a believer in a long stretch of darkness, and it helps to know it before you need it: you will preach the same sermon to your own soul more than once, and it will not feel like progress. The poem will say it a third time in the next psalm, which is the other half of this one. God's people have always sung this in the dry season, and the thirst it begins with is answered in the end by a voice on the last page of the Bible: To the thirsty I will give from the spring of the water of life without payment (Rev 21:6).

42.title: As a Deer Pants for Flowing Streams
42.overview: Book Two opens with a thirst. A soul pants for the living God like a deer for water, longing to come and appear before him (vv. 1-2), while tears replace food and a taunt repeats all day: Where is your God? (v. 3). He remembers leading the festival procession to God's house (v. 4), and then speaks to himself: Why are you cast down, O my soul? ... Hope in God (v. 5). From the far north, by the waterfalls of Hermon, deep calls to deep and God's breakers go over him (vv. 6-7); yet by day God commands his steadfast love and at night gives a song (v. 8). Why have you forgotten me? — and the taunt again (vv. 9-10) — and the same refrain again (v. 11).
42.theology:
Psalms 42 and 43 are one poem with one refrain (42:5, 11; 43:5), and Book Two begins here; across Pss 42-83 God largely replaces the LORD, which makes the single LORD of v. 8 stand out.

Desire for God is described as bodily need, not mood (vv. 1-2), and the loss felt most is access to corporate worship (v. 4).

The refrain is a man preaching to his own soul rather than listening to it, and the ground he gives is future praise, not present improvement (v. 5).

The waves are called God's own (v. 7) — as Jonah said from the fish (Jonah 2:3) — and the same God commands steadfast love by day and gives a song at night (v. 8).

Nothing is resolved by the end: the refrain is simply repeated (v. 11), which is what a long darkness actually looks like.
42.examples:
The choir descended from the man the ground swallowed.

A panting deer is in trouble, not in a mood.

Tears instead of meals, and a question all day long.

The memory that hurts: he used to lead the singing.

Two questions to his own soul, then an order.

Your breakers, your waves.

Steadfast love dispatched by day; a song issued at night.

The same sermon preached twice to the same soul.

43.text: <sup>1</sup>Vindicate me, O God, and defend my cause against an ungodly people, from the deceitful and unjust man deliver me!<sup>2</sup>For you are the God in whom I take refuge; why have you rejected me? Why do I go about mourning because of the oppression of the enemy?<sup>3</sup>Send out your light and your truth; let them lead me; let them bring me to your holy hill and to your dwelling!<sup>4</sup>Then I will go to the altar of God, to God my exceeding joy, and I will praise you with the lyre, O God, my God.<sup>5</sup>Why are you cast down, O my soul, and why are you in turmoil within me? Hope in God; for I shall again praise him, my salvation and my God.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–5 — To God My Exceeding Joy
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Vindicate me, O God, and defend my cause against an ungodly people (v. 1); why have you rejected me? Why do I go about mourning? (v. 2). Send out your light and your truth; let them lead me; let them bring me to your holy hill and to your dwelling! (v. 3). Then I will go to the altar of God, to God my exceeding joy (v. 4). And the refrain a third time: Why are you cast down, O my soul ... Hope in God (v. 5).
verseByVerse.theology: The thirst of Psalm 42 becomes a request for guides, and the destination is not a place but a person.

verseByVerse.quote: Vindicate me, O God, and defend my cause against an ungodly people, from the deceitful and unjust man deliver me! For you are the God in whom I take refuge; why have you rejected me? Why do I go about mourning because of the oppression of the enemy?
verseByVerse.commentary:
Vindicate me, O God, and defend my cause against an ungodly people, from the deceitful and unjust man deliver me! For you are the God in whom I take refuge; why have you rejected me? Why do I go about mourning because of the oppression of the enemy?

This psalm has no heading, and it needs none: it is the last stanza of the one before. The refrain at verse 5 is the refrain of 42:5 and 42:11, and verse 2 here repeats 42:9 almost word for word. Somewhere in the transmission the poem was split in two; it should be read straight through.

What has changed is the direction. Psalm 42 was memory and thirst; this half asks. And the first question is the hardest one a believer ever has to hold: you are the God in whom I take refuge — and — why have you rejected me? Both in one sentence, neither cancelling the other. That is not confusion. It is what faith sounds like when the evidence has gone the wrong way.

verseByVerse.quote: Send out your light and your truth; let them lead me; let them bring me to your holy hill and to your dwelling! Then I will go to the altar of God, to God my exceeding joy, and I will praise you with the lyre, O God, my God.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Send out your light and your truth; let them lead me; let them bring me to your holy hill and to your dwelling!

Notice what he does not ask for. Not the destruction of the ungodly people, not an explanation, not even transport. He asks God to send out two servants — light and truth — to come and get him and walk him home. They are pictured as guides sent from the sanctuary to fetch a man who cannot find his own way back, the way the pillar of cloud and fire went ahead of Israel (Exod 13:21).

And the two named are exactly the two a person in his condition has lost. He is in the dark and he is being lied about; he wants light to see by and truth to stand on. A Christian reading this cannot help hearing who arrived: I am the light of the world (John 8:12), and I am the way, and the truth, and the life (John 14:6). What the psalmist asked God to send out, God sent.

Then I will go to the altar of God, to God my exceeding joy, and I will praise you with the lyre, O God, my God.

The destination gets named twice, and the second naming is the real one. He wants to reach the altar — and then he corrects himself: to God my exceeding joy. The Hebrew is doubled, the gladness of my joy. It is not the building he misses, or the music, or the crowd he used to lead. It is the person at the end of the journey.

That is the test of any longing for church that has been interrupted. What exactly do you miss? This man wants the altar because God is there, and he says so in case anybody mistook his homesickness for nostalgia.

verseByVerse.quote: Why are you cast down, O my soul, and why are you in turmoil within me? Hope in God; for I shall again praise him, my salvation and my God.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Why are you cast down, O my soul, and why are you in turmoil within me? Hope in God; for I shall again praise him, my salvation and my God.

The third time, word for word. The poem ends exactly where it has been twice already, with a man asking his own soul the same two questions and giving it the same order.

Nothing has been resolved. He is still far from the sanctuary; the ungodly people are still there; the taunt of 42:3 has not been answered. What he has is a refrain, and the discipline to say it again.

Take that as the psalm's gift rather than its failure. Christians in a long stretch of darkness often expect that the right insight will lift it once and for all, and are ashamed when they find themselves back at the same sentence a week later. This poem, printed twice over in two psalms, says that repetition is not defeat. Preach it to yourself again. I shall again praise him was true the first time, and it is still true now.

43.title: Send Out Your Light and Your Truth
43.overview: The second half of Psalm 42. He asks God to vindicate him against an ungodly people and to deliver him from the deceitful, while asking in the same breath why God has rejected him (vv. 1-2). His request is for guides: Send out your light and your truth; let them lead me; let them bring me to your holy hill and to your dwelling! (v. 3). Then he will come to the altar — and past it, to God my exceeding joy (v. 4). The refrain closes the poem for the third time: Hope in God; for I shall again praise him (v. 5).
43.theology:
This psalm has no heading because it completes Psalm 42: same refrain, and v. 2 repeats 42:9. Faith holds you are the God in whom I take refuge and why have you rejected me? in one sentence without either cancelling the other.

What is asked for is escort rather than rescue (v. 3): light and truth sent out from God to fetch a man who cannot find his way back (cf. Exod 13:21) — and precisely what he lacks in the dark and under slander. The New Testament names both in one person (John 8:12; 14:6).

The destination is corrected as it is named: the altar, and then God my exceeding joy (v. 4). Longing for worship is longing for God, not for the building or the music.

The poem ends with its refrain unchanged for the third time (v. 5): in a long darkness, repetition is not failure.
43.examples:
No heading, because it is the last stanza of the psalm before.

Refuge and rejection in the same sentence.

Light and truth sent out like servants to fetch him home.

Exactly what a man in the dark and under slander has lost.

Past the altar to the God at it.

The same sermon, a third time, and not a defeat.

44.text: To the choirmaster. A Maskil of the Sons of Korah. 1O God, we have heard with our ears, our fathers have told us, what deeds you performed in their days, in the days of old:2you with your own hand drove out the nations, but them you planted; you afflicted the peoples, but them you set free;3for not by their own sword did they win the land, nor did their own arm save them, but your right hand and your arm, and the light of your face, for you delighted in them.4You are my King, O God; ordain salvation for Jacob!5Through you we push down our foes; through your name we tread down those who rise up against us.6For not in my bow do I trust, nor can my sword save me.7But you have saved us from our foes and have put to shame those who hate us.8In God we have boasted continually, and we will give thanks to your name forever. Selah9But you have rejected us and disgraced us and have not gone out with our armies.10You have made us turn back from the foe, and those who hate us have gotten spoil.11You have made us like sheep for slaughter and have scattered us among the nations.12You have sold your people for a trifle, demanding no high price for them.13You have made us the taunt of our neighbors, the derision and scorn of those around us.14You have made us a byword among the nations, a laughingstock among the peoples.15All day long my disgrace is before me, and shame has covered my face16at the sound of the taunter and reviler, at the sight of the enemy and the avenger.17All this has come upon us, though we have not forgotten you, and we have not been false to your covenant.18Our heart has not turned back, nor have our steps departed from your way;19yet you have broken us in the place of jackals and covered us with the shadow of death.20If we had forgotten the name of our God or spread out our hands to a foreign god,21would not God discover this? For he knows the secrets of the heart.22Yet for your sake we are killed all the day long; we are regarded as sheep to be slaughtered.23Awake! Why are you sleeping, O Lord? Rouse yourself! Do not reject us forever!24Why do you hide your face? Why do you forget our affliction and oppression?25For our soul is bowed down to the dust; our belly clings to the ground.26Rise up; come to our help! Redeem us for the sake of your steadfast love!

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–8 — Not by Their Own Sword
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: O God, we have heard with our ears, our fathers have told us, what deeds you performed in their days — you drove out nations and planted them, for not by their own sword did they win the land, but by your right hand and the light of your face (vv. 1-3). You are my King, O God: through you we push down our foes, for not in my bow do I trust, and in God we have boasted continually (vv. 4-8).
verseByVerse.theology: The nation's whole history is told as something God did, with the army as a bystander.

verseByVerse.quote: O God, we have heard with our ears, our fathers have told us, what deeds you performed in their days, in the days of old: you with your own hand drove out the nations, but them you planted; you afflicted the peoples, but them you set free; for not by their own sword did they win the land, nor did their own arm save them, but your right hand and your arm, and the light of your face, for you delighted in them. You are my King, O God; ordain salvation for Jacob! Through you we push down our foes; through your name we tread down those who rise up against us. For not in my bow do I trust, nor can my sword save me. But you have saved us from our foes and have put to shame those who hate us. In God we have boasted continually, and we will give thanks to your name forever. Selah
verseByVerse.commentary:
O God, we have heard with our ears, our fathers have told us, what deeds you performed in their days, in the days of old: you with your own hand drove out the nations, but them you planted ... for not by their own sword did they win the land, nor did their own arm save them, but your right hand and your arm, and the light of your face, for you delighted in them.

Another Maskil of the sons of Korah, and this one is sung by a whole nation. It opens as a history lesson passed down at the table: our fathers told us. And the whole conquest is told with Israel as the beneficiary rather than the agent — you drove out, you planted, and explicitly not their sword, not their arm. Even the reason is on God's side: for you delighted in them. Nothing in the founding story is a national achievement.

You are my King, O God; ordain salvation for Jacob! Through you we push down our foes ... For not in my bow do I trust, nor can my sword save me.

And the present generation says the same about itself. This is Psalm 20's some trust in chariots made into a creed, and it matters enormously for what follows: these are not people presuming on their own strength. They have boasted in God ... continually.

Hold that, because the next verse begins with But you, and everything after it is unbearable.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 9–22 — You Have Made Us Like Sheep for Slaughter
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: But you have rejected us and disgraced us: made them retreat, like sheep for slaughter, scattered, sold for a trifle, made a byword and a laughingstock, with shame covering their faces all day (vv. 9-16). All this has come upon us, though we have not forgotten you, and we have not been false to your covenant — let God search the secrets of the heart (vv. 17-21). Yet for your sake we are killed all the day long; we are regarded as sheep to be slaughtered (v. 22).
verseByVerse.theology: A whole people insisting they have not deserved this, and naming God as the one who did it.

verseByVerse.quote: But you have rejected us and disgraced us and have not gone out with our armies. You have made us turn back from the foe, and those who hate us have gotten spoil. You have made us like sheep for slaughter and have scattered us among the nations. You have sold your people for a trifle, demanding no high price for them. You have made us the taunt of our neighbors, the derision and scorn of those around us. You have made us a byword among the nations, a laughingstock among the peoples. All day long my disgrace is before me, and shame has covered my face at the sound of the taunter and reviler, at the sight of the enemy and the avenger.
verseByVerse.commentary:
But you have rejected us and disgraced us and have not gone out with our armies. You have made us turn back from the foe, and those who hate us have gotten spoil. You have made us like sheep for slaughter and have scattered us among the nations.

Count the accusations, because the psalm means them to land: you rejected, you disgraced, you stayed home from the battle, you made us retreat, you made us sheep for the knife, you scattered us. Twelve times in this section God is the subject of the verb. Nobody in the Bible blames circumstances.

You have sold your people for a trifle, demanding no high price for them.

This is the most bitter line in the psalm, and it should be allowed to stay as bitter as it is. God is pictured as a man selling his own household — and not even driving a hard bargain. He let them go cheap. When a believer feels that God has not merely allowed a loss but seems to have valued them at nothing, this verse has been there first.

You have made us the taunt of our neighbors ... a byword among the nations, a laughingstock among the peoples. All day long my disgrace is before me, and shame has covered my face at the sound of the taunter and reviler.

The wound is public. The ESV notes that byword is literally "a shaking of the head" — the gesture strangers make when they pass. It is the same taunt that ran through Psalm 42, now aimed at a whole nation, and it goes on all day long.

verseByVerse.quote: All this has come upon us, though we have not forgotten you, and we have not been false to your covenant. Our heart has not turned back, nor have our steps departed from your way; yet you have broken us in the place of jackals and covered us with the shadow of death. If we had forgotten the name of our God or spread out our hands to a foreign god, would not God discover this? For he knows the secrets of the heart. Yet for your sake we are killed all the day long; we are regarded as sheep to be slaughtered.
verseByVerse.commentary:
All this has come upon us, though we have not forgotten you, and we have not been false to your covenant. Our heart has not turned back, nor have our steps departed from your way; yet you have broken us in the place of jackals and covered us with the shadow of death.

Here is what makes this psalm so difficult, and so necessary. The standard explanation for national disaster in the Old Testament is national sin — and this psalm refuses it. They have not forgotten God, not gone after other gods, not turned back. This is the book of Job, written for a whole people.

If we had forgotten the name of our God or spread out our hands to a foreign god, would not God discover this? For he knows the secrets of the heart.

And they put the claim under oath in the strongest way available: if we were lying, you would know. They invite the examination rather than avoiding it. That is not arrogance; it is the only honest thing a person can say when the standard diagnosis does not fit their case, and it is a great relief to anyone who has been told that their suffering must be the result of some hidden sin.

Yet for your sake we are killed all the day long; we are regarded as sheep to be slaughtered.

Not merely undeserved — suffered for your sake, because they belong to him. And this is the verse Paul reaches for in the greatest passage he ever wrote about God's love. Having asked whether tribulation or famine or sword can separate us from Christ, he quotes it exactly: As it is written, For your sake we are being killed all the day long; we are regarded as sheep to be slaughtered (Rom 8:36). And then: No, in all these things we are more than conquerors through him who loved us (Rom 8:37).

Notice what Paul does not do. He does not soften the verse or say the psalmist overstated it. He grants the whole of it — yes, this happens, to God's own people, all day long — and denies the conclusion everyone draws from it. The slaughter is real; the separation is not.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 23–26 — Awake! Why Are You Sleeping?
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Awake! Why are you sleeping, O Lord? Rouse yourself! Do not reject us forever! Why do you hide your face? (vv. 23-24). Their soul is bowed to the dust and their belly clings to the ground (v. 25). Rise up; come to our help! Redeem us for the sake of your steadfast love! (v. 26).
verseByVerse.theology: The rudest prayer in the Psalter ends by appealing to the one thing that never depended on them.

verseByVerse.quote: Awake! Why are you sleeping, O Lord? Rouse yourself! Do not reject us forever! Why do you hide your face? Why do you forget our affliction and oppression? For our soul is bowed down to the dust; our belly clings to the ground. Rise up; come to our help! Redeem us for the sake of your steadfast love!
verseByVerse.commentary:
Awake! Why are you sleeping, O Lord? Rouse yourself! Do not reject us forever!

It is the rudest thing anybody says to God in the Psalter, and it is in Scripture, in the hymnbook, for congregational use. They do not believe God is asleep — the previous verse said he knows the secrets of the heart. They are describing how it looks, and asking him to stop looking like that.

There is one place in the Gospels where God incarnate really was asleep in a crisis, and his friends woke him with almost this sentence: Teacher, do you not care that we are perishing? (Mark 4:38). He did not rebuke the waking. He rebuked the wind.

Why do you hide your face? Why do you forget our affliction and oppression? For our soul is bowed down to the dust; our belly clings to the ground.

Bodies in the dust, face down, unable to get up. That is the posture of the nation, and it is also the posture of prayer — they are flat on the ground either way, and they have decided to speak from there.

Rise up; come to our help! Redeem us for the sake of your steadfast love!

And after all that insistence on their innocence — twenty-five verses of it, sworn to and offered for inspection — look at the ground they finally stand on. Not "for the sake of our faithfulness". For the sake of your steadfast love. They were right that they had not deserved this; they know better than to ask for rescue on the strength of it.

The psalm ends unanswered. No deliverance is reported, no explanation given. What is given is a verse that Paul would take up centuries later to tell Christians under Roman swords that they were not abandoned, and a last line that shows a battered people still asking, and still asking on the right ground.

44.title: Sheep to Be Slaughtered
44.overview: The fathers told the children what God did: he drove out nations and planted Israel, not by their sword or arm but by his right hand and the light of his face (vv. 1-3). The same generation says the same of itself — not in my bow do I trust (vv. 4-8). But you have rejected us: made them retreat, sheep for slaughter, scattered, sold for a trifle, a byword and a laughingstock with shame all day long (vv. 9-16). And they have not deserved it: they have not forgotten God or turned to another god, and they invite him to search the secrets of the heart (vv. 17-21). Yet for your sake we are killed all the day long (v. 22). Awake! Why are you sleeping, O Lord? Their bodies are in the dust; the last request stands on God's steadfast love, not their innocence (vv. 23-26).
44.theology:
The founding story is told with Israel as beneficiary, never agent (vv. 1-3), and the present generation disowns its own bow (v. 6) — so this is not a psalm of presumption.

It then refuses the standard explanation of disaster. These sufferers are not guilty (vv. 17-21) and they invite God's inspection: the book of Job, written for a whole nation. That refusal is a relief to anyone told their suffering must conceal a sin.

Paul quotes v. 22 in Rom 8:36 without softening it: he grants the slaughter and denies the conclusion, since in all these things we are more than conquerors (Rom 8:37).

Awake! Why are you sleeping? (v. 23) describes how God's inaction looks, not what they believe about him; the sleeping Christ of Mark 4:38 rebuked the wind, not the waking.

After twenty-five verses of protested innocence, the appeal is made for the sake of your steadfast love (v. 26).
44.examples:
A history lesson in which the army is a bystander.

Twelve accusations, every one beginning with you.

Sold cheap, with no haggling.

A byword: literally a shaking of the head.

Suffering that does not fit the standard diagnosis — and is not made to.

Paul grants the verse and denies the conclusion.

The rudest prayer in the Psalter, printed for congregational use.

Innocent, and still asking on the ground of steadfast love.

45.text: To the choirmaster: according to Lilies. A Maskil of the Sons of Korah; a love song. 1My heart overflows with a pleasing theme; I address my verses to the king; my tongue is like the pen of a ready scribe.2You are the most handsome of the sons of men; grace is poured upon your lips; therefore God has blessed you forever.3Gird your sword on your thigh, O mighty one, in your splendor and majesty!4In your majesty ride out victoriously for the cause of truth and meekness and righteousness; let your right hand teach you awesome deeds!5Your arrows are sharp in the heart of the king's enemies; the peoples fall under you.6Your throne, O God, is forever and ever. The scepter of your kingdom is a scepter of uprightness;7you have loved righteousness and hated wickedness. Therefore God, your God, has anointed you with the oil of gladness beyond your companions;8your robes are all fragrant with myrrh and aloes and cassia. From ivory palaces stringed instruments make you glad;9daughters of kings are among your ladies of honor; at your right hand stands the queen in gold of Ophir.10Hear, O daughter, and consider, and incline your ear: forget your people and your father's house,11and the king will desire your beauty. Since he is your lord, bow to him.12The people of Tyre will seek your favor with gifts, the richest of the people.13All glorious is the princess in her chamber, with robes interwoven with gold.14In many-colored robes she is led to the king, with her virgin companions following behind her.15With joy and gladness they are led along as they enter the palace of the king.16In place of your fathers shall be your sons; you will make them princes in all the earth.17I will cause your name to be remembered in all generations; therefore nations will praise you forever and ever.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–9 — Gird Your Sword on Your Thigh
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: My heart overflows with a pleasing theme (v. 1). The king is the most handsome of men, with grace poured on his lips (v. 2); let him gird his sword and ride out victoriously for the cause of truth and meekness and righteousness (vv. 3-5). Your throne, O God, is forever and ever ... you have loved righteousness and hated wickedness. Therefore God, your God, has anointed you with the oil of gladness beyond your companions (vv. 6-7). His robes smell of myrrh; the queen stands at his right hand in gold (vv. 8-9).
verseByVerse.theology: A wedding song that calls the bridegroom God, and is quoted in the New Testament as the Father speaking to the Son.

verseByVerse.quote: My heart overflows with a pleasing theme; I address my verses to the king; my tongue is like the pen of a ready scribe. You are the most handsome of the sons of men; grace is poured upon your lips; therefore God has blessed you forever. Gird your sword on your thigh, O mighty one, in your splendor and majesty! In your majesty ride out victoriously for the cause of truth and meekness and righteousness; let your right hand teach you awesome deeds! Your arrows are sharp in the heart of the king's enemies; the peoples fall under you.
verseByVerse.commentary:
My heart overflows with a pleasing theme; I address my verses to the king; my tongue is like the pen of a ready scribe.

The only psalm the headings call a love song, written for a royal wedding, and the poet says his heart is boiling over and his tongue can hardly keep up with it. Scripture is not embarrassed by a love song, and it puts one in the middle of its prayer book.

You are the most handsome of the sons of men; grace is poured upon your lips; therefore God has blessed you forever.

He starts with the groom's face and then his speech: grace is poured upon your lips. When Jesus preached in Nazareth the crowd marveled at the gracious words that were coming from his mouth (Luke 4:22), which is this line come to life.

Gird your sword on your thigh, O mighty one, in your splendor and majesty! In your majesty ride out victoriously for the cause of truth and meekness and righteousness ... Your arrows are sharp in the heart of the king's enemies.

A sword at a wedding. The bridegroom is a warrior, and the psalm names the cause he rides for — truth and meekness and righteousness. Meekness is not what any nation writes on its banners, and it is one of the three things this King fights for. John saw the same rider: in righteousness he judges and makes war (Rev 19:11).

verseByVerse.quote: Your throne, O God, is forever and ever. The scepter of your kingdom is a scepter of uprightness; you have loved righteousness and hated wickedness. Therefore God, your God, has anointed you with the oil of gladness beyond your companions; your robes are all fragrant with myrrh and aloes and cassia. From ivory palaces stringed instruments make you glad; daughters of kings are among your ladies of honor; at your right hand stands the queen in gold of Ophir.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Your throne, O God, is forever and ever. The scepter of your kingdom is a scepter of uprightness; you have loved righteousness and hated wickedness. Therefore God, your God, has anointed you with the oil of gladness beyond your companions.

Read that slowly, because something has happened that the Old Testament almost never does. The king being married is addressed as God — and in the next line has a God of his own who anoints him. Israelite poets did not flatter kings like this; the language bursts the occasion it was written for.

The letter to the Hebrews takes it as settled. Arguing that the Son is greater than any angel, it quotes these two verses word for word and says who is speaking to whom: But of the Son he says, Your throne, O God, is forever and ever, the scepter of uprightness is the scepter of your kingdom. You have loved righteousness and hated wickedness; therefore God, your God, has anointed you with the oil of gladness beyond your companions (Heb 1:8-9). The Father calls the Son God. A Jewish wedding song is one of the New Testament's proofs of the deity of Christ.

And notice what the anointing is for. Not merely office — the oil of gladness, and beyond your companions. The word for anointed is the word Messiah. Isaiah promised the same oil to people in mourning (Isa 61:3); here the King has more of it than anyone in the room, and the joy is part of the job.

Your robes are all fragrant with myrrh and aloes and cassia. From ivory palaces stringed instruments make you glad; daughters of kings are among your ladies of honor; at your right hand stands the queen in gold of Ophir.

Perfume, music, gold: the psalm is enjoying the wedding. Christian readers sometimes hurry past this to get to the theology, but the theology is that the King's wedding day is a day of scent and music and a bride standing beside him. The last book of the Bible describes the end of everything as exactly that (Rev 19:7-9).

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Hear, O daughter, and consider, and incline your ear: forget your people and your father's house, and the king will desire your beauty (vv. 10-11). Tyre comes with gifts; the princess is glorious in gold-woven robes and is led to the king with her companions, with joy and gladness (vv. 12-15). His sons will be princes in all the earth, and his name will be remembered in all generations (vv. 16-17).
verseByVerse.theology: The bride leaves everything to belong to him, and what she gets is his desire and his house.

verseByVerse.quote: Hear, O daughter, and consider, and incline your ear: forget your people and your father's house, and the king will desire your beauty. Since he is your lord, bow to him. The people of Tyre will seek your favor with gifts, the richest of the people. All glorious is the princess in her chamber, with robes interwoven with gold. In many-colored robes she is led to the king, with her virgin companions following behind her. With joy and gladness they are led along as they enter the palace of the king.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Hear, O daughter, and consider, and incline your ear: forget your people and your father's house, and the king will desire your beauty. Since he is your lord, bow to him.

The poem turns to the bride, and what it asks of her is total. In that world a royal marriage usually meant a foreign princess, and she is told to leave her nation behind — not merely to travel, to forget. Genesis says a man shall leave his father and mother and hold fast to his wife; here it is the bride who leaves everything.

And the promise attached is not security or status: the king will desire your beauty. She is not being acquired; she is wanted. That is the order of every conversion — a leaving, and then the discovery that the one you came to has been desiring you.

All glorious is the princess in her chamber, with robes interwoven with gold. In many-colored robes she is led to the king, with her virgin companions following behind her. With joy and gladness they are led along as they enter the palace of the king.

She is dressed by others and led in; the procession is joyful, and her friends come with her. Paul saw the church this way and said who does the dressing: Christ gave himself for her so that he might present the church to himself in splendor, without spot or wrinkle or any such thing (Eph 5:27). The glorious robes are not her contribution.

verseByVerse.quote: In place of your fathers shall be your sons; you will make them princes in all the earth. I will cause your name to be remembered in all generations; therefore nations will praise you forever and ever.
verseByVerse.commentary:
In place of your fathers shall be your sons; you will make them princes in all the earth. I will cause your name to be remembered in all generations; therefore nations will praise you forever and ever.
