The poet promises the king two things at the end: a future, and a name. In place of your fathers shall be your sons — the line will run forward instead of backward, which for a dynasty is everything. And the singer's own contribution is memory: my song will keep your name alive.

It was a large promise for a court poet to make about a monarch whose name we no longer know. And it came true in a way he did not expect. The wedding this psalm celebrated is forgotten; the psalm is read every week somewhere in the world, because the King it turned out to be about has a throne forever and ever, and his sons will indeed be princes in all the earth.

So read the last line as it stands and let it be as large as it is: nations will praise you forever and ever. That is not wedding flattery. It is what is happening.

45.title: Your Throne, O God, Is Forever
45.overview: A wedding song for a king. The poet's heart overflows: the groom is the most handsome of men, grace poured on his lips (vv. 1-2); let him ride out with his sword for truth, meekness and righteousness (vv. 3-5). Then the king is addressed as God: Your throne, O God, is forever and ever ... therefore God, your God, has anointed you with the oil of gladness beyond your companions (vv. 6-7). His robes are fragrant, music plays, and the queen stands at his right hand in gold (vv. 8-9). The bride is told to forget her people and her father's house, for the king desires her beauty (vv. 10-11); she is led to him in gold-woven robes with her companions, in joy and gladness (vv. 12-15). His sons will be princes in all the earth and his name remembered in every generation (vv. 16-17).
45.theology:
The king of this psalm is addressed as God and also has a God who anoints him (vv. 6-7), language that bursts the occasion it was written for. Hebrews quotes both verses as the Father speaking to the Son, to prove his deity and his superiority to the angels (Heb 1:8-9). A wedding song is one of the New Testament's proofs of the deity of Christ.

The cause he fights for includes meekness (v. 4; cf. Rev 19:11), and his anointing is the oil of gladness beyond his companions (v. 7; Isa 61:3) — joy is part of the office.

The bride's call is to leave and forget in order to belong, and the promise is desire rather than status (vv. 10-11); she is dressed and led in by others, which Paul applies to the church Christ presents to himself in splendour (Eph 5:27; cf. Rev 19:7-9).

The closing promise of a remembered name and princely sons (vv. 16-17) outran the king it was written for.
45.examples:
The Bible's prayer book contains a love song.

Grace poured on his lips, and a synagogue marvelling at his words.

A sword at a wedding, and meekness on the banner.

A king called God, who has a God — and Hebrews saying who is speaking.

Anointed with gladness beyond everyone else in the room.

Forget your father's house: the shape of every conversion.

Robes she did not weave.

The name the poet promised to keep alive.

46.text: To the choirmaster. Of the Sons of Korah. According to Alamoth. A Song. 1God is our refuge and strength, a very present help in trouble.2Therefore we will not fear though the earth give way, though the mountains be moved into the heart of the sea,3though its waters roar and foam, though the mountains tremble at its swelling. Selah4There is a river whose streams make glad the city of God, the holy habitation of the Most High.5God is in the midst of her; she shall not be moved; God will help her when morning dawns.6The nations rage, the kingdoms totter; he utters his voice, the earth melts.7The LORD of hosts is with us; the God of Jacob is our fortress. Selah8Come, behold the works of the LORD, how he has brought desolations on the earth.9He makes wars cease to the end of the earth; he breaks the bow and shatters the spear; he burns the chariots with fire.10"Be still, and know that I am God. I will be exalted among the nations, I will be exalted in the earth!"11The LORD of hosts is with us; the God of Jacob is our fortress. Selah

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–7 — Though the Earth Give Way
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: God is our refuge and strength, a very present help in trouble. Therefore we will not fear though the earth give way, though the mountains be moved into the heart of the sea (vv. 1-3). There is a river whose streams make glad the city of God; God is in her midst and she shall not be moved, and he helps her when morning dawns (vv. 4-5). The nations rage, the kingdoms totter; he utters his voice, the earth melts. The LORD of hosts is with us; the God of Jacob is our fortress (vv. 6-7).
verseByVerse.theology: The psalm names the end of the world in its second verse, and then mentions a quiet river.

verseByVerse.quote: God is our refuge and strength, a very present help in trouble. Therefore we will not fear though the earth give way, though the mountains be moved into the heart of the sea, though its waters roar and foam, though the mountains tremble at its swelling. Selah
verseByVerse.commentary:
God is our refuge and strength, a very present help in trouble.

Another song of the sons of Korah, set to a tune whose name the ESV can only call a musical term. Three words for what God is, and the third is the one that does the work. A very present help — the ESV notes the phrase may be rendered well proved — means help that is already on site. Not summoned, not dispatched, not on its way. The trouble and the help arrive together because the help was there first.

Therefore we will not fear though the earth give way, though the mountains be moved into the heart of the sea, though its waters roar and foam, though the mountains tremble at its swelling.

Most comfort begins small and works up. This psalm begins at the top. If the ground itself failed, if the mountains — the standing symbol of permanence — slid into the sea and the sea went wild, we would still not be afraid. It is the end of the world described in two verses, and the psalm's answer is already in verse 1.

Which is the right order for a frightened person. You do not calm someone by telling them the worst will not happen. You tell them who is with them if it does.

verseByVerse.quote: There is a river whose streams make glad the city of God, the holy habitation of the Most High. God is in the midst of her; she shall not be moved; God will help her when morning dawns. The nations rage, the kingdoms totter; he utters his voice, the earth melts. The LORD of hosts is with us; the God of Jacob is our fortress. Selah
verseByVerse.commentary:
There is a river whose streams make glad the city of God, the holy habitation of the Most High.

After the roaring sea, a river — and the first thing to say is that Jerusalem had no river. Every other great city of the ancient world sat on one: Babylon on the Euphrates, Thebes on the Nile, Nineveh on the Tigris. The city of God had a spring and a tunnel, and that is all. So the river here is not geography.

Set it against verse 3. The sea roars and foams and shakes the mountains; this water has streams, and what they do is make glad. The world's power is loud and destructive; God's provision to his city is quiet and gladdening, and it does not run dry. Ezekiel saw a river coming out from under the temple threshold and deepening as it went; John saw it at the end, the river of the water of life, bright as crystal, flowing from the throne of God and of the Lamb (Rev 22:1). And Jesus stood up at a festival and said that whoever believed in him would have rivers of living water flowing out of him (John 7:38).

God is in the midst of her; she shall not be moved; God will help her when morning dawns.

The mountains were moved in verse 2 and the city is not moved in verse 5 — the same word, and the difference is the middle clause: God is in the midst of her. Her stability is not structural.

And do not hurry past when morning dawns. The help comes at daybreak, which means there was a night. Once in Jerusalem's history the Assyrian army camped outside her walls and in the morning the city woke to find them dead (2 Kgs 19:35). God's people are not spared the night; they are met at the end of it.

The nations rage, the kingdoms totter; he utters his voice, the earth melts. The LORD of hosts is with us; the God of Jacob is our fortress.

The nations rage as they did in Psalm 2, and the kingdoms wobble — and then God clears his throat. He does not raise an army; he utters his voice, and the earth melts. What the roaring waters of verse 3 could not do to the city, God's voice does to the world.

Then the refrain, which is the whole psalm in nine words: The LORD of hosts is with us. The LORD of armies, and the God of Jacob — the God who bound himself to a schemer and kept his word. Immanuel, God with us, long before the name was given to a child.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 8–11 — Be Still, and Know That I Am God
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Come, behold the works of the LORD: he makes wars cease, breaks the bow, shatters the spear and burns the chariots (vv. 8-9). Be still, and know that I am God. I will be exalted among the nations, I will be exalted in the earth! (v. 10). And the refrain again: The LORD of hosts is with us; the God of Jacob is our fortress (v. 11).
verseByVerse.theology: The famous command is spoken to the armies, not to the anxious: stop fighting and look at who this is.

verseByVerse.quote: Come, behold the works of the LORD, how he has brought desolations on the earth. He makes wars cease to the end of the earth; he breaks the bow and shatters the spear; he burns the chariots with fire. "Be still, and know that I am God. I will be exalted among the nations, I will be exalted in the earth!" The LORD of hosts is with us; the God of Jacob is our fortress. Selah
verseByVerse.commentary:
Come, behold the works of the LORD, how he has brought desolations on the earth. He makes wars cease to the end of the earth; he breaks the bow and shatters the spear; he burns the chariots with fire.

We are invited to come and look at a battlefield after God has finished with it. And what has been destroyed is not armies but weapons: bows snapped, spears shattered, chariots burning. God's way of ending war is to ruin the equipment.

Be still, and know that I am God. I will be exalted among the nations, I will be exalted in the earth!

This is one of the best known sentences in the Bible and it is usually quoted to an anxious Christian over a cup of tea. Look at who is being addressed. The verse comes in the middle of smashed weapons and raging nations, and God is speaking to them. It is not primarily "calm down, dear"; it is closer to "stop, drop it, and look at who I am" — the word means to let go, to cease striving.

That does not remove the comfort; it grounds it. The believer overhears God telling the nations to stand down, and stands down himself, because the God who can silence the armies of the earth can certainly handle what is on his mind at 2 a.m. Stillness is possible for us because it is commanded to them.

And the reason God gives is not peace for its own sake: I will be exalted among the nations, I will be exalted in the earth. That is the settled end of history, stated in the future tense with no conditions attached.

The LORD of hosts is with us; the God of Jacob is our fortress.

The refrain a second time, and it is where the psalm leaves us. Not "the earth is stable" — it may give way. Not "the nations are calm" — they are raging. The one fixed point is a presence: he is with us, and the walls we are behind are a person.

46.title: A Very Present Help in Trouble
46.overview: God is refuge, strength, and help already on site — therefore no fear even if the earth gives way, the mountains slide into the sea, and the waters roar (vv. 1-3). Against that sea, a river: quiet streams that make the city of God glad, because God is in her midst and helps her when morning dawns (vv. 4-5). The nations rage and kingdoms totter until God utters his voice and the earth melts; the LORD of hosts is with us; the God of Jacob is our fortress (vv. 6-7). Come and see what he has done: wars ended, bows broken, spears shattered, chariots burned (vv. 8-9). Be still, and know that I am God. I will be exalted among the nations (v. 10) — and the refrain again (v. 11).
46.theology:
Help is very present (v. 1): already there when the trouble starts. The psalm states the worst case first (vv. 2-3), because the way to steady a frightened person is not to deny the worst but to name who is with them in it.

Jerusalem had no river; the streams of v. 4 are set deliberately against the roaring sea of v. 3 — God's provision is quiet and gladdening where the world's power is loud (cf. Ezek 47; John 7:38; Rev 22:1). The city is not moved because God is in her midst (v. 5), and help comes when morning dawns, so the night is not skipped (cf. 2 Kgs 19:35).

Be still, and know that I am God (v. 10) is addressed to the raging nations: stop fighting and look at who I am. The believer's calm is grounded in that command to them, and in God's stated end: I will be exalted.

The refrain (vv. 7, 11) puts the whole security in a presence: the LORD of hosts is with us.
46.examples:
Help that was on site before the trouble.

Comfort that begins with the end of the world.

A city with no river, and a river anyway.

The sea roars; the streams make glad.

Moved, and not moved — the same word, one clause apart.

Help at daybreak, which means there was a night.

God ends wars by ruining the equipment.

Be still, said to the armies, overheard by the anxious.

47.text: To the choirmaster. A Psalm of the Sons of Korah. 1Clap your hands, all peoples! Shout to God with loud songs of joy!2For the LORD, the Most High, is to be feared, a great king over all the earth.3He subdued peoples under us, and nations under our feet.4He chose our heritage for us, the pride of Jacob whom he loves. Selah5God has gone up with a shout, the LORD with the sound of a trumpet.6Sing praises to God, sing praises! Sing praises to our King, sing praises!7For God is the King of all the earth; sing praises with a psalm!8God reigns over the nations; God sits on his holy throne.9The princes of the peoples gather as the people of the God of Abraham. For the shields of the earth belong to God; he is highly exalted!

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–4 — Clap Your Hands, All Peoples
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Clap your hands, all peoples! Shout to God with loud songs of joy! For the LORD, the Most High, is to be feared, a great king over all the earth (vv. 1-2). He subdued peoples under Israel and chose their heritage for them, the pride of Jacob whom he loves (vv. 3-4).
verseByVerse.theology: The command to worship is addressed to every nation, and the reason given is that God is king of all of them.

verseByVerse.quote: Clap your hands, all peoples! Shout to God with loud songs of joy! For the LORD, the Most High, is to be feared, a great king over all the earth. He subdued peoples under us, and nations under our feet. He chose our heritage for us, the pride of Jacob whom he loves. Selah
verseByVerse.commentary:
Clap your hands, all peoples! Shout to God with loud songs of joy! For the LORD, the Most High, is to be feared, a great king over all the earth.

The first word is addressed to everybody. Not Israel, clap: all peoples. This little psalm is missionary from its opening line, and it does not invite the nations, it commands them — which only makes sense if the second line is true, that the LORD is a great king over all the earth and not merely the local deity of a small country.

And notice what it asks for: clapping and shouting. Worship in the Psalter is regularly noisy, and there is no suggestion that volume is a lesser form of devotion. In the same breath God is to be feared. Loud joy and awe are not alternatives.

He subdued peoples under us, and nations under our feet. He chose our heritage for us, the pride of Jacob whom he loves.

The reason the nations should rejoice is, at first sight, an odd one: God gave Israel victories over them. But watch where the psalm is going. The nations are being summoned to celebrate the rule of a God whose people they have been losing to — and by verse 9 they are standing in the assembly as family. The conquest is not the end of the story.

He chose our heritage for us: even the land was not selected by them. And the one thing said about Jacob is that God loves him.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 5–9 — Sing Praises with a Psalm
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: God has gone up with a shout, the LORD with the sound of a trumpet (v. 5). Sing praises to God, sing praises! Sing praises to our King, sing praises! — with understanding, for God is the King of all the earth and sits on his holy throne (vv. 6-8). The princes of the peoples gather as the people of the God of Abraham, for the shields of the earth belong to God (v. 9).
verseByVerse.theology: God goes up with a shout, and the last verse has foreign rulers counted as Abraham's family.

verseByVerse.quote: God has gone up with a shout, the LORD with the sound of a trumpet. Sing praises to God, sing praises! Sing praises to our King, sing praises! For God is the King of all the earth; sing praises with a psalm! God reigns over the nations; God sits on his holy throne.
verseByVerse.commentary:
God has gone up with a shout, the LORD with the sound of a trumpet.

Something has been carried up the hill. The picture is almost certainly the ark going up to Zion with shouting and the blast of the horn (2 Sam 6:15) — God enthroned in the city, the procession arriving.

From the earliest centuries the church has read this verse on Ascension Day, and the instinct is right. A man went up with his disciples watching, and a cloud took him out of their sight (Acts 1:9); Paul quotes another psalm the same way — When he ascended on high he led a host of captives (Eph 4:8). The ark going up to its throne is a small rehearsal of a greater going-up, and the trumpet in this verse will sound again when he comes back.

Sing praises to God, sing praises! Sing praises to our King, sing praises! For God is the King of all the earth; sing praises with a psalm!

Five times in two verses. The psalm has one idea and cannot leave it alone, which is what happens to people who are actually glad.

And the last phrase adds the qualification that keeps the noise from being empty. The ESV notes the word is maskil: sing with understanding, with skill, with the mind engaged. Loud and thoughtful are not opposites either, and a church that has one without the other has lost half the verse.

God reigns over the nations; God sits on his holy throne. The tense is present. Not will reign — reigns, now, over nations that do not know it and would not agree.

verseByVerse.quote: The princes of the peoples gather as the people of the God of Abraham. For the shields of the earth belong to God; he is highly exalted!
verseByVerse.commentary:
The princes of the peoples gather as the people of the God of Abraham. For the shields of the earth belong to God; he is highly exalted!

The last verse is the biggest thing in the psalm. Foreign rulers — the princes of the very peoples subdued in verse 3 — are gathered in, and they are counted not as prisoners or vassals but as the people of the God of Abraham. They have joined the family.

That promise goes back to the beginning: God told Abraham that in you all the families of the earth shall be blessed (Gen 12:3). Paul says the point of Abraham's story was always that he would be the father of all who believe without being circumcised (Rom 4:11). Here, in nine verses of a wedding-sized psalm, is the whole Gentile mission in one line.

The shields of the earth belong to God — shields being a way of naming the rulers themselves, the protectors of their nations. Every defence the world has is God's property. The princes come in and hand them over.

So the psalm that began by ordering the nations to clap ends with their leaders standing inside the congregation, and the last words are what everybody in that gathering can agree on: he is highly exalted! Every Christian reading this is standing in verse 9. We are the princes of the peoples who came in.

47.title: God Has Gone Up with a Shout
47.overview: All peoples are commanded to clap and shout, because the LORD Most High is a great king over the whole earth (vv. 1-2); he subdued nations and chose Israel's heritage for her (vv. 3-4). God has gone up with a shout, the LORD with the sound of a trumpet (v. 5). Five times in two verses: sing praises — and sing with understanding, for God is King of all the earth and sits on his holy throne (vv. 6-8). The princes of the peoples gather as the people of the God of Abraham, and the shields of the earth belong to God (v. 9).
47.theology:
The psalm is missionary in its first line: the nations are commanded, not invited, to worship (v. 1), which only follows if God is king of all the earth (v. 2). Loud joy and fear stand together, as do volume and understanding (v. 7, maskil).

God's going up with a shout (v. 5) pictures the ark ascending Zion (2 Sam 6:15), and the church has long read it of the Ascension (Acts 1:9; cf. Eph 4:8).

God's reign over the nations is present tense (v. 8), exercised over peoples who neither know nor agree.

The last verse gathers Gentile rulers as the people of the God of Abraham (v. 9) — the promise of Gen 12:3 and the argument of Rom 4:11 in a single line. Their shields, the defences of the nations, are handed in.
47.examples:
The first word is addressed to everybody.

Clapping and fear in the same breath.

The nations told to celebrate a rule they have been losing to.

The ark going up the hill, and a cloud taking him out of sight.

Five "sing praises" in two verses.

Sing with understanding: volume is not the whole of it.

Foreign princes counted as Abraham's family.

We are the princes who came in.

48.text: A Song. A Psalm of the Sons of Korah. 1Great is the LORD and greatly to be praised in the city of our God! His holy mountain,2beautiful in elevation, is the joy of all the earth, Mount Zion, in the far north, the city of the great King.3Within her citadels God has made himself known as a fortress.4For behold, the kings assembled; they came on together.5As soon as they saw it, they were astounded; they were in panic; they took to flight.6Trembling took hold of them there, anguish as of a woman in labor.7By the east wind you shattered the ships of Tarshish.8As we have heard, so have we seen in the city of the LORD of hosts, in the city of our God, which God will establish forever. Selah9We have thought on your steadfast love, O God, in the midst of your temple.10As your name, O God, so your praise reaches to the ends of the earth. Your right hand is filled with righteousness.11Let Mount Zion be glad! Let the daughters of Judah rejoice because of your judgments!12Walk about Zion, go around her, number her towers,13consider well her ramparts, go through her citadels, that you may tell the next generation14that this is God, our God forever and ever. He will guide us forever.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–8 — The Kings Assembled, and Fled
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Great is the LORD and greatly to be praised in the city of our God! — his holy mountain, beautiful in elevation, the joy of all the earth ... the city of the great King, where God has made himself known as a fortress (vv. 1-3). Kings assembled and came on together; as soon as they saw it they panicked and fled, trembling like a woman in labour, shattered like the ships of Tarshish (vv. 4-7). As we have heard, so have we seen in the city of the LORD of hosts (v. 8).
verseByVerse.theology: An army arrives, looks, and runs — and no battle is described at all.

verseByVerse.quote: Great is the LORD and greatly to be praised in the city of our God! His holy mountain, beautiful in elevation, is the joy of all the earth, Mount Zion, in the far north, the city of the great King. Within her citadels God has made himself known as a fortress.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Great is the LORD and greatly to be praised in the city of our God! His holy mountain, beautiful in elevation, is the joy of all the earth, Mount Zion, in the far north, the city of the great King.

Two things in this verse are geographically false and theologically exact. Zion is not beautiful in elevation by any standard — it is a modest ridge, overlooked by the Mount of Olives, unimpressive beside the mountains of Lebanon. And it is not in the far north; it is in the south of the country, and the hill itself sits on the southern side of the city.

What the poet is doing is borrowing. The nations around Israel spoke of a great mountain in the far north where the gods held court, and this psalm takes that language and pins it on a low hill in Judah. The real mountain of God is not the impressive one; it is the one he chose. Paul makes the same move about people: God chose what is low and despised.

The joy of all the earth is an extravagant claim for a small city, and it was remembered when the claim collapsed — after Jerusalem fell, passers-by jeered, Is this the city that was called the perfection of beauty, the joy of all the earth? (Lam 2:15). Jesus called it the city of the great King and told people not to swear by it (Matt 5:35). And Hebrews tells Christians that they have already come to Mount Zion ... the heavenly Jerusalem (Heb 12:22), which is where the psalm's language finally fits.

Within her citadels God has made himself known as a fortress. Not the walls — God, inside them, has shown what he is. The strong point of the city is a person.

verseByVerse.quote: For behold, the kings assembled; they came on together. As soon as they saw it, they were astounded; they were in panic; they took to flight. Trembling took hold of them there, anguish as of a woman in labor. By the east wind you shattered the ships of Tarshish. As we have heard, so have we seen in the city of the LORD of hosts, in the city of our God, which God will establish forever. Selah
verseByVerse.commentary:
For behold, the kings assembled; they came on together. As soon as they saw it, they were astounded; they were in panic; they took to flight. Trembling took hold of them there, anguish as of a woman in labor. By the east wind you shattered the ships of Tarshish.

This is the strangest battle report in Scripture, because there is no battle. The kings gather, advance, arrive — and then four verbs in a row happen to them: astounded, panicked, fled, seized with trembling. Israel does nothing. Not a single defender is mentioned.

The comparison in verse 6 is deliberately undignified for an army: anguish as of a woman in labor — pain that cannot be postponed or fought off, arriving in waves. And the ships of Tarshish, the ocean-going merchant vessels, the largest things anyone in that world had built, are broken by a wind.

Jerusalem saw this happen more than once, most famously when Sennacherib's army camped outside and went home without a fight (2 Kgs 19), and again when Jehoshaphat's choir went out in front of the soldiers and found the enemy destroyed (2 Chr 20:22-24).

As we have heard, so have we seen in the city of the LORD of hosts, in the city of our God, which God will establish forever.

Psalm 44 began we have heard with our ears, our fathers have told us — and complained that the experience had not been repeated. This generation says the other thing: what we were told, we have now watched. Both psalms are true, and a believer will have both kinds of decade.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: We have thought on your steadfast love, O God, in the midst of your temple; his praise reaches the ends of the earth (vv. 9-11). Walk about Zion, go around her, number her towers, consider well her ramparts, go through her citadels, that you may tell the next generation that this is God, our God forever and ever. He will guide us forever (vv. 12-14).
verseByVerse.theology: Count the towers, and then tell the children — not about the towers, but about God.

verseByVerse.quote: We have thought on your steadfast love, O God, in the midst of your temple. As your name, O God, so your praise reaches to the ends of the earth. Your right hand is filled with righteousness. Let Mount Zion be glad! Let the daughters of Judah rejoice because of your judgments!
verseByVerse.commentary:
We have thought on your steadfast love, O God, in the midst of your temple. As your name, O God, so your praise reaches to the ends of the earth. Your right hand is filled with righteousness.

After the deliverance, they go inside and think. We have thought on your steadfast love — the verb is deliberate, the same kind of work as the murmuring of Psalm 1. Something happened outside the walls; the meaning of it is worked out inside the temple.

That is the right order after any rescue, and most of us skip it. The kings ran away, the city survived — and the psalm's response is not a party but a congregation sitting down to turn God's covenant love over in their minds.

Let Mount Zion be glad! Let the daughters of Judah rejoice because of your judgments! The villages around the city celebrate too. God's judgments — his decisions, carried out — are a reason for ordinary people in ordinary towns to be glad.

verseByVerse.quote: Walk about Zion, go around her, number her towers, consider well her ramparts, go through her citadels, that you may tell the next generation that this is God, our God forever and ever. He will guide us forever.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Walk about Zion, go around her, number her towers, consider well her ramparts, go through her citadels, that you may tell the next generation that this is God, our God forever and ever. He will guide us forever.

Five commands, and they are all physical: walk, go round, count, consider, go through. The congregation is sent out on a tour of the walls the morning after the siege lifted. Count the towers — they are all still standing. Look at the ramparts — not a stone gone.

And then the reason, which is the point of the whole psalm: that you may tell the next generation. The survey is not nostalgia or civic pride. It is evidence-gathering for the children, who will need to know that this happened, in this city, in a year that can be named.

But notice carefully what they are told to report. Not "this is our city", not "these are our towers". That this is God, our God forever and ever. The towers are the visual aid; God is the message. Which is just as well, because in 587 BC every one of those towers came down, and the psalm was still true — it always had been about the one inside the walls, not the walls.

The last line is the promise a survey of masonry cannot give: He will guide us forever. The ESV notes another reading — "He will guide us beyond death". Either way it reaches past the lifetime of the generation doing the counting, and past the city they are counting in, to the Zion that is above (Heb 12:22) and the city coming down out of heaven (Rev 21:2), whose walls will never need surveying again.

48.title: Walk About Zion
48.overview: Great is the LORD in the city of God: his holy mountain, beautiful in elevation, the joy of all the earth, where God has made himself known as a fortress (vv. 1-3). Kings assembled and advanced, and as soon as they saw it they were astounded, panicked and fled, trembling like a woman in labour; the ships of Tarshish were shattered by an east wind (vv. 4-7). As we have heard, so have we seen (v. 8). Inside the temple they turn God's steadfast love over in their minds, and his praise reaches the ends of the earth (vv. 9-11). Then: Walk about Zion, go around her, number her towers ... that you may tell the next generation that this is God, our God forever and ever. He will guide us forever (vv. 12-14).
48.theology:
The psalm's geography is deliberately wrong: Zion is neither lofty nor northern (v. 2). The language of the nations' mountain of the gods is planted on a modest ridge God chose — and Jesus calls it the city of the great King (Matt 5:35), while Hebrews says believers have come to the heavenly Zion (Heb 12:22).

The deliverance is described with no battle at all: four verbs happen to the attackers and Israel does nothing (vv. 4-7). And the fortress is a person known within the citadels (v. 3).

As we have heard, so have we seen (v. 8) answers the complaint of 44:1: both kinds of decade are real.

Deliverance is followed by deliberate meditation indoors (v. 9), and the tour of the walls exists to furnish testimony for the children — whose content is not the towers but God (vv. 12-14). Those towers fell in 587 BC and the last line held: He will guide us forever (the ESV notes the reading beyond death).
48.examples:
A low ridge given the language of the mountain of the gods.

The strong point of the city is a person inside it.

A battle report with no battle in it.

Labour pains: pain that cannot be fought off.

Heard from the fathers, and then seen with their own eyes.

The morning-after tour: count the towers, none missing.

Tell the children about God, not about the masonry.

The towers came down; the last line did not.

49.text: To the choirmaster. A Psalm of the Sons of Korah. 1Hear this, all peoples! Give ear, all inhabitants of the world,2both low and high, rich and poor together!3My mouth shall speak wisdom; the meditation of my heart shall be understanding.4I will incline my ear to a proverb; I will solve my riddle to the music of the lyre.5Why should I fear in times of trouble, when the iniquity of those who cheat me surrounds me,6those who trust in their wealth and boast of the abundance of their riches?7Truly no man can ransom another, or give to God the price of his life,8for the ransom of their life is costly and can never suffice,9that he should live on forever and never see the pit.10For he sees that even the wise die; the fool and the stupid alike must perish and leave their wealth to others.11Their graves are their homes forever, their dwelling places to all generations, though they called lands by their own names.12Man in his pomp will not remain; he is like the beasts that perish.13This is the path of those who have foolish confidence; yet after them people approve of their boasts. Selah14Like sheep they are appointed for Sheol; death shall be their shepherd, and the upright shall rule over them in the morning. Their form shall be consumed in Sheol, with no place to dwell.15But God will ransom my soul from the power of Sheol, for he will receive me. Selah16Be not afraid when a man becomes rich, when the glory of his house increases.17For when he dies he will carry nothing away; his glory will not go down after him.18For though, while he lives, he counts himself blessed— and though you get praise when you do well for yourself—19his soul will go to the generation of his fathers, who will never again see light.20Man in his pomp yet without understanding is like the beasts that perish.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–12 — The Ransom of Their Life Is Costly
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Hear this, all peoples ... both low and high, rich and poor together! — the psalmist will speak wisdom and solve his riddle to music (vv. 1-4). Why fear those who trust in wealth? Truly no man can ransom another, or give to God the price of his life, for the ransom of their life is costly and can never suffice (vv. 5-9). The wise die like the fool and leave their wealth to others; their graves are their homes. Man in his pomp will not remain; he is like the beasts that perish (vv. 10-12).
verseByVerse.theology: The one purchase no fortune can make is the one everybody needs.

verseByVerse.quote: Hear this, all peoples! Give ear, all inhabitants of the world, both low and high, rich and poor together! My mouth shall speak wisdom; the meditation of my heart shall be understanding. I will incline my ear to a proverb; I will solve my riddle to the music of the lyre. Why should I fear in times of trouble, when the iniquity of those who cheat me surrounds me, those who trust in their wealth and boast of the abundance of their riches?
verseByVerse.commentary:
Hear this, all peoples! Give ear, all inhabitants of the world, both low and high, rich and poor together! My mouth shall speak wisdom; the meditation of my heart shall be understanding. I will incline my ear to a proverb; I will solve my riddle to the music of the lyre.

This psalm is not addressed to God at all. It is a lecture, and the lecture hall is the world — low and high, rich and poor, summoned to the same seat. Death is the one subject on which the classes cannot be separated.

And the poet is careful about his own standing: he will incline my ear to a proverb before he opens his mouth. He is a listener first. Then he calls what follows a riddle and says he will solve it to music. Some truths are so hard that they have to be sung before they can be borne.

Why should I fear in times of trouble, when the iniquity of those who cheat me surrounds me, those who trust in their wealth and boast of the abundance of their riches?

The situation is Psalm 37's and Psalm 73's: dishonest people with money, and a believer who is losing to them. The question is not "why do they prosper?" but why should I fear? — and the answer, when it comes, has nothing to do with their fortunes being reversed. It has to do with a funeral.

verseByVerse.quote: Truly no man can ransom another, or give to God the price of his life, for the ransom of their life is costly and can never suffice, that he should live on forever and never see the pit. For he sees that even the wise die; the fool and the stupid alike must perish and leave their wealth to others. Their graves are their homes forever, their dwelling places to all generations, though they called lands by their own names. Man in his pomp will not remain; he is like the beasts that perish.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Truly no man can ransom another, or give to God the price of his life, for the ransom of their life is costly and can never suffice, that he should live on forever and never see the pit.

Here is the riddle solved, and it lands on the rich man's own ground: money. A ransom was the payment that bought a man out of slavery or off a death sentence, and the psalm says flatly that the one purchase everybody needs is the one no fortune can make. Costly, and it can never suffice — not "rarely", not "only for the very rich". Never.

Jesus put the same question to a crowd: For what can a man give in return for his soul? (Mark 8:37). The expected answer is nothing, and it is the reason the New Testament describes salvation as a purchase made by someone else: you were ransomed from the futile ways inherited from your forefathers, not with perishable things such as silver or gold, but with the precious blood of Christ (1 Pet 1:18-19). Peter says silver and gold in the same breath as this psalm, and then names the price that did suffice.

For he sees that even the wise die; the fool and the stupid alike must perish and leave their wealth to others. Their graves are their homes forever, their dwelling places to all generations, though they called lands by their own names.

Three kinds of people — wise, foolish, stupid — and one exit. The detail that stings is the last: they called lands by their own names, and their actual permanent address turned out to be a grave. Every country has estates and streets named after men nobody can identify.

Man in his pomp will not remain; he is like the beasts that perish. The word is the one for splendour and display — everything a life looks like from outside.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 13–20 — But God Will Ransom My Soul
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: This is the path of foolish confidence, admired by those who come after (v. 13). Like sheep they are appointed for Sheol; death shall be their shepherd (v. 14). But God will ransom my soul from the power of Sheol, for he will receive me (v. 15). Do not be afraid when a man grows rich: when he dies he will carry nothing away (vv. 16-19). Man in his pomp yet without understanding is like the beasts that perish (v. 20).
verseByVerse.theology: Everyone in the psalm dies; the difference is who is shepherding them out of it.

verseByVerse.quote: This is the path of those who have foolish confidence; yet after them people approve of their boasts. Selah Like sheep they are appointed for Sheol; death shall be their shepherd, and the upright shall rule over them in the morning. Their form shall be consumed in Sheol, with no place to dwell. But God will ransom my soul from the power of Sheol, for he will receive me. Selah
verseByVerse.commentary:
This is the path of those who have foolish confidence; yet after them people approve of their boasts.

The saddest half-line in the psalm: after they are dead, the next generation quotes them admiringly. The biographies get written, the buildings keep the name, and young men set out to copy a life that is now demonstrably over.

Like sheep they are appointed for Sheol; death shall be their shepherd, and the upright shall rule over them in the morning.

This is the anti-Psalm 23. There the LORD is my shepherd; here death shall be their shepherd, herding a flock down into Sheol. Everyone is being led by someone. The question the psalm asks is not whether you are being shepherded but who is doing it.

And there is a morning in the verse: the upright shall rule over them in the morning. The night of death has a daybreak in it, and the people who were losing to the rich all through this psalm are on top when the light comes.

But God will ransom my soul from the power of Sheol, for he will receive me.

After eight verses insisting no man can pay the ransom, the psalm says who can. But God will ransom my soul — the same word, now with God as the purchaser. It is the hinge of the whole poem: the impossibility in verse 7 is a statement about men, not about God.

And he will receive me is the verb used of Enoch, whom God took (Gen 5:24). Hosea puts the same promise in God's own mouth: I shall ransom them from the power of Sheol; I shall redeem them from Death (Hos 13:14) — which Paul quotes at the resurrection chapter's climax. This is an Old Testament believer, with the doctrine of resurrection still in shadow, saying the one thing that makes the rest of the psalm bearable.

verseByVerse.quote: Be not afraid when a man becomes rich, when the glory of his house increases. For when he dies he will carry nothing away; his glory will not go down after him. For though, while he lives, he counts himself blessed— and though you get praise when you do well for yourself— his soul will go to the generation of his fathers, who will never again see light. Man in his pomp yet without understanding is like the beasts that perish.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Be not afraid when a man becomes rich, when the glory of his house increases. For when he dies he will carry nothing away; his glory will not go down after him.

The command is not do not envy but do not be afraid, which is more honest about what wealth in other people's hands actually does to us. It is intimidating. The psalm's cure is a single fact: he will carry nothing away. Paul says it plainly — we brought nothing into the world, and we cannot take anything out of the world (1 Tim 6:7). The glory stays at the graveside with the mourners.

For though, while he lives, he counts himself blessed — and though you get praise when you do well for yourself — his soul will go to the generation of his fathers, who will never again see light.

Notice the aside in the middle: you get praise when you do well for yourself. The world congratulates self-interest, and the psalm is not surprised by it; that is simply how applause works. It is set against a sentence about never seeing light again.

Man in his pomp yet without understanding is like the beasts that perish.

The refrain returns from verse 12 with one phrase added, and everything turns on it: yet without understanding. The psalm has not been attacking wealth. A rich man who understands — who knows he cannot buy the ransom, and that God can — is not the man in this verse. The one who is like the beasts is the one who lives in splendour and never thinks about the end of it.

So the psalm that began by summoning rich and poor to the same lecture ends by dividing them along a different line altogether: not what a man owns, but whether he has understood who pays.

49.title: No Man Can Ransom Another
49.overview: A wisdom lecture addressed to everyone, rich and poor alike: the psalmist will solve a riddle to music (vv. 1-4). Why fear people who trust in wealth? Truly no man can ransom another, or give to God the price of his life — the price is beyond every fortune (vv. 5-9). The wise die like fools and leave their money behind; their permanent address is a grave, though they named lands after themselves (vv. 10-12). Their heirs still admire them; they are a flock with death for a shepherd (vv. 13-14). But God will ransom my soul from the power of Sheol, for he will receive me (v. 15). So do not be afraid when a man grows rich: he carries nothing away (vv. 16-19). Man in his pomp yet without understanding is like the beasts that perish (v. 20).
49.theology:
The psalm is addressed to the world, not to God, and its subject levels every class: death (vv. 1-2).

Its centre is a statement about money: the ransom for a life can never suffice (vv. 7-9). Jesus asks the same question (Mark 8:37), and the New Testament names the price that worked — not silver or gold but the blood of Christ (1 Pet 1:18-19).

Everyone is shepherded; the question is by whom. Death shall be their shepherd (v. 14) is the reverse of Psalm 23, and there is a morning in the verse.

What men cannot do God does: God will ransom my soul ... he will receive me (v. 15), the verb used of Enoch (Gen 5:24; cf. Hos 13:14).

The refrain changes one phrase between v. 12 and v. 20: the danger is not wealth but pomp without understanding.
49.examples:
Rich and poor summoned to the same seat.

A truth so hard it has to be sung.

The one purchase no fortune can make.

Estates named after men nobody can identify.

The next generation admiring a life that is demonstrably over.

Death as shepherd — Psalm 23 in reverse.

Enoch's verb: he will receive me.

Not "do not envy" but "do not be afraid".

50.text: A Psalm of Asaph. 1The Mighty One, God the LORD, speaks and summons the earth from the rising of the sun to its setting.2Out of Zion, the perfection of beauty, God shines forth.3Our God comes; he does not keep silence; before him is a devouring fire, around him a mighty tempest.4He calls to the heavens above and to the earth, that he may judge his people:5"Gather to me my faithful ones, who made a covenant with me by sacrifice!"6The heavens declare his righteousness, for God himself is judge! Selah7"Hear, O my people, and I will speak; O Israel, I will testify against you. I am God, your God.8Not for your sacrifices do I rebuke you; your burnt offerings are continually before me.9I will not accept a bull from your house or goats from your folds.10For every beast of the forest is mine, the cattle on a thousand hills.11I know all the birds of the hills, and all that moves in the field is mine.12"If I were hungry, I would not tell you, for the world and its fullness are mine.13Do I eat the flesh of bulls or drink the blood of goats?14Offer to God a sacrifice of thanksgiving, and perform your vows to the Most High,15and call upon me in the day of trouble; I will deliver you, and you shall glorify me."16But to the wicked God says: "What right have you to recite my statutes or take my covenant on your lips?17For you hate discipline, and you cast my words behind you.18If you see a thief, you are pleased with him, and you keep company with adulterers.19"You give your mouth free rein for evil, and your tongue frames deceit.20You sit and speak against your brother; you slander your own mother's son.21These things you have done, and I have been silent; you thought that I was one like yourself. But now I rebuke you and lay the charge before you.22"Mark this, then, you who forget God, lest I tear you apart, and there be none to deliver!23The one who offers thanksgiving as his sacrifice glorifies me; to one who orders his way rightly I will show the salvation of God!"

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–6 — Our God Comes; He Does Not Keep Silence
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: The Mighty One, God the LORD, speaks and summons the earth from the rising of the sun to its setting; out of Zion God shines forth (vv. 1-2). Our God comes; he does not keep silence; before him is a devouring fire, around him a mighty tempest (v. 3). He calls heaven and earth as witnesses and gathers his faithful ones, who made a covenant with me by sacrifice — for God himself is judge! (vv. 4-6).
verseByVerse.theology: The court is convened, the witnesses are the sky and the ground, and the defendants are his own people.

verseByVerse.quote: The Mighty One, God the LORD, speaks and summons the earth from the rising of the sun to its setting. Out of Zion, the perfection of beauty, God shines forth. Our God comes; he does not keep silence; before him is a devouring fire, around him a mighty tempest. He calls to the heavens above and to the earth, that he may judge his people: "Gather to me my faithful ones, who made a covenant with me by sacrifice!" The heavens declare his righteousness, for God himself is judge! Selah
verseByVerse.commentary:
The Mighty One, God the LORD, speaks and summons the earth from the rising of the sun to its setting. Out of Zion, the perfection of beauty, God shines forth. Our God comes; he does not keep silence; before him is a devouring fire, around him a mighty tempest.

The first psalm of Asaph, one of David's chief musicians, and it opens like a courtroom. Three names for God stacked in the first line, and then a summons issued to the whole earth, east to west. The ESV notes that verse 3 can be read as a prayer — "May our God come, and not keep silence" — but either way the point is that the silence is ending.

He calls to the heavens above and to the earth, that he may judge his people: Gather to me my faithful ones, who made a covenant with me by sacrifice! The heavens declare his righteousness, for God himself is judge!

Heaven and earth are called as witnesses, exactly as Moses called them when the covenant was made (Deut 32:1). This is a covenant lawsuit, and the shock of it is who is in the dock. Not the nations. That he may judge his people — and the defendants are addressed as my faithful ones, who made a covenant with me by sacrifice. These are the committed, the church-going, the sacrificing. That is who this psalm is for.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 7–15 — If I Were Hungry, I Would Not Tell You
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Hear, O my people ... I am God, your God. Not for your sacrifices do I rebuke you; your burnt offerings are continually before me (vv. 7-8). He needs no bull or goat: every beast of the forest is mine, the cattle on a thousand hills, and if I were hungry, I would not tell you (vv. 9-13). Offer to God a sacrifice of thanksgiving, and perform your vows to the Most High, and call upon me in the day of trouble; I will deliver you, and you shall glorify me (vv. 14-15).
verseByVerse.theology: The offerings were faultless; the theology behind them was that God needed feeding.

verseByVerse.quote: "Hear, O my people, and I will speak; O Israel, I will testify against you. I am God, your God. Not for your sacrifices do I rebuke you; your burnt offerings are continually before me. I will not accept a bull from your house or goats from your folds. For every beast of the forest is mine, the cattle on a thousand hills. I know all the birds of the hills, and all that moves in the field is mine. "If I were hungry, I would not tell you, for the world and its fullness are mine. Do I eat the flesh of bulls or drink the blood of goats?
verseByVerse.commentary:
Hear, O my people, and I will speak; O Israel, I will testify against you. I am God, your God. Not for your sacrifices do I rebuke you; your burnt offerings are continually before me.

God begins by clearing away the obvious charge. He is not complaining about attendance. Their sacrifices are continually before him — the rota is being kept, the animals are arriving, nobody has skipped a feast. Whatever is wrong is wrong underneath a faultless religious practice, which is the most frightening kind of thing to be told.

I will not accept a bull from your house or goats from your folds. For every beast of the forest is mine, the cattle on a thousand hills. I know all the birds of the hills, and all that moves in the field is mine.

Here is the problem: they had come to think of sacrifice as supply. God answers by pointing out that the animal on the altar was already his before they bought it. The cattle on a thousand hills has become a proverb, and the sentence beside it is just as good — I know all the birds of the hills. Not owns merely: knows, individually.

If I were hungry, I would not tell you, for the world and its fullness are mine. Do I eat the flesh of bulls or drink the blood of goats?

The sarcasm is deliberate and it is aimed at a religion the surrounding nations practised in earnest — feeding the gods, who were thought to need it. Paul said the same to Athens: God is not served by human hands, as though he needed anything (Acts 17:25).

The application is not difficult. Any religion that treats God as needy — needing our attendance, our money, our defence — has become this psalm's target, however orthodox the paperwork. He does not need you. That is precisely why what he wants from you is not supply.

verseByVerse.quote: Offer to God a sacrifice of thanksgiving, and perform your vows to the Most High, and call upon me in the day of trouble; I will deliver you, and you shall glorify me."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Offer to God a sacrifice of thanksgiving, and perform your vows to the Most High, and call upon me in the day of trouble; I will deliver you, and you shall glorify me.

Three things instead, and none of them feeds God. Thanksgiving — the ESV notes it may be "Make thanksgiving your sacrifice to God": gratitude is what he is after, and gratitude by definition admits that everything came from him. Perform your vows: keep the promises you made when you were desperate, which most people do not.

And then the third, which is astonishing in a lawsuit: call upon me in the day of trouble. In the middle of testifying against them, God tells them to ask him for help. The worship he wants from his people is that they should need him and say so.

I will deliver you, and you shall glorify me. There is the whole transaction, and notice which way the supply runs. He delivers; we glorify. A man who has been rescued and says so has given God exactly what the bulls could not.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 16–23 — You Thought That I Was One Like Yourself
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: To the wicked God says: What right have you to recite my statutes or take my covenant on your lips? — they hate discipline, keep company with thieves and adulterers, and slander their own brothers (vv. 16-20). These things you have done, and I have been silent; you thought that I was one like yourself. But now I rebuke you and lay the charge before you (v. 21). Mark this, then, you who forget God (v. 22): thanksgiving glorifies him, and to the one who orders his way rightly he will show the salvation of God (v. 23).
verseByVerse.theology: God's silence had been read as agreement. It was not.

verseByVerse.quote: But to the wicked God says: "What right have you to recite my statutes or take my covenant on your lips? For you hate discipline, and you cast my words behind you. If you see a thief, you are pleased with him, and you keep company with adulterers. "You give your mouth free rein for evil, and your tongue frames deceit. You sit and speak against your brother; you slander your own mother's son. These things you have done, and I have been silent; you thought that I was one like yourself. But now I rebuke you and lay the charge before you.
verseByVerse.commentary:
But to the wicked God says: What right have you to recite my statutes or take my covenant on your lips? For you hate discipline, and you cast my words behind you.

Now the second charge, and it is against people who can quote Scripture. They recite my statutes — they know the texts, they say the words in the service — and they cast my words behind them, which is the gesture of throwing something over your shoulder to get it out of sight while walking on.

If you see a thief, you are pleased with him, and you keep company with adulterers. You give your mouth free rein for evil, and your tongue frames deceit. You sit and speak against your brother; you slander your own mother's son.

The list runs from the eighth and seventh commandments to the ninth, and it ends closest to home. You sit — comfortably, at length — and take apart your own brother. The psalm has moved from the cattle on a thousand hills to a man being unpleasant about his family at a dinner table, and treats the second as the more serious evidence.

These things you have done, and I have been silent; you thought that I was one like yourself. But now I rebuke you and lay the charge before you.

And here is the sentence the whole psalm has been building to. God's silence had been read as agreement. Because nothing happened, they concluded that nothing was wrong — that God shared their standards, kept the same company, found the same jokes funny. You thought that I was one like yourself.

It is the commonest theological error there is, and it is not committed by atheists. It is committed by people in the congregation with the statutes on their lips. God's patience is not his approval, and one day he says so.

verseByVerse.quote: "Mark this, then, you who forget God, lest I tear you apart, and there be none to deliver! The one who offers thanksgiving as his sacrifice glorifies me; to one who orders his way rightly I will show the salvation of God!"
verseByVerse.commentary:
Mark this, then, you who forget God, lest I tear you apart, and there be none to deliver!

The warning is violent and it is a mercy: it is given before anything happens. You who forget God is the psalm's final description of them — not deniers, forgetters. And the second half removes the assumption every person in this psalm has been living on, that there will always be a way out.

The one who offers thanksgiving as his sacrifice glorifies me; to one who orders his way rightly I will show the salvation of God!

The psalm ends by restating the whole case positively. Thanksgiving — again — is what glorifies God; and the one who orders his way, who arranges his actual conduct rather than only his liturgy, is promised a sight of the salvation of God.

That is where the courtroom lands. The defendants are not told to bring more animals or to try harder at the festivals. They are told to be grateful, to keep their word, to call for help, to mend their behaviour — and that the God who needs nothing from them has salvation to show them.

50.title: The Cattle on a Thousand Hills
50.overview: God convenes a court. He summons the earth from sunrise to sunset, shines out of Zion, comes with fire and tempest, and calls heaven and earth as witnesses to judge his own people — the ones who made a covenant with him by sacrifice (vv. 1-6). The charge is not neglect: their burnt offerings are continually before him (vv. 7-8). It is that they think he needs feeding — every beast of the forest is already his, and if I were hungry, I would not tell you (vv. 9-13). What he wants is thanksgiving, kept vows, and to be called on in the day of trouble (vv. 14-15). Then a second charge, against those who recite his statutes while keeping company with thieves and adulterers and slandering their own brothers: you thought that I was one like yourself (vv. 16-21). Mark this, you who forget God — and to the one who orders his way rightly, God will show his salvation (vv. 22-23).
50.theology:
The psalm is a covenant lawsuit with heaven and earth as witnesses (v. 4; cf. Deut 32:1), and the defendants are God's own committed, sacrificing people (vv. 5, 7). Faultless religious practice is explicitly not the issue (v. 8).

The error is treating sacrifice as supply. God owns the animal before it is bought (vv. 10-11) and needs nothing (v. 12; cf. Acts 17:25) — so any religion that makes God needy, however orthodox, is this psalm's target.

What he asks instead is thanksgiving, kept vows, and prayer in trouble (vv. 14-15): the worship God wants from his people is that they should need him and say so. I will deliver you, and you shall glorify me.

The second charge falls on people who can quote Scripture (v. 16) and ends at the family table (v. 20). Its verdict names the commonest error of religious people: you thought that I was one like yourself (v. 21). God's patience is not his approval.
50.examples:
A summons issued from sunrise to sunset.

The defendants are the ones who kept the rota.

The bull was already his before they bought it.

He knows the birds individually.

In the middle of a lawsuit: call on me.

He delivers; we glorify. That is the whole transaction.

Casting God's words over the shoulder while walking on.

Silence mistaken for agreement.

51.text: To the choirmaster. A Psalm of David, when Nathan the prophet went to him, after he had gone in to Bathsheba. 1Have mercy on me, O God, according to your steadfast love; according to your abundant mercy blot out my transgressions.2Wash me thoroughly from my iniquity, and cleanse me from my sin!3For I know my transgressions, and my sin is ever before me.4Against you, you only, have I sinned and done what is evil in your sight, so that you may be justified in your words and blameless in your judgment.5Behold, I was brought forth in iniquity, and in sin did my mother conceive me.6Behold, you delight in truth in the inward being, and you teach me wisdom in the secret heart.7Purge me with hyssop, and I shall be clean; wash me, and I shall be whiter than snow.8Let me hear joy and gladness; let the bones that you have broken rejoice.9Hide your face from my sins, and blot out all my iniquities.10Create in me a clean heart, O God, and renew a right spirit within me.11Cast me not away from your presence, and take not your Holy Spirit from me.12Restore to me the joy of your salvation, and uphold me with a willing spirit.13Then I will teach transgressors your ways, and sinners will return to you.14Deliver me from bloodguiltiness, O God, O God of my salvation, and my tongue will sing aloud of your righteousness.15O Lord, open my lips, and my mouth will declare your praise.16For you will not delight in sacrifice, or I would give it; you will not be pleased with a burnt offering.17The sacrifices of God are a broken spirit; a broken and contrite heart, O God, you will not despise.18Do good to Zion in your good pleasure; build up the walls of Jerusalem;19then will you delight in right sacrifices, in burnt offerings and whole burnt offerings; then bulls will be offered on your altar.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–6 — Against You, You Only, Have I Sinned
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Have mercy on me, O God, according to your steadfast love ... blot out my transgressions. Wash me thoroughly from my iniquity, and cleanse me from my sin! (vv. 1-2). For I know my transgressions, and my sin is ever before me. Against you, you only, have I sinned (vv. 3-4). Behold, I was brought forth in iniquity — and God delights in truth in the inward being (vv. 5-6).
verseByVerse.theology: Three words for sin, three for pardon, and an admission that the trouble goes back further than the crime.

verseByVerse.quote: Have mercy on me, O God, according to your steadfast love; according to your abundant mercy blot out my transgressions. Wash me thoroughly from my iniquity, and cleanse me from my sin! For I know my transgressions, and my sin is ever before me. Against you, you only, have I sinned and done what is evil in your sight, so that you may be justified in your words and blameless in your judgment.
verseByVerse.commentary:
To the choirmaster. A Psalm of David, when Nathan the prophet went to him, after he had gone in to Bathsheba.

The heading does not spare him. It names the woman, names the prophet, and dates the psalm to the worst afternoon of his life — and then hands the whole thing to the choirmaster to be sung in public. Israel's king made his confession into a national hymn.

Have mercy on me, O God, according to your steadfast love; according to your abundant mercy blot out my transgressions. Wash me thoroughly from my iniquity, and cleanse me from my sin!

He does not open with an explanation. The first words are a plea for mercy, and the measure asked for is not the size of the sin but the size of God: according to your steadfast love ... according to your abundant mercy.

Three words for what he has done — transgression (rebellion), iniquity (crookedness), sin (falling short) — and three for what he wants done about it. Blot out is to erase writing from a record. Wash is the word for laundering cloth, trampling and beating a garment until the stain comes out. Cleanse is the priest's word for declaring someone ritually clean. The record, the stain, the status: all three.

For I know my transgressions, and my sin is ever before me. Against you, you only, have I sinned and done what is evil in your sight, so that you may be justified in your words and blameless in your judgment.

Against you, you only has puzzled readers, because he had plainly sinned against Uriah, who was dead, and against Bathsheba, and against his army and his people. He is not denying that. He is saying who the offended party ultimately is: every wrong done to a person is a wrong done to the God who made them, and it is God alone who can pardon it. A man can apologise to his neighbour and still be unforgiven.

And the last clause concedes the verdict before it is passed: so that you may be justified in your words. Paul quotes exactly this to prove that God is in the right when he judges (Rom 3:4). Real confession does not negotiate over the sentence.

verseByVerse.quote: Behold, I was brought forth in iniquity, and in sin did my mother conceive me. Behold, you delight in truth in the inward being, and you teach me wisdom in the secret heart.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Behold, I was brought forth in iniquity, and in sin did my mother conceive me.

This is not an excuse, and it is not a slur on his mother. It is the deepest thing in the psalm. Having confessed the act, he goes underneath it: the act came out of a nature that was bent before he could walk. If he only confessed the adultery, he would be treating himself as a good man who did a bad thing.

Every serious repentance reaches this point eventually. The problem is not that I made a mistake; the problem is what I am. And it is the reason verse 10 will ask for something a decent effort cannot produce.

Behold, you delight in truth in the inward being, and you teach me wisdom in the secret heart.

Two beholds side by side: here is what I am, and here is what you want. God's interest is in the inward being and the secret heart — the part David had been managing carefully in public for the best part of a year while the affair was covered up.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 7–12 — Create in Me a Clean Heart
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Purge me with hyssop, and I shall be clean; wash me, and I shall be whiter than snow; let the bones God has broken rejoice (vv. 7-8). Hide your face from my sins ... Create in me a clean heart, O God, and renew a right spirit within me. Cast me not away from your presence, and take not your Holy Spirit from me. Restore to me the joy of your salvation (vv. 9-12).
verseByVerse.theology: He does not ask for repair. He asks for the verb of Genesis 1.

verseByVerse.quote: Purge me with hyssop, and I shall be clean; wash me, and I shall be whiter than snow. Let me hear joy and gladness; let the bones that you have broken rejoice. Hide your face from my sins, and blot out all my iniquities. Create in me a clean heart, O God, and renew a right spirit within me. Cast me not away from your presence, and take not your Holy Spirit from me. Restore to me the joy of your salvation, and uphold me with a willing spirit.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Purge me with hyssop, and I shall be clean; wash me, and I shall be whiter than snow.

Hyssop is a small bushy plant used as a brush. It was hyssop that daubed the lamb's blood on the doorposts at Passover, hyssop that sprinkled a cleansed leper, hyssop that applied the water of purification to a man who had touched a corpse (Num 19:18). David is asking to be treated as an unclean man with blood on his hands — which is precisely what he is — and he wants the ritual to work.

Whiter than snow is the promise Isaiah would later put in God's own mouth: though your sins are like scarlet, they shall be as white as snow (Isa 1:18). Not less scarlet. White.

Let me hear joy and gladness; let the bones that you have broken rejoice.

He says God broke his bones, and asks that the broken bones be made to dance. It is the honest account of what conviction of sin feels like — an injury, inflicted by God, and survivable only if the same hand heals it.

Hide your face from my sins, and blot out all my iniquities. Create in me a clean heart, O God, and renew a right spirit within me.

The word create is not a general word for making. It is bara, the verb of Genesis 1:1, used in the Old Testament only with God as its subject. David does not ask for his heart to be cleaned up, mended or improved. He asks for an act of creation out of nothing, because he has just said in verse 5 that there is nothing in him to work with. This is the Old Testament asking for the new birth.

Cast me not away from your presence, and take not your Holy Spirit from me.

David had watched this happen. The Spirit of the LORD departed from Saul, and David was in the room as the replacement (1 Sam 16:14). He is not speculating about a doctrine; he is terrified of a precedent. Christians under the new covenant are given a better promise — the Spirit is a seal for the day of redemption (Eph 4:30) — but feel the horror of the request before hurrying to the comfort. Whatever else sin costs, it should never cost us this fear lightly.

Restore to me the joy of your salvation, and uphold me with a willing spirit.

Notice what he asks to have restored. Not his salvation — the joy of it. He knows the difference between being saved and being glad about it, and he has lost the second. And he asks for a willing spirit: not merely to be forgiven but to want to obey, which is the thing sin destroys first and quietest.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 13–19 — A Broken and Contrite Heart
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Then I will teach transgressors your ways; deliver me from bloodguiltiness and my tongue will sing (vv. 13-15). For you will not delight in sacrifice, or I would give it ... The sacrifices of God are a broken spirit; a broken and contrite heart, O God, you will not despise (vv. 16-17). Do good to Zion ... build up the walls of Jerusalem, and then right sacrifices will be offered (vv. 18-19).
verseByVerse.theology: A forgiven man immediately becomes a teacher, and the only offering he has is the state he is in.

verseByVerse.quote: Then I will teach transgressors your ways, and sinners will return to you. Deliver me from bloodguiltiness, O God, O God of my salvation, and my tongue will sing aloud of your righteousness. O Lord, open my lips, and my mouth will declare your praise. For you will not delight in sacrifice, or I would give it; you will not be pleased with a burnt offering. The sacrifices of God are a broken spirit; a broken and contrite heart, O God, you will not despise.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Then I will teach transgressors your ways, and sinners will return to you.

Then — after the clean heart, not before. A forgiven man becomes a teacher of exactly the people he now belongs to: transgressors, sinners. This is what David is doing in this very psalm, and it is why it went to the choirmaster. The most useful thing about a restored believer is that he knows the way back because he has walked it.

Deliver me from bloodguiltiness, O God, O God of my salvation, and my tongue will sing aloud of your righteousness. O Lord, open my lips, and my mouth will declare your praise.

He names the crime without softening it: there is a man dead because of him. And he cannot even begin the praise on his own — open my lips, because guilt had shut them. Churches have opened their services with this verse for centuries, which is exactly right: nobody starts worship under their own power.

For you will not delight in sacrifice, or I would give it; you will not be pleased with a burnt offering.

There is a reason this is not false piety. Under the law there was no sacrifice for deliberate adultery and premeditated murder; the sacrificial system covered sins of ignorance and weakness, not these. David has nothing to bring, and he says so: I would give it if it would work. He is standing outside the mechanism of his own religion with nothing in his hands.

The sacrifices of God are a broken spirit; a broken and contrite heart, O God, you will not despise.

So the only offering he has left is the state he is in. Broken is the word used of the bones in verse 8; contrite means crushed small. And the promise is put as a double negative, which is gentler than an assurance: God will not despise it. He will not look at a man in pieces and turn away.

That is the mercy the tax collector was relying on when he stood at a distance and beat his breast, and Jesus said he went home justified (Luke 18:13-14). It is the only entry requirement this psalm mentions, and the whole of Christianity runs through it.

verseByVerse.quote: Do good to Zion in your good pleasure; build up the walls of Jerusalem; then will you delight in right sacrifices, in burnt offerings and whole burnt offerings; then bulls will be offered on your altar.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Do good to Zion in your good pleasure; build up the walls of Jerusalem; then will you delight in right sacrifices, in burnt offerings and whole burnt offerings; then bulls will be offered on your altar.

The ending surprises readers who have just been told that God does not delight in sacrifice. It is not a contradiction; it is the proper sequel. What God rejected in verse 16 was sacrifice offered instead of a broken heart. What he delights in here is sacrifice offered by people whose hearts have been dealt with — then will you delight in right sacrifices. The same altar, with a different man standing at it.

And notice that the king's private repentance ends by praying for the city. He knows his sin did not stay private: a nation is affected by what its leaders do in the dark, and the walls of Jerusalem are on his conscience along with Uriah. Real repentance always widens; it starts with have mercy on me and ends asking God to do good to everybody else.

51.title: Create in Me a Clean Heart
51.overview: David's confession after Nathan confronted him over Bathsheba, handed to the choirmaster to be sung in public. He asks for mercy measured by God's steadfast love: blot out, wash, cleanse (vv. 1-2). He knows his transgressions, and against you, you only, have I sinned (vv. 3-4); the trouble reaches back to his conception, and God wants truth in the inward being (vv. 5-6). Purge me with hyssop; let the bones you broke rejoice; create in me a clean heart, O God ... take not your Holy Spirit from me. Restore to me the joy of your salvation (vv. 7-12). Then he will teach transgressors God's ways; deliver him from bloodguilt and open his lips (vv. 13-15). God does not want sacrifice: the sacrifices of God are a broken spirit; a broken and contrite heart, O God, you will not despise (vv. 16-17). And the psalm ends praying for Zion, where right sacrifices will then be offered (vv. 18-19).
51.theology:
Pardon is asked for on the scale of God's mercy, not the scale of the sin (v. 1), with three words for sin answered by three for forgiveness — record erased, stain laundered, status declared clean (vv. 1-2).

Against you, you only (v. 4) does not deny the human victims; it names who alone can pardon, and concedes God's verdict in advance — which Paul cites at Rom 3:4.

Verse 5 takes repentance beneath the act to the nature: the problem is not a mistake but a condition. So v. 10 asks for bara, the Genesis 1 verb used only of God: creation, not repair — the Old Testament praying for the new birth.

The fear in v. 11 is drawn from Saul (1 Sam 16:14); believers now have a better promise (Eph 4:30). What is asked back is the joy of salvation (v. 12), not salvation itself.

The law provided no sacrifice for deliberate adultery and murder, so David has nothing to bring (v. 16) — only what he is (v. 17), which God will not despise (cf. Luke 18:13-14). Repentance then widens from have mercy on me to prayer for the whole city (v. 18).
51.examples:
The heading names the woman and the prophet, and sends it to the choir.

Blot out, launder, declare clean.

Apologising to your neighbour and remaining unforgiven.

Under the act, a nature: brought forth in iniquity.

Hyssop — the brush used on doorposts and lepers.

Broken bones asked to dance.

Create: the verb only God is ever the subject of.

He had watched the Spirit leave Saul.

Not salvation restored — the joy of it.

No sacrifice in the law fitted his case.

52.text: To the choirmaster. A Maskil of David, when Doeg, the Edomite, came and told Saul, "David has come to the house of Ahimelech." 1Why do you boast of evil, O mighty man? The steadfast love of God endures all the day.2Your tongue plots destruction, like a sharp razor, you worker of deceit.3You love evil more than good, and lying more than speaking what is right. Selah4You love all words that devour, O deceitful tongue.5But God will break you down forever; he will snatch and tear you from your tent; he will uproot you from the land of the living. Selah6The righteous shall see and fear, and shall laugh at him, saying,7"See the man who would not make God his refuge, but trusted in the abundance of his riches and sought refuge in his own destruction!"8But I am like a green olive tree in the house of God. I trust in the steadfast love of God forever and ever.9I will thank you forever, because you have done it. I will wait for your name, for it is good, in the presence of the godly.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Why do you boast of evil, O mighty man? His tongue plots destruction like a sharp razor; he loves evil more than good and lying more than truth, and all words that devour (vv. 1-4). But God will break you down forever; he will snatch and tear you from your tent; he will uproot you from the land of the living (v. 5). The righteous will see and fear and laugh: See the man who would not make God his refuge (vv. 6-7).
verseByVerse.theology: A hero whose great exploit was informing, and a tongue that did the work of a razor.

verseByVerse.quote: Why do you boast of evil, O mighty man? The steadfast love of God endures all the day. Your tongue plots destruction, like a sharp razor, you worker of deceit. You love evil more than good, and lying more than speaking what is right. Selah You love all words that devour, O deceitful tongue.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The heading takes us to one of the darkest pages in Samuel. David, on the run, came to the priests at Nob and was given bread and Goliath's sword.
