A man of Saul's was there and saw it: Doeg the Edomite. He went to the king and reported it — accurately — and when Saul's own soldiers refused to touch the priests, Doeg killed eighty-five of them himself, and then the town (1 Sam 22:9-10, 18).

So this psalm is about an informer. Nothing he said was false. That is what makes it such a precise study of what a tongue can do.

Why do you boast of evil, O mighty man? The steadfast love of God endures all the day.

O mighty man is sarcasm, and it stings: the title belongs to a champion, and this champion's great exploit was carrying a report. And notice the answer set against his boasting — not David's strength, but God's steadfast love, which endures all the day, outlasting whatever the man is currently enjoying.

Your tongue plots destruction, like a sharp razor, you worker of deceit. You love evil more than good, and lying more than speaking what is right. You love all words that devour, O deceitful tongue.

A razor is a small blade, useful, ordinary, kept close to the face — and capable of opening a throat. James makes the same point with a spark and a forest (Jas 3:5-6). What Doeg did required no army; it required a sentence.

And twice the psalm says he loves it. This is not a man who lost his temper. He prefers evil to good and lying to truth as a settled taste, the way another man prefers salt to sugar. The phrase words that devour is exact: some speech is eating somebody.

verseByVerse.quote: But God will break you down forever; he will snatch and tear you from your tent; he will uproot you from the land of the living. Selah The righteous shall see and fear, and shall laugh at him, saying, "See the man who would not make God his refuge, but trusted in the abundance of his riches and sought refuge in his own destruction!"
verseByVerse.commentary:
But God will break you down forever; he will snatch and tear you from your tent; he will uproot you from the land of the living.

Four verbs, all God's, and all violent: break down, snatch, tear away, uproot. The tent is his settled place, and he is pulled out of it like a peg. A man who made his living by loyalty to a king will be evicted by the King who was not consulted.

The righteous shall see and fear, and shall laugh at him, saying, See the man who would not make God his refuge, but trusted in the abundance of his riches and sought refuge in his own destruction!

The laughter needs care. It is not amusement at another man's pain; it follows fear in the same sentence, and what it laughs at is the collapse of a boast. Here was a man with money and access who declined the one refuge that holds, and the ESV notes his alternative may be read as "his work of destruction" — he took shelter in the very thing that ruined him. Every generation watches somebody do it, and when the structure falls, the laughter is at the absurdity, not the funeral.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 8–9 — But I Am Like a Green Olive Tree
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: But I am like a green olive tree in the house of God. I trust in the steadfast love of God forever and ever. I will thank you forever, because you have done it. I will wait for your name, for it is good, in the presence of the godly (vv. 8-9).
verseByVerse.theology: One man is torn out of his tent; the other is planted indoors, and gives thanks before anything has visibly changed.

verseByVerse.quote: But I am like a green olive tree in the house of God. I trust in the steadfast love of God forever and ever. I will thank you forever, because you have done it. I will wait for your name, for it is good, in the presence of the godly.
verseByVerse.commentary:
But I am like a green olive tree in the house of God. I trust in the steadfast love of God forever and ever.

Set the two pictures side by side, because the psalm means you to. One man is torn from his tent and uprooted; the other is a tree in the house of God — planted indoors, in the courts, where trees do not normally grow. An olive tree is slow, long-lived and productive for centuries; Jeremiah used the same image of Israel, a green olive tree, beautiful with good fruit (Jer 11:16).

And David writes this while living in caves. He has no tent worth tearing down, and he is not currently allowed anywhere near the house of God. The claim is not about his circumstances; it is about where his roots are.

I will thank you forever, because you have done it. I will wait for your name, for it is good, in the presence of the godly.

Because you have done it — past tense, about a rescue that has not yet occurred. And then, in the same breath, I will wait. Thanking God for a finished work while still waiting for it is not a contradiction; it is faith's ordinary posture, and every Christian at the Lord's Table does exactly that.

The last phrase is where the psalm ends: in the presence of the godly. Doeg had the king's ear and the king's favour and died alone in the record. David, hunted, names the company he intends to keep.

52.title: A Green Olive Tree in the House of God
52.overview: Written about Doeg the Edomite, who told Saul where David had been and then slaughtered the priests of Nob. Why do you boast of evil, O mighty man? — his tongue is a sharp razor, he loves evil more than good and lying more than truth, and delights in words that devour (vv. 1-4). God will break him down, snatch him from his tent and uproot him from the land of the living (v. 5), and the righteous will see, fear, and laugh at the collapse of a man who would not make God his refuge but trusted his riches (vv. 6-7). But I am like a green olive tree in the house of God: trusting God's steadfast love forever, thanking him for what he has done, and waiting for his name among the godly (vv. 8-9).
52.theology:
The informer's report was true, and it killed eighty-five priests (1 Sam 22): the psalm is a study of what a tongue can do without a weapon (v. 2; cf. Jas 3:5-6).

The sin is an affection, not an outburst: twice he is said to love evil and lying (vv. 3-4). A razor is small, ordinary and kept near the face.

The righteous laugh only after they fear (v. 6), and what they laugh at is a collapsed boast — a man who sheltered in the thing that ruined him (v. 7).

Two pictures are set against each other: uprooted from a tent, and planted as a green olive tree indoors (vv. 5, 8; cf. 1:3; Jer 11:16). David writes it from a cave, so the claim is about roots rather than circumstances, and he thanks God in the past tense for a rescue still awaited (v. 9).
52.examples:
An informer who told the truth, and eighty-five dead priests.

O mighty man: the hero whose exploit was a report.

A razor — small, ordinary, kept near the face.

Twice: he loves it. Not a lapse, a taste.

Words that devour: some speech is eating somebody.

Torn from a tent; planted in a house.

A cave-dweller calling himself a tree in God's courts.

Thanks for a finished work, and still waiting.

53.text: To the choirmaster: according to Mahalath. A Maskil of David. 1The fool says in his heart, "There is no God." They are corrupt, doing abominable iniquity; there is none who does good.2God looks down from heaven on the children of man to see if there are any who understand, who seek after God.3They have all fallen away; together they have become corrupt; there is none who does good, not even one.4Have those who work evil no knowledge, who eat up my people as they eat bread, and do not call upon God?5There they are, in great terror, where there is no terror! For God scatters the bones of him who encamps against you; you put them to shame, for God has rejected them.6Oh, that salvation for Israel would come out of Zion! When God restores the fortunes of his people, let Jacob rejoice, let Israel be glad.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–6 — The Same Verdict, Sung Again
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: The fool says in his heart, There is no God; God looks down from heaven and finds no one who understands or seeks him — there is none who does good, not even one (vv. 1-3). The evildoers eat up God's people like bread and never pray (v. 4). There they are, in great terror, where there is no terror! — for God scatters the bones of the besiegers (v. 5). Oh, that salvation for Israel would come out of Zion! (v. 6).
verseByVerse.theology: Psalm 14 printed a second time, with the divine name changed throughout and one verse rewritten after a deliverance.

verseByVerse.quote: The fool says in his heart, "There is no God." They are corrupt, doing abominable iniquity; there is none who does good. God looks down from heaven on the children of man to see if there are any who understand, who seek after God. They have all fallen away; together they have become corrupt; there is none who does good, not even one. Have those who work evil no knowledge, who eat up my people as they eat bread, and do not call upon God?
verseByVerse.commentary:
The fool says in his heart, There is no God. They are corrupt, doing abominable iniquity; there is none who does good.

You have read this before. Psalm 53 is Psalm 14 a second time, and the exposition of what it means belongs there: the fool is a moral category rather than an intellectual one, the creed is held in the heart and proved by a way of life, God conducts the search himself and finds nobody, and Paul quotes the verdict to open his case that the whole world is accountable (Rom 3:10-12).

Even the heading has changed: Psalm 14 was simply "To the choirmaster. Of David"; this one is set according to Mahalath and called a Maskil — musical or liturgical terms, says the ESV, whose meaning is no longer known. The same words have been given a new setting for a new occasion.

What this chapter is for is the differences, because the Psalter does not print a poem twice by accident.

The first is the name of God. In Psalm 14 the covenant name, the LORD, appears four times. In Psalm 53 it does not appear at all; every occurrence has become God. That is not a slip. Psalm 53 sits in Book Two of the Psalter, where the covenant name is largely replaced by the general name for God — and the effect here is to widen the verdict. Psalm 14 said this about human beings before the God of Israel. Psalm 53 says it about human beings before God as such, and lets no one plead a different deity.

The small verbal changes run the same way. Psalm 14 has abominable deeds; this has abominable iniquity. Psalm 14 says they have turned aside; this says they have fallen away. Nothing in the diagnosis has softened with the years.

verseByVerse.quote: There they are, in great terror, where there is no terror! For God scatters the bones of him who encamps against you; you put them to shame, for God has rejected them. Oh, that salvation for Israel would come out of Zion! When God restores the fortunes of his people, let Jacob rejoice, let Israel be glad.
verseByVerse.commentary:
There they are, in great terror, where there is no terror! For God scatters the bones of him who encamps against you; you put them to shame, for God has rejected them.

Here is the one verse that is genuinely rewritten, and the two should be set side by side. Psalm 14 said: There they are in great terror, for God is with the generation of the righteous. You would shame the plans of the poor, but the LORD is his refuge. This version says something sharper: their terror came where there is no terror — panic with no cause, the kind that empties a camp overnight — and God scatters the bones of him who encamps against you.

Something has happened between the two editions. An army had encamped, and it is not there any more, and what is left is unburied bones. Israel could point to more than one such morning; the most famous is the night the Assyrian camp outside Jerusalem was found dead (2 Kgs 19:35).

So the psalm of universal human corruption has been reissued with a war story in the middle of it. The verdict did not change; the evidence for God's answer to it grew. That is how a congregation sings an old song after something has happened to them — same words, one verse updated, because they now know something they did not.

Oh, that salvation for Israel would come out of Zion! When God restores the fortunes of his people, let Jacob rejoice, let Israel be glad.

And the longing is unchanged, except that here it is God who restores rather than the LORD. If there is none who does good, no reform will do; salvation has to come from outside, out of Zion. It did. The wish at the end of both psalms was answered by one man walking out of that city to die.

53.title: There Is None Who Does Good: A Second Time
53.overview: Psalm 14 printed a second time. The fool says in his heart there is no God; God looks down from heaven and finds no one who understands or seeks him — none who does good, not even one (vv. 1-3). The evildoers consume God's people like bread and never call on him (v. 4). Then the one rewritten verse: There they are, in great terror, where there is no terror!, for God scatters the bones of the army encamped against his people (v. 5). And the same closing longing: Oh, that salvation for Israel would come out of Zion! (v. 6).
53.theology:
The exposition of this psalm's content stands at Psalm 14; here only the differences are treated, because the Psalter prints it twice on purpose.

Every LORD of Psalm 14 has become God (Book Two's pattern), which widens the verdict: the corruption is stated before God as such, and no one may plead a different deity.

Verse 5 is genuinely rewritten. Psalm 14:5-6 spoke of God being with the righteous generation; this speaks of causeless terror and scattered bones — a siege lifted between the two editions (cf. 2 Kgs 19:35). The verdict on humanity did not change; the evidence of God's answer grew.

The unchanged ending keeps the point: if none does good, salvation must come from outside, out of Zion (v. 6).
53.examples:
The Psalter does not print a poem twice by accident.

Four covenant names in Psalm 14; none here.

Turned aside becomes fallen away.

Terror where there was nothing to be afraid of.

An army that encamped, and the bones left behind.

Same song, one verse updated, because something happened.

54.text: To the choirmaster: with stringed instruments. A Maskil of David, when the Ziphites went and told Saul, "Is not David hiding among us?" 1O God, save me by your name, and vindicate me by your might.2O God, hear my prayer; give ear to the words of my mouth.3For strangers have risen against me; ruthless men seek my life; they do not set God before themselves. Selah4Behold, God is my helper; the Lord is the upholder of my life.5He will return the evil to my enemies; in your faithfulness put an end to them.6With a freewill offering I will sacrifice to you; I will give thanks to your name, O LORD, for it is good.7For he has delivered me from every trouble, and my eye has looked in triumph on my enemies.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–7 — Save Me by Your Name
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: O God, save me by your name, and vindicate me by your might. O God, hear my prayer (vv. 1-2), for strangers and ruthless men who do not set God before themselves are after his life (v. 3). Behold, God is my helper; the Lord is the upholder of my life (v. 4). He will return the evil to his enemies (v. 5). With a freewill offering I will sacrifice to you ... For he has delivered me from every trouble (vv. 6-7).
verseByVerse.theology: Seven verses from betrayal by his own tribe to thanksgiving in the past tense, with nothing in between but God.

verseByVerse.quote: O God, save me by your name, and vindicate me by your might. O God, hear my prayer; give ear to the words of my mouth. For strangers have risen against me; ruthless men seek my life; they do not set God before themselves. Selah
verseByVerse.commentary:
The heading names the occasion: when the Ziphites went and told Saul, Is not David hiding among us? (1 Sam 23:19). The Ziphites were men of Judah — David's own tribe. He was hiding in their hills, and they sent word to the king who wanted him dead. They did it twice (1 Sam 26:1).

O God, save me by your name, and vindicate me by your might. O God, hear my prayer; give ear to the words of my mouth.

Save me by your name. Not by your army, not by an angel: by your name — everything God has revealed himself to be, treated as the instrument of rescue. A man who knows what God is like has something to appeal to, and this is why learning God's character is not an academic exercise. It is the thing you reach for when your neighbours have sold you.

For strangers have risen against me; ruthless men seek my life; they do not set God before themselves.

The ESV notes that some manuscripts read insolent men here. If the text is strangers, the word is bitter: these men were not foreigners at all, they were his own kin, and he can no longer tell the difference. Betrayal turns family into strangers.

And the diagnosis at the end explains everything: they do not set God before themselves. Once God is out of view, a man becomes a calculation of advantage, and handing over a fugitive to a murderous king is simply good politics.

verseByVerse.quote: Behold, God is my helper; the Lord is the upholder of my life. He will return the evil to my enemies; in your faithfulness put an end to them. With a freewill offering I will sacrifice to you; I will give thanks to your name, O LORD, for it is good. For he has delivered me from every trouble, and my eye has looked in triumph on my enemies.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Behold, God is my helper; the Lord is the upholder of my life.

The behold is the turn, and it comes in verse 4 of seven with nothing whatever having changed. Saul is still coming; the Ziphites have still informed. What David does is look away from the situation to a fact, and announce it as if pointing at something in the room.

The writer to the Hebrews teaches Christians to say the same thing in the same tone: So we can confidently say, The Lord is my helper; I will not fear; what can man do to me? (Heb 13:6).

He will return the evil to my enemies; in your faithfulness put an end to them.

Again the pattern of these psalms: the evil goes back, and God is the one who returns it. David had the opportunity to settle this himself — twice he was close enough to kill Saul and twice he walked away. A man who believes verse 5 does not need to act on it.

With a freewill offering I will sacrifice to you; I will give thanks to your name, O LORD, for it is good.

A freewill offering was the one sacrifice nobody owed: not required by the calendar, not demanded for a sin, not the payment of a vow. It was brought because a man wanted to. That is what he promises from a cave.

For he has delivered me from every trouble, and my eye has looked in triumph on my enemies.

And the last verse is in the past tense, written by a man still in the wilderness with the search parties out. He has delivered me — from every trouble, which at the time of writing is not yet visibly true.

That is not self-deception; it is how faith speaks about a God who does not lose. Every believer has a version of this to say, and the shortest psalm in this stretch of the Psalter shows the whole movement in seven verses: betrayed by his own people, praying to a name, seeing a helper, handing over the vengeance, planning a gift nobody required, and giving thanks for a rescue not yet in sight.

54.title: God Is My Helper
54.overview: Written when the Ziphites — men of David's own tribe — told Saul where he was hiding. O God, save me by your name, and vindicate me by your might (vv. 1-2), for ruthless men who do not set God before themselves are seeking his life (v. 3). Then the turn, with nothing changed: Behold, God is my helper; the Lord is the upholder of my life (v. 4). God will return the evil to his enemies (v. 5), and David promises a freewill offering and thanks (v. 6) — for he has delivered me from every trouble, said in the past tense while the search parties are still out (v. 7).
54.theology:
Rescue is asked for by your name (v. 1): God's revealed character is treated as the instrument, which is why knowing what he is like is not academic.

The betrayal is by his own tribe, and the text may call them strangers — betrayal turns kin into foreigners. Its root is named: they do not set God before themselves (v. 3).

The hinge comes in v. 4 with no change of circumstances, and the New Testament teaches believers the same sentence (Heb 13:6). Vengeance is returned by God, not taken by David, who twice spared Saul (v. 5; cf. Rom 12:19).

He promises the one offering nobody owed (v. 6) and gives thanks in the past tense for a deliverance not yet visible (v. 7).
54.examples:
His own tribe sent word to the king who wanted him dead.

Saved by a name: what you reach for when neighbours sell you.

Betrayal turns family into strangers.

A behold in verse 4, with nothing changed.

Twice close enough to kill Saul, and twice he walked away.

A freewill offering: the sacrifice nobody owed.

Past-tense thanks from a man still being hunted.

55.text: To the choirmaster: with stringed instruments. A Maskil of David. 1Give ear to my prayer, O God, and hide not yourself from my plea for mercy!2Attend to me, and answer me; I am restless in my complaint and I moan,3because of the noise of the enemy, because of the oppression of the wicked. For they drop trouble upon me, and in anger they bear a grudge against me.4My heart is in anguish within me; the terrors of death have fallen upon me.5Fear and trembling come upon me, and horror overwhelms me.6And I say, "Oh, that I had wings like a dove! I would fly away and be at rest;7yes, I would wander far away; I would lodge in the wilderness; Selah8I would hurry to find a shelter from the raging wind and tempest."9Destroy, O Lord, divide their tongues; for I see violence and strife in the city.10Day and night they go around it on its walls, and iniquity and trouble are within it;11ruin is in its midst; oppression and fraud do not depart from its marketplace.12For it is not an enemy who taunts me— then I could bear it; it is not an adversary who deals insolently with me— then I could hide from him.13But it is you, a man, my equal, my companion, my familiar friend.14We used to take sweet counsel together; within God's house we walked in the throng.15Let death steal over them; let them go down to Sheol alive; for evil is in their dwelling place and in their heart.16But I call to God, and the LORD will save me.17Evening and morning and at noon I utter my complaint and moan, and he hears my voice.18He redeems my soul in safety from the battle that I wage, for many are arrayed against me.19God will give ear and humble them, he who is enthroned from of old, Selah because they do not change and do not fear God.20My companion stretched out his hand against his friends; he violated his covenant.21His speech was smooth as butter, yet war was in his heart; his words were softer than oil, yet they were drawn swords.22Cast your burden on the LORD, and he will sustain you; he will never permit the righteous to be moved.23But you, O God, will cast them down into the pit of destruction; men of blood and treachery shall not live out half their days. But I will trust in you.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–8 — Oh, That I Had Wings Like a Dove
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Give ear to my prayer, O God: he is restless and moaning, his heart in anguish, the terrors of death have fallen upon me (vv. 1-5). Oh, that I had wings like a dove! I would fly away and be at rest — away to the wilderness, out of the raging wind (vv. 6-8).
verseByVerse.theology: A man in a violent city who would rather be a bird, and says so to God.

verseByVerse.quote: Give ear to my prayer, O God, and hide not yourself from my plea for mercy! Attend to me, and answer me; I am restless in my complaint and I moan, because of the noise of the enemy, because of the oppression of the wicked. For they drop trouble upon me, and in anger they bear a grudge against me. My heart is in anguish within me; the terrors of death have fallen upon me. Fear and trembling come upon me, and horror overwhelms me. And I say, "Oh, that I had wings like a dove! I would fly away and be at rest; yes, I would wander far away; I would lodge in the wilderness; Selah I would hurry to find a shelter from the raging wind and tempest."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Give ear to my prayer, O God, and hide not yourself from my plea for mercy! Attend to me, and answer me; I am restless in my complaint and I moan ... My heart is in anguish within me; the terrors of death have fallen upon me. Fear and trembling come upon me, and horror overwhelms me.

Five words for the state he is in: restless, moaning, anguish, fear and trembling, horror. This is not a man being brave about it. The terrors of death have fallen upon me — fallen, like something dropped on him from above.

And I say, Oh, that I had wings like a dove! I would fly away and be at rest; yes, I would wander far away; I would lodge in the wilderness; I would hurry to find a shelter from the raging wind and tempest.

Here is one of the most human sentences in the Bible, and God saw fit to have it sung in church. He does not want to fight, or to win, or even to be vindicated. He wants to leave. A dove, of all birds — not an eagle to fight with, a dove to get out quietly.

Scripture prints the wish without a word of rebuke. It is not treated as unbelief. Anyone who has sat at a desk or in a house and thought, I would give anything to be somewhere else and out of this, is in good company and in the Psalter. What the psalm does with the wish is the point: he tells it to God, and keeps talking.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 9–21 — It Is You, My Familiar Friend
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: For it is not an enemy who taunts me — then I could bear it ... But it is you, a man, my equal, my companion, my familiar friend. We used to take sweet counsel together; within God's house we walked in the throng (vv. 12-14). Let death take them (v. 15). But I call to God, and the LORD will save me. Evening and morning and at noon I utter my complaint and moan, and he hears my voice (vv. 16-19). The friend broke his covenant: his speech was smooth as butter, yet war was in his heart (vv. 20-21).
verseByVerse.theology: What makes it unbearable is not the enmity but the address: it is you, and we used to walk to church together.

verseByVerse.quote: Destroy, O Lord, divide their tongues; for I see violence and strife in the city. Day and night they go around it on its walls, and iniquity and trouble are within it; ruin is in its midst; oppression and fraud do not depart from its marketplace. For it is not an enemy who taunts me— then I could bear it; it is not an adversary who deals insolently with me— then I could hide from him. But it is you, a man, my equal, my companion, my familiar friend. We used to take sweet counsel together; within God's house we walked in the throng. Let death steal over them; let them go down to Sheol alive; for evil is in their dwelling place and in their heart.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Destroy, O Lord, divide their tongues; for I see violence and strife in the city. Day and night they go around it on its walls, and iniquity and trouble are within it; ruin is in its midst; oppression and fraud do not depart from its marketplace.

Divide their tongues is the prayer of Babel in reverse — God confused the language of the builders so the project stopped (Gen 11:7), and David asks for the same treatment for a conspiracy. It is a shrewd request: not that the plotters be destroyed first, but that they stop being able to understand each other.

The city is described as patrolled by the wrong things. Violence and strife walk the walls where the watchmen should be; fraud keeps regular hours in the market. This is a description of somewhere respectable and rotten, and it is Jerusalem.

For it is not an enemy who taunts me — then I could bear it; it is not an adversary who deals insolently with me — then I could hide from him. But it is you, a man, my equal, my companion, my familiar friend. We used to take sweet counsel together; within God's house we walked in the throng.

Everything in the psalm has been leading here, and the psalm stops to say it slowly. If this were an enemy, he could bear it; enmity is survivable. What cannot be borne is the identity of the man: you, a man, my equal, my companion, my familiar friend. Four descriptions, each closer in than the last.

And then the detail that makes it unbearable: within God's house we walked in the throng. They went to worship together. Whatever this man now is, David and he once walked up to the temple in the same crowd, talking — sweet counsel — about the things they both believed.

Church betrayal is its own category of wound, and Scripture has a psalm for it. David's own counsellor Ahithophel went over to Absalom (2 Sam 15:31), and Jesus, at a table, said He who has dipped his hand in the dish with me will betray me (Matt 26:23). The man who wrote this verse and the Lord who quoted its cousin both know exactly what it costs.

Let death steal over them; let them go down to Sheol alive; for evil is in their dwelling place and in their heart.

The prayer is savage, and it is a prayer — addressed to God, not a plan. The phrase recalls Korah's rebellion, where the ground opened and the conspirators went down alive (Num 16:33). David asks God to do what God once did. He does not reach for a knife, and the wish is handed over to the only one with the right to grant it.

verseByVerse.quote: But I call to God, and the LORD will save me. Evening and morning and at noon I utter my complaint and moan, and he hears my voice. He redeems my soul in safety from the battle that I wage, for many are arrayed against me. God will give ear and humble them, he who is enthroned from of old, Selah because they do not change and do not fear God. My companion stretched out his hand against his friends; he violated his covenant. His speech was smooth as butter, yet war was in his heart; his words were softer than oil, yet they were drawn swords.
verseByVerse.commentary:
But I call to God, and the LORD will save me. Evening and morning and at noon I utter my complaint and moan, and he hears my voice.

Three times a day, at set hours, he brings the same complaint. There is no suggestion he has found new words or a better attitude; it is the same moaning as verse 2. And the verse ends, without fuss, he hears my voice.

That is a picture of ordinary prayer in a long trouble: fixed times, repeated content, and a God who does not get tired of the subject. Daniel prayed three times a day in Babylon, and the hours held him steady when everything else was against him.

He redeems my soul in safety from the battle that I wage, for many are arrayed against me. God will give ear and humble them, he who is enthroned from of old, because they do not change and do not fear God.

The diagnosis is two-part: they do not change and they do not fear God, and the first follows from the second. A man with nothing above him has no reason to become anything other than what he is.

My companion stretched out his hand against his friends; he violated his covenant. His speech was smooth as butter, yet war was in his heart; his words were softer than oil, yet they were drawn swords.

Two comparisons, both about texture: butter and oil, smooth and soft — and underneath, war and drawn swords. The psalm is not describing rudeness. It is describing the most dangerous kind of speech there is, the kind that sounds like friendship. Anyone who has been undone by someone unfailingly pleasant knows the taste of butter in this verse.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 22–23 — Cast Your Burden on the LORD
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Cast your burden on the LORD, and he will sustain you; he will never permit the righteous to be moved (v. 22). But you, O God, will cast them down into the pit of destruction ... But I will trust in you (v. 23).
verseByVerse.theology: Two castings in two verses: the burden thrown onto God, and the treacherous thrown down by him.

verseByVerse.quote: Cast your burden on the LORD, and he will sustain you; he will never permit the righteous to be moved. But you, O God, will cast them down into the pit of destruction; men of blood and treachery shall not live out half their days. But I will trust in you.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Cast your burden on the LORD, and he will sustain you; he will never permit the righteous to be moved.

The psalm turns outward and speaks to whoever is listening. Cast is a decisive verb — throw it, get it off you — and the noun is the thing that has been given you to carry, your assigned load. The promise is not that the load will be removed but that he will sustain you: God holds the man rather than lifting the weight.

Peter gives the same instruction to a church under pressure and adds the reason: casting all your anxieties on him, because he cares for you (1 Pet 5:7). The psalmist has spent twenty-one verses doing exactly this in public — the horror, the wish to fly away, the name of the friend, the savage prayer — and only then turns round and tells us to do it too. He is not giving advice from a comfortable chair.

But you, O God, will cast them down into the pit of destruction; men of blood and treachery shall not live out half their days. But I will trust in you.

The same verb twice in two verses: we cast our burden onto God, and God casts the treacherous down. Both throwings are his to handle, and neither is ours.

And the last four words are the psalm's real ending: But I will trust in you. Nothing has been resolved. The friend is still a traitor, the city is still violent, the wings have not been given. What he has is a decision, said out loud, in the present tense.

55.title: Cast Your Burden on the LORD
55.overview: David is restless, moaning, in anguish, with the terrors of death fallen on him (vv. 1-5), and wishes aloud for wings like a dove to fly away and be at rest in the wilderness (vv. 6-8). He asks God to divide the conspirators' tongues, for violence patrols the city walls and fraud keeps hours in the market (vv. 9-11). Then the wound: it is not an enemy but you, a man, my equal, my companion, my familiar friend, with whom he once walked to the house of God (vv. 12-14). Let death take them (v. 15). But he calls to God evening, morning and noon, and is heard (vv. 16-19); his friend's speech was smooth as butter with war in his heart (vv. 20-21). Cast your burden on the LORD, and he will sustain you (v. 22) — and God will cast the treacherous down, but I will trust in you (v. 23).
55.theology:
The wish to escape is printed without rebuke (vv. 6-8): Scripture does not treat I would fly away as unbelief, provided it is said to God.

The prayer against the plotters asks for Babel's remedy — divided tongues (v. 9; Gen 11:7) — and the imprecation of v. 15 is handed to God rather than acted on.

What cannot be borne is not enmity but betrayal by a worship companion (vv. 12-14; cf. 41:9; 2 Sam 15:31; Matt 26:23). Smooth speech with war underneath is named as the most dangerous kind (v. 21).

Prayer in a long trouble is fixed hours and repeated content, and it is heard (v. 17). The refusal to change is traced to the absence of the fear of God (v. 19).

Cast your burden (v. 22; cf. 1 Pet 5:7) promises sustaining rather than removal — God holds the man, not the weight — and the psalm ends undelivered, on a decision: But I will trust in you.
55.examples:
Five words for panic, none of them brave.

A dove, not an eagle: he wants out, not a fight.

Babel prayed for on purpose.

Violence walking the walls where watchmen should be.

Four descriptions, each closer in than the last.

They used to walk up to the temple in the same crowd.

Butter and oil on the surface; drawn swords underneath.

Two castings: the burden onto God, the traitor by God.

56.text: To the choirmaster: according to The Dove on Far-off Terebinths. A Miktam of David, when the Philistines seized him in Gath. 1Be gracious to me, O God, for man tramples on me; all day long an attacker oppresses me;2my enemies trample on me all day long, for many attack me proudly.3When I am afraid, I put my trust in you.4In God, whose word I praise, in God I trust; I shall not be afraid. What can flesh do to me?5All day long they injure my cause; all their thoughts are against me for evil.6They stir up strife, they lurk; they watch my steps, as they have waited for my life.7For their crime will they escape? In wrath cast down the peoples, O God!8You have kept count of my tossings; put my tears in your bottle. Are they not in your book?9Then my enemies will turn back in the day when I call. This I know, that God is for me.10In God, whose word I praise, in the LORD, whose word I praise,11in God I trust; I shall not be afraid. What can man do to me?12I must perform my vows to you, O God; I will render thank offerings to you.13For you have delivered my soul from death, yes, my feet from falling, that I may walk before God in the light of life.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Be gracious to me, O God, for man tramples on me all day long (vv. 1-2). When I am afraid, I put my trust in you. In God, whose word I praise, in God I trust; I shall not be afraid. What can flesh do to me? (vv. 3-4). They injure his cause, stir up strife, lurk and watch his steps (vv. 5-6). For their crime will they escape? In wrath cast down the peoples, O God! (v. 7).
verseByVerse.theology: Fear and trust in the same sentence, and the trust is the thing he does about the fear.

verseByVerse.quote: Be gracious to me, O God, for man tramples on me; all day long an attacker oppresses me; my enemies trample on me all day long, for many attack me proudly. When I am afraid, I put my trust in you. In God, whose word I praise, in God I trust; I shall not be afraid. What can flesh do to me? All day long they injure my cause; all their thoughts are against me for evil. They stir up strife, they lurk; they watch my steps, as they have waited for my life. For their crime will they escape? In wrath cast down the peoples, O God!
verseByVerse.commentary:
The heading puts this in Gath: when the Philistines seized him in Gath, the enemy city where David escaped by pretending to be insane (1 Sam 21:10-15). Psalm 34 came out of the same week, written afterwards in relief. This one is written from inside the fear, and the difference in tone shows.

Be gracious to me, O God, for man tramples on me; all day long an attacker oppresses me; my enemies trample on me all day long, for many attack me proudly.

Trample twice, all day long twice. The word is used of an animal snapping at something, and the repetition is the point: it is the relentlessness that wears a person down, not any single blow.

When I am afraid, I put my trust in you.

Six words that have carried more frightened Christians through more nights than almost any others. Notice what they do not say. Not "I am never afraid"; not "if I trusted properly I would not be afraid". The fear is assumed, given a time — "when", not "if" — and the trust is what he does inside it. Faith here is not a feeling that replaces fear; it is an action taken while afraid.

In God, whose word I praise, in God I trust; I shall not be afraid. What can flesh do to me?

And then the next verse says he will not be afraid, one line after admitting that he is. Both are true, and the psalm sees no contradiction: the fear is what he feels, and the fearlessness is where the argument lands.

Notice the ground: God, whose word I praise. Not his circumstances, not his record — a word God has given, praised while the danger is still in the room. And what can flesh do to me? is a real question with a real answer: flesh can do a great deal, including kill him. The psalm means: nothing that finally counts.

All day long they injure my cause; all their thoughts are against me for evil. They stir up strife, they lurk; they watch my steps, as they have waited for my life. For their crime will they escape? In wrath cast down the peoples, O God!

The ESV notes that verse 5 may be "they twist my words", which is exactly what people do to a man they have already decided about. And the surveillance is patient: lurking, watching his steps, waiting. Then the question a wronged person always asks — will they escape? — handed over to God rather than answered by his own hand.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 8–13 — Put My Tears in Your Bottle
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: You have kept count of my tossings; put my tears in your bottle. Are they not in your book? (v. 8). This I know, that God is for me (v. 9). The refrain again: in God I trust; I shall not be afraid. What can man do to me? (vv. 10-11). He will pay his vows and give thank offerings, for you have delivered my soul from death ... that I may walk before God in the light of life (vv. 12-13).
verseByVerse.theology: Every sleepless turn counted, every tear kept — and the rescue is for walking, not just surviving.

verseByVerse.quote: You have kept count of my tossings; put my tears in your bottle. Are they not in your book? Then my enemies will turn back in the day when I call. This I know, that God is for me. In God, whose word I praise, in the LORD, whose word I praise, in God I trust; I shall not be afraid. What can man do to me? I must perform my vows to you, O God; I will render thank offerings to you. For you have delivered my soul from death, yes, my feet from falling, that I may walk before God in the light of life.
verseByVerse.commentary:
You have kept count of my tossings; put my tears in your bottle. Are they not in your book?

Three pictures, and all three say the same thing: God keeps records of what nobody else notices.

My tossings — the ESV notes it may be wanderings. Either the turning of a man who cannot sleep, or the miles of a fugitive's aimless travel; and God has kept count. Someone has been keeping a tally of the nights.

Put my tears in your bottle. Tears are the least durable thing a person produces; they dry in minutes and nobody sees most of them. He asks God to collect them in a flask and keep them. It is one of the tenderest requests in Scripture, and it assumes a God who would want to.

Are they not in your book? The question expects yes. What is happening to you is written down. Nobody else is keeping this record; your employer is not, the people who wronged you are not, and history will not. God is.

Then my enemies will turn back in the day when I call. This I know, that God is for me.

This I know — the one certainty he claims in the psalm, and it is not about the outcome. God is for me. Paul asks the same thing as a question that cannot be answered: If God is for us, who can be against us? (Rom 8:31). Both know how many are against them. The point is who is on the other side.

In God, whose word I praise, in the LORD, whose word I praise, in God I trust; I shall not be afraid. What can man do to me?

The refrain a second time, expanded, and with the covenant name added in the middle — rare in this part of the Psalter. Flesh in verse 4 has become man here: the question is asked twice, because a frightened man has to say it more than once. The writer to the Hebrews teaches Christians to say it too (Heb 13:6).

I must perform my vows to you, O God; I will render thank offerings to you. For you have delivered my soul from death, yes, my feet from falling, that I may walk before God in the light of life.

Past tense again, from a man in an enemy city: you have delivered. And the purpose clause at the end is the best thing in the psalm. He was not rescued merely to be alive. He was rescued that I may walk before God in the light of life — to live in the open, in daylight, in God's presence, after weeks of hiding and pretending to be mad.

That is what God saves people for. Not survival, and not even safety: the light, and a walk.

56.title: When I Am Afraid, I Put My Trust in You
56.overview: Written when the Philistines seized David in Gath. Men trample him all day long and attack proudly (vv. 1-2). When I am afraid, I put my trust in you — in God, whose word he praises, he will not be afraid; what can flesh do to him (vv. 3-4)? They twist his cause, lurk, and watch his steps; will they escape (vv. 5-7)? You have kept count of my tossings; put my tears in your bottle. Are they not in your book? (v. 8). This I know, that God is for me (v. 9), and the refrain returns (vv. 10-11). He will pay his vows, for God has delivered his soul from death and his feet from falling, that I may walk before God in the light of life (vv. 12-13).
56.theology:
Psalm 34 came out of the same week in relief; this one is prayed from inside the fear.

Verse 3 grants the fear and acts anyway: "when", not "if". Faith here is not a feeling that replaces fear but a decision taken while afraid, grounded in a word God has given (v. 4). What can flesh do to me? does not deny that flesh can kill; it denies that it can finally count (cf. Heb 13:6).

God keeps three records nobody else keeps: the count of sleepless turnings, the tears bottled, the book (v. 8).

The one certainty claimed is not the outcome but the alignment: God is for me (v. 9; cf. Rom 8:31).

Deliverance has a purpose beyond survival: that I may walk before God in the light of life (v. 13).
56.examples:
The same week as Psalm 34 — but written from inside it.

Trampled all day long: relentlessness, not one blow.

When I am afraid, not "if".

Afraid in verse 3, unafraid in verse 4, and both true.

Sleepless turnings, counted by someone.

Tears kept in a bottle; nothing else keeps them.

The one thing he knows is not the outcome.

Rescued for a walk in the light, not merely for survival.

57.text: To the choirmaster: according to Do Not Destroy. A Miktam of David, when he fled from Saul, in the cave. 1Be merciful to me, O God, be merciful to me, for in you my soul takes refuge; in the shadow of your wings I will take refuge, till the storms of destruction pass by.2I cry out to God Most High, to God who fulfills his purpose for me.3He will send from heaven and save me; he will put to shame him who tramples on me. Selah God will send out his steadfast love and his faithfulness!4My soul is in the midst of lions; I lie down amid fiery beasts— the children of man, whose teeth are spears and arrows, whose tongues are sharp swords.5Be exalted, O God, above the heavens! Let your glory be over all the earth!6They set a net for my steps; my soul was bowed down. They dug a pit in my way, but they have fallen into it themselves. Selah7My heart is steadfast, O God, my heart is steadfast! I will sing and make melody!8Awake, my glory! Awake, O harp and lyre! I will awake the dawn!9I will give thanks to you, O Lord, among the peoples; I will sing praises to you among the nations.10For your steadfast love is great to the heavens, your faithfulness to the clouds.11Be exalted, O God, above the heavens! Let your glory be over all the earth!

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–6 — In the Shadow of Your Wings
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Be merciful to me, O God ... in the shadow of your wings I will take refuge, till the storms of destruction pass by (v. 1). He cries to God who fulfills his purpose for me, who will send out his steadfast love and faithfulness (vv. 2-3). My soul is in the midst of lions, men whose teeth are spears and tongues are swords (v. 4). Be exalted, O God, above the heavens! (v. 5). They dug a pit and fell into it themselves (v. 6).
verseByVerse.theology: A man hiding in a cave says he is sheltering under wings, and asks first for God's glory.

verseByVerse.quote: Be merciful to me, O God, be merciful to me, for in you my soul takes refuge; in the shadow of your wings I will take refuge, till the storms of destruction pass by. I cry out to God Most High, to God who fulfills his purpose for me. He will send from heaven and save me; he will put to shame him who tramples on me. Selah God will send out his steadfast love and his faithfulness!
verseByVerse.commentary:
The heading says he was in the cave, fleeing from Saul — either Adullam (1 Sam 22:1) or En-gedi, where he crept up in the dark and cut the corner off the king's robe and then refused to touch him (1 Sam 24). The tune is called Do Not Destroy, which happens to be exactly what David said to his men that day.

Be merciful to me, O God, be merciful to me, for in you my soul takes refuge; in the shadow of your wings I will take refuge, till the storms of destruction pass by.

He is in a cave, which is a refuge made of rock, and he describes his refuge as feathers. The shadow of your wings is the bird covering her young — the image of Psalm 17, of Ruth coming under God's wings, of Jesus over Jerusalem. The stone is keeping the rain off; he says God is keeping him.

And the timing is modest: till the storms of destruction pass by. He does not ask for the storm to stop, only to be covered while it goes over. That is often the whole of what can be prayed.

I cry out to God Most High, to God who fulfills his purpose for me.

A remarkable thing for a man with a price on his head to say. He has been anointed king and is living in a hole in the ground, and he calls God the one who fulfills his purpose for me — present tense, mid-cave. The purpose is not suspended while the circumstances are bad; the cave is part of it.

He will send from heaven and save me; he will put to shame him who tramples on me. God will send out his steadfast love and his faithfulness!

Two things are dispatched from heaven like messengers: steadfast love and faithfulness. The same pair that Psalm 43 asked God to send out as guides. God's attributes are pictured as personnel, sent on errands to particular people in particular caves.

verseByVerse.quote: My soul is in the midst of lions; I lie down amid fiery beasts— the children of man, whose teeth are spears and arrows, whose tongues are sharp swords. Be exalted, O God, above the heavens! Let your glory be over all the earth! They set a net for my steps; my soul was bowed down. They dug a pit in my way, but they have fallen into it themselves. Selah
verseByVerse.commentary:
My soul is in the midst of lions; I lie down amid fiery beasts — the children of man, whose teeth are spears and arrows, whose tongues are sharp swords.

The menagerie turns out to be men, and their weapons are their mouths. Teeth ... spears and arrows, tongues ... sharp swords. This is the psalm's third mention of speech as weaponry in six psalms (52:2; 55:21), and the phrase I lie down should not be missed: he sleeps among them. The lions are his neighbours.

Be exalted, O God, above the heavens! Let your glory be over all the earth!

And here, in the middle of the lions, is the psalm's actual request. Not "get me out". The first thing he asks for is that God be exalted and his glory fill the earth — a request that has nothing to do with David's situation and will not shorten it by a day.

Sit with that. A hunted man's top priority is God's reputation in places he will never visit. The refrain will come back at the end of the psalm, so it frames everything in between: the lions, the pit, the singing.

They set a net for my steps; my soul was bowed down. They dug a pit in my way, but they have fallen into it themselves.

The pit again (7:15; 9:15), and the middle clause is the honest one: my soul was bowed down. The trap worked on him before it caught them. Faith in these psalms is rarely undented; it is bowed down and still speaking.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: My heart is steadfast, O God, my heart is steadfast! I will sing and make melody! Awake, my glory! Awake, O harp and lyre! I will awake the dawn! (vv. 7-8). He will give thanks among the peoples and sing among the nations, for God's steadfast love is great to the heavens (vv. 9-10). Be exalted, O God, above the heavens! Let your glory be over all the earth! (v. 11).
verseByVerse.theology: The refrain returns, and the fugitive announces that he intends to wake the sunrise.

verseByVerse.quote: My heart is steadfast, O God, my heart is steadfast! I will sing and make melody! Awake, my glory! Awake, O harp and lyre! I will awake the dawn! I will give thanks to you, O Lord, among the peoples; I will sing praises to you among the nations. For your steadfast love is great to the heavens, your faithfulness to the clouds. Be exalted, O God, above the heavens! Let your glory be over all the earth!
verseByVerse.commentary:
My heart is steadfast, O God, my heart is steadfast! I will sing and make melody!

He says it twice, the way people do when they are telling themselves as much as God. Steadfast is fixed, settled, prepared — the opposite of the bowed-down soul three verses earlier. Nothing outside has changed between verse 6 and verse 7; the lions are still there and the cave is still a cave.

Awake, my glory! Awake, O harp and lyre! I will awake the dawn!

One of the most extraordinary sentences in the Psalter. He wakes himself first — the ESV notes my glory may be my whole being — then his instruments, which he apparently has with him in the cave, and then he announces that he will wake up the sunrise.

Think about the order. Normally the dawn wakes the singer. David proposes to be up before it, singing, so that the sun comes up to find the music already going. A man hiding from a king with soldiers outside decides to be the first thing awake in the country.

I will give thanks to you, O Lord, among the peoples; I will sing praises to you among the nations. For your steadfast love is great to the heavens, your faithfulness to the clouds.

And the audience he has in mind is not the cave. Among the peoples ... among the nations: he expects this song to travel, and Paul quotes the verse that matches it from Psalm 18 to prove that God always intended the Gentiles to praise him with his people (Rom 15:9). The song written underground did travel, further than the man singing it could have guessed.

Be exalted, O God, above the heavens! Let your glory be over all the earth!

The refrain closes it, unchanged. The psalm began with a man asking to be covered until the storm passed, and ends with the same man asking for nothing at all for himself — only that God be high and his glory wide. Verses 7-11 were thought good enough to be reprinted later as the opening of Psalm 108, which is where they are taken up again.

57.title: I Will Awake the Dawn
57.overview: From the cave, hiding from Saul. Be merciful to me, O God ... in the shadow of your wings I will take refuge, till the storms of destruction pass by (v. 1). He cries to the God who fulfils his purpose for him and sends out steadfast love and faithfulness from heaven (vv. 2-3). He is among lions whose teeth are spears and whose tongues are swords (v. 4). Be exalted, O God, above the heavens! (v. 5). They dug a pit and fell into it (v. 6). My heart is steadfast ... Awake, my glory! Awake, O harp and lyre! I will awake the dawn! (vv. 7-8). He will give thanks among the peoples, for God's steadfast love reaches the heavens (vv. 9-10) — and the refrain closes the psalm (v. 11).
57.theology:
A refuge of rock is described as a refuge of feathers (v. 1; cf. 17:8; Ruth 2:12; Matt 23:37), and what is asked is covering until the storm passes, not the cancelling of the storm.

A hunted man calls God the one who fulfills his purpose for me in the present tense (v. 2): the cave is not an interruption of the purpose.

God's steadfast love and faithfulness are dispatched like messengers (v. 3; cf. 43:3).

The psalm's own petition is the refrain, and it asks nothing for the psalmist: Be exalted, O God ... let your glory be over all the earth (vv. 5, 11).

Faith here is bowed down and still speaking (v. 6), and steadfastness is declared with nothing outside changed (v. 7). The singing is aimed at the nations (v. 9), and vv. 7-11 are reprinted as the opening of Psalm 108.
57.examples:
A tune called Do Not Destroy, and a man who had just said it.

Stone overhead, feathers in the prayer.

Covered while the storm goes over, not spared the storm.

God's purpose being fulfilled, mid-cave.

Love and faithfulness sent out like staff on an errand.

He lies down among the lions: they are his neighbours.

The first request is God's glory in places he will never visit.

Up before the sun, so it rises to find the music going.

58.text: To the choirmaster: according to Do Not Destroy. A Miktam of David. 1Do you indeed decree what is right, you gods? Do you judge the children of man uprightly?2No, in your hearts you devise wrongs; your hands deal out violence on earth.3The wicked are estranged from the womb; they go astray from birth, speaking lies.4They have venom like the venom of a serpent, like the deaf adder that stops its ear,5so that it does not hear the voice of charmers or of the cunning enchanter.6O God, break the teeth in their mouths; tear out the fangs of the young lions, O LORD!7Let them vanish like water that runs away; when he aims his arrows, let them be blunted.8Let them be like the snail that dissolves into slime, like the stillborn child who never sees the sun.9Sooner than your pots can feel the heat of thorns, whether green or ablaze, may he sweep them away!10The righteous will rejoice when he sees the vengeance; he will bathe his feet in the blood of the wicked.11Mankind will say, "Surely there is a reward for the righteous; surely there is a God who judges on earth."

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–5 — Do You Indeed Decree What Is Right?
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Do you indeed decree what is right, you gods? Do you judge the children of man uprightly? No, in your hearts you devise wrongs; your hands deal out violence on earth (vv. 1-2). The wicked are estranged from the womb and go astray from birth, speaking lies (v. 3), with venom like a serpent's, deaf as an adder that stops its ear against the charmer (vv. 4-5).
verseByVerse.theology: The psalm opens by cross-examining the judges, and finds that the bench is where the violence is being planned.

verseByVerse.quote: Do you indeed decree what is right, you gods? Do you judge the children of man uprightly? No, in your hearts you devise wrongs; your hands deal out violence on earth. The wicked are estranged from the womb; they go astray from birth, speaking lies. They have venom like the venom of a serpent, like the deaf adder that stops its ear, so that it does not hear the voice of charmers or of the cunning enchanter.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Do you indeed decree what is right, you gods? Do you judge the children of man uprightly? No, in your hearts you devise wrongs; your hands deal out violence on earth.

The tune is the same as Psalm 57's, Do Not Destroy, and this time the psalm asks God to do a great deal of destroying. Read the ESV's note before anything else: the word rendered you gods may be read you mighty lords. The people being addressed are judges. Scripture can call human judges gods because they do God's own work — deciding between right and wrong for other people (Ps 82:1, 6; and see Exod 22:8-9, where a case is brought "before God", meaning before the judges).

So this is a psalm about a corrupt courtroom, and it opens by putting the bench in the dock. The questions are not rhetorical politeness: do you indeed decree what is right? And the answer is given in the same breath. The violence on the streets was devised in their hearts and dealt out by their hands. When justice is for sale, the men in robes are not bystanders to the violence; they are its wholesale suppliers.

The wicked are estranged from the womb; they go astray from birth, speaking lies.

The same doctrine as 51:5, turned outward. This is not a comment on any individual baby; it is the psalm saying that the corruption in that courtroom is not an accident of training or circumstance. It goes back further than the career.

They have venom like the venom of a serpent, like the deaf adder that stops its ear, so that it does not hear the voice of charmers or of the cunning enchanter.

Two images, and the second is the more frightening. A snake charmer can handle a snake that listens. This one has stopped its ear — deliberately, the picture suggests, pressing itself down so that the music cannot reach it. There is a deafness that is chosen, and it is proof against every reasonable appeal. Argument, evidence, eloquence: nothing gets in.

That is why the psalm turns to God in the next verse. It has already tried talking.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 6–11 — Surely There Is a God Who Judges
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: O God, break the teeth in their mouths; tear out the fangs of the young lions — let them vanish like water, be blunted like arrows, dissolve like a snail, be swept away (vv. 6-9). The righteous will rejoice when he sees the vengeance (v. 10). Mankind will say, Surely there is a reward for the righteous; surely there is a God who judges on earth (v. 11).
verseByVerse.theology: Every request is handed to God, and what the psalm finally wants is for the world to know that justice exists.

verseByVerse.quote: O God, break the teeth in their mouths; tear out the fangs of the young lions, O LORD! Let them vanish like water that runs away; when he aims his arrows, let them be blunted. Let them be like the snail that dissolves into slime, like the stillborn child who never sees the sun. Sooner than your pots can feel the heat of thorns, whether green or ablaze, may he sweep them away!
verseByVerse.commentary:
O God, break the teeth in their mouths; tear out the fangs of the young lions, O LORD! Let them vanish like water that runs away; when he aims his arrows, let them be blunted. Let them be like the snail that dissolves into slime, like the stillborn child who never sees the sun.

This is the hardest passage in this stretch of the Psalter and there is no honest way to make it comfortable. Broken teeth, blunted arrows, a snail leaving nothing but a trail, a child that never drew breath. The ESV notes that verse 9 is obscure in Hebrew; the rest is only too clear.

Three things hold it in place. First, every verb is addressed to God. O God, break ... tear out ... let them vanish. The psalmist asks for nothing he intends to do himself, which is precisely the difference between imprecation and revenge — and precisely what Paul commands: never avenge yourselves, but leave it to the wrath of God (Rom 12:19). A man praying this way has disarmed himself.

Second, the images are of disabling, not torture. Teeth and fangs are what the predator bites with; arrows are what the archer kills with. The prayer is that the weapons stop working — and these are judges, so their weapon is their mouth.

Third, the psalm is not personal. Nothing here is about the psalmist's reputation or comfort. It is about a legal system devouring the helpless, which God has said he hates. A person who feels nothing when the courts are bought has a defective conscience, not a superior one.

And the Christian still prays this psalm through the cross — where God's judgment on the wicked fell on his own Son, so that the men who deserve verse 6 may be offered verse 11's God on other terms. That does not cancel the prayer. Revelation has the martyrs praying it still (Rev 6:10).

verseByVerse.quote: The righteous will rejoice when he sees the vengeance; he will bathe his feet in the blood of the wicked. Mankind will say, "Surely there is a reward for the righteous; surely there is a God who judges on earth."
verseByVerse.commentary:
The righteous will rejoice when he sees the vengeance; he will bathe his feet in the blood of the wicked.

The picture is a battlefield after God has acted — a man walking through the aftermath, the ground so wet that his feet are washed as he goes. It is deliberately shocking, and notice who did the killing: not the righteous man. He arrives afterwards. The nearest New Testament image is the rider whose own robe is dipped in blood, who will tread the winepress of the fury of the wrath of God the Almighty (Rev 19:13, 15), and the armies who follow him are dressed in white and carry nothing.

The rejoicing is not glee at suffering. It is the relief of people who had begun to believe that nothing would ever be put right, when it finally is.

Mankind will say, Surely there is a reward for the righteous; surely there is a God who judges on earth.

And here is what the whole psalm has been after. Not the destruction of the judges for its own sake — the public re-establishment of the fact that justice exists. The two surelys answer the two questions of verse 1.

Corrupt courts do not merely rob individuals; they teach a whole society that nobody is above the bench and nothing is finally settled. That is the lie this psalm is written against. Anyone who has watched the guilty walk free with a smile knows how much they want verse 11 to be true, and this psalm is God's own word saying it is — on earth, not only in eternity.

58.title: A God Who Judges on Earth
58.overview: The psalm cross-examines corrupt judges: do you decree what is right? No — they devise wrongs in their hearts and deal out violence with their hands (vv. 1-2). The wicked go astray from birth, venomous as serpents, deaf as an adder that stops its own ear against the charmer (vv. 3-5). So the prayer is handed to God: break the teeth in their mouths, let them vanish like water, dissolve like a snail, be swept away (vv. 6-9). The righteous will rejoice when he sees the vengeance and walk through the aftermath (v. 10), and everyone will say: Surely there is a reward for the righteous; surely there is a God who judges on earth (v. 11).
58.theology:
The addressees are human judges, called gods because they exercise God's function (v. 1; see the ESV's note; cf. Ps 82:1, 6; Exod 22:8-9). This is a psalm against bought courts, and it treats the bench as the source of the street's violence (v. 2).

The adder that stops its own ear (vv. 4-5) is chosen deafness, proof against every reasonable appeal — which is why the psalm turns from argument to prayer.

The imprecation is not softened, and three things hold it: every verb is addressed to God, so the psalmist has disarmed himself (Rom 12:19); the images are of disabling a predator's weapons rather than torture; and nothing in it is personal — it is about a legal system devouring the helpless.

The righteous do not do the killing; they walk through the aftermath (v. 10; cf. Rev 19:13-15), and the rejoicing is relief that wrong is finally put right. The psalm's goal is v. 11: the public re-establishment of the fact that there is a God who judges on earth (cf. Rev 6:10).
58.examples:
The bench put in the dock.

Judges called gods because they do God's own work.

Violence devised in chambers and dealt out on the street.

A snake that presses its ear down so the music cannot reach it.

Every verb of the curse is addressed to God.

Teeth and arrows: the weapons disabled, not the man tortured.

The righteous arrive after the battle, carrying nothing.

Two surelys answering the two questions of verse 1.

59.text: To the choirmaster: according to Do Not Destroy. A Miktam of David, when Saul sent men to watch his house in order to kill him. 1Deliver me from my enemies, O my God; protect me from those who rise up against me;2deliver me from those who work evil, and save me from bloodthirsty men.3For behold, they lie in wait for my life; fierce men stir up strife against me. For no transgression or sin of mine, O LORD,4for no fault of mine, they run and make ready. Awake, come to meet me, and see!5You, LORD God of hosts, are God of Israel. Rouse yourself to punish all the nations; spare none of those who treacherously plot evil. Selah6Each evening they come back, howling like dogs and prowling about the city.7There they are, bellowing with their mouths with swords in their lips— for "Who," they think, "will hear us?"8But you, O LORD, laugh at them; you hold all the nations in derision.9O my Strength, I will watch for you, for you, O God, are my fortress.10My God in his steadfast love will meet me; God will let me look in triumph on my enemies.11Kill them not, lest my people forget; make them totter by your power and bring them down, O Lord, our shield!12For the sin of their mouths, the words of their lips, let them be trapped in their pride. For the cursing and lies that they utter,13consume them in wrath; consume them till they are no more, that they may know that God rules over Jacob to the ends of the earth. Selah14Each evening they come back, howling like dogs and prowling about the city.15They wander about for food and growl if they do not get their fill.16But I will sing of your strength; I will sing aloud of your steadfast love in the morning. For you have been to me a fortress and a refuge in the day of my distress.17O my Strength, I will sing praises to you, for you, O God, are my fortress, the God who shows me steadfast love.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–8 — For No Fault of Mine
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Deliver me from my enemies, O my God — they lie in wait for his life for no transgression or sin of mine ... for no fault of mine (vv. 1-4). Rouse yourself to punish all the nations (v. 5). Each evening they come back, howling like dogs and prowling about the city, bellowing with swords in their lips and asking who will hear them (vv. 6-7). But you, O LORD, laugh at them (v. 8).
verseByVerse.theology: Surveillance at nightfall, a man who has done nothing, and a God who laughs at the watchers.

verseByVerse.quote: Deliver me from my enemies, O my God; protect me from those who rise up against me; deliver me from those who work evil, and save me from bloodthirsty men. For behold, they lie in wait for my life; fierce men stir up strife against me. For no transgression or sin of mine, O LORD, for no fault of mine, they run and make ready. Awake, come to meet me, and see! You, LORD God of hosts, are God of Israel. Rouse yourself to punish all the nations; spare none of those who treacherously plot evil. Selah Each evening they come back, howling like dogs and prowling about the city. There they are, bellowing with their mouths with swords in their lips— for "Who," they think, "will hear us?" But you, O LORD, laugh at them; you hold all the nations in derision.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The heading fixes the night: when Saul sent men to watch his house in order to kill him (1 Sam 19:11). David is inside; the assassins are outside in the dark, waiting for morning. His wife let him down through a window and put an idol in the bed to buy him time.

Deliver me from my enemies, O my God; protect me from those who rise up against me; deliver me from those who work evil, and save me from bloodthirsty men.

Four requests in two verses, and the piling up is the sound of urgency. He is not composing; he is asking the same thing four ways because the men are outside.

For behold, they lie in wait for my life; fierce men stir up strife against me. For no transgression or sin of mine, O LORD, for no fault of mine, they run and make ready.

Twice he says it: no transgression or sin of mine ... no fault of mine. He is not claiming to be a sinless man — the psalms of this same author say the opposite — but that in this matter he has done nothing to deserve a death squad. It matters that Scripture lets an innocent man say so plainly.

Each evening they come back, howling like dogs and prowling about the city. There they are, bellowing with their mouths with swords in their lips — for Who, they think, will hear us?

Here is the image that gives the psalm its atmosphere. Not wolves in the wild: dogs, the scavenging packs that came into ancient towns after dark, circling, howling, looking for anything left out. Saul's men are reduced to a nuisance that comes with nightfall.

And their creed is the creed of Psalm 10 and Psalm 50: "Who ... will hear us?" The ESV notes the Hebrew lacks they think, so it may be a shout as much as a thought — either way, men who have decided nobody is listening.

But you, O LORD, laugh at them; you hold all the nations in derision.

Somebody is listening. The laugh is the one from Psalm 2 and Psalm 37, and it lands on a besieged house in a small town: the men outside think they are unobserved, and heaven finds them funny.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 9–17 — Kill Them Not, Lest My People Forget
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: O my Strength, I will watch for you, for you, O God, are my fortress (vv. 9-10). Kill them not, lest my people forget; make them totter by your power and bring them down (v. 11); let them be trapped in their pride, that they may know that God rules over Jacob to the ends of the earth (vv. 12-13). The dogs come back again at evening, prowling and growling for food (vv. 14-15). But I will sing of your strength; I will sing aloud of your steadfast love in the morning (vv. 16-17).
verseByVerse.theology: He asks God not to kill them, so the lesson lasts — and schedules his singing for dawn.

verseByVerse.quote: O my Strength, I will watch for you, for you, O God, are my fortress. My God in his steadfast love will meet me; God will let me look in triumph on my enemies. Kill them not, lest my people forget; make them totter by your power and bring them down, O Lord, our shield! For the sin of their mouths, the words of their lips, let them be trapped in their pride. For the cursing and lies that they utter, consume them in wrath; consume them till they are no more, that they may know that God rules over Jacob to the ends of the earth. Selah
verseByVerse.commentary:
O my Strength, I will watch for you, for you, O God, are my fortress. My God in his steadfast love will meet me; God will let me look in triumph on my enemies.

They are watching the house; he will watch for God. The same verb, turned into worship. And he is inside a house that is surrounded, calling God his fortress — which is what a house exactly is not, tonight.

Kill them not, lest my people forget; make them totter by your power and bring them down, O Lord, our shield!

This is the strangest petition in the Psalter, and it repays a slow reading. He does not ask for the men to be killed. He asks for them to be left alive and reduced — made to stagger, brought down — and gives his reason: lest my people forget.

A dead enemy is forgotten by the next generation. A humbled one, still walking about the city with everyone knowing what he tried and what became of him, is a standing lesson. The psalm wants the teaching to outlast the incident, and is prepared to let the men live to get it. That is a long way from bloodlust, and it comes from a man who could have asked for anything.

For the sin of their mouths, the words of their lips, let them be trapped in their pride ... consume them in wrath; consume them till they are no more, that they may know that God rules over Jacob to the ends of the earth.

The two petitions sit oddly together — do not kill them, and consume them — and the psalm does not tidy it up. That is what praying under threat actually sounds like. But notice the end that both requests are aimed at: that they may know. Even the fiercest line in the psalm wants knowledge as its outcome, and the knowledge is about God's rule reaching to the ends of the earth, not about David's safety.

verseByVerse.quote: Each evening they come back, howling like dogs and prowling about the city. They wander about for food and growl if they do not get their fill. But I will sing of your strength; I will sing aloud of your steadfast love in the morning. For you have been to me a fortress and a refuge in the day of my distress. O my Strength, I will sing praises to you, for you, O God, are my fortress, the God who shows me steadfast love.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Each evening they come back, howling like dogs and prowling about the city. They wander about for food and growl if they do not get their fill.

The refrain returns unchanged, which is the psalm's honesty: after all that prayer, the dogs are still doing their rounds. Nothing has been fixed. The only addition is a detail about their appetite — they growl when they go unfed, which is what has been happening every night that David survives.

But I will sing of your strength; I will sing aloud of your steadfast love in the morning. For you have been to me a fortress and a refuge in the day of my distress.

But I will sing — and look at the hour. The dogs come at evening; he schedules his singing for the morning. He is planning, while the noise is still going on outside, what he will do when the sun comes up. Psalm 57 had him waking the dawn with a harp in a cave; here he sets the alarm from inside a besieged house.

And the tense has turned: you have been to me a fortress and a refuge. Past tense, written at night, about a siege that is not over.

O my Strength, I will sing praises to you, for you, O God, are my fortress, the God who shows me steadfast love.

The psalm ends on the title it began the second half with — my Strength — and adds the one word that makes the difference between a fortress and a friend: the God who shows me steadfast love. Any strong God can be a wall. This one is fond of him, and that is what gets a hunted man through a night of howling.

59.title: Howling Like Dogs
59.overview: Written the night Saul's men surrounded David's house. Deliver me, protect me, save me — they lie in wait for no transgression or sin of mine (vv. 1-5). Each evening they come back, howling like dogs and prowling about the city, sure that no one hears them (vv. 6-7) — but you, O LORD, laugh at them (v. 8). He will watch for God, his fortress (vv. 9-10). Then the strangest request in the Psalter: Kill them not, lest my people forget — humble them instead, so that everyone learns that God rules over Jacob to the ends of the earth (vv. 11-13). The dogs come back again (vv. 14-15). But I will sing of your strength; I will sing aloud of your steadfast love in the morning (vv. 16-17).
59.theology:
Scripture lets an innocent man say twice that he has done nothing to deserve this (vv. 3-4), without any claim to be sinless in general.

The enemies are scavenging dogs on their nightly round (vv. 6, 14), and their creed is that nobody hears them (v. 7; cf. 10:11; 50:21) — answered by heaven's laughter (v. 8; cf. 2:4; 37:13).

Verse 11 asks that the enemies be spared and humbled rather than killed, because a living warning teaches longer than a dead one: the psalm wants the lesson to outlast the incident. Even the fiercest petition aims at knowledge — that they may know that God rules over Jacob (v. 13).

The refrain returns unchanged after all the praying (v. 14): nothing has been fixed. The singing is scheduled for morning while the howling is still going on (v. 16), and the last word is not power but affection: the God who shows me steadfast love (v. 17).
59.examples:
Assassins outside; a window and an idol in the bed.

Four requests in two verses: the sound of urgency.

Scavenging dogs doing the rounds after dark.

"Who ... will hear us?" — and heaven laughing.

They watch the house; he watches for God.

Spare them, so the lesson lasts longer than they do.

The refrain returns: the dogs are still there.

Singing booked for dawn, from inside a siege.

60.text: To the choirmaster: according to Shushan Eduth. A Miktam of David; for instruction; when he strove with Aram-naharaim and with Aram-zobah, and when Joab on his return struck down twelve thousand of Edom in the Valley of Salt. 1O God, you have rejected us, broken our defenses; you have been angry; oh, restore us.2You have made the land to quake; you have torn it open; repair its breaches, for it totters.3You have made your people see hard things; you have given us wine to drink that made us stagger.4You have set up a banner for those who fear you, that they may flee to it from the bow.
