Selah5That your beloved ones may be delivered, give salvation by your right hand and answer us!6God has spoken in his holiness: "With exultation I will divide up Shechem and portion out the Vale of Succoth.7Gilead is mine; Manasseh is mine; Ephraim is my helmet; Judah is my scepter.8Moab is my washbasin; upon Edom I cast my shoe; over Philistia I shout in triumph."9Who will bring me to the fortified city? Who will lead me to Edom?10Have you not rejected us, O God? You do not go forth, O God, with our armies.11Oh, grant us help against the foe, for vain is the salvation of man!12With God we shall do valiantly; it is he who will tread down our foes.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–5 — You Have Made Your People See Hard Things
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: O God, you have rejected us, broken our defenses; you have been angry; oh, restore us (v. 1). You have made the land to quake; you have torn it open ... You have made your people see hard things; you have given us wine to drink that made us stagger (vv. 2-3). He has set up a banner for those who fear him to flee to (v. 4). That your beloved ones may be delivered, give salvation by your right hand and answer us! (v. 5).
verseByVerse.theology: A defeat described as God's own work, and prayed about in exactly those terms.

verseByVerse.quote: O God, you have rejected us, broken our defenses; you have been angry; oh, restore us. You have made the land to quake; you have torn it open; repair its breaches, for it totters. You have made your people see hard things; you have given us wine to drink that made us stagger. You have set up a banner for those who fear you, that they may flee to it from the bow. Selah That your beloved ones may be delivered, give salvation by your right hand and answer us!
verseByVerse.commentary:
The heading is the longest yet and names real campaigns — Aram-naharaim, Aram-zobah, Joab's return after twelve thousand Edomites were struck down in the Valley of Salt. (The histories give the figure as eighteen thousand, 2 Sam 8:13 and 1 Chr 18:12, and credit Abishai in Chronicles; the heading counts differently, and the psalm is not written to settle it.) And in the middle of it, two words that change how the whole psalm is read: for instruction. This defeat was written up as a teaching document. Israel put her worst days on the syllabus.

O God, you have rejected us, broken our defenses; you have been angry; oh, restore us. You have made the land to quake; you have torn it open; repair its breaches, for it totters.

Every verb belongs to God. Not we were outnumbered, not the alliance failed: you rejected, you broke, you were angry, you made the land quake, you tore it open. A modern account of a military reverse would reach for logistics. This one goes straight past the second causes to the first.

And notice that the same God is asked to mend it — oh, restore us ... repair its breaches. There is no one else to ask. The hand that tore is the only hand that can stitch.

You have made your people see hard things; you have given us wine to drink that made us stagger.

Two images for a national disaster. Hard things — literally a hard sight, something you cannot unsee. And a cup of wine that leaves a people reeling in the street, unable to walk straight. The prophets would use that cup again and again, and it would end up in Gethsemane, where a greater Son of David asked whether it could pass and then drank it.

You have set up a banner for those who fear you, that they may flee to it from the bow.

A banner in that world was a rallying point — a standard planted on high ground so scattered soldiers could find each other. But look at what this one is for: not to march behind, to flee to. God gives a beaten army a place to regroup rather than a slogan. The ESV notes an alternative reading, that the banner is displayed because of truth.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 6–12 — Vain Is the Salvation of Man
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: God speaks, walking his estate: Shechem, Succoth, Gilead, Manasseh, Ephraim is my helmet; Judah is my scepter — and the neighbours are furniture: Moab is my washbasin; upon Edom I cast my shoe (vv. 6-8). Who will bring him to Edom's fortified city — have you not rejected us, O God? (vv. 9-10). Oh, grant us help against the foe, for vain is the salvation of man! With God we shall do valiantly; it is he who will tread down our foes (vv. 11-12).
verseByVerse.theology: God's survey of the map, and a beaten army's two-line creed.

verseByVerse.quote: God has spoken in his holiness: "With exultation I will divide up Shechem and portion out the Vale of Succoth. Gilead is mine; Manasseh is mine; Ephraim is my helmet; Judah is my scepter. Moab is my washbasin; upon Edom I cast my shoe; over Philistia I shout in triumph."
verseByVerse.commentary:
God has spoken in his holiness: With exultation I will divide up Shechem and portion out the Vale of Succoth. Gilead is mine; Manasseh is mine; Ephraim is my helmet; Judah is my scepter.

God answers, and the tone is of a landowner walking his property with obvious pleasure. He names places on both sides of the Jordan — Shechem and Succoth, Gilead and Manasseh — as a man might name fields. The ESV notes that in his holiness may be in his sanctuary.

Then two tribes get jobs. Ephraim is my helmet: the largest northern tribe is God's headgear in battle. Judah is my scepter: the southern tribe is the staff in his hand, which is where the kings come from and eventually the King. The army that has just been beaten is being told whose equipment it is.

Moab is my washbasin; upon Edom I cast my shoe; over Philistia I shout in triumph.

And now the neighbours, and the language is deliberately humiliating. Moab, the old enemy across the Dead Sea, is the bowl God washes his feet in. Edom is where he tosses his sandals when he comes indoors — the gesture of a man arriving home and dropping his shoes on a servant. Philistia gets a shout.

The point is not contempt for those peoples as such. It is scale. Israel has just been mauled by these nations and cannot see over the top of them; God describes the same nations as household items.

verseByVerse.quote: Who will bring me to the fortified city? Who will lead me to Edom? Have you not rejected us, O God? You do not go forth, O God, with our armies. Oh, grant us help against the foe, for vain is the salvation of man! With God we shall do valiantly; it is he who will tread down our foes.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Who will bring me to the fortified city? Who will lead me to Edom? Have you not rejected us, O God? You do not go forth, O God, with our armies.

Straight after that magnificent speech, the psalm goes back to the facts on the ground. There is still a fortified city nobody has taken, and the honest sentence is still true: You do not go forth, O God, with our armies.

This is the shape of faith in a bad season, and the psalm refuses to resolve it prematurely. God's ownership of the world (vv. 6-8) and God's apparent absence from this campaign (v. 10) are both put in the same poem, and neither is used to silence the other.

Oh, grant us help against the foe, for vain is the salvation of man! With God we shall do valiantly; it is he who will tread down our foes.

Two lines, and they are the creed of a defeated army. First the negative, and it is brutal about what they have just tried: vain is the salvation of man — empty, a puff of breath. Everything human — the alliances, the generals, the numbers — has been weighed and found to be nothing.

Then the positive, and it is not passive: with God we shall do valiantly. They are going back out. This is not a psalm about retiring from the field; it is about who goes with them. And the last clause hands the outcome over: it is he who will tread down our foes.

Hold the two halves together and you have the Christian's working position in any hard enterprise. Nothing you can do will save you; and with God you will act bravely and the result belongs to him. These five verses were thought worth reprinting — they appear again in Psalm 108 — because a beaten people needs this sentence more than once.

60.title: With God We Shall Do Valiantly
60.overview: A defeat, written up for instruction. God has rejected them, broken their defences, made the land quake and given them wine that made them stagger (vv. 1-3); he has set up a banner for his people to flee to (v. 4), and they ask to be delivered by his right hand (v. 5). Then God speaks, walking his estate: Shechem, Succoth, Gilead, Manasseh, Ephraim is my helmet; Judah is my scepter, while Moab is his washbasin and Edom the place he throws his sandal (vv. 6-8). Yet the fortified city is still unconquered and you do not go forth, O God, with our armies (vv. 9-10). Oh, grant us help against the foe, for vain is the salvation of man! With God we shall do valiantly (vv. 11-12).
60.theology:
The disaster is attributed to God in every verb (vv. 1-3), and the God who tore is the only one asked to mend. Israel filed her worst days under instruction.

The banner is a rallying point to flee to, not a slogan to march behind (v. 4): God gives a beaten army somewhere to regroup.

God's speech surveys the land as an owner (vv. 6-8), gives Ephraim and Judah jobs in his own kit, and reduces the nations that have just mauled Israel to household items — a statement of scale, not contempt.

The psalm then returns to the facts and refuses to resolve them: God's ownership of everything and his absence from this campaign stand in the same poem (vv. 9-10).

Its closing creed has two halves in order: vain is the salvation of man, and with God we shall do valiantly (vv. 11-12) — not retirement from the field but a different companion, with the outcome handed over. Verses 5-12 are reprinted at 108:6-13.
60.examples:
A defeat put on the syllabus.

Every verb of the disaster belongs to God.

The hand that tore is the only one that can stitch.

Wine that leaves a nation unable to walk straight.

A banner to flee to, not to march behind.

Ephraim as helmet, Judah as staff.

The nations that mauled them, described as a washbasin.

Two lines: man's salvation is empty, and we are going back out.

61.text: To the choirmaster: with stringed instruments. Of David. 1Hear my cry, O God, listen to my prayer;2from the end of the earth I call to you when my heart is faint. Lead me to the rock that is higher than I,3for you have been my refuge, a strong tower against the enemy.4Let me dwell in your tent forever! Let me take refuge under the shelter of your wings! Selah5For you, O God, have heard my vows; you have given me the heritage of those who fear your name.6Prolong the life of the king; may his years endure to all generations!7May he be enthroned forever before God; appoint steadfast love and faithfulness to watch over him!8So will I ever sing praises to your name, as I perform my vows day after day.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–8 — Lead Me to the Rock
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Hear my cry, O God ... from the end of the earth I call to you when my heart is faint. Lead me to the rock that is higher than I (vv. 1-2), for God has been his refuge and strong tower (v. 3). Let me dwell in your tent forever! Let me take refuge under the shelter of your wings! (v. 4). God has heard his vows and given him the heritage of those who fear his name (v. 5). Prolong the life of the king ... may he be enthroned forever before God, with steadfast love and faithfulness set to watch over him (vv. 6-7) — so will I ever sing praises to your name (v. 8).
verseByVerse.theology: A faint man at the far edge of things asks to be taken up to a rock he cannot climb.

verseByVerse.quote: Hear my cry, O God, listen to my prayer; from the end of the earth I call to you when my heart is faint. Lead me to the rock that is higher than I, for you have been my refuge, a strong tower against the enemy. Let me dwell in your tent forever! Let me take refuge under the shelter of your wings! Selah
verseByVerse.commentary:
Hear my cry, O God, listen to my prayer; from the end of the earth I call to you when my heart is faint. Lead me to the rock that is higher than I.

Three things are true of him at once, and each makes the next harder. He is far away — from the end of the earth, which may be geography or may be how the distance feels. He is exhausted: when my heart is faint, the word for a man about to pass out. And the thing he needs is above him.

The rock that is higher than I is one of the great phrases of the Psalter, and the whole of it is in the last two words. A rock at his own level would be no use; the water rises to that. He wants the high ledge, the one out of reach — and therefore he cannot ask to be shown it. He asks to be led there, which is a request made by people who have run out of strength rather than out of information.

For you have been my refuge, a strong tower against the enemy. The reason he can ask is the record. Proverbs says the same: The name of the LORD is a strong tower; the righteous man runs into it and is safe (Prov 18:10).

Let me dwell in your tent forever! Let me take refuge under the shelter of your wings!

Two shelters, and there is a lovely incongruity in the first. A tent is the most temporary building there is, and he asks to live in one forever. What makes it permanent is not the canvas but the owner. And under the roof of the tent, a second and softer covering — the wings of the bird, the image of Psalms 17, 57 and 63. He wants to be God's guest and God's chick at the same time.

verseByVerse.quote: For you, O God, have heard my vows; you have given me the heritage of those who fear your name. Prolong the life of the king; may his years endure to all generations! May he be enthroned forever before God; appoint steadfast love and faithfulness to watch over him! So will I ever sing praises to your name, as I perform my vows day after day.
verseByVerse.commentary:
For you, O God, have heard my vows; you have given me the heritage of those who fear your name.

Between verse 4 and verse 5 something has settled. He asked to be led to the rock; now he reports that God has heard, and that he has already been given the inheritance that belongs to God-fearers. The prayer has not been answered in his circumstances; it has been answered in his certainty.

Prolong the life of the king; may his years endure to all generations! May he be enthroned forever before God; appoint steadfast love and faithfulness to watch over him!

The psalm turns to pray for the king — and if David is the author he is praying about himself in the third person, which is what a man does when he is thinking of the office rather than the occupant. But look at the size of the request. may his years endure to all generations; may he be enthroned forever before God. No king of Judah got that. They all died, and most of them badly.

The prayer is reaching past every actual occupant to the promise God had made to David's house — your throne shall be established forever (2 Sam 7:16) — and it was answered when an angel said of a child, he will reign over the house of Jacob forever, and of his kingdom there will be no end (Luke 1:33). A prayer prayed for centuries in Israel's worship was finally granted to one man, who is enthroned before God now and does not die.

And the two courtiers appointed to attend him are the ones this book keeps sending out on errands: steadfast love and faithfulness, set to watch over him like a bodyguard (cf. 43:3; 57:3).

So will I ever sing praises to your name, as I perform my vows day after day.

The psalm ends with two things that go together and are usually separated: singing, and doing what he promised. Vows are performed day after day — not in one grand gesture but in instalments, which is how promises are actually kept. The man who began at the end of the earth with a fainting heart finishes with a daily routine and a song.

61.title: The Rock That Is Higher Than I
61.overview: From the end of the earth, with his heart failing, he asks God to lead him to the rock that is higher than I, since God has been his refuge and strong tower (vv. 1-3). He asks to live in God's tent forever and to shelter under his wings (v. 4). God has heard his vows and given him the heritage of those who fear his name (v. 5). Then he prays for the king: long life, years enduring to all generations, enthroned forever before God, guarded by steadfast love and faithfulness (vv. 6-7). So will I ever sing praises to your name, as I perform my vows day after day (v. 8).
61.theology:
The help needed is above him and out of reach, so he asks to be led rather than shown (v. 2): the prayer of someone out of strength, not out of information.

He asks to live forever in a tent (v. 4) — permanence belongs to the owner, not the structure — and to be at once God's guest and God's fledgling (cf. 15:1; 17:8; 27:5; 57:1).

The prayer is answered first in certainty rather than circumstances (v. 5).

The petition for the king asks what no king of Judah received — years to all generations, enthroned forever (vv. 6-7) — reaching past every occupant to the promise of 2 Sam 7:16, granted at last to the child of Luke 1:33. God's steadfast love and faithfulness are appointed as his bodyguard.

Vows are kept in instalments, day after day, alongside the singing (v. 8).
61.examples:
Far away, fainting, and needing something above him.

A rock at your own level is no use: the water rises to that.

Led, not shown — the prayer of a man out of strength.

A tent asked for forever.

God's guest and God's chick in the same verse.

A prayer no Judean king could carry, granted to one.

Steadfast love and faithfulness posted as bodyguards.

Promises kept in instalments.

62.text: To the choirmaster: according to Jeduthun. A Psalm of David. 1For God alone my soul waits in silence; from him comes my salvation.2He alone is my rock and my salvation, my fortress; I shall not be greatly shaken.3How long will all of you attack a man to batter him, like a leaning wall, a tottering fence?4They only plan to thrust him down from his high position. They take pleasure in falsehood. They bless with their mouths, but inwardly they curse. Selah5For God alone, O my soul, wait in silence, for my hope is from him.6He only is my rock and my salvation, my fortress; I shall not be shaken.7On God rests my salvation and my glory; my mighty rock, my refuge is God.8Trust in him at all times, O people; pour out your heart before him; God is a refuge for us. Selah9Those of low estate are but a breath; those of high estate are a delusion; in the balances they go up; they are together lighter than a breath.10Put no trust in extortion; set no vain hopes on robbery; if riches increase, set not your heart on them.11Once God has spoken; twice have I heard this: that power belongs to God,12and that to you, O Lord, belongs steadfast love. For you will render to a man according to his work.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–7 — He Alone Is My Rock
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: For God alone my soul waits in silence; from him comes my salvation. He alone is my rock and my salvation, my fortress; I shall not be greatly shaken (vv. 1-2). How long will they batter a man like a leaning wall, a tottering fence, blessing with their mouths and cursing inwardly (vv. 3-4)? For God alone, O my soul, wait in silence, for my hope is from him — rock, salvation, fortress, glory, refuge (vv. 5-7).
verseByVerse.theology: The same confession twice, first as a report and then as an order he gives himself.

verseByVerse.quote: For God alone my soul waits in silence; from him comes my salvation. He alone is my rock and my salvation, my fortress; I shall not be greatly shaken. How long will all of you attack a man to batter him, like a leaning wall, a tottering fence? They only plan to thrust him down from his high position. They take pleasure in falsehood. They bless with their mouths, but inwardly they curse. Selah For God alone, O my soul, wait in silence, for my hope is from him. He only is my rock and my salvation, my fortress; I shall not be shaken. On God rests my salvation and my glory; my mighty rock, my refuge is God.
verseByVerse.commentary:
For God alone my soul waits in silence; from him comes my salvation. He alone is my rock and my salvation, my fortress; I shall not be greatly shaken.

One small Hebrew word opens six verses of this psalm, and the English has to spread it about: alone, only, but. Twice it is used of God (vv. 1-2), twice of the enemies and their plans (v. 4), twice of how much a human being weighs (v. 9). The poem is built on a single adverb, and the effect is a man narrowing his options until one is left.

Waits in silence is not sulking. It is the stillness of someone who has stopped arguing his case and stopped casting about for alternatives. And notice the honest qualification at the end of verse 2: I shall not be greatly shaken. He does not claim to be unshakable. He claims a limit on how far the shaking can go.

How long will all of you attack a man to batter him, like a leaning wall, a tottering fence? They only plan to thrust him down from his high position. They take pleasure in falsehood. They bless with their mouths, but inwardly they curse.

They see him as a wall already out of true — one good shove and it comes down. It is a horrible image of how a group treats someone they have decided is finished: not a fight, a demolition of something already leaning.

And the method is words. They bless with their mouths, but inwardly they curse — the same double heart as 55:21, where the speech was butter and the intention was war.

For God alone, O my soul, wait in silence, for my hope is from him. He only is my rock and my salvation, my fortress; I shall not be shaken.

Now the opening confession comes back, but something has changed. Verse 1 was a statement: my soul waits in silence. Verse 5 is an imperative: O my soul, WAIT in silence. He turns round and commands himself to do what he has just claimed to be doing. That is not hypocrisy; it is how faith works under pressure, and Psalm 42 does the same thing with its refrain.

One more difference: verse 2 said not GREATLY shaken; verse 6 drops the qualifier — I shall not be shaken. Between the two, all that has happened is that he has preached to himself.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 8–12 — Pour Out Your Heart Before Him
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Trust in him at all times, O people; pour out your heart before him; God is a refuge for us (v. 8). High and low alike are lighter than a breath in the scales (v. 9); set no hope on extortion, and if riches increase, do not set your heart on them (v. 10). Once God has spoken; twice have I heard this: that power belongs to God, and that to you, O Lord, belongs steadfast love. For you will render to a man according to his work (vv. 11-12).
verseByVerse.theology: One utterance of God, two things heard in it — and neither of them is what a frightened man expects.

verseByVerse.quote: Trust in him at all times, O people; pour out your heart before him; God is a refuge for us. Selah Those of low estate are but a breath; those of high estate are a delusion; in the balances they go up; they are together lighter than a breath. Put no trust in extortion; set no vain hopes on robbery; if riches increase, set not your heart on them.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Trust in him at all times, O people; pour out your heart before him; God is a refuge for us.

He turns from his own soul to everyone else's, and the middle command is one of the kindest sentences in Scripture. Pour out your heart before him — empty it, tip the whole thing up, the way Hannah described her own praying: I have been pouring out my soul before the LORD (1 Sam 1:15).

Notice that it stands beside wait in silence and does not contradict it. The silence of verses 1 and 5 is towards other people and towards alternatives; the pouring out is towards God. A believer may be quite silent in public about his trouble and entirely unrestrained in private.

Those of low estate are but a breath; those of high estate are a delusion; in the balances they go up; they are together lighter than a breath.

Put every human being on the scales — the nobodies and the somebodies together — and the pan holding them rises. They do not register. This is Psalm 39's mere breath again, and it is said here to a man being battered by people who seemed to have all the power. They weigh nothing. It is not an insult; it is a correction of the terror.

Put no trust in extortion; set no vain hopes on robbery; if riches increase, set not your heart on them.

And the last clause is for the people who never robbed anyone. Wealth can arrive honestly — if riches increase — and the danger is not in the money but in the heart's quiet migration towards it. The command is not to give it away but to watch where your heart goes when the balance grows.

verseByVerse.quote: Once God has spoken; twice have I heard this: that power belongs to God, and that to you, O Lord, belongs steadfast love. For you will render to a man according to his work.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Once God has spoken; twice have I heard this: that power belongs to God, and that to you, O Lord, belongs steadfast love.

The psalm ends with a formula the Old Testament uses for something said with great weight — once ... twice, as Elihu says God speaks in one way, and in two (Job 33:14). God said one thing, and the listener heard two.

And the two are exactly the pair a battered man needs, in that order. Power belongs to God — so the leaning-wall treatment in verse 3 is not the last word about his strength. To you, O Lord, belongs steadfast love — so that power is not neutral, and not against him.

Either half alone would be unbearable. Power without love is a tyrant; love without power is a sympathetic bystander. The Christian faith holds the two together at a cross, where God's power looked like weakness and his love did the costliest thing available.

For you will render to a man according to his work.

And the last line puts both to use. The men who bless with their mouths and curse inwardly will be paid according to what they actually did, not what they said — which is the promise Paul makes (Rom 2:6) and Jesus repeats about his own return (Matt 16:27). The psalm that began by narrowing everything down to God alone ends by leaving the accounts with him.

62.title: For God Alone My Soul Waits in Silence
62.overview: For God alone my soul waits in silence — he alone is rock, salvation and fortress, so the psalmist will not be greatly shaken (vv. 1-2). His attackers treat him as a leaning wall to be pushed over, blessing with their mouths while cursing inwardly (vv. 3-4). So he commands himself: For God alone, O my soul, wait in silence (vv. 5-7). Then he turns to everyone: Trust in him at all times, O people; pour out your heart before him (v. 8), for high and low alike weigh less than a breath, and riches are not to be trusted or loved (vv. 9-10). Once God has spoken; twice have I heard this: that power belongs to God, and that to you, O Lord, belongs steadfast love — and he will render to each according to his work (vv. 11-12).
62.theology:
One Hebrew adverb opens six verses, narrowing the options to God alone (vv. 1, 2, 4, 5, 6, 9). Waiting in silence is the stillness of a man who has stopped looking for alternatives, and the honest limit of v. 2 (not greatly shaken) becomes the plain claim of v. 6 after he has preached to himself.

The statement of v. 1 returns as a command in v. 5: faith under pressure orders the soul to do what it has claimed to be doing (cf. 42:5).

Silence towards alternatives and pouring out towards God are not in conflict (vv. 5, 8; cf. 1 Sam 1:15): a believer may be quiet in public and unrestrained in private.

Weighed together, all human power is lighter than a breath (v. 9) — a correction of terror, not an insult; and honest wealth is dangerous to the heart's affections (v. 10).

God's single utterance yields two things (v. 11; cf. Job 33:14): power and steadfast love. Either without the other would be unbearable, and both meet at the cross. Judgment follows deeds, not speech (v. 12; Rom 2:6; Matt 16:27).
62.examples:
A psalm built on one small adverb.

Not unshakable — not greatly shaken.

A demolition of something already leaning.

The statement of verse 1 given as an order in verse 5.

Silence outwards, pouring out upwards.

Everyone on the scales, and the pan rises.

The heart's quiet migration when the balance grows.

Power without love is a tyrant; love without power is a bystander.

63.text: A Psalm of David, when he was in the wilderness of Judah. 1O God, you are my God; earnestly I seek you; my soul thirsts for you; my flesh faints for you, as in a dry and weary land where there is no water.2So I have looked upon you in the sanctuary, beholding your power and glory.3Because your steadfast love is better than life, my lips will praise you.4So I will bless you as long as I live; in your name I will lift up my hands.5My soul will be satisfied as with fat and rich food, and my mouth will praise you with joyful lips,6when I remember you upon my bed, and meditate on you in the watches of the night;7for you have been my help, and in the shadow of your wings I will sing for joy.8My soul clings to you; your right hand upholds me.9But those who seek to destroy my life shall go down into the depths of the earth;10they shall be given over to the power of the sword; they shall be a portion for jackals.11But the king shall rejoice in God; all who swear by him shall exult, for the mouths of liars will be stopped.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–8 — My Soul Thirsts for You
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: O God, you are my God; earnestly I seek you; my soul thirsts for you; my flesh faints for you, as in a dry and weary land where there is no water (v. 1). He remembers looking on God in the sanctuary (v. 2). Because your steadfast love is better than life, my lips will praise you (vv. 3-4). His soul is satisfied as with fat and rich food when he remembers God on his bed in the night watches (vv. 5-7). My soul clings to you; your right hand upholds me (v. 8).
verseByVerse.theology: A man with no water calls God better than life, and describes a feast in a desert.

verseByVerse.quote: O God, you are my God; earnestly I seek you; my soul thirsts for you; my flesh faints for you, as in a dry and weary land where there is no water. So I have looked upon you in the sanctuary, beholding your power and glory. Because your steadfast love is better than life, my lips will praise you. So I will bless you as long as I live; in your name I will lift up my hands.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The heading puts him in the wilderness of Judah — the badlands east of the hill country, either during the Saul years (1 Sam 23:14) or the flight from Absalom (2 Sam 15:23). Either way he is in a place with no water.

O God, you are my God; earnestly I seek you; my soul thirsts for you; my flesh faints for you, as in a dry and weary land where there is no water.

The first four words are the whole relationship: O God, you are my God. Not the God, not a God — mine, which is the difference between theology and faith.

Then the thirst, and notice that it is not a figure of speech laid over a comfortable life. He is actually parched, in an actual desert, and he says that what his body is doing for water his soul is doing for God. My flesh faints for you: even the physical craving has been drawn into the longing. Psalm 42 used the deer at the stream for the same thing; this one has the advantage of a man who is genuinely dry.

So I have looked upon you in the sanctuary, beholding your power and glory.

He is remembering. Cut off from the place of worship, he goes back over what he saw there. That is what a believer in a dry season lives on — not new experiences but stored ones, gone over carefully.

Because your steadfast love is better than life, my lips will praise you. So I will bless you as long as I live; in your name I will lift up my hands.

Here is the most extreme valuation anywhere in the Psalter, and the circumstances make it. A man whose life is actually in danger, in a place that could kill him within days, says that God's covenant love is better than life.

Not better than comfort, or than wealth, or than reputation — better than the thing everybody else is trying to hold on to. Test it by the alternative: if life is the highest good, then anyone who can threaten your life owns you. This man's enemies have no leverage, and it is not bravado; it is arithmetic. Paul does the same sum and reaches the same answer — to live is Christ, and to die is gain (Phil 1:21).

verseByVerse.quote: My soul will be satisfied as with fat and rich food, and my mouth will praise you with joyful lips, when I remember you upon my bed, and meditate on you in the watches of the night; for you have been my help, and in the shadow of your wings I will sing for joy. My soul clings to you; your right hand upholds me.
verseByVerse.commentary:
My soul will be satisfied as with fat and rich food, and my mouth will praise you with joyful lips.

He is in a desert, and the word he reaches for is a banquet: fat and rich food, the best cuts at a feast. Whatever he is living on, it is not rations. This is one of Scripture's plainest statements that God himself is enjoyable, not merely necessary.

When I remember you upon my bed, and meditate on you in the watches of the night.

And here is when the feast happens: at night, awake, in the hours when the mind normally works against a man. The watches of the night were the sentry shifts, and while somebody was standing guard over the camp he was lying there going over God. Psalm 16 said the same about the night teaching him; Psalm 4 told the angry to ponder on their beds. Scripture keeps turning insomnia into an appointment.

For you have been my help, and in the shadow of your wings I will sing for joy. My soul clings to you; your right hand upholds me.

The last verse holds two grips. My soul clings to you — the verb is the one Genesis uses of a man holding fast to his wife, the strongest word for attachment in the language. And immediately: your right hand upholds me.

Both are true and the order matters. He is holding on, and underneath his grip is a hand that is doing the actual holding. Anyone who has ever worried that their grip on God is too weak should read the second half of the verse. The clinging is real; the security is in the upholding.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 9–11 — The King Shall Rejoice in God
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Those who seek his life will go down into the depths, be given to the sword and become a portion for jackals (vv. 9-10). But the king shall rejoice in God; all who swear by him shall exult, for the mouths of liars will be stopped (v. 11).
verseByVerse.theology: The psalm ends with the liars silenced — not answered, stopped.

verseByVerse.quote: But those who seek to destroy my life shall go down into the depths of the earth; they shall be given over to the power of the sword; they shall be a portion for jackals. But the king shall rejoice in God; all who swear by him shall exult, for the mouths of liars will be stopped.
verseByVerse.commentary:
But those who seek to destroy my life shall go down into the depths of the earth; they shall be given over to the power of the sword; they shall be a portion for jackals.

Three sentences of stark reversal. A body unburied and left for scavengers was the ancient world's picture of total disgrace — and the men who hunted him through the wilderness will be left in it. He is not planning any of this; it is stated as their end, not his project.

But the king shall rejoice in God; all who swear by him shall exult, for the mouths of liars will be stopped.

David speaks of himself as the king, as he did in Psalm 61 — the office rather than the man. And note what the last clause actually says about the liars. Not that they will be refuted, or that the truth will come out and everyone will apologise. Their mouths will be stopped.

That is a considerable comfort to anyone being lied about, and it is realistic. Slander is very often never answered in this life; the correction does not catch up with the rumour. What this psalm promises is that there is a day when the talking simply ends, and until then a man in a waterless place can lie awake at night enjoying God as though at a banquet.

63.title: Better Than Life
63.overview: From the wilderness of Judah: O God, you are my God ... my soul thirsts for you; my flesh faints for you, as in a dry and weary land where there is no water (v. 1). He remembers seeing God's power and glory in the sanctuary (v. 2). Because your steadfast love is better than life, my lips will praise you (vv. 3-4). His soul is satisfied as at a feast when he remembers God on his bed through the night watches (vv. 5-7). My soul clings to you; your right hand upholds me (v. 8). Those hunting him will fall to the sword and be left for jackals (vv. 9-10), but the king shall rejoice in God ... for the mouths of liars will be stopped (v. 11).
63.theology:
The thirst is literal and spiritual at once: his flesh as well as his soul is doing the longing (v. 1; cf. 42:1-2). Cut off from worship, he lives on remembered worship (v. 2).

Better than life (v. 3) is the Psalter's most extreme valuation, and it is made by a man in real danger. Its logic is plain: if life is the highest good, anyone who can threaten it owns you. Paul reaches the same conclusion (Phil 1:21).

God is described as enjoyable, not merely necessary — a banquet in a desert (v. 5) — and the feast is eaten at night, in the sentry watches (v. 6; cf. 4:4; 16:7).

Two grips are named in v. 8, and their order matters: the soul clings (the Gen 2:24 verb), and underneath it God's right hand upholds. The security is in the upholding.

The liars' mouths are stopped rather than refuted (v. 11) — realistic comfort for the slandered, since corrections rarely catch up with rumours.
63.examples:
Four words that are the whole relationship: you are my God.

A real desert, and a body doing the longing.

Living on stored worship rather than new experiences.

If life is the highest good, whoever can end it owns you.

Fat and rich food, ordered in a wilderness.

Insomnia turned into an appointment.

He clings; the right hand holds.

Not refuted — stopped.

64.text: To the choirmaster. A Psalm of David. 1Hear my voice, O God, in my complaint; preserve my life from dread of the enemy.2Hide me from the secret plots of the wicked, from the throng of evildoers,3who whet their tongues like swords, who aim bitter words like arrows,4shooting from ambush at the blameless, shooting at him suddenly and without fear.5They hold fast to their evil purpose; they talk of laying snares secretly, thinking, "Who can see them?"6They search out injustice, saying, "We have accomplished a diligent search." For the inward mind and heart of a man are deep.7But God shoots his arrow at them; they are wounded suddenly.8They are brought to ruin, with their own tongues turned against them; all who see them will wag their heads.9Then all mankind fears; they tell what God has brought about and ponder what he has done.10Let the righteous one rejoice in the LORD and take refuge in him! Let all the upright in heart exult!

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–6 — Shooting from Ambush at the Blameless
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Hear my voice, O God, in my complaint; preserve my life from dread of the enemy. Hide me from the secret plots of the wicked (vv. 1-2), who whet their tongues like swords, who aim bitter words like arrows, shooting from ambush at the blameless, shooting at him suddenly and without fear (vv. 3-4). They hold to their purpose, lay snares secretly, and ask Who can see them?; they search out injustice diligently (vv. 5-6).
verseByVerse.theology: Sharpened tongues, arrows fired from cover, and a great deal of hard work put into malice.

verseByVerse.quote: Hear my voice, O God, in my complaint; preserve my life from dread of the enemy. Hide me from the secret plots of the wicked, from the throng of evildoers, who whet their tongues like swords, who aim bitter words like arrows, shooting from ambush at the blameless, shooting at him suddenly and without fear. They hold fast to their evil purpose; they talk of laying snares secretly, thinking, "Who can see them?" They search out injustice, saying, "We have accomplished a diligent search." For the inward mind and heart of a man are deep.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Hear my voice, O God, in my complaint; preserve my life from dread of the enemy.

Read that request carefully. He does not ask first to be preserved from the enemy but from dread of him. The fear is treated as a separate danger, and it is: a man can be destroyed by the anticipation of an attack that never comes. Anyone lying awake rehearsing what someone might do has asked for the wrong thing if he has only asked for the trouble to be removed.

Hide me from the secret plots of the wicked, from the throng of evildoers, who whet their tongues like swords, who aim bitter words like arrows, shooting from ambush at the blameless, shooting at him suddenly and without fear.

This is the sixth psalm in a row where the weapon is a mouth, and here it becomes the entire subject. Two military images: a sword put to the whetstone — deliberate, unhurried preparation, a man sitting down to make his words sharper — and arrows shot from cover.

The ambush is what makes it unbearable. Shooting from ambush at the blameless: the victim has no warning, cannot see who fired, and often does not know he has been hit until the damage is done. That is exactly how a reputation is taken apart. And without fear — they are not nervous about it, because ambushers are never identified.

They hold fast to their evil purpose; they talk of laying snares secretly, thinking, Who can see them?

Their creed once more: Who can see them? Psalm 10's predator and Psalm 59's dogs said the same. Every campaign of this kind runs on the assumption that the meetings are private.

They search out injustice, saying, We have accomplished a diligent search. For the inward mind and heart of a man are deep.

Two sobering observations. The first is the sheer industry of malice: they search out, they call it a diligent search, and they congratulate each other on the thoroughness. People will work harder to damage someone than they ever worked at their job.

The second is the line that ends the verse: the inward mind and heart of a man are deep. There is more in a human being than anyone can see down into — which is why the plotting stays hidden, and why only God can reach the bottom of it.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 7–10 — But God Shoots His Arrow
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: But God shoots his arrow at them; they are wounded suddenly. They are brought to ruin, with their own tongues turned against them; all who see them will wag their heads (vv. 7-8). Then all mankind fears; they tell what God has brought about and ponder what he has done (v. 9). Let the righteous one rejoice in the LORD and take refuge in him! (v. 10).
verseByVerse.theology: The ambush is answered in kind, by an archer they never saw, and the outcome is a world that has learned something.

verseByVerse.quote: But God shoots his arrow at them; they are wounded suddenly. They are brought to ruin, with their own tongues turned against them; all who see them will wag their heads. Then all mankind fears; they tell what God has brought about and ponder what he has done. Let the righteous one rejoice in the LORD and take refuge in him! Let all the upright in heart exult!
verseByVerse.commentary:
But God shoots his arrow at them; they are wounded suddenly.

But God — and the reply is in the same currency. They fired arrows from cover; God fires one. They shot suddenly (v. 4); they are wounded suddenly (v. 7), the very same word. The ambushers are ambushed, by an archer they never saw taking aim.

This is not the psalmist's revenge. He has not touched a bow; he asked in verse 1 to be hidden. The answer to the archers comes from somewhere above the tree line.

They are brought to ruin, with their own tongues turned against them; all who see them will wag their heads.

And the mechanism of the ruin is beautifully exact: their own tongues turned against them. Not a thunderbolt — their own words, coming back. The thing they sharpened cut them. Paul states the principle generally: whatever one sows, that will he also reap (Gal 6:7).

The head-wagging is the same gesture the psalms have suffered under elsewhere (22:7; 44:14). It has changed address.

Then all mankind fears; they tell what God has brought about and ponder what he has done.

Notice what the outcome is not. It is not the righteous man gloating, and it is not even his vindication being announced. It is that everybody now takes God seriously: they fear, they tell, they ponder. A public act of God turns into a public conversation, and people go away thinking.

Let the righteous one rejoice in the LORD and take refuge in him! Let all the upright in heart exult!

And the last verse tells the righteous where to put their gladness: in the LORD, not in the outcome. The psalm has spent six verses on the anatomy of a whispering campaign and three on God's answer, and it ends by sending the victim back to the refuge he asked for in verse 2 — not to enjoy the downfall, but to enjoy God.

64.title: They Whet Their Tongues Like Swords
64.overview: He asks God to preserve him from dread of the enemy and to hide him from secret plots (vv. 1-2), where men whet their tongues like swords and shoot bitter words like arrows from ambush at the blameless, suddenly and without fear (vv. 3-4), certain that nobody can see them, and working diligently at their malice (vv. 5-6). But God shoots his arrow at them; they are wounded suddenly, brought to ruin by their own tongues, with onlookers wagging their heads (vv. 7-8). Then everyone fears and tells what God has done and ponders it (v. 9), and the righteous are told to rejoice and take refuge in the LORD (v. 10).
64.theology:
The first petition is against the dread rather than the enemy (v. 1): anticipation does its own damage.

This is the sixth consecutive psalm whose weapon is speech, and it makes it the subject. The whetstone shows deliberation, and the ambush explains the pain: no warning, no face, and no fear of identification (vv. 3-4). Malice is industrious and congratulates itself on thoroughness (v. 6), and it hides in an interior too deep for anyone but God to sound.

God's answer comes in the same currency and with the same adverb: they shot suddenly, they are wounded suddenly (vv. 4, 7), by an archer they never saw. The psalmist has not touched a bow.

The ruin works through their own tongues (v. 8; cf. Gal 6:7), and the outcome is neither gloating nor even vindication but a world that fears, tells and ponders (v. 9). Joy is finally located in the LORD, not in the downfall (v. 10).
64.examples:
Asking to be spared the dread, not only the danger.

A man sitting down at a whetstone to make his words sharper.

Shot from cover: no warning, and no face.

People work harder at malice than at their jobs.

An interior too deep for anyone but God to reach.

Suddenly, and suddenly: the same word, both ways.

The thing they sharpened cut them.

The end is not gloating but a world that goes away thinking.

65.text: To the choirmaster. A Psalm of David. A Song. 1Praise is due to you, O God, in Zion, and to you shall vows be performed.2O you who hear prayer, to you shall all flesh come.3When iniquities prevail against me, you atone for our transgressions.4Blessed is the one you choose and bring near, to dwell in your courts! We shall be satisfied with the goodness of your house, the holiness of your temple!5By awesome deeds you answer us with righteousness, O God of our salvation, the hope of all the ends of the earth and of the farthest seas;6the one who by his strength established the mountains, being girded with might;7who stills the roaring of the seas, the roaring of their waves, the tumult of the peoples,8so that those who dwell at the ends of the earth are in awe at your signs. You make the going out of the morning and the evening to shout for joy.9You visit the earth and water it; you greatly enrich it; the river of God is full of water; you provide their grain, for so you have prepared it.10You water its furrows abundantly, settling its ridges, softening it with showers, and blessing its growth.11You crown the year with your bounty; your wagon tracks overflow with abundance.12The pastures of the wilderness overflow, the hills gird themselves with joy,13the meadows clothe themselves with flocks, the valleys deck themselves with grain, they shout and sing together for joy.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–8 — O You Who Hear Prayer
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Praise is due to you, O God, in Zion ... O you who hear prayer, to you shall all flesh come (vv. 1-2). When iniquities prevail against me, you atone for our transgressions (v. 3). Blessed is the one you choose and bring near, to dwell in your courts! (v. 4). By awesome deeds he answers, the hope of the ends of the earth, who established the mountains and stills the roaring of the seas ... the tumult of the peoples, so that morning and evening shout for joy (vv. 5-8).
verseByVerse.theology: A God whose title is that he hears, who deals with sin and stills both oceans and nations.

verseByVerse.quote: Praise is due to you, O God, in Zion, and to you shall vows be performed. O you who hear prayer, to you shall all flesh come. When iniquities prevail against me, you atone for our transgressions. Blessed is the one you choose and bring near, to dwell in your courts! We shall be satisfied with the goodness of your house, the holiness of your temple!
verseByVerse.commentary:
Praise is due to you, O God, in Zion, and to you shall vows be performed. O you who hear prayer, to you shall all flesh come.

The ESV notes an alternative for the first line: "Praise waits for you in silence" — praise standing by, ready, like a servant in an anteroom.

And then God is given a name made out of a habit: O you who hear prayer. Not "you who answered once"; this is what he is. The promise attached is as wide as the world — to you shall all flesh come — which is a startling thing to say in a psalm sung at the temple in a small country.

When iniquities prevail against me, you atone for our transgressions.

Watch the pronouns: iniquities prevail against me, and God atones for our transgressions. One man's experience of being overwhelmed by his own sin turns immediately into the congregation's forgiveness.

And the verb is the great one: atone, kaphar, the word of the Day of Atonement when the blood was taken behind the curtain (Lev 16). It is God who does it here. The sinner is the object, not the agent: sin prevails against him and God covers it.

Blessed is the one you choose and bring near, to dwell in your courts! We shall be satisfied with the goodness of your house, the holiness of your temple!

Two verbs and both are God's: choose and bring near. Nobody in this psalm arrives under his own steam. And what they find when they get there is not merely safety but satisfaction — the same word that Psalm 63 used of fat and rich food. God's house feeds people.

verseByVerse.quote: By awesome deeds you answer us with righteousness, O God of our salvation, the hope of all the ends of the earth and of the farthest seas; the one who by his strength established the mountains, being girded with might; who stills the roaring of the seas, the roaring of their waves, the tumult of the peoples, so that those who dwell at the ends of the earth are in awe at your signs. You make the going out of the morning and the evening to shout for joy.
verseByVerse.commentary:
By awesome deeds you answer us with righteousness, O God of our salvation, the hope of all the ends of the earth and of the farthest seas.

The horizon keeps widening. In verse 2 all flesh comes; here God is the hope of all the ends of the earth and of the farthest seas — of people this congregation had never met and sailors beyond the known map.

The one who by his strength established the mountains, being girded with might; who stills the roaring of the seas, the roaring of their waves, the tumult of the peoples.

Three things in one sentence, and the third is the surprise: the roaring sea and the roaring nations are handled by the same hand and named in the same breath (as in Psalm 46). Political chaos and physical chaos are the same kind of problem to God.

And the line has a New Testament echo that would have stopped any Jewish reader. One night on a lake a man stood up in a boat and rebuked the wind and said to the sea, Peace! Be still! — and the men with him asked who he could possibly be (Mark 4:39-41). This psalm answers their question.

So that those who dwell at the ends of the earth are in awe at your signs. You make the going out of the morning and the evening to shout for joy.

A lovely line, and easy to hurry past: sunrise and sunset are pictured as two gates the day goes out of, and both of them are shouting. Every dawn and every dusk, somewhere on the planet, is a noise of gladness.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 9–13 — The Valleys Deck Themselves with Grain
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: You visit the earth and water it; you greatly enrich it; you water the furrows, settle the ridges, soften it with showers and bless its growth (vv. 9-10). You crown the year with your bounty; your wagon tracks overflow with abundance; the pastures overflow, the hills gird themselves with joy, the meadows clothe themselves with flocks, the valleys deck themselves with grain, they shout and sing together for joy (vv. 11-13).
verseByVerse.theology: God goes round the fields himself, and the countryside dresses up and sings.

verseByVerse.quote: You visit the earth and water it; you greatly enrich it; the river of God is full of water; you provide their grain, for so you have prepared it. You water its furrows abundantly, settling its ridges, softening it with showers, and blessing its growth. You crown the year with your bounty; your wagon tracks overflow with abundance. The pastures of the wilderness overflow, the hills gird themselves with joy, the meadows clothe themselves with flocks, the valleys deck themselves with grain, they shout and sing together for joy.
verseByVerse.commentary:
You visit the earth and water it; you greatly enrich it; the river of God is full of water; you provide their grain, for so you have prepared it.

Now God becomes a farmer, and the psalm follows him round the fields. You visit — he comes in person, the same verb used of God visiting his people to help them. The ESV notes the middle phrase may be "make it overflow".

You water its furrows abundantly, settling its ridges, softening it with showers, and blessing its growth.

Five verbs, and they are the work of a man who knows soil. Furrows watered, the ridges between them knocked down and settled, the crust softened by rain so the seed can get up through it. This is not poetic vagueness about nature. It is what a farmer prays for in order, and the psalm says God does each step himself.

You crown the year with your bounty; your wagon tracks overflow with abundance.

The picture is God driving a loaded cart round the countryside, and so much is spilling off the back that the ruts left by the wheels are overflowing with it. That is the Bible's image of a good harvest: not careful measures, but a God who is messy with his generosity.

The pastures of the wilderness overflow, the hills gird themselves with joy, the meadows clothe themselves with flocks, the valleys deck themselves with grain, they shout and sing together for joy.

The land gets dressed. The hills belt themselves with gladness, the meadows put on sheep like a coat, the valleys wrap themselves in wheat — and then the whole landscape starts singing. There is no embarrassment in Scripture about God's pleasure in ordinary fertility.

Paul preached this to a crowd of pagans in a country town: God did not leave himself without witness, for he did good by giving you rains from heaven and fruitful seasons, satisfying your hearts with food and gladness (Acts 14:17). The rain that fell on people who did not know his name was already his sermon. And the psalm that began with atonement in Zion ends in a field, because the God who forgives sin is the same one who softens soil.

65.title: You Crown the Year with Your Bounty
65.overview: Praise waits for God in Zion, and vows are paid to you who hear prayer, to whom all flesh will come (vv. 1-2). When iniquities overwhelm one man, God atones for the congregation's transgressions (v. 3); blessed is the one God chooses and brings near to his courts (v. 4). He answers with awesome deeds, the hope of the ends of the earth; he set the mountains and stills the roaring of seas and the tumult of peoples alike, so that morning and evening shout for joy (vv. 5-8). Then God goes round the fields: visiting, watering, enriching, settling the ridges, softening the soil with showers, crowning the year with bounty until his wagon tracks overflow — and the hills, meadows and valleys dress themselves and sing (vv. 9-13).
65.theology:
God's name here is a habit: you who hear prayer (v. 2), and the invitation is universal — all flesh, the ends of the earth, the farthest seas (vv. 2, 5).

Atonement is God's own act (v. 3, the Day of Atonement verb; Lev 16), and access is by his choosing and bringing near (v. 4): nobody arrives under his own power, and what they find is satisfaction.

Roaring seas and roaring nations are one kind of problem to God (v. 7; cf. 46:3, 6) — which is the question the disciples asked about Jesus on the lake (Mark 4:39-41).

Providence is described as farming done by God in person, step by step (vv. 9-10), with a harvest so generous that the cart spills into the ruts (v. 11). Paul preached this creation-kindness to pagans as God's witness to them (Acts 14:17): the God who forgives sin is the one who softens soil.
65.examples:
Praise standing by in an anteroom.

A name made out of a habit: the one who hears.

Sin prevails against me; God atones for our.

Chosen and brought near — nobody walks in.

Seas and nations, hushed by the same hand.

Sunrise and sunset as two gates, both shouting.

Ruts overflowing behind a loaded cart.

The countryside getting dressed and singing.

66.text: To the choirmaster. A Song. A Psalm. 1Shout for joy to God, all the earth;2sing the glory of his name; give to him glorious praise!3Say to God, "How awesome are your deeds! So great is your power that your enemies come cringing to you.4All the earth worships you and sings praises to you; they sing praises to your name." Selah5Come and see what God has done: he is awesome in his deeds toward the children of man.6He turned the sea into dry land; they passed through the river on foot. There did we rejoice in him,7who rules by his might forever, whose eyes keep watch on the nations— let not the rebellious exalt themselves. Selah8Bless our God, O peoples; let the sound of his praise be heard,9who has kept our soul among the living and has not let our feet slip.10For you, O God, have tested us; you have tried us as silver is tried.11You brought us into the net; you laid a crushing burden on our backs;12you let men ride over our heads; we went through fire and through water; yet you have brought us out to a place of abundance.13I will come into your house with burnt offerings; I will perform my vows to you,14that which my lips uttered and my mouth promised when I was in trouble.15I will offer to you burnt offerings of fattened animals, with the smoke of the sacrifice of rams; I will make an offering of bulls and goats. Selah16Come and hear, all you who fear God, and I will tell what he has done for my soul.17I cried to him with my mouth, and high praise was on my tongue.18If I had cherished iniquity in my heart, the Lord would not have listened.19But truly God has listened; he has attended to the voice of my prayer.20Blessed be God, because he has not rejected my prayer or removed his steadfast love from me!

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–7 — Come and See What God Has Done
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Shout for joy to God, all the earth ... give to him glorious praise! (vv. 1-2). Say to God how awesome his deeds are; all the earth worships him (vv. 3-4). Come and see what God has done: he is awesome in his deeds toward the children of man. He turned the sea into dry land; they passed through the river on foot. There did we rejoice in him, who rules forever and watches the nations (vv. 5-7).
verseByVerse.theology: The whole earth is called to look at one nation's history, and the singers say we about a crossing centuries before they were born.

verseByVerse.quote: Shout for joy to God, all the earth; sing the glory of his name; give to him glorious praise! Say to God, "How awesome are your deeds! So great is your power that your enemies come cringing to you. All the earth worships you and sings praises to you; they sing praises to your name." Selah Come and see what God has done: he is awesome in his deeds toward the children of man. He turned the sea into dry land; they passed through the river on foot. There did we rejoice in him, who rules by his might forever, whose eyes keep watch on the nations— let not the rebellious exalt themselves. Selah
verseByVerse.commentary:
Shout for joy to God, all the earth; sing the glory of his name; give to him glorious praise! Say to God, How awesome are your deeds! So great is your power that your enemies come cringing to you.

The psalm opens at maximum range — all the earth — and it will narrow steadily: the world here, the congregation from verse 8, and a single man from verse 13. That funnel is the shape of the whole poem, and it ends with one person telling a small group what happened to him.

Come and see what God has done: he is awesome in his deeds toward the children of man. He turned the sea into dry land; they passed through the river on foot. There did we rejoice in him.

Two crossings in one line: the Red Sea, where the water stood up and Israel walked out of Egypt (Exod 14), and the Jordan, where it happened again on the way in (Josh 3). Two generations, forty years apart, one God.

And then the phrase that should stop any reader: THERE did WE rejoice in him. The singer was not born for centuries. He says we anyway, because what God did to his people then was done to him. This is how Scripture teaches a congregation to hold its history — not as something that happened to other people but as family memory. Christians say the same thing about a cross they did not stand at.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 8–15 — Tried as Silver Is Tried
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Bless our God, O peoples, who has kept us alive and not let our feet slip (vv. 8-9). For you, O God, have tested us; you have tried us as silver is tried. You brought us into the net; you laid a crushing burden on our backs; you let men ride over our heads; we went through fire and through water; yet you have brought us out to a place of abundance (vv. 10-12). So he will come into God's house and pay the vows his lips uttered when he was in trouble (vv. 13-15).
verseByVerse.theology: Every verb of the ordeal belongs to God, including the net — and so does the way out.

verseByVerse.quote: Bless our God, O peoples; let the sound of his praise be heard, who has kept our soul among the living and has not let our feet slip. For you, O God, have tested us; you have tried us as silver is tried. You brought us into the net; you laid a crushing burden on our backs; you let men ride over our heads; we went through fire and through water; yet you have brought us out to a place of abundance.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Bless our God, O peoples; let the sound of his praise be heard, who has kept our soul among the living and has not let our feet slip.

Two modest mercies, and most people have them and never count them: still alive, and not fallen. The psalm wants the nations to hear about those.

For you, O God, have tested us; you have tried us as silver is tried. You brought us into the net; you laid a crushing burden on our backs; you let men ride over our heads; we went through fire and through water; yet you have brought us out to a place of abundance.

Read the verbs and notice whose they are. You tested, you tried, you brought us into the net, you laid the burden, you let men ride over our heads. Scripture does not offer the comfort that the trouble came from somewhere else. The net was God's.

And the image for it is a refinery: you have tried us as silver is tried. Silver is not purified by being left alone; it is melted, and the dross rises so that it can be lifted off. Peter says the same of Christians, that the testing of their faith is more precious than gold that perishes though it is tested by fire (1 Pet 1:7).

Men ride over our heads is the picture of a defeated army being ridden across — the ultimate humiliation, bodies used as ground. And then two elements in three words: fire and water, the two ways the ancient world knew a person could be destroyed. Isaiah promised both by name: When you pass through the waters, I will be with you ... when you walk through fire you shall not be burned (Isa 43:2). Not round: through.

And then the hinge of the psalm, one word: yet. Yet you have brought us out to a place of abundance. The same hand that held them in the net has set them down somewhere wide and well supplied. The destination explains the route without cancelling how bad the route was.

verseByVerse.quote: I will come into your house with burnt offerings; I will perform my vows to you, that which my lips uttered and my mouth promised when I was in trouble. I will offer to you burnt offerings of fattened animals, with the smoke of the sacrifice of rams; I will make an offering of bulls and goats. Selah
verseByVerse.commentary:
I will come into your house with burnt offerings; I will perform my vows to you, that which my lips uttered and my mouth promised when I was in trouble. I will offer to you burnt offerings of fattened animals, with the smoke of the sacrifice of rams; I will make an offering of bulls and goats.

The plural becomes singular here — I — and the first thing the rescued man does is pay for what he said in the crisis. He is honest about when the promises were made: when I was in trouble. Vows made in a hospital corridor are real vows.

And the list is expensive: fattened animals, rams, bulls, goats. Most people's gratitude shrinks as the memory of the danger fades. This man's has kept its size.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 16–20 — Come and Hear What He Has Done for My Soul
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Come and hear, all you who fear God, and I will tell what he has done for my soul (v. 16). He cried out with praise on his tongue (v. 17). If I had cherished iniquity in my heart, the Lord would not have listened. But truly God has listened; he has attended to the voice of my prayer (vv. 18-19). Blessed be God, because he has not rejected my prayer or removed his steadfast love from me! (v. 20).
verseByVerse.theology: The psalm narrows from the whole earth to one man's testimony, and ends on two things God did not do.

verseByVerse.quote: Come and hear, all you who fear God, and I will tell what he has done for my soul. I cried to him with my mouth, and high praise was on my tongue. If I had cherished iniquity in my heart, the Lord would not have listened. But truly God has listened; he has attended to the voice of my prayer. Blessed be God, because he has not rejected my prayer or removed his steadfast love from me!
verseByVerse.commentary:
Come and hear, all you who fear God, and I will tell what he has done for my soul.

Verse 5 said come and see what God did for the nation; this says come and hear what he has done for one soul. Both are needed. A church that only has the big story becomes a history lecture, and a church that only has personal testimony becomes a series of anecdotes. This psalm has the Red Sea and one man's answered prayer in the same song.

I cried to him with my mouth, and high praise was on my tongue. If I had cherished iniquity in my heart, the Lord would not have listened.

The word is cherished, and everything depends on it. He does not say "if I had any sin in my heart" — that would end all prayer, his own included. He says: if I had looked at it, and kept it, and been fond of it, and had no intention of giving it up.

Proverbs puts the same principle sharply: If one turns away his ear from hearing the law, even his prayer is an abomination (Prov 28:9). Deliberate, cuddled sin is a closed line, and the remedy is not to pray louder. It is to stop cherishing it.

But truly God has listened; he has attended to the voice of my prayer. Blessed be God, because he has not rejected my prayer or removed his steadfast love from me!

The psalm ends by blessing God for two things that did not happen: the prayer was not turned away, and the love was not withdrawn. That is a strange and very honest way to finish. He had evidently feared both.

So had the nation, in the net and under the horses. The whole psalm holds them together: the God who put them in the fire is the God who did not withdraw his steadfast love, and the man who came out the other side is standing in the congregation with a bull, telling everybody.

66.title: We Went Through Fire and Through Water
66.overview: All the earth is called to shout for joy and to say how awesome God's deeds are (vv. 1-4). Come and see what God has done: he turned the sea into dry land and they crossed the river on foot — there did we rejoice in him (vv. 5-7). Bless him, you peoples: he has kept us alive and not let our feet slip (vv. 8-9). You have tried us as silver is tried. You brought us into the net ... we went through fire and through water; yet you have brought us out to a place of abundance (vv. 10-12). So he pays in public the vows he made in trouble (vv. 13-15). Come and hear ... what he has done for my soul: had he cherished iniquity the Lord would not have listened, but God has listened (vv. 16-19). Blessed be God, because he has not rejected my prayer or removed his steadfast love from me! (v. 20).
66.theology:
The psalm funnels from all the earth (vv. 1-4) to the congregation (vv. 8-12) to one man (vv. 13-20). A later generation says we of the Red Sea and the Jordan (v. 6): Scripture teaches a people to hold its history as family memory.

Every verb of the ordeal belongs to God, including the net and the crushing burden (vv. 10-12); the testing is refinery work, as silver is purified by melting (cf. 1 Pet 1:7), and the way through fire and water is through, not round (Isa 43:2). The hinge is yet: the same hand that held them in the net set them down in abundance.

Vows made in trouble are paid at cost when the danger has passed (vv. 13-15).

Cherished iniquity, not merely committed sin, is what closes the line (v. 18; cf. Prov 28:9) — and the remedy is not louder prayer but letting go. The psalm ends blessing God for two things that did not happen (v. 20), which the singer had evidently feared.
66.examples:
All the earth, then the congregation, then one man.

A singer saying we about a crossing centuries earlier.

Two mercies nobody counts: alive, and not fallen.

The net was God's.

Silver is not purified by being left alone.

Bodies used as ground for cavalry.

Through the fire and the water, not round them.

Cherished, not merely committed.

67.text: To the choirmaster: with stringed instruments. A Psalm. A Song. 1May God be gracious to us and bless us and make his face to shine upon us, Selah2that your way may be known on earth, your saving power among all nations.3Let the peoples praise you, O God; let all the peoples praise you!4Let the nations be glad and sing for joy, for you judge the peoples with equity and guide the nations upon earth. Selah5Let the peoples praise you, O God; let all the peoples praise you!6The earth has yielded its increase; God, our God, shall bless us.7God shall bless us; let all the ends of the earth fear him!

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–7 — That Your Way May Be Known on Earth
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: May God be gracious to us and bless us and make his face to shine upon us, that your way may be known on earth, your saving power among all nations (vv. 1-2). Let the peoples praise you, O God; let all the peoples praise you! (v. 3). Let the nations be glad and sing for joy, for you judge the peoples with equity and guide the nations upon earth (v. 4), and the refrain returns (v. 5). The earth has yielded its increase; God, our God, shall bless us. God shall bless us; let all the ends of the earth fear him! (vv. 6-7).
verseByVerse.theology: Israel asks for the priestly blessing and gives God a reason: so that the nations will find out what he is like.

verseByVerse.quote: May God be gracious to us and bless us and make his face to shine upon us, Selah that your way may be known on earth, your saving power among all nations.
verseByVerse.commentary:
May God be gracious to us and bless us and make his face to shine upon us.

Every Israelite would have recognised this instantly. It is the blessing Aaron and his sons were told to say over the people: The LORD bless you and keep you; the LORD make his face to shine upon you and be gracious to you (Num 6:24-25). The priest said it to them; here the congregation says it back to God as a request.

Notice what that teaches about praying. The best material is what God has already said he wants to give. Praying Scripture back is not a technique; it is asking for things you already know are in his hand.

That your way may be known on earth, your saving power among all nations.

And here is what makes this little psalm remarkable. The blessing has been given a purpose clause, and the purpose is not Israel's comfort. "Bless us — so that they may know you."

It is the promise to Abraham turned into a prayer. God said, I will bless you ... so that you will be a blessing ... and in you all the families of the earth shall be blessed (Gen 12:2-3). Israel is asking to be blessed in the way a lamp asks to be lit — for the sake of the room.

Which puts an uncomfortable question to anyone praying for God's favour. Ask for it; the psalm does. But the psalm gives a reason, and the reason is other people. A church praying only for its own health has dropped the second half of this verse.

verseByVerse.quote: Let the peoples praise you, O God; let all the peoples praise you! Let the nations be glad and sing for joy, for you judge the peoples with equity and guide the nations upon earth. Selah Let the peoples praise you, O God; let all the peoples praise you!
verseByVerse.commentary:
Let the peoples praise you, O God; let all the peoples praise you!

The refrain, and it will come again unchanged in verse 5, framing the middle verse. Note that the request is not that the nations be conquered, or converted to Israel, or brought under her government. It is that they should praise — that they should end up enjoying God.

Let the nations be glad and sing for joy, for you judge the peoples with equity and guide the nations upon earth.

This is the centre of the psalm, and the reason given for Gentile gladness is startling: God's judgment. Let the nations be GLAD ... FOR you judge the peoples with equity.

We are used to hearing judgment as bad news. To people who have been governed by the strong and the corrupt, a judge who cannot be bought is the best news there is. Equity means the case is heard on its merits; and guide the nations upon earth means their history is not drifting. For nations that have been someone else's plaything, that is a reason to sing.

verseByVerse.quote: The earth has yielded its increase; God, our God, shall bless us. God shall bless us; let all the ends of the earth fear him!
verseByVerse.commentary:
The earth has yielded its increase; God, our God, shall bless us. God shall bless us; let all the ends of the earth fear him!

The tense changes and a fact appears: the earth has yielded its increase. A harvest has come in. Whatever else is uncertain, the barns are filling, and the congregation takes that as evidence — not merely for themselves but for everybody.

The logic is the same as Psalm 65, and Paul preached it to pagans in Lystra: God gave rains from heaven and fruitful seasons as his witness to people who had never heard his name (Acts 14:17). A good harvest is an argument, and this psalm wants the argument made to the ends of the earth.

Then the last line, which is the psalm's whole aim stated once more: let all the ends of the earth fear him. Not admire, not acknowledge — fear, in the sense this book has taught throughout, which is the beginning of wisdom and the door into friendship with God (25:14).

Seven verses, and the word peoples or nations appears in five of them. It is a missionary prayer written centuries before there was a mission, and its answer is a scene John was shown at the end: a great multitude that no one could number, from every nation, from all tribes and peoples and languages, standing before the throne (Rev 7:9). They are doing exactly what verse 3 asked for.

67.title: Let All the Peoples Praise You
67.overview: The congregation prays the priestly blessing back to God — May God be gracious to us and bless us and make his face to shine upon us — and attaches a purpose: that your way may be known on earth, your saving power among all nations (vv. 1-2). Twice the refrain: Let the peoples praise you, O God; let all the peoples praise you! (vv. 3, 5), framing the reason the nations should be glad — God judges with equity and guides them (v. 4). The harvest is in, God will bless his people, and the psalm ends where it has been aiming: let all the ends of the earth fear him! (vv. 6-7).
67.theology:
Verse 1 is the Aaronic blessing (Num 6:24-25) turned into a petition: the best material for prayer is what God has already said he wants to give.

The blessing is asked for with a purpose clause, and the purpose is other people (v. 2) — Gen 12:2-3 in prayer form. A church praying only for its own health has dropped the second half of the verse.

What is wanted for the nations is not conquest or absorption but praise (vv. 3, 5), and the reason given for Gentile gladness is God's judgment (v. 4): to people governed by the strong and the corrupt, an unbribable judge is good news, and guide the nations means their history is not drifting.

A harvest already gathered is treated as evidence for the whole world (v. 6; cf. Ps 65; Acts 14:17), and the goal is the fear of God at the ends of the earth (v. 7) — answered in Rev 7:9.
67.examples:
The priest's blessing prayed back to God as a request.

Bless us — so that they may know you.

A lamp asking to be lit for the sake of the room.

Not conquered, not absorbed: praising.

Judgment as the reason the nations should sing.

A judge who cannot be bought is the best news the weak ever hear.

A full barn used as an argument to the ends of the earth.

Verse 3's request, seen finished in Revelation 7.

68.text: To the choirmaster. A Psalm of David.
