A Song. 1God shall arise, his enemies shall be scattered; and those who hate him shall flee before him!2As smoke is driven away, so you shall drive them away; as wax melts before fire, so the wicked shall perish before God!3But the righteous shall be glad; they shall exult before God; they shall be jubilant with joy!4Sing to God, sing praises to his name; lift up a song to him who rides through the deserts; his name is the LORD; exult before him!5Father of the fatherless and protector of widows is God in his holy habitation.6God settles the solitary in a home; he leads out the prisoners to prosperity, but the rebellious dwell in a parched land.7O God, when you went out before your people, when you marched through the wilderness, Selah8the earth quaked, the heavens poured down rain, before God, the One of Sinai, before God, the God of Israel.9Rain in abundance, O God, you shed abroad; you restored your inheritance as it languished;10your flock found a dwelling in it; in your goodness, O God, you provided for the needy.11The Lord gives the word; the women who announce the news are a great host:12"The kings of the armies—they flee, they flee!" The women at home divide the spoil—13though you men lie among the sheepfolds— the wings of a dove covered with silver, its pinions with shimmering gold.14When the Almighty scatters kings there, let snow fall on Zalmon.15O mountain of God, mountain of Bashan; O many-peaked mountain, mountain of Bashan!16Why do you look with hatred, O many-peaked mountain, at the mount that God desired for his abode, yes, where the LORD will dwell forever?17The chariots of God are twice ten thousand, thousands upon thousands; the Lord is among them; Sinai is now in the sanctuary.18You ascended on high, leading a host of captives in your train and receiving gifts among men, even among the rebellious, that the LORD God may dwell there.19Blessed be the Lord, who daily bears us up; God is our salvation. Selah20Our God is a God of salvation, and to GOD, the Lord, belong deliverances from death.21But God will strike the heads of his enemies, the hairy crown of him who walks in his guilty ways.22The Lord said, "I will bring them back from Bashan, I will bring them back from the depths of the sea,23that you may strike your feet in their blood, that the tongues of your dogs may have their portion from the foe."24Your procession is seen, O God, the procession of my God, my King, into the sanctuary—25the singers in front, the musicians last, between them virgins playing tambourines:26"Bless God in the great congregation, the LORD, O you who are of Israel's fountain!"27There is Benjamin, the least of them, in the lead, the princes of Judah in their throng, the princes of Zebulun, the princes of Naphtali.28Summon your power, O God, the power, O God, by which you have worked for us.29Because of your temple at Jerusalem kings shall bear gifts to you.30Rebuke the beasts that dwell among the reeds, the herd of bulls with the calves of the peoples. Trample underfoot those who lust after tribute; scatter the peoples who delight in war.31Nobles shall come from Egypt; Cush shall hasten to stretch out her hands to God.32O kingdoms of the earth, sing to God; sing praises to the Lord, Selah33to him who rides in the heavens, the ancient heavens; behold, he sends out his voice, his mighty voice.34Ascribe power to God, whose majesty is over Israel, and whose power is in the skies.35Awesome is God from his sanctuary; the God of Israel—he is the one who gives power and strength to his people. Blessed be God!

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–6 — God Settles the Solitary in a Home
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: God shall arise, his enemies shall be scattered; as smoke is driven away and wax melts, the wicked perish, while the righteous are jubilant (vv. 1-4). Father of the fatherless and protector of widows is God in his holy habitation. God settles the solitary in a home; he leads out the prisoners to prosperity (vv. 5-6).
verseByVerse.theology: The war-cry of the ark is followed at once by a description of God as a father to orphans.

verseByVerse.quote: God shall arise, his enemies shall be scattered; and those who hate him shall flee before him! As smoke is driven away, so you shall drive them away; as wax melts before fire, so the wicked shall perish before God! But the righteous shall be glad; they shall exult before God; they shall be jubilant with joy! Sing to God, sing praises to his name; lift up a song to him who rides through the deserts; his name is the LORD; exult before him! Father of the fatherless and protector of widows is God in his holy habitation. God settles the solitary in a home; he leads out the prisoners to prosperity, but the rebellious dwell in a parched land.
verseByVerse.commentary:
God shall arise, his enemies shall be scattered; and those who hate him shall flee before him!

Israel knew this sentence. It is what Moses said every time the ark was lifted to lead the next stage of the march: Arise, O LORD, and let your enemies be scattered (Num 10:35). So the psalm begins as a procession song — and verses 24-27 will show us the parade arriving.

As smoke is driven away, so you shall drive them away; as wax melts before fire, so the wicked shall perish before God!

Two images of things that cannot hold their shape: smoke in wind, wax near flame. Neither is destroyed by force; they simply cannot persist in the presence of something stronger.

Sing to God, sing praises to his name; lift up a song to him who rides through the deserts; his name is the LORD; exult before him!

God is pictured as a rider crossing open country — the God of a people on the move rather than a deity fixed to one shrine.

Father of the fatherless and protector of widows is God in his holy habitation. God settles the solitary in a home; he leads out the prisoners to prosperity, but the rebellious dwell in a parched land.

And here, four verses into a war song, is the heart of the psalm. The God whose enemies scatter like smoke, who has twenty thousand chariots (v. 17), describes himself by his care for four kinds of people with nothing: orphans, widows, the lonely and prisoners.

Look at what he does for each. He is father to the fatherless — not patron, father. He is the widow's protector, the word for a legal advocate, because in that world her problem was that nobody would take her case. He settles the solitary in a home: the isolated person is not merely visited but given a household to belong to, which is exactly what God does when he puts lonely people into a church. And he leads prisoners out into prosperity.

All of this is said of God in his holy habitation — that is, this is not what he does on his days off. It is what he is like at home.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: He marched before his people through the wilderness; the earth quaked, the rain fell, and the needy were provided for (vv. 7-10). The word is given and the women announce the rout; kings flee and the spoil is divided (vv. 11-14). Why should the great mountains of Bashan envy the little hill God chose (vv. 15-16)? God's chariots are twice ten thousand (v. 17). You ascended on high, leading a host of captives in your train and receiving gifts among men (v. 18). Blessed be the Lord, who daily bears us up; God is our salvation — to him belong deliverances from death, and his enemies will be struck (vv. 19-23).
verseByVerse.theology: The verse Paul quotes of Christ's ascension sits next to the verse about God carrying his people every day.

verseByVerse.quote: O God, when you went out before your people, when you marched through the wilderness, Selah the earth quaked, the heavens poured down rain, before God, the One of Sinai, before God, the God of Israel. Rain in abundance, O God, you shed abroad; you restored your inheritance as it languished; your flock found a dwelling in it; in your goodness, O God, you provided for the needy. The Lord gives the word; the women who announce the news are a great host: "The kings of the armies—they flee, they flee!" The women at home divide the spoil— though you men lie among the sheepfolds— the wings of a dove covered with silver, its pinions with shimmering gold. When the Almighty scatters kings there, let snow fall on Zalmon.
verseByVerse.commentary:
O God, when you went out before your people, when you marched through the wilderness, the earth quaked, the heavens poured down rain, before God, the One of Sinai, before God, the God of Israel.

The psalm remembers the march out of Egypt in the language of Deborah's old victory song, which says almost the same words (Judg 5:4-5). And note the title: the One of Sinai. The mountain got its reputation from him, not the other way round.

Rain in abundance, O God, you shed abroad; you restored your inheritance as it languished; your flock found a dwelling in it; in your goodness, O God, you provided for the needy.

The thunderstorm of verse 8 becomes agricultural rain in verse 9. The same weather that terrifies at Sinai waters a field in Canaan, and the beneficiary is named: the needy. Verse 5's orphans and widows are being fed.

The Lord gives the word; the women who announce the news are a great host: The kings of the armies — they flee, they flee!

A lovely detail, easily missed: the heralds are women, and there are a great many of them. The news of the victory is carried by the ones who stayed behind — as Miriam and the women sang after the sea, and Deborah sang after Sisera. And the report is a stammer of delight: they flee, they flee!

Verses 12-14 are among the most obscure in the Psalter — spoil divided at home, a dove covered with silver, snow falling on Zalmon. The shape is clear even where the detail is not: an army routed, treasure carried home, and something beautiful glinting in the light after a night of fear.

verseByVerse.quote: O mountain of God, mountain of Bashan; O many-peaked mountain, mountain of Bashan! Why do you look with hatred, O many-peaked mountain, at the mount that God desired for his abode, yes, where the LORD will dwell forever? The chariots of God are twice ten thousand, thousands upon thousands; the Lord is among them; Sinai is now in the sanctuary. You ascended on high, leading a host of captives in your train and receiving gifts among men, even among the rebellious, that the LORD God may dwell there.
verseByVerse.commentary:
O mountain of God, mountain of Bashan; O many-peaked mountain, mountain of Bashan! Why do you look with hatred, O many-peaked mountain, at the mount that God desired for his abode, yes, where the LORD will dwell forever?

The psalm turns and teases the mountains. Bashan's range in the north is high, rugged and spectacular — the ESV notes the word may mean hunch-backed — and Zion is a low ridge in the south. Why the jealous stare? Because God chose the small one.

That is the Bible's pattern with mountains, nations, families and people: the impressive one is passed over, and the unimpressive one gets the visit.

The chariots of God are twice ten thousand, thousands upon thousands; the Lord is among them; Sinai is now in the sanctuary. You ascended on high, leading a host of captives in your train and receiving gifts among men, even among the rebellious, that the LORD God may dwell there.

Twenty thousand chariots, and then an ascent: God going up the hill with a column of prisoners behind him and tribute being handed over — the standard scene when a victorious king came home.

Paul quotes this verse of Jesus, and makes one startling change. When he ascended on high he led a host of captives, and he GAVE gifts to men (Eph 4:8). The psalm says the conqueror received gifts; Paul says he gave them — because that is what the victor does with tribute when he gets home, and because what the ascended Christ distributed was apostles, prophets, evangelists, pastors and teachers to his church.

And note the psalm's own last clause: the tribute is received even among the rebellious, so that the LORD God may dwell there. The conquest ends in God moving in among the people who fought him.

verseByVerse.quote: Blessed be the Lord, who daily bears us up; God is our salvation. Selah Our God is a God of salvation, and to GOD, the Lord, belong deliverances from death. But God will strike the heads of his enemies, the hairy crown of him who walks in his guilty ways. The Lord said, "I will bring them back from Bashan, I will bring them back from the depths of the sea, that you may strike your feet in their blood, that the tongues of your dogs may have their portion from the foe."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Blessed be the Lord, who daily bears us up; God is our salvation.

One verse after the great ascent, the psalm says this. The God who was carried up the hill in procession is the God who daily bears us up — the word is used of loading a pack animal. He carries us, every day, as a load he has taken on.

Set that beside verse 17's twenty thousand chariots. Overwhelming power, and the daily work of carrying somebody who cannot manage.

Our God is a God of salvation, and to GOD, the Lord, belong deliverances from death.

The plural is striking: deliverances, more than one, and the phrase is literally escapes belonging to God. Every way out of death there has ever been is his property.

But God will strike the heads of his enemies, the hairy crown of him who walks in his guilty ways ... that you may strike your feet in their blood.

The battlefield language returns, and it is grim — long hair worn as a warrior's pride, and a victor walking through the aftermath. As at Psalm 58, the killing is God's and the imagery is of a war already decided; Christians pray it with the cross in view, where the head of the serpent was struck by a man whose own heel was bruised.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 24–35 — Cush Shall Hasten to Stretch Out Her Hands
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: The procession comes into the sanctuary — singers, musicians, girls with tambourines, and the tribes, with little Benjamin in the lead (vv. 24-27). Kings will bring gifts to Jerusalem; scatter the peoples who delight in war (vv. 28-30). Nobles shall come from Egypt; Cush shall hasten to stretch out her hands to God (v. 31). O kingdoms of the earth, sing to God ... Awesome is God from his sanctuary ... he is the one who gives power and strength to his people. Blessed be God! (vv. 32-35).
verseByVerse.theology: The parade ends with the nations invited in and the last word given to the strength God hands out.

verseByVerse.quote: Your procession is seen, O God, the procession of my God, my King, into the sanctuary— the singers in front, the musicians last, between them virgins playing tambourines: "Bless God in the great congregation, the LORD, O you who are of Israel's fountain!" There is Benjamin, the least of them, in the lead, the princes of Judah in their throng, the princes of Zebulun, the princes of Naphtali. Summon your power, O God, the power, O God, by which you have worked for us. Because of your temple at Jerusalem kings shall bear gifts to you. Rebuke the beasts that dwell among the reeds, the herd of bulls with the calves of the peoples. Trample underfoot those who lust after tribute; scatter the peoples who delight in war. Nobles shall come from Egypt; Cush shall hasten to stretch out her hands to God.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Your procession is seen, O God, the procession of my God, my King, into the sanctuary — the singers in front, the musicians last, between them virgins playing tambourines.

Here is the parade the psalm began with, arriving. And notice the order of march: singers at the front, players at the back, girls with tambourines in the middle. No soldiers are mentioned.

There is Benjamin, the least of them, in the lead, the princes of Judah in their throng, the princes of Zebulun, the princes of Naphtali.

Benjamin, the smallest tribe — and nearly wiped out in Judges — walks at the head. Two southern tribes and two northern ones are named together, which in Israel's history was itself a small miracle.

Summon your power, O God ... Because of your temple at Jerusalem kings shall bear gifts to you. Rebuke the beasts that dwell among the reeds ... scatter the peoples who delight in war.

The ESV notes that verse 30 is obscure in Hebrew; the beasts among the reeds are usually taken as Egypt, whose emblem was the crocodile or the hippopotamus of the Nile marshes. What is clear is the last line, which is a prayer for the end of a particular kind of nation: those who delight in war. Not merely those who fight — those who enjoy it.

Nobles shall come from Egypt; Cush shall hasten to stretch out her hands to God.

Egypt is the house of slavery, and Cush is the land beyond the southern edge of the known world. Both are pictured coming in with their hands out. Centuries later Philip met a man from Cush on a desert road, reading Isaiah in a chariot, and baptised him (Acts 8:27-39). This verse was walking down that road.

verseByVerse.quote: O kingdoms of the earth, sing to God; sing praises to the Lord, Selah to him who rides in the heavens, the ancient heavens; behold, he sends out his voice, his mighty voice. Ascribe power to God, whose majesty is over Israel, and whose power is in the skies. Awesome is God from his sanctuary; the God of Israel—he is the one who gives power and strength to his people. Blessed be God!
verseByVerse.commentary:
O kingdoms of the earth, sing to God; sing praises to the Lord, to him who rides in the heavens, the ancient heavens; behold, he sends out his voice, his mighty voice.

The rider of verse 4 crossed deserts; here he rides the sky. And the psalm that has been full of chariots and armies ends with the only weapon God actually needs: he sends out his voice.

Ascribe power to God, whose majesty is over Israel, and whose power is in the skies. Awesome is God from his sanctuary; the God of Israel — he is the one who gives power and strength to his people. Blessed be God!

The last line brings the whole thing home. All that power — twenty thousand chariots, a voice that carries across the heavens, kings bringing tribute — and the final clause is about distribution: he is the one who gives power and strength to his people.

It is the same movement as verse 18 read through Paul: the conqueror comes home and hands out what he has won. And it is the same God as verse 5, the father of the fatherless. The psalm's whole argument is that these are not two Gods but one — the strength in the skies and the kindness to the widow are the same strength and the same kindness, and both of them arrive at the same address: his people.

68.title: Father of the Fatherless
68.overview: The ark's marching song: God shall arise, his enemies shall be scattered — driven off like smoke, melted like wax, while the righteous rejoice (vv. 1-4). Then his character: Father of the fatherless and protector of widows ... God settles the solitary in a home (vv. 5-6). He marched through the wilderness with earthquake and rain, and provided for the needy (vv. 7-10). Women announce the rout of kings and the spoil is divided (vv. 11-14). Why should the great mountains envy the hill God chose (vv. 15-16)? With twenty thousand chariots he ascended on high, leading a host of captives ... and receiving gifts among men (vv. 17-18) — and daily bears us up (vv. 19-23). The procession enters the sanctuary, singers first, little Benjamin in the lead (vv. 24-27); kings bring gifts, Egypt and Cush stretch out their hands (vv. 28-31), and the kingdoms of the earth are told to sing to the God who gives power and strength to his people (vv. 32-35).
68.theology:
The psalm opens with the words spoken whenever the ark set out (v. 1; Num 10:35) and is built as a procession that arrives at vv. 24-27.

Its centre is that the God of twenty thousand chariots defines himself by orphans, widows, the lonely and prisoners (vv. 5-6) — and does so in his holy habitation, which is to say this is what he is like at home. He settles the solitary in a household, which is what he does when lonely people are put into a church.

God chose the low hill over the spectacular ranges (vv. 15-16), as he chooses throughout Scripture.

Paul quotes v. 18 of Christ's ascension and changes received to gave (Eph 4:8), because a conqueror distributes his tribute at home — and the psalm's own end says the same: he gives power and strength to his people (v. 35). The tribute is even taken among the rebellious, so that God may dwell among the people who fought him.

Between the ascent and the battlefield stands v. 19: the God carried in procession is the God who carries his people daily. Egypt and Cush coming in (v. 31) is met on a desert road in Acts 8:27-39.
68.examples:
The sentence Moses said whenever the ark moved.

Smoke and wax: things that cannot hold their shape.

Father, not patron; advocate for the widow nobody would represent.

The solitary given a household to belong to.

Sinai got its name from him, not the other way round.

The heralds are women, and there are a great many of them.

The mountains stare jealously at the little hill God picked.

Paul's one-word change: received becomes gave.

Twenty thousand chariots, and a daily load carried.

69.text: To the choirmaster: according to Lilies. Of David. 1Save me, O God! For the waters have come up to my neck.2I sink in deep mire, where there is no foothold; I have come into deep waters, and the flood sweeps over me.3I am weary with my crying out; my throat is parched. My eyes grow dim with waiting for my God.4More in number than the hairs of my head are those who hate me without cause; mighty are those who would destroy me, those who attack me with lies. What I did not steal must I now restore?5O God, you know my folly; the wrongs I have done are not hidden from you.6Let not those who hope in you be put to shame through me, O Lord GOD of hosts; let not those who seek you be brought to dishonor through me, O God of Israel.7For it is for your sake that I have borne reproach, that dishonor has covered my face.8I have become a stranger to my brothers, an alien to my mother's sons.9For zeal for your house has consumed me, and the reproaches of those who reproach you have fallen on me.10When I wept and humbled my soul with fasting, it became my reproach.11When I made sackcloth my clothing, I became a byword to them.12I am the talk of those who sit in the gate, and the drunkards make songs about me.13But as for me, my prayer is to you, O LORD. At an acceptable time, O God, in the abundance of your steadfast love answer me in your saving faithfulness.14Deliver me from sinking in the mire; let me be delivered from my enemies and from the deep waters.15Let not the flood sweep over me, or the deep swallow me up, or the pit close its mouth over me.16Answer me, O LORD, for your steadfast love is good; according to your abundant mercy, turn to me.17Hide not your face from your servant, for I am in distress; make haste to answer me.18Draw near to my soul, redeem me; ransom me because of my enemies!19You know my reproach, and my shame and my dishonor; my foes are all known to you.20Reproaches have broken my heart, so that I am in despair. I looked for pity, but there was none, and for comforters, but I found none.21They gave me poison for food, and for my thirst they gave me sour wine to drink.22Let their own table before them become a snare; and when they are at peace, let it become a trap.23Let their eyes be darkened, so that they cannot see, and make their loins tremble continually.24Pour out your indignation upon them, and let your burning anger overtake them.25May their camp be a desolation; let no one dwell in their tents.26For they persecute him whom you have struck down, and they recount the pain of those you have wounded.27Add to them punishment upon punishment; may they have no acquittal from you.28Let them be blotted out of the book of the living; let them not be enrolled among the righteous.29But I am afflicted and in pain; let your salvation, O God, set me on high!30I will praise the name of God with a song; I will magnify him with thanksgiving.31This will please the LORD more than an ox or a bull with horns and hoofs.32When the humble see it they will be glad; you who seek God, let your hearts revive.33For the LORD hears the needy and does not despise his own people who are prisoners.34Let heaven and earth praise him, the seas and everything that moves in them.35For God will save Zion and build up the cities of Judah, and people shall dwell there and possess it;36the offspring of his servants shall inherit it, and those who love his name shall dwell in it.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–12 — The Waters Have Come Up to My Neck
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Save me, O God! For the waters have come up to my neck. I sink in deep mire, where there is no foothold; he is worn out with crying and his eyes fail with waiting (vv. 1-3). Those who hate him without cause outnumber his hairs (v. 4), and yet O God, you know my folly (v. 5). Let his disgrace not shame those who hope in God (v. 6), for it is for your sake that I have borne reproach — a stranger to his brothers, consumed by zeal for God's house, mocked for his fasting, the subject of drunkards' songs (vv. 7-12).
verseByVerse.theology: A man drowning, who admits his own folly and whose chief fear is that his shame will hurt other believers.

verseByVerse.quote: Save me, O God! For the waters have come up to my neck. I sink in deep mire, where there is no foothold; I have come into deep waters, and the flood sweeps over me. I am weary with my crying out; my throat is parched. My eyes grow dim with waiting for my God. More in number than the hairs of my head are those who hate me without cause; mighty are those who would destroy me, those who attack me with lies. What I did not steal must I now restore? O God, you know my folly; the wrongs I have done are not hidden from you. Let not those who hope in you be put to shame through me, O Lord GOD of hosts; let not those who seek you be brought to dishonor through me, O God of Israel.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Save me, O God! For the waters have come up to my neck. I sink in deep mire, where there is no foothold; I have come into deep waters, and the flood sweeps over me.

The tune is Lilies, the one Psalm 45 used for a royal wedding; the same melody now carries a man drowning.

Psalm 40 described a man hauled out of a miry bog. This one is still in it, and the water is at his chin. No foothold is the horror of the image: nothing to push against, nothing to stand on, and the more he struggles the deeper he goes. The ESV notes the first line may read "the waters threaten my life".

I am weary with my crying out; my throat is parched. My eyes grow dim with waiting for my God.

He has prayed himself hoarse. This is not a man who has failed to pray; it is a man whose praying has exhausted him, whose voice has gone and whose eyes have given out from scanning the horizon. Anyone who has waited that long knows that the waiting is its own labour.

More in number than the hairs of my head are those who hate me without cause ... What I did not steal must I now restore?

Without cause is the phrase Jesus took from this psalm and Psalm 35 and applied to the world's hatred of himself: They hated me without a cause (John 15:25). And the last line is the exact sensation of being wrongly accused — being made to pay back something you never took.

O God, you know my folly; the wrongs I have done are not hidden from you.

Stop here, because this verse must be handled honestly. The man praying this psalm is a sinner and says so. He is not claiming that every charge against him is false, only that the hatred is undeserved.

And the New Testament still applies this psalm to Christ — but notice exactly which parts. It quotes the suffering: the hatred without cause, the zeal, the reproaches, the sour wine. It never quotes verse 5. The psalm gives us a righteous sufferer who is nevertheless a sinner, and in him we see the shape of one who suffered the same way and had no folly to confess.

Let not those who hope in you be put to shame through me ... let not those who seek you be brought to dishonor through me.

And here is his first request — not for rescue but for damage limitation. His fear is that his public disgrace will make other believers ashamed of their God. A man at the end of his strength is still thinking about what his situation is doing to the faith of people watching.

verseByVerse.quote: For it is for your sake that I have borne reproach, that dishonor has covered my face. I have become a stranger to my brothers, an alien to my mother's sons. For zeal for your house has consumed me, and the reproaches of those who reproach you have fallen on me. When I wept and humbled my soul with fasting, it became my reproach. When I made sackcloth my clothing, I became a byword to them. I am the talk of those who sit in the gate, and the drunkards make songs about me.
verseByVerse.commentary:
For it is for your sake that I have borne reproach, that dishonor has covered my face. I have become a stranger to my brothers, an alien to my mother's sons.

The trouble is religious in origin: for your sake. And it has cost him his family — not distant relatives but my mother's sons, the boys he grew up with. John records the same of Jesus in one flat sentence: For not even his brothers believed in him (John 7:5).

For zeal for your house has consumed me, and the reproaches of those who reproach you have fallen on me.

Both halves of this verse are quoted in the New Testament, of two different moments. When Jesus drove the traders out of the temple, his disciples remembered that it was written, Zeal for your house will consume me (John 2:17) — and the tense they remembered it in is future, because they had just watched the thing that would get him killed.

And Paul quotes the second half to teach Christians to carry other people's burdens: For Christ did not please himself, but as it is written, The reproaches of those who reproached you fell on me (Rom 15:3). The insults aimed at God landed on him. That is what happens to anyone who stands close enough to God to be in the line of fire, and it is what happened to Christ absolutely.

When I wept and humbled my soul with fasting, it became my reproach. When I made sackcloth my clothing, I became a byword to them. I am the talk of those who sit in the gate, and the drunkards make songs about me.

His devotion is the joke. He fasted, and it was held against him; he wore mourning, and became a nickname. The two audiences named are the respectable and the disreputable: those who sit in the gate are the elders and businessmen who ran the town, and the drunks are writing songs about him in the tavern. Top and bottom of society, united in finding him ridiculous.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 13–21 — I Looked for Pity, but There Was None
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: But as for me, my prayer is to you, O LORD. At an acceptable time ... answer me (v. 13). Deliver him from the mire and the flood, and do not hide God's face (vv. 14-18). You know my reproach, and my shame and my dishonor (v. 19). Reproaches have broken my heart ... I looked for pity, but there was none, and for comforters, but I found none. They gave me poison for food, and for my thirst they gave me sour wine to drink (vv. 20-21).
verseByVerse.theology: The loneliest verses in the Psalter, and the Gospels record the last of them happening.

verseByVerse.quote: But as for me, my prayer is to you, O LORD. At an acceptable time, O God, in the abundance of your steadfast love answer me in your saving faithfulness. Deliver me from sinking in the mire; let me be delivered from my enemies and from the deep waters. Let not the flood sweep over me, or the deep swallow me up, or the pit close its mouth over me. Answer me, O LORD, for your steadfast love is good; according to your abundant mercy, turn to me. Hide not your face from your servant, for I am in distress; make haste to answer me. Draw near to my soul, redeem me; ransom me because of my enemies! You know my reproach, and my shame and my dishonor; my foes are all known to you. Reproaches have broken my heart, so that I am in despair. I looked for pity, but there was none, and for comforters, but I found none. They gave me poison for food, and for my thirst they gave me sour wine to drink.
verseByVerse.commentary:
But as for me, my prayer is to you, O LORD. At an acceptable time, O God, in the abundance of your steadfast love answer me in your saving faithfulness.

At an acceptable time is a remarkable thing for a drowning man to say. He asks for an answer and leaves the timing with God — not because he is calm, but because he believes there is such a thing as God's right moment.

Deliver me from sinking in the mire ... Let not the flood sweep over me, or the deep swallow me up, or the pit close its mouth over me.

Three mouths are open to swallow him: the flood, the deep, and the pit. The last image is of a grave closing its lid, and he asks that it be kept open a little longer.

Answer me, O LORD, for your steadfast love is good ... Hide not your face from your servant, for I am in distress; make haste to answer me. Draw near to my soul, redeem me; ransom me because of my enemies!

Five imperatives in three verses: answer, turn, do not hide, make haste, draw near. And the two great words at the end — redeem and ransom — are commercial: buy me back, pay whatever it costs to get me out.

Reproaches have broken my heart, so that I am in despair. I looked for pity, but there was none, and for comforters, but I found none.

These are the loneliest lines in the book. Broken my heart is literal in Hebrew and unimprovable in English. And then the search: he looked round for one person to feel something for him, and for anyone at all who would sit with him, and there was nobody.

Whoever is reading this psalm from inside that experience should know that it is here, in Scripture, without correction or rebuke. And that a man in Gethsemane came back three times to friends who were asleep.

They gave me poison for food, and for my thirst they gave me sour wine to drink.

At the cross they offered Jesus wine to drink, mixed with gall, and he would not take it (Matt 27:34); later, when he said I thirst, they put a sponge of sour wine to his mouth (John 19:28-29). The Gospel writers plainly have this verse in view. The last kindness offered to a dying man was a mouthful of vinegar, and it had been written down a thousand years before.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 22–36 — Let Their Own Table Become a Snare
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Let their own table before them become a snare ... let their eyes be darkened; pour out indignation, may their camp be a desolation, blot them out of the book of the living (vv. 22-28). But I am afflicted and in pain; let your salvation, O God, set me on high! (v. 29). Praise will please the LORD more than an ox (vv. 30-31); the humble will be glad, for the LORD hears the needy (vv. 32-33). Let heaven and earth praise him, for God will save Zion (vv. 34-36).
verseByVerse.theology: The Psalter's longest curse, and then a song that costs nothing and pleases God more than cattle.

verseByVerse.quote: Let their own table before them become a snare; and when they are at peace, let it become a trap. Let their eyes be darkened, so that they cannot see, and make their loins tremble continually. Pour out your indignation upon them, and let your burning anger overtake them. May their camp be a desolation; let no one dwell in their tents. For they persecute him whom you have struck down, and they recount the pain of those you have wounded. Add to them punishment upon punishment; may they have no acquittal from you. Let them be blotted out of the book of the living; let them not be enrolled among the righteous.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Let their own table before them become a snare; and when they are at peace, let it become a trap. Let their eyes be darkened, so that they cannot see, and make their loins tremble continually.

Here begins the longest curse in the Psalter, and there is no point pretending it is gentle. The table is the place of safety and fellowship, and he asks that it turn into a trap; the eyes are asked to go dark; the body is asked to shake.

Two things keep it in its place. First, as always, it is prayer: he asks God to do it. Second, and more startling, Paul quotes these very verses — of Israel's hardening against the gospel, in the same letter where he says my heart's desire and prayer to God for them is that they may be saved (Rom 11:9-10; 10:1). Paul can pray this psalm and weep over the people it describes at the same time, because the curse is God's to administer and the pleading is ours to do.

Pour out your indignation upon them ... May their camp be a desolation; let no one dwell in their tents.

Peter quoted verse 25 in the upper room about one man: May his camp become desolate, and let there be no one to dwell in it (Acts 1:20), of Judas, whose place had to be filled. The psalm of the betrayed one supplied the words for what happened to the betrayer.

For they persecute him whom you have struck down, and they recount the pain of those you have wounded.

This is the charge underneath the curse, and it deserves weighing. Their sin is not that they attacked a strong man; it is that they went after someone God had already brought low, and then talked about his pain for entertainment. Kicking a man who is already down, and making a story of it, is what this psalm asks God to judge.

Add to them punishment upon punishment; may they have no acquittal from you. Let them be blotted out of the book of the living; let them not be enrolled among the righteous.

The book of the living is the register of God's people, and the last request is that these names be struck off it. It is the most terrible thing anyone asks for in the Psalter. The risen Christ says the opposite to a faithful church: I will never blot his name out of the book of life (Rev 3:5). Both sentences are about the same register, and between them lies the whole difference that the gospel makes.

verseByVerse.quote: But I am afflicted and in pain; let your salvation, O God, set me on high! I will praise the name of God with a song; I will magnify him with thanksgiving. This will please the LORD more than an ox or a bull with horns and hoofs. When the humble see it they will be glad; you who seek God, let your hearts revive. For the LORD hears the needy and does not despise his own people who are prisoners. Let heaven and earth praise him, the seas and everything that moves in them. For God will save Zion and build up the cities of Judah, and people shall dwell there and possess it; the offspring of his servants shall inherit it, and those who love his name shall dwell in it.
verseByVerse.commentary:
But I am afflicted and in pain; let your salvation, O God, set me on high!

After all that, he is still in the water. The curse changed nothing about his condition, and that matters: praying imprecation does not relieve the sufferer. What he actually needs is the next line — God's salvation lifting him on high, out of the mire and onto a rock.

I will praise the name of God with a song; I will magnify him with thanksgiving. This will please the LORD more than an ox or a bull with horns and hoofs.

And here the psalm turns, and its poorest verse is its best. He has nothing. He cannot bring a bull — he is drowning, disgraced, abandoned by his family, mocked in the tavern. What he has is a voice, and God prefers it. The detail about horns and hoofs makes the point: a fully grown, perfect animal, the most expensive thing a man could offer, and a song of thanks outranks it (as at 50:14 and 51:17).

When the humble see it they will be glad; you who seek God, let your hearts revive. For the LORD hears the needy and does not despise his own people who are prisoners.

His rescue will be other people's medicine. The humble will see it and take heart — which answers his fear back in verse 6 that his disgrace would damage their faith. And the reason given is a straight statement of God's policy: he hears the needy and does not despise his people who are prisoners, wherever they are being held.

Let heaven and earth praise him, the seas and everything that moves in them. For God will save Zion and build up the cities of Judah ... the offspring of his servants shall inherit it, and those who love his name shall dwell in it.

The psalm that began with one man up to his neck in water ends with the sea itself praising, the cities rebuilt, and children living safely in them generations later. That is the true shape of the Christian hope: the personal rescue is real, and it is the smallest part of what God is doing.

69.title: Zeal for Your House Has Consumed Me
69.overview: The waters are at his neck and there is no foothold; he has prayed himself hoarse (vv. 1-3). Those who hate him without cause outnumber his hairs, and he is made to repay what he never stole (v. 4) — though God knows his folly (v. 5). His fear is that his disgrace will shame other believers (v. 6). He has borne reproach for God's sake, become a stranger to his own brothers, been consumed by zeal for God's house, mocked for fasting, and made the subject of drunkards' songs (vv. 7-12). He prays for God's acceptable time, for rescue from mire and flood, and for God's face not to be hidden (vv. 13-18). Reproaches have broken my heart ... I looked for pity, but there was none; they gave him poison and sour wine (vv. 19-21). Then the Psalter's longest curse (vv. 22-28). But I am afflicted and in pain (v. 29): he will praise with a song, which pleases God more than an ox; the needy will hear and revive; and God will save Zion for the generations to come (vv. 30-36).
69.theology:
The psalmist is a sinner and says so (v. 5), and the New Testament still applies the psalm to Christ — quoting the suffering (vv. 4, 9, 21, 22-23, 25) and never v. 5. The righteous sufferer here is the shape of one who suffered the same way with no folly to confess.

His first petition is not rescue but that his disgrace should not damage the faith of others (v. 6), answered at v. 32.

Verse 9 is quoted twice: the temple cleansing (John 2:17) and the principle that insults aimed at God fall on those who stand close to him — which Paul applies to Christ and then to us (Rom 15:3).

Verse 21 was fulfilled at the cross (Matt 27:34; John 19:28-29), and v. 20's search for pity has a counterpart in Gethsemane.

The imprecation is prayer, and Paul quotes part of it (Rom 11:9-10) while praying for the salvation of the very people (Rom 10:1). Its charge is specific: they persecuted a man God had already struck down and made entertainment of his pain (v. 26). Against v. 28's blotting out stands Rev 3:5.

The curse changes nothing; what lifts him is salvation (v. 29). A song from a man with nothing pleases God more than the most expensive animal (vv. 30-31; cf. 50:14; 51:17).
69.examples:
Still in the bog of Psalm 40, and now up to the neck.

Prayed hoarse: the waiting is its own labour.

Made to pay back what he never took.

The New Testament quotes the suffering and never verse 5.

His first request: do not let my shame hurt their faith.

Mocked at the gate and sung about in the tavern.

He looked for one person to sit with him.

Vinegar, written down a thousand years early.

A song from a man with nothing, preferred to a prize bull.

70.text: To the choirmaster. Of David, for the memorial offering. 1Make haste, O God, to deliver me! O LORD, make haste to help me!2Let them be put to shame and confusion who seek my life! Let them be turned back and brought to dishonor who delight in my hurt!3Let them turn back because of their shame who say, "Aha, Aha!"4May all who seek you rejoice and be glad in you! May those who love your salvation say evermore, "God is great!"5But I am poor and needy; hasten to me, O God! You are my help and my deliverer; O LORD, do not delay!

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Make haste, O God, to deliver me! O LORD, make haste to help me! (v. 1). Let those who seek his life be shamed and those who say Aha, Aha! be turned back (vv. 2-3). May all who seek you rejoice and be glad in you! May those who love your salvation say evermore, God is great! (v. 4). But I am poor and needy; hasten to me, O God! You are my help and my deliverer; O LORD, do not delay! (v. 5).
verseByVerse.theology: Psalm 40's closing prayer, reissued on its own with every unhurried word removed.

verseByVerse.quote: Make haste, O God, to deliver me! O LORD, make haste to help me! Let them be put to shame and confusion who seek my life! Let them be turned back and brought to dishonor who delight in my hurt! Let them turn back because of their shame who say, "Aha, Aha!" May all who seek you rejoice and be glad in you! May those who love your salvation say evermore, "God is great!" But I am poor and needy; hasten to me, O God! You are my help and my deliverer; O LORD, do not delay!
verseByVerse.commentary:
One thing has been added rather than cut: the heading. This is now for the memorial offering, as Psalm 38 was — the handful of grain burned to bring a worshipper to God's remembrance. The emergency prayer has been given a place in the liturgy.

This psalm has been printed already. It is Psalm 40:13-17, lifted out of the end of that psalm and issued as a prayer in its own right, and the exposition of what it means stands there. What this chapter is for is the differences — because the Psalter does not reprint five verses by accident.

Make haste, O God, to deliver me! O LORD, make haste to help me!

Compare the opening of the original: Be pleased, O LORD, to deliver me! O LORD, make haste to help me! (40:13). The courteous first clause — be pleased — has gone. What is left begins at a run: make haste, and then make haste again.

That is the whole character of this edition. Every unhurried word has been cut. Psalm 40 had eleven verses of testimony before it reached this prayer — the pit, the new song, the scroll of the book, the great congregation. Here there is none of that. The psalm opens in the emergency.

And the Psalter keeps both versions on purpose. There are days for the long version, where you rehearse everything God has done before you ask for anything. And there are days when the house is on fire, and Scripture provides a prayer for those too: five verses, no preamble, twice make haste and once do not delay.

Let them be put to shame and confusion who seek my life! ... Let them turn back because of their shame who say, Aha, Aha!

The petitions against the enemies stand almost word for word as in Psalm 40, and Aha, Aha! is the same noise of delighted malice heard at 35:21. Some sounds do not change.

May all who seek you rejoice and be glad in you! May those who love your salvation say evermore, God is great!

Here is the first of the two real changes, and it is one word. Psalm 40:16 has them saying Great is the LORD!, using the covenant name; this has God is great! That is the pattern right through Book Two of the Psalter (Psalms 42-83), where the general name for God largely replaces the covenant name — as Psalm 53 did with Psalm 14.

And notice what he wants for other people even in an emergency. He is five verses from death and still asking that everyone who seeks God should be glad. Panic has not made him selfish.

But I am poor and needy; hasten to me, O God! You are my help and my deliverer; O LORD, do not delay!

The second change is here, and it is the most telling in the psalm. Psalm 40:17 reads: As for me, I am poor and needy, but the Lord takes thought for me. That was a reflection — a man pausing, in the middle of trouble, to remember that God is thinking about him.

This version replaces the reflection with another plea: hasten to me, O God! The quiet line has been cut and the urgency put in its place.

Which tells you exactly what this little psalm is for. It is the same prayer with the reflective parts removed, kept in the book for the moment when a believer cannot manage reflection and can still manage hurry. The content of faith has not changed — he is poor and needy, God is his help and deliverer — but the pace has, and God's word makes room for both.

70.title: Make Haste, O God
70.overview: Psalm 40:13-17, reissued on its own as a prayer for emergencies. Make haste, O God, to deliver me! (v. 1). Let those who hunt him be shamed and those who jeer be turned back (vv. 2-3); let all who seek God rejoice and say God is great! (v. 4). But I am poor and needy; hasten to me, O God! You are my help and my deliverer; O LORD, do not delay! (v. 5).
70.theology:
The exposition stands at Psalm 40; this chapter carries the differences, which are consistent: everything unhurried has been removed. The courteous be pleased of 40:13 is gone, and the reflective the Lord takes thought for me (40:17) has become another plea for speed.

The divine name shifts as it does throughout Book Two: Great is the LORD! (40:16) becomes God is great! (v. 4), the same change Psalm 53 made to Psalm 14.

The Psalter keeps both editions deliberately. There are days for the long version with its history of rescues, and days when a believer can manage nothing but make haste — and Scripture supplies a prayer for those too.

Even in the emergency, the request that all who seek God be glad is retained (v. 4): panic has not made him selfish.
70.examples:
Five verses lifted out of Psalm 40 and given their own heading.

The polite opening cut; it starts at a run.

No preamble: none of the pit, the new song, or the congregation.

Great is the LORD becomes God is great.

The reflection replaced by another hurry.

Still asking that other people be glad, five verses from death.

A prayer kept in the book for when there is no time.

71.text: <sup>1</sup>In you, O LORD, do I take refuge; let me never be put to shame!<sup>2</sup>In your righteousness deliver me and rescue me; incline your ear to me, and save me!<sup>3</sup>Be to me a rock of refuge, to which I may continually come; you have given the command to save me, for you are my rock and my fortress.<sup>4</sup>Rescue me, O my God, from the hand of the wicked, from the grasp of the unjust and cruel man.<sup>5</sup>For you, O Lord, are my hope, my trust, O LORD, from my youth.<sup>6</sup>Upon you I have leaned from before my birth; you are he who took me from my mother's womb. You who have done great things, O God, who is like you?<sup>20</sup>You who have made me see many troubles and calamities will revive me again; from the depths of the earth you will bring me up again.<sup>21</sup>You will increase my greatness and comfort me again.<sup>22</sup>I will also praise you with the harp for your faithfulness, O my God; I will sing praises to you with the lyre, O Holy One of Israel.<sup>23</sup>My lips will shout for joy, when I sing praises to you; my soul also, which you have redeemed.<sup>24</sup>And my tongue will talk of your righteous help all the day long, for they have been put to shame and disappointed who sought to do me hurt.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: In you, O LORD, do I take refuge — be a rock of refuge to which he may continually come (vv. 1-4). For you, O Lord, are my hope, my trust, O LORD, from my youth. Upon you I have leaned from before my birth (vv. 5-6); he has been a portent to many, his mouth filled with praise (vv. 7-8). Do not cast me off in the time of old age; forsake me not when my strength is spent (v. 9), for his enemies say God has forsaken him (vv. 10-11). O God, be not far from me; O my God, make haste to help me! (vv. 12-13).
verseByVerse.theology: A man who has leaned on God since before he could speak, asking not to be dropped now that he is weak.

verseByVerse.quote: In you, O LORD, do I take refuge; let me never be put to shame! In your righteousness deliver me and rescue me; incline your ear to me, and save me! Be to me a rock of refuge, to which I may continually come; you have given the command to save me, for you are my rock and my fortress. Rescue me, O my God, from the hand of the wicked, from the grasp of the unjust and cruel man. For you, O Lord, are my hope, my trust, O LORD, from my youth. Upon you I have leaned from before my birth; you are he who took me from my mother's womb. My praise is continually of you. I have been as a portent to many, but you are my strong refuge. My mouth is filled with your praise, and with your glory all the day.
verseByVerse.commentary:
This psalm has no heading, and it does not need one: the man who wrote it is unmistakable from the first line. He is old, and he is praying in words he has used all his life.

Read verses 1-3 beside Psalm 31:1-3 and they are nearly identical. Verse 6 is Psalm 22:9-10. Verse 12 is Psalm 22:11 and 40:13. Verse 13 comes out of Psalm 35. This is not a lack of originality; it is what a lifetime of praying does. The phrases he learned as a young man are the ones that come to hand when his strength is gone, and anyone who has sat with a dying believer has heard old hymns doing the same work.

In you, O LORD, do I take refuge; let me never be put to shame! ... Be to me a rock of refuge, to which I may continually come.

Continually is the psalm's own word for itself — it will come four more times. He is describing a habit of a lifetime, not a crisis visit.

For you, O Lord, are my hope, my trust, O LORD, from my youth. Upon you I have leaned from before my birth; you are he who took me from my mother's womb. My praise is continually of you.

He measures the relationship in decades, and then further back than decades. From my youth, and behind that, from before my birth — God acting as the midwife who took him out and handed him over. Psalm 22 said the same. What an old man wants to tell you is not how long he has believed, but how long he has been held.

I have been as a portent to many, but you are my strong refuge.

A portent is a sign, something people point at. It can be a wonder or a warning, and the word is neutral enough to cover both: his life has been unusual enough that people watch it and draw conclusions. Long lives are read by other people whether or not their owners intend it.

verseByVerse.quote: Do not cast me off in the time of old age; forsake me not when my strength is spent. For my enemies speak concerning me; those who watch for my life consult together and say, "God has forsaken him; pursue and seize him, for there is none to deliver him." O God, be not far from me; O my God, make haste to help me! May my accusers be put to shame and consumed; with scorn and disgrace may they be covered who seek my hurt.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Do not cast me off in the time of old age; forsake me not when my strength is spent.

Here is the request this psalm exists for, and nowhere else in the Psalter is it made at length. The fear is specific: that God's interest was in his usefulness, and that when the usefulness runs out the relationship will quietly end. Cast me off is the word for discarding something.

Anyone who has watched a capable person become dependent knows the fear from the inside: the shrinking of attention, the sense of being stored somewhere rather than wanted. This psalm brings it to God directly — and the God it brings it to had already answered through Isaiah: even to your old age I am he, and to gray hairs I will carry you. I have made, and I will bear; I will carry and will save (Isa 46:4).

For my enemies speak concerning me; those who watch for my life consult together and say, God has forsaken him; pursue and seize him, for there is none to deliver him.

And there is the cruelty. They read his decline as a verdict — God has forsaken him — which is the taunt thrown at the sufferer of Psalm 22 and Psalm 42. Weakness is taken as evidence of abandonment, and the weak person, watching his own strength go, is tempted to agree with them.

O God, be not far from me; O my God, make haste to help me! Two more borrowed lines (22:11; 40:13), and an old man in a hurry.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 14–24 — Until I Proclaim Your Might to Another Generation
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: But I will hope continually and will praise you yet more and more; his mouth will tell of God's righteous acts all day (vv. 14-16). O God, from my youth you have taught me ... So even to old age and gray hairs, O God, do not forsake me, until I proclaim your might to another generation (vv. 17-18). You who have made me see many troubles and calamities will revive me again; from the depths of the earth you will bring me up again (vv. 19-21). He will praise with harp and lyre, O Holy One of Israel, with lips that shout for joy (vv. 22-24).
verseByVerse.theology: The one thing he asks to live for is to tell the next generation what God is like.

verseByVerse.quote: But I will hope continually and will praise you yet more and more. My mouth will tell of your righteous acts, of your deeds of salvation all the day, for their number is past my knowledge. With the mighty deeds of the Lord GOD I will come; I will remind them of your righteousness, yours alone. O God, from my youth you have taught me, and I still proclaim your wondrous deeds. So even to old age and gray hairs, O God, do not forsake me, until I proclaim your might to another generation, your power to all those to come.
verseByVerse.commentary:
But I will hope continually and will praise you yet more and more.

Yet more and more is a startling thing for a man in decline to say. Everything else about him is diminishing; the praise is to increase. It is the same arithmetic Paul does: Though our outer self is wasting away, our inner self is being renewed day by day (2 Cor 4:16).

My mouth will tell of your righteous acts, of your deeds of salvation all the day, for their number is past my knowledge.

He has lost count. A long life with God ends with a man who cannot remember all the rescues, which is the best possible reason for not being able to keep quiet.

O God, from my youth you have taught me, and I still proclaim your wondrous deeds. So even to old age and gray hairs, O God, do not forsake me, until I proclaim your might to another generation, your power to all those to come.

The request of verse 9 comes back, and now it has a purpose attached, and the purpose is not himself. He does not ask for more years to enjoy his grandchildren or to finish his work. He asks to be kept going until I proclaim your might to another generation.

That is the great use of old age in Scripture, and it should be said plainly to a church full of people who think their usefulness has ended. The old know what God has done over fifty years; nobody else in the room does. The young have energy and no memory. This psalm makes the handover the reason for staying alive.

verseByVerse.quote: Your righteousness, O God, reaches the high heavens. You who have done great things, O God, who is like you? You who have made me see many troubles and calamities will revive me again; from the depths of the earth you will bring me up again. You will increase my greatness and comfort me again. I will also praise you with the harp for your faithfulness, O my God; I will sing praises to you with the lyre, O Holy One of Israel. My lips will shout for joy, when I sing praises to you; my soul also, which you have redeemed. And my tongue will talk of your righteous help all the day long, for they have been put to shame and disappointed who sought to do me hurt.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Your righteousness, O God, reaches the high heavens. You who have done great things, O God, who is like you?

The question is asked by a man who has had the whole of his life to look for a rival and has not found one.

You who have made me see many troubles and calamities will revive me again; from the depths of the earth you will bring me up again. You will increase my greatness and comfort me again.

This is the summary of a long life with God, and both halves are addressed to the same person. You who have made me see many troubles — he does not pretend they came from somewhere else, and he does not itemise them either. And the same you will revive me again.

Three times again in two verses. He has been revived before; he expects it once more. From the depths of the earth you will bring me up is language that reaches past any recovery of health: for an old man near the end, being brought up from the depths of the earth is resurrection, and the Old Testament's hope is showing through the floor of this psalm.

I will also praise you with the harp for your faithfulness, O my God; I will sing praises to you with the lyre, O Holy One of Israel. My lips will shout for joy, when I sing praises to you; my soul also, which you have redeemed.

He gets his instruments out. And the title he reaches for is Isaiah's — O Holy One of Israel, rare in the Psalter — the God whose holiness had been the terror of the prophets, addressed as my God by a man with grey hair and a harp.

And my tongue will talk of your righteous help all the day long, for they have been put to shame and disappointed who sought to do me hurt.

The last verse answers verse 11. They said God had forsaken him; they were wrong, and the psalm ends with the old man still talking — all the day long — which is exactly what he asked for in verse 18.

71.title: Even to Old Age and Gray Hairs
71.overview: An old man prays in the words he has used all his life, stitched from Psalms 22, 31, 35 and 40. He takes refuge in God and asks for a rock he may come to continually (vv. 1-4); God has been his hope from his youth and he has leaned on him since before birth (vv. 5-8). Do not cast me off in the time of old age; forsake me not when my strength is spent (v. 9) — for his enemies read his decline as a verdict: God has forsaken him (vv. 10-13). But I will hope continually and will praise you yet more and more (vv. 14-16), and the one thing he asks to live for is this: until I proclaim your might to another generation (vv. 17-18). The God who made him see many troubles will revive him again and bring him up from the depths of the earth (vv. 19-21), and he ends with harp and lyre and a tongue that will not stop (vv. 22-24).
71.theology:
The psalm is assembled out of earlier psalms, which is what a lifetime of praying produces: the phrases learned young are the ones that come to hand when strength is gone.

Its subject is old age, treated nowhere else at length. The fear in v. 9 is that God's interest was in usefulness and will end with it — answered already by Isa 46:4, where God promises to carry to grey hairs. The enemies read weakness as abandonment (v. 11), the taunt of 22:8 and 42:3.

Praise is to increase as the body declines (v. 14; cf. 2 Cor 4:16), and the rescues are past counting (v. 15).

The purpose attached to more life is not enjoyment but handover: until I proclaim your might to another generation (v. 18). The old hold a memory of God's acts that nobody else in the room has.

Troubles and reviving are addressed to the same God (v. 20), and from the depths of the earth you will bring me up again reaches past recovery towards resurrection.
71.examples:
No heading needed: the voice is unmistakable.

Old hymns doing the work at the end of a life.

Not how long he has believed — how long he has been held.

A portent: a life other people read and draw conclusions from.

The fear of being stored rather than wanted.

Praise increasing while everything else diminishes.

He has lost count of the rescues.

Asking for years in order to hand something over.

72.text: Of Solomon. 1Give the king your justice, O God, and your righteousness to the royal son!2May he judge your people with righteousness, and your poor with justice!3Let the mountains bear prosperity for the people, and the hills, in righteousness!4May he defend the cause of the poor of the people, give deliverance to the children of the needy, and crush the oppressor!5May they fear you while the sun endures, and as long as the moon, throughout all generations!6May he be like rain that falls on the mown grass, like showers that water the earth!7In his days may the righteous flourish, and peace abound, till the moon be no more!8May he have dominion from sea to sea, and from the River to the ends of the earth!9May desert tribes bow down before him, and his enemies lick the dust!10May the kings of Tarshish and of the coastlands render him tribute; may the kings of Sheba and Seba bring gifts!11May all kings fall down before him, all nations serve him!12For he delivers the needy when he calls, the poor and him who has no helper.13He has pity on the weak and the needy, and saves the lives of the needy.14From oppression and violence he redeems their life, and precious is their blood in his sight.15Long may he live; may gold of Sheba be given to him! May prayer be made for him continually, and blessings invoked for him all the day!16May there be abundance of grain in the land; on the tops of the mountains may it wave; may its fruit be like Lebanon; and may people blossom in the cities like the grass of the field!17May his name endure forever, his fame continue as long as the sun! May people be blessed in him, all nations call him blessed!18Blessed be the LORD, the God of Israel, who alone does wondrous things.19Blessed be his glorious name forever; may the whole earth be filled with his glory! Amen and Amen!20The prayers of David, the son of Jesse, are ended.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–7 — Like Rain on the Mown Grass
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Give the king your justice, O God, and your righteousness to the royal son! — that he may judge the people rightly and defend the cause of the poor ... and crush the oppressor (vv. 1-4). May he endure as long as sun and moon, and come like rain that falls on the mown grass (vv. 5-7). May he have dominion from sea to sea, with desert tribes bowing and the kings of Tarshish, Sheba and Seba bringing tribute: may all kings fall down before him, all nations serve him (vv. 8-11).
verseByVerse.theology: A prayer for a government measured entirely by what it does for people with no leverage.

verseByVerse.quote: Give the king your justice, O God, and your righteousness to the royal son! May he judge your people with righteousness, and your poor with justice! Let the mountains bear prosperity for the people, and the hills, in righteousness! May he defend the cause of the poor of the people, give deliverance to the children of the needy, and crush the oppressor! May they fear you while the sun endures, and as long as the moon, throughout all generations! May he be like rain that falls on the mown grass, like showers that water the earth! In his days may the righteous flourish, and peace abound, till the moon be no more!
verseByVerse.commentary:
Give the king your justice, O God, and your righteousness to the royal son! May he judge your people with righteousness, and your poor with justice!

The psalm is headed Of Solomon, and it reads like the answer to the request he actually made when God offered him anything: Give your servant therefore an understanding mind to govern your people, that I may discern between good and evil (1 Kgs 3:9). Here that is turned into a prayer: the justice a king administers has to be given to him first, because it is your justice and your righteousness before it is his.

And note whose the people are. Twice in one verse: your people, your poor. The king is a steward, not an owner, which is the sentence every government in history has needed and few have believed.

May he defend the cause of the poor of the people, give deliverance to the children of the needy, and crush the oppressor!

Here is the test this psalm applies to a reign, and it is applied four times (vv. 2, 4, 12, 13). Not the borders, not the buildings, not the economy in general: what happens to the people with no leverage. And the positive and the negative go together — you cannot defend the cause of the poor without crushing the oppressor, because someone is doing the oppressing.

May they fear you while the sun endures, and as long as the moon, throughout all generations! May he be like rain that falls on the mown grass, like showers that water the earth!

And here is the loveliest picture of government in the Bible. Not a sword, not a wall: rain on a field that has just been cut. Mown grass looks finished; rain on it brings it back. A good reign is weather that makes things grow — quiet, general, and noticed mostly by its absence.

In his days may the righteous flourish, and peace abound, till the moon be no more!

The time-scale keeps overshooting. As long as the moon, till the moon be no more, throughout all generations. Solomon reigned forty years and then his kingdom split in two. Israel prayed this for every king she had, and no king came close.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 8–20 — Precious Is Their Blood in His Sight
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: May his dominion run from sea to sea, with kings of Tarshish, Sheba and Seba bringing tribute and all nations serving him (vv. 8-11). For he delivers the needy when he calls, the poor and him who has no helper; he pities the weak and redeems them from oppression and violence, and precious is their blood in his sight (vv. 12-14). Long may he live, with grain abundant on the hilltops and people blossoming in the cities (vv. 15-16). May his name endure forever ... May people be blessed in him, all nations call him blessed! (v. 17). Blessed be the LORD, the God of Israel, who alone does wondrous things ... Amen and Amen! (vv. 18-19). The prayers of David, the son of Jesse, are ended (v. 20).
verseByVerse.theology: The reason for the king's worldwide dominion is that he rescues people nobody else will help.

verseByVerse.quote: May he have dominion from sea to sea, and from the River to the ends of the earth! May desert tribes bow down before him, and his enemies lick the dust! May the kings of Tarshish and of the coastlands render him tribute; may the kings of Sheba and Seba bring gifts! May all kings fall down before him, all nations serve him! For he delivers the needy when he calls, the poor and him who has no helper. He has pity on the weak and the needy, and saves the lives of the needy. From oppression and violence he redeems their life, and precious is their blood in his sight.
verseByVerse.commentary:
May he have dominion from sea to sea, and from the River to the ends of the earth! May desert tribes bow down before him, and his enemies lick the dust! May the kings of Tarshish and of the coastlands render him tribute; may the kings of Sheba and Seba bring gifts! May all kings fall down before him, all nations serve him!

The map opens out. The ESV notes that the River is the Euphrates; Tarshish is far west in the Mediterranean and Sheba far south in Arabia. Kings arrive from both directions with gifts — and Matthew tells of wise men coming from the east to a house in Bethlehem and opening treasures of gold and frankincense and myrrh (Matt 2:11).

Held against any actual Israelite king this is embarrassing. Solomon's reach was respectable and regional. All kings ... all nations is not a description of the tenth century BC; it is a prayer that outgrew every man it was prayed for.

For he delivers the needy when he calls, the poor and him who has no helper. He has pity on the weak and the needy, and saves the lives of the needy.

And now the reason for the worldwide dominion, introduced by for. He deserves the whole earth because of what he does for one particular kind of person — him who has no helper. That phrase is the psalm's definition of the poor: not merely those without money, those without anyone.

From oppression and violence he redeems their life, and precious is their blood in his sight.

The last clause is the measure of a civilisation. Precious is their blood in his sight: the lives of people who can do nothing for him are costly in his eyes — valuable, expensive, not to be spent. Every king in the ancient world spent the poor; this one prices them high.

verseByVerse.quote: Long may he live; may gold of Sheba be given to him! May prayer be made for him continually, and blessings invoked for him all the day! May there be abundance of grain in the land; on the tops of the mountains may it wave; may its fruit be like Lebanon; and may people blossom in the cities like the grass of the field! May his name endure forever, his fame continue as long as the sun! May people be blessed in him, all nations call him blessed!
verseByVerse.commentary:
Long may he live; may gold of Sheba be given to him! May prayer be made for him continually, and blessings invoked for him all the day!

A people who are governed like this will pray for their king, continually, and mean it. That is the natural result of the previous verses rather than a duty added to them.

May there be abundance of grain in the land; on the tops of the mountains may it wave; may its fruit be like Lebanon; and may people blossom in the cities like the grass of the field!

Grain waving on the mountain tops is an agricultural joke — the hilltops are the last place you would plant. The picture is of such fertility that even the bad ground is heavy with wheat, and the cedars of Lebanon standing in for the size of the fruit. And then the cities: may people blossom ... like the grass of the field, which is what happens to a population when the government of verses 12-14 is in place.

May his name endure forever, his fame continue as long as the sun! May people be blessed in him, all nations call him blessed!

And here the prayer reaches all the way back to Abraham. God's promise was: in you all the families of the earth shall be blessed (Gen 12:3). This verse asks that the promise be fulfilled through the king.

No son of David could carry that. They knew it; they went on praying it anyway, because the promise had been made and a king would have to fill it. Isaiah saw him coming — a shoot from the stump of Jesse of whom he wrote, with righteousness he shall judge the poor, and decide with equity for the meek of the earth (Isa 11:4), which is this psalm's own test. And the wise men who came with gifts came to a child whose kingdom would have no end.

verseByVerse.quote: Blessed be the LORD, the God of Israel, who alone does wondrous things. Blessed be his glorious name forever; may the whole earth be filled with his glory! Amen and Amen! The prayers of David, the son of Jesse, are ended.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Blessed be the LORD, the God of Israel, who alone does wondrous things. Blessed be his glorious name forever; may the whole earth be filled with his glory! Amen and Amen!

This is not part of Solomon's prayer. It is the doxology that closes Book Two of the Psalter, matching the one at 41:13 and answered later at 89:52 and 106:48. Notice how it corrects the psalm it ends: seventeen verses have asked enormous things for a king, and the doxology says who ALONE does wondrous things. Whatever the king achieves, God did it.

And the horizon is bigger than the psalm's. The prayer wanted the king's fame to fill the earth; the doxology wants the whole earth to be filled with his glory. That is the sentence Habakkuk and Isaiah both saw coming true, and John saw a city where it had.

The prayers of David, the son of Jesse, are ended.

An editor's note, and a moving one. The collection that began with a man saying Blessed is the man ends with an old king's prayers running out — and the last thing he prays for is his son, and a reign that will treat the poor as precious.

David's prayers are ended. The Psalter is not: three more books follow, and psalms attributed to David appear again later. But this is the natural close of the great Davidic collection, and it ends where the whole Bible is going — with the earth full of God's glory and all nations calling one king blessed.

72.title: May All Kings Fall Down Before Him
72.overview: A prayer for the king: give him God's own justice, that he may judge the people rightly, defend the poor and crush the oppressor (vv. 1-4). May he endure as long as sun and moon and come like rain on mown grass (vv. 5-7). May his rule reach from sea to sea, with kings from Tarshish, Sheba and Seba bringing tribute and all nations serving him (vv. 8-11) — for he delivers the needy when he calls, the poor and him who has no helper, and precious is their blood in his sight (vv. 12-14). Long may he live, with grain waving on the hilltops and people blossoming in the cities (vv. 15-16); may people be blessed in him, all nations call him blessed (v. 17). Then Book Two's doxology: Blessed be the LORD, the God of Israel, who alone does wondrous things ... may the whole earth be filled with his glory! Amen and Amen! (vv. 18-19), and the note: The prayers of David, the son of Jesse, are ended (v. 20).
72.theology:
The justice a king administers must first be given to him, and the people are God's people and God's poor (vv. 1-2): the king is steward, not owner.

The psalm's test of a reign is applied four times and is always the same — what happens to those with no leverage (vv. 2, 4, 12, 13), and defending them requires crushing their oppressors. Its picture of good government is rain on cut grass (v. 6): weather that makes things grow.

The dominion asked for outgrew every king it was prayed for (vv. 8-11), and its stated ground is mercy to him who has no helper (v. 12), whose blood is precious is their blood in his sight (v. 14).

Verse 17 attaches the Abrahamic promise (Gen 12:3) to the king — which no son of David carried, and which Isaiah saw coming in one who would judge the poor with righteousness (Isa 11:4; cf. Matt 2:11).

The closing doxology corrects the whole prayer: God alone does wondrous things, and the horizon is the earth filled with his glory (vv. 18-19; cf. 41:13; 89:52; 106:48). Verse 20 closes the Davidic collection.
72.examples:
Solomon's own request at Gibeon, turned into a prayer.

Your people, your poor: the king is a steward.

You cannot defend the poor without crushing somebody.

Government as rain on mown grass.
